Dexter Morgan is back on the prowl in the Season 2 premiere of Dexter: Resurrection, and I saw my favorite character again from last season! Eric Stonestreet returned once again as the Rapunzel Killer, but unfortunately, the return was short-lived.

Al Walker was tracked down by Dexter while on vacation with his family, as he was "working" while traveling to parks with his wife and kids. Dex was able to "do what he does," as Harrison puts it, and now no pony-tailed women have to worry about Rapunzel anymore. As satisfying as it was, I'm upset that Dexter: Resurrection is once again killing off fun guest stars.

Last season, Dexter: Resurrection gave us a great plot twist with the Serial Killers Club, which was quickly decimated by the Bay Harbor Butcher. There was a stacked cast of great guest stars, but by the end of the season, they were all dead except for Eric Stonestreet's character.

I had high hopes he'd be a big bad in Season 2, but that hope was squashed pretty quickly. I kind of guessed that would be the case given how many new guest stars were a part of this season, but it's disappointing the show didn't hold off and do a season dedicated to Rapunzel where Dex was on the road.

Dexter: Resurrection has two major guest stars this season, with Dan Stevens playing the Five Boroughs Killer and Brian Cox playing the New York Ripper. Both are big names tied to the Season 2 plot, and with Dexter being so concerned about legacy, it feels as though he's going to try to take out both of them.

I Have A Theory About Dexter: Resurrection And His Downfall. Why I Think Season 2 Could Address It

That's kind of the point of Dexter, to be fair. He's a serial killer who hunts other killers, so I can't sit here and act like Resurrection is going against what this series is about. I just feel as though he's felt very untouchable thus far, and maybe that these serial killers aren't as crafty as the ones from the original series?

I guess I fear that Dexter is becoming an Avengers-level type of anti-hero, and it feels like we haven't seen him face any real adversity. I know that's funny to say with him having been shot by his own son, but he and Harrison were able to put that aside really quickly. I'm just hoping we see Dex face a little more adversity in these upcoming episodes on the 2026 TV schedule, because I fear he's untouchable.

Catch new episodes of Dexter: Resurrection on Paramount+ on Fridays. I'm eager to see how the rest of this season plays out, and if Dexter and Harrison end the season in some trouble with the law.

#3598. Godzilla Minus Zero's King Ghidorah Design Leaks Online Thanks To Merchandise

Not even the King of the Monsters is immune to that most terrifying and undefeated of foes: merchandise. "Godzilla Minus Zero" director Takashi Yamazaki has kept his cards close to the vest on the highly-anticipated sequel, even with multiple full-length trailers hyping up the carnage that's to come in post-War Japan (and possibly New York City). But, as we creep closer to the impending release and what looks like a potential box office record in the making, there are always certain aspects bound to escape containment no matter how hard the concerned parties try — like the look of the kaiju-sized villain that Godzilla will be squaring off against this time around. Needless to say, what follows will count as major spoilers for those who wish to go in 100% fresh and unblemished, so don't say we didn't warn you!

For those who're still here and decided to ignore my helpful advice, well, it's hard to blame any of you. In fact, it's kind of hard to consider this a "spoiler" in any real conventional sense, either. "Godzilla" fans who've been following along closely already know that Ghidorah, the famous three-headed dragon from outer space, is set to play a huge role in "Minus Zero." But, despite keeping any actual glimpse of the flying, electricity-spewing monster away from the marketing, the bad guy's final look has leaked out courtesy of a Desktop Monster toy listing that you can see here.

Ghidorah Minus Zero toy design pic.twitter.com/g7slE3UPNr

Yup, sure looks like a three-headed dragon to me! The thing is, the whole look and feel of Ghidorah has been fairly set in stone over the years, and any deviations would have to be considered minor cosmetic tweaks, at best. That's certainly the case here, though diehards will inevitably notice some key details. Let's break them all down below.

Love it, hate it, or something in between, there's no denying the fact that 2019's "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" managed to visualize each and every one of its iconic kaiju — from Big G to Mothra to Rodan — in all their majestic splendor. But everyone's favorite extraterrestrial from outer space, Ghidorah, was a particular highlight. Lifted directly out of the old Toho movies with an updated and modernized spin, the final result raised the bar impossibly high for any other adaptation to come in the future. Needless to say, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has embraced that challenge and come out swinging with its own spin ... and it looks just different enough.

Let's get the obvious disclaimer out of the way: There's only so much you can do with the general look of a giant, golden, three-headed dragon, and "Minus Zero" certainly isn't reinventing the wheel. The snakelike heads, the webbed wings, and club-like tails are all present and accounted for this time around. But a closer look reveals some key differences. There's some gnarly-looking quills/spikes running up and down King Ghidorah's back, reminiscent of the spikey plates Godzilla sports. The wings are more of a wyvern-like design, too, with Ghidorah's "arms" resembling that of a pterosaur (those birdlike beasts that coexisted with dinosaurs, for the uninitiated).

But the most interesting twist is how much this Ghidorah resembles the one featured in Japan's "Godzilla the Ride: Giant Monsters Ultimate Battle" — an indoor theme park with a short film directed by Takashi Yamazaki himself, featuring his design for Ghidorah. If it ain't broke, don't fix it! Yamazaki appears to have taken that to heart.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" stomps into theaters November 6, 2026.

#3596. You Should Enable This Chrome Feature That Flags Suspicious Websites

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you use Google Chrome, you can turn on a new safety feature that will warn you if you navigate to a suspicious website that looks like others already known for malicious behavior. The alerts are part of Enhanced Protection mode in Chrome's Safe Browsing, which checks your activity against potentially harmful sites and warns you if you're at risk of encountering malware, phishing, intrusive ads, or social engineering attacks.

Most internet users are familiar with the full-page alerts that appear if you navigate to a site that's known to be malicious. These red "dangerous site" warnings indicate a high risk of harm to the user and can't really be ignored since they take up the entire screen and urge you to go back to safety.

The new "suspicious site" alerts indicate possible risk of harm based on patterns consistent with other known malicious sites. This means that Google isn't as confident that the website is actually dangerous, but it looks a lot like others that are spreading malware or running phishing scams. These suspicious site warnings are smaller pop-ups with the text "This site doesn't seem right" and two button options: Mark as safe or Back to safety. The different colors, text, and formatting make it easy for users to distinguish between what Google deems dangerous versus suspicious.

Safe Browsing in Chrome has three options: standard protection, enhanced protection, and no protection at all (which isn't recommended). Standard protection checks your browsing activity, extensions, and downloads against Google's list of unsafe sites, which is updated periodically. By contrast, enhanced protection works in real time and uses AI analysis. Note that enhanced protection does require you to share more information about your activity to Google, and the data are linked to your Google Account.

Now that the spooky season has officially ended, a certain celebrity family is already decked out in their favorite Christmas attire and bringing in a stylish cheer that’ll last until New Year. The Kardashian-Jenner brood have traded scary movies and creepy costumes for a holiday campaign that brought (nearly) the whole family together. Just two days out from Halloween, the stars are already bringing what they call "SKIMSmas" to the forefront.

This isn’t the first time the famous sisters have come right out of Halloween launching a Christmas-themed campaign for Kim Kardashian’s SKIMS brand. A few years ago, they did a whole photoshoot with a polar bear, and this year fans have been treated to a 1970s inspired vintage photoshoot for the brand's 2026 Holiday Shop that brought Kim together with her sisters, Khloé and Kourtney Kardashian, and half-sisters Kylie and Kendall Jenner. Khloé shared her portion of the campaign on Instagram, and honestly, this is hitting me in my holiday feels:

A post shared by Khloé Kardashian (@khloekardashian)

I’m just loving the nostalgia in the campaign, especially with Khloé’s red and white onesie, paired perfectly with white gloves and boots. There’s a "kid on Christmas" feel to the video due to her sneaking up on Santa and shaking presents under the tree. (Also, don’t think I didn’t catch her being a little Grinch-y by mimicking two of the Dr. Seuss character's iconic moves.)

However, while Kardashian was distracting herself from Halloween, I was almost distracted by Dick Van Dyke's voice. The media personality’s post features a few lines from Mary Poppins. In the 1964 movie, Van Dyke stops his performance of his “One Man Band” to sing that he feels “like somethin’ is brewin’ and ‘bout to begin.” Now, the change in the wind that he feels signals the return of Julie Andrews’ titular nanny, but Kardashian is using the beloved lyrics to signal the return of Christmas. (An act usually done by Mariah Carey’s “All I Want For Christmas Is You.”)

That aside, I’m also not the only one that’s loving this campaign. Fans have called it "cinematic," but what really caught my eye was a sweet comment from Khloé's mom, Kris Jenner:

The cutest Santa’s helper I ever did see 🎅🏽🤶

Kardashian is definitely giving Mrs. Claus vibes and is clearly having fun with the festive fashion. This is only the most recent stage in the Kardashian-Jenner fashion evolution we’ve seen this year. Just a few months ago, the sisters sported some summer-friendly looks and are now trading those in for some autumn-inspired attire. (Just check out Kim wearing a bunch of brown leather to promote the opening of a new SKIMS London store.)

I wasn’t expecting to skip straight to Christmas before the turkey’s even in the oven. However, I also shouldn’t be surprised by all this, as the Kardashians are known to indulge in fun, flirty and stylish seasonal campaigns.

Kylie Jenner actually beat her sisters to the Christmas punch with a winter kissed cosmetic collection she promoted on her Instagram. The limited time collection features “four best-selling formulas, reimagined in the signature winter kissed pink.” Jenner even promoted the collection while wearing blush pink lingerie and a Christmas hat. She’s proving that, once again, she has a full Christmas dance card as she’s continuing to bring in the holiday cheer with products available through her KHY brand. The holiday wear features a black, white, pink, and olive color scheme for a more Kardashian/Jenner-esque aesthetic.

See if you can spot some SKIMS fits or fun holiday looks in Season 8 of The Kardashians, which hit the 2026 TV schedule in early October and will continue into December. New episodes can be watched every Thursday with a Hulu subscription.

#3594. Why Criminal Minds: Evolution Was Canceled At Paramount Plus

"Criminal Minds" has been running since September 2005. But the show is set to come a close with its upcoming 20th Season, marking the end of an incredible run that already included one previous cancellation. The original "Criminal Minds" aired on CBS and ended after its fifteenth season back in 2020, after which the show was reborn as "Criminal Minds: Evolution." This latest incarnation of the procedural crime drama has been available on streaming service Paramount+ since 2022, but it seems the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Unit (BAU) will finally close up shop after Season 20.

Originally created by Jeff Davis, "Criminal Minds" has followed the investigations of the BAU as they've help track down dangerous criminals via their profiling expertise. The show debuted with Mandy Patinkin playing FBI Senior Supervisory Special Agent Jason Gideon, alongside Lola Glaudini as FBI Supervisory Special Agent Elle Greenaway, Thomas Gibson as FBI Supervisory Special Agent and Behavioral Analysis Unit Chief Aaron Hotchner, Matthew Gray Gubler as Spencer Reid, Kirsten Vangsness as Penelope Garcia, and A.J. Cook as Jennifer "JJ" Jareau. But as you might expect given the show's impressive run, "Criminal Minds" has undergone major changes over the years, with Mandy Patinkin's Jason Gideon leaving after just two seasons ahead of several other major departures.

Today, only Cook and Vangsness remain from the original cast, and it seems it's now time for their "Criminal Minds" journey to come to a close. For fans, the show's cancellation will have come as somewhat of a shock, especially since "Evolution" seems to have been faring well on Paramount+. For now, it remains unclear exactly why the series was canceled, but it likely has to do with a combination of cost, the show's broadcast roots, and new leadership at Paramount.

"Criminal Minds: Evolution" Season 19 debuted in May 2026, by which time the show had already been given an early Season 20 renewal in March 2026, with Paramount+ announcing a 2027 debut for Season 20. All of which seemed to bode well for the show. But this was prior to the completion of the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger becoming official in October 2026. Paramount's takeover of the historic studio completed early that month, and by October 30 Deadline reported that "Criminal Minds: Evolution" had been cancelled, making the 20th season its last.

As such, the show became the first victim of the new Paramount+ leadership, but it seems the writing was on the wall even before the merger. Deadline cited sources as having claimed that the previous Paramount+ regime recommended cancelling the series prior to new Co-Chair & Chief Content Officer for Skydance Direct to Consumer, Casey Bloys, taking over. The outlet also noted that "Evolution" was still performing well and could, at the time of writing, be found in the Paramount+ Top 10. As such, it's likely the show's cancellation came down to cost or, as Deadline notes, the fact that "Evolution" retains much of the broadcast sensibility of the original show despite being a streaming series.

Meanwhile, HBO Max, which is now under the same leadership as Paramount+, is following a new "The Pitt"-style approach that, like broadcast, keeps the episode count high each season and follows a yearly release schedule while maintaining the production values of premium streaming series. It seems as though "Criminal Minds: Evolution" might not have fit that approach.

"Criminal Minds" executive producer/showrunner Erica Messer seemed surprised by the news of its cancellation. "It's hard to put into words what 'Criminal Minds' has meant to all of us who have been fortunate enough to be part of this extraordinary journey," she said (via Deadline). "[...] While suddenly navigating the end of this chapter, I'm filled with gratitude for our remarkable cast, writers, directors and crew who have poured their hearts into this show, and for the incredible fans around the world whose unwavering loyalty has kept 'Criminal Minds' going for two decades." The showrunner added that she was looking forward to Season 20, which wrapped filming by the time the cancellation was confirmed, meaning it likely won't provide a definite ending to the story.

Elsewhere, the "Criminal Minds: Evolution" cast reacted to the cancellation via social media. Emily Prentiss actor Paget Brewster kept things simple, posting a photo to Instagram of herself smiling with the words, "Free Agent..." Similarly, A.J. Cook took to Instagram to post a photo of herself in front of a tombstone for her character, alongside the caption "Rest in peace JJ (for now)."

Meanwhile, RJ Hatanaka, who plays Special Agent Tyler Green, posted a photo of the cast alongside the caption, "Just the finest group of people." Finally, Penelope Garcia actor Kirsten Vangsness — who has been part of every season of "Criminal Minds" — posted an Instagram video expressing her gratitude. "My heart fireworks in appreciation for the time at this job," she wrote, while using the video to speculate that the show could still continue elsewhere. For now, nothing has been confirmed, but as Vangsness points out in her video, showrunner Erica Messer has said that there are still stories to tell.

#3593. Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s Tragic Love Story

“I think you’re the saddest girl I ever met.”

“You’re the first man that ever said that. I’m usually told how happy I am.”

This exchange, from The Misfits, written by Arthur Miller, shows Marilyn Monroe drawing closer to something other than the “dumb blonde” persona for which Hollywood praised her.

After all, the actor—who was born in Los Angeles in 1926 and died in the City of Angels in 1962 at the age of 36—wanted to be taken seriously as a performer. She never fully identified with the image Hollywood created for her. She spent her limited free time enjoying uncharacteristic pastimes, as evidenced by one of her most famous photographs, which depicts her reading James Joyce’s Ulysses while donning a striped tank top, black shorts, and a deep, melancholic gaze.

Marilyn Monroe reads a book in her room at the Hotel Ambassador in midtown Manhattan, March 1955.

“A sex symbol becomes a thing. I just hate to be a thing,” said Monroe to Life magazine in 1962, reflecting on her strained relationship with Hollywood.

Miller, who was born in New York in 1915 and passed away in 2005, initially believed he would be a good partner for Monroe, whose life was marked by great successes, but also abandonment and her unfortunate inability to have children—one of the most painful issues for Monroe.

Monroe and Miller first met in 1950, when he was in Los Angeles with director Elia Kazan. It was Kazan who introduced them.

Monroe and Miller began talking, and he emphasized her potential to become a dramatic actor on New York stages. He struck a chord.

In the mid-1950s, the star left Hollywood and moved to New York to study, attending The Actors Studio and working with Lee Strasberg. She met with Miller again in the Big Apple, and in 1955, they began dating seriously, joining two seemingly distant worlds.

Marilyn Monroe and playwright Arthur Miller play with his dog Hugo,at Miller’s summer home on June 25, 1956.

Monroe felt respected by him, unlike the way she felt in Hollywood, which she once called “an overcrowded brothel, a merry-go-round with beds for horses,” in her unfinished memoir, My Story.

Miller, who had won the Pulitzer Prize in 1949 for Death of a Salesman, was captivated by her and ended his failing marriage.

The subsequent marriage between Monroe and Miller—her third marriage, his second—took place on June 29, 1956, in White Plains, New York. A few days later, a private Jewish ceremony was also held, following the actor’s conversion to Judaism.

The first major rift in their marriage stemmed from ongoing tension between public and private life. Miller wanted a more secluded, domestic life; Monroe wanted a family, but she was not willing to give up the career she had so painstakingly built.

For the 1957 film The Prince and the Showgirl—directed by and starring Laurence Olivier, with Monroe as the female lead and coproducer—the actor and her husband moved to England, where tensions rose.

Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe after their wedding.

Monroe found some of Miller’s notes, in which he expressed disappointment with their marriage and admitted to sometimes feeling embarrassed around his friends in the cultural world.

It was one of the hardest moments in their relationship: Monroe discovered that the man who seemed to recognize her talent and intelligence also viewed her through the very same lens from which she was trying to free herself.

In her own notebooks, she reflected on her fear of becoming “someone’s wife” and losing her independence.

Miller would later say that he wrote very little during the years of his marriage.

Monroe, meanwhile, was struggling to become a mother. During her marriage, she experienced a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy, and another spontaneous termination of pregnancy.

On the set of The Prince and the Showgirl, her difficulties increased: She often arrived late, struggled to work consistently, and her relationship with Laurence Olivier became strained.

In the background, Miller faced a trial, as he had refused to name Communist Party members and sympathizers. He was convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, but the conviction was overturned the following year.

Marilyn Monroe and her former husband Arthur Miller as they leave Doctors Hospital on August 10, 1957, after she recovered from a 10-day hospital stay following an ectopic pregnancy.

Despite Monroe publicly expressing her support for her husband, the cracks in their marriage turned into chasms. Arguments, a lack of trust, disillusionment, drugs, alcohol, all of it became too difficult to contain.

The point of no return was another feature film, The Misfits, written by Miller for Monroe.

The desert setting where it was filmed didn’t help. Amid hellish temperatures, Monroe and Miller were no longer on speaking terms, even though they were staying at the same hotel. Intermediaries were needed just to get them to communicate.

It was during this shoot that Miller met the photographer Inge Morath, whom he would later marry in February 1962.

They divorced shortly after The Misfits was released in theaters.

After The Misfits, Monroe went through one of the most difficult periods of her life. In 1961 she was admitted to the Payne Whitney Psychiatric Clinic in New York. Joe DiMaggio intervened to have her transferred to another facility.

Marilyn Monroe’s photo shoot at Hollywood agent Johnny Hyde’s backyard in Beverly Hills, California, 1957.

Before her death, Monroe nevertheless continued to work, seek roles, and imagine a life different from the one others intended for her.

In a 1988 interview that aired on the Italian network Rai, journalist and writer Enzo Biagi asked Miller: “How do you want to remember Marilyn Monroe?”

He replied: “She made everyone believe she was very happy, but I didn’t believe it. She was very depressed, but she had the extraordinary talent of being able to mask her state of mind. She wore a mask because she was suffering too much. She was completely unable to cope with her depression, but she had been an abused child. She was looking for someone to save her.”

Originally published by Vanity Fair Italia.

#3592. What to Wear When Exercising Outdoors, Based on How Cold It Is

I fell in love with cold weather running while I was training for a spring marathon. It wasn’t a choice at first: Some weeks, the weather was bad for days on end, and if I stayed home, I would fall behind in my training. Everybody else in my training group was braving the elements, so I did too—with no regrets.

I got to run on quiet mornings while snow was softly falling. I signed up for a winter race that herded finishers into a heated barn for hot chocolate and soup. I set a personal record at a spring race, during which I pushed myself hard without breaking a sweat. I now find it sad when somebody tells me they’re afraid of running in the cold, or that they would run in the winter but don’t know what to wear.

No, cold weather doesn’t have to stop you from running, but getting dressed can be a puzzle: How do you keep from freezing your butt off at first and avoid overheating once you start to sweat? Fortunately, it isn’t as tough as it looks. With the right gear, your fingers and ears can stay toasty while you jog through a winter wonderland. Below, I’ll give you a temperature-by-temperature running cheat sheet, and then dive into the specifics on how to buy the best socks, shirts, and more.

When I get dressed to run in winter, I take a look at the “feels like” temperature, not the actual high or low. I also make sure to check the weather for the time I’ll go running, not for the whole day. It doesn’t matter how warm it will be at 2 p.m. if my run will be happening at 6 a.m., before the sun is up. I use the Carrot Weather app, but any app that gives you hourly feels-like temps will work just fine.

Next, use the 20-degree rule. Imagine that the temperature is 20 degrees (Fahrenheit) warmer than it really is. What would you wear then? Here's an example: if it’s 50 degrees out, you should dress as if it were 70: in a T-shirt and shorts, most likely. If it’s 30 degrees, you’d dress as if it were 50: long pants and maybe a light jacket. Get the idea?

Everybody has their own preferences. Some people wear shorts even when it’s snowing, while others will pop a beanie on as soon as there’s a detectable chill in the air. I’m a pretty middle-of-the-road runner when it comes to keeping warm, so here’s what I wear at each “feels like” temperature, starting with warmer weather and working our way colder. I'll give a guide to each type of garment or accessory at the end.

At 50+ degrees Fahrenheit, I’m wearing basically the same things I would for a summer run.

Head and hands: Nothing special. No gloves and no hat, unless it’s a baseball cap to shade my eyes from the sun.

We’re starting to feel the first bit of a chill. This is where I may start bringing gloves, although they’ll probably get stuffed into a pocket by the end of the run. Remember, with the 20-degree rule, it will feel like 60 degrees by the time you're warmed up.

Bottoms: Leggings, lightweight long pants, or shorts.

Top: Something with long sleeves, but ideally made of thin material (think long-sleeved T-shirt, not a full-on sweatshirt or jacket). If you wore a sun shirt in the summer, that's a good layering option for these cool temps. I like my REI Sahara Shade hoodie here, but any long sleeve will do. If you run fall and winter races, you'll probably be handed a free long-sleeved version at some point.

Hands: I usually just pull my shirt's sleeves over my hands, but you could wear knit gloves if you want. Consider something like Flipmits for an intermediate option (they can be folded down into a wrist cuff when your hands warm up).

Head: A headband if you need protection for your ears.

You may see a few snowflakes drifting down, but don’t bundle up in a snowsuit. Once you’re warmed up, it will only feel like 50 degrees—so go for something in “light jacket” territory.

Bottoms: Leggings or running tights. The fleece-lined kind can be nice. (I have these.)

Top: You’ll want some kind of jacket or sweatshirt. A lightweight, reflective rain jacket is great here, or just throw on a regular hoodie over your T-shirt. (I go with cotton sweats in dry weather or light snow, but I'd go for synthetics or wool if there's rain or sleet.)

Hands: Definitely wear gloves. The cheap knit ones are usually good enough, but consider treating yourself to a nice pair of running gloves.

Head: Your choice of hat or headband; I’d stick with the headband.

Feet: This is around the temperature you may start to want warmer socks. That goes double if snow is in play: snow that falls onto your shoes will work its way through the mesh, melt, and make your feet wet. Wool is a good material here, so consider something like these from Smartwool.

This is where I’ll officially say it’s “cold.” Whatever warm-weather gear you were getting away with at warmer temps, you’ll probably have to swap it out now. Shorts people will break out their long pants. Headband people will wear a real hat.

Bottoms: Leggings and shorts. I don’t care if you think it looks goofy to wear both; this is an A+ hack. Or try a puffer skirt.

Top: It’s definitely jacket weather. Rather than getting a warmer jacket, I like to wear the same light jacket as I did at 30 degrees, but this time with a long-sleeved fleece or wool base layer underneath.

Hands: Real gloves, please. You can keep wearing your little knit gloves if you’re able to tuck your hands inside your jacket sleeves, or if you have a pair of mittens to wear over top; otherwise, get windproof gloves.

Head: A hat, and maybe also a buff for your nose and mouth. (If you have any cloth masks still hanging around from the early COVID days, they’re perfect for cold weather runs.)

Feet: Warm socks for sure. If you’ll be doing a lot of running in these temperatures, you may want shoes that are specialized for the elements. Look for ones with Gore-Tex uppers, like the Brooks Ghost GTX.

This is where I tap out. If a run is just barely in the teens, I’ll make do with the 20-degree items I mentioned above, adding an extra layer wherever needed. But if that isn't enough, I opt for the treadmill. You certainly can run in this weather if you are determined. You’ll want windproof everything, some kind of face covering, and you may need eye protection such as goggles.

Whenever the weather gets to your own personal “too cold” temperature, remember that you still have options. The early afternoon is often the warmest part of the day, so a run may be tolerable then. There’s also no shame in using a treadmill (even if you have to join a cheap gym for this reason alone).

Everybody has different preferences, and with practice you’ll figure out if you’re the kind of person who wears three shirts before it hits freezing or the type to run through the snow in shorts. But this should give you a starting point when you head out for your first (or next) cold weather run.

As you continue on your cold-weather running journey, you may need to buy some new gear or repurpose things from elsewhere in your closet. And yes, the first few minutes of your run will feel chilly. But if you’re wearing the right shoes and clothes (and planning routes with a few extra factors in mind, which I’ll discuss below), winter running is not just feasible; it’s actually fun. So here are the items you may want to consider.

Your feet need to be warm and, if possible, dry. Warm socks go without saying, but there are some extra considerations when you’re picking socks to run in. Wool socks are ideal because they keep your feet warm even when they get wet. You may not think of winter as a wet time, but any snow that meets up with your body heat will turn into water. If you don’t have wool socks, synthetic wicking fabrics are a good second choice. Cotton is a no-no

First, the socks have to be able to fit into your shoes. If you’ve been running in super thin cotton or synthetic socks all summer, thick socks may not fit. Smartwool run socks are available in a thin version that can fit no problem—but in colder weather you’ll want some thickness for extra warmth. That thickness, in turn, may mean that your winter running shoes need to be roomier than the shoes you wear in summer. If you’re buying a new pair, make sure to try them on with the type of socks you intend to run in.

If your warm socks fit, you can make do with the same shoes you wore in the summer. Your feet will stay dry if the weather is dry and you stay out of puddles. If you encounter snow and slush, though, your feet will have to endure warm-but-wet conditions for the rest of your run. That can be okay for short runs, but for serious winter running, consider upgrading your shoes.

Some running shoes are available with water-resistant uppers. This level of water resistance will keep stray snowflakes out of your socks, but it isn’t reliable if you’ll be stepping in slush puddles. In that case, you’ll want something more waterproof, like Gore-Tex shoes, many of which are made for running trails.

If you expect to run on a lot of ice or packed snow, especially on trails, spikes can give you a little extra grip.

Yaktrax makes a rubber harness that stretches to fit your shoe, with steel coils and small spikes, for about $40.

Microspikes are a notch up from there, costing around $90 for what look like a miniature version of the chains you’d put on car tires.

And if you’re really dedicated—and are seeking a purpose-built pair of snow shoes—you can attach individual spikes: either these traction spikes from IceSpike, or via a DIY approach using sheet metal screws. (There’s a tutorial here.)

The versions that include rubber, like Yaktrax, can wear out quickly on pavement, so it’s best to save these for runs on trails or on unplowed paths. You’ll also want to be careful about the fit. I tried a pair that were similar to Yaktrax, but they were a tad too big. Shortly into my run, I found that the rubber stretched enough to pull the front set of spikes up over the top of my shoe. I've since gotten better-fitting ones, and they work great.

Spikes and specialized shoes help you go more places, in worse weather—but remember that they’re not required to just head out on a chilly day. Regular shoes are fine if the weather is cold but dry, or if you’re willing to put up with a little moisture.

I actually love when the weather gets cold enough that I need a jacket, because then I get to wear something that gives me extra pockets! Stick with thin jackets that have some room inside. By the time temps dip into the 20s or below, you’ll be doing some serious layering: for example, an undershirt, a long-sleeved warm layer, and a jacket. A great option for that warm layer is a wool base layer like this one. (Don’t worry, it’s not itchy.) If you can’t wear wool, a synthetic fleece is a good alternative.

Before you run out to buy all new clothes, experiment with what’s in your closet. Try repurposing a thin sweater, for example. Some people would never wear cotton for running (it can be cold when wet), but I wear it as my undershirt layer and have lived to tell the tale. Just make sure to shower or change after your run, so you aren't sitting around in cold, wet clothes.

The jacket is the most important layer. You can grab a sweatshirt in a pinch, but to be really well-equipped for nasty weather, you’ll want a jacket that is windproof and water-resistant. Jackets made for running are lightweight, for layering. Consider ones that are visible at night, with bright colors and reflective areas, and that come with zippered pockets.

Once it’s too cold for shorts, you’ll want to start layering your bottoms, too. Loose pants let cold air in, which is why leggings or “running tights” like these are standard winter wear for all genders. Running tights come in different thicknesses; go for something fleece-lined for your coldest runs, or layer two pairs.

You need to keep your ears warm, but don’t reach for a winter hat right away: an ear warmer or headband can cover your ears while still letting heat escape from the top of your head. And if anything is falling from the sky (say, snow), a baseball cap will keep it out of your eyes.

Fleece or knit hats are great for cold enough days, of course. The dividing line between earwarmer weather and hat weather is a personal one, and depends on whether you’re overheating. If you’re wearing a hat but sweating into your base layers, the hat is probably overkill.

Gloves, however, are essential. I keep a pair of cheap knit gloves in my jacket pockets, but windy or very cold days call for something stronger. You can layer gloves; I find gloves under mittens work well. You can also get windproof insulated gloves, which are warmer than any number of layers of holey knit gloves.

Your face will freeze on windy or very cold days, so this is where your old stash of pandemic face masks really shines. Consider a balaclava or even a fleece-lined bandana. A neck gaiter stays on better than a scarf if your neck is cold. At this point, every inch of you is covered but your eyes. Sunglasses can take care of that.

#3591. Who Is The Longbow Killer In Absolute Green Arrow? DC's Murder Mystery, Explained

This article contains spoilers for "Absolute Green Arrow."

DC Comics' "Absolute" Universe has made major changes to classic heroes like Batman. "Absolute Green Arrow," which recently completed its first arc, "The Longbow Killer," leans more toward mystery. Despite the title, the main character here is Dinah Lance, the Black Canary, and she's investigating who the Green Arrow is.

An "Absolute Green Arrow" series from writer Pornsak Pichetshote and artist Rafael Albuquerque was announced in July 2025. Classic Green Arrow Oliver Queen (aka Ollie) then debuted in the "Absolute" Universe in October one-shot "Absolute Evil," by Al Ewing and Giuseppe Camuncoli. An archery-loving billionaire who wants to be a hero, Oliver is murdered by the evil oligarchs who call themselves "The Justice League."

In "Absolute Green Arrow," the murder mystery isn't who killed Oliver Queen; the audience already knows that. The question is why the "Longbow Killer," dressed like a cross of Robin Hood and the Grim Reaper, is murdering people connected to Oliver's death.

The comic presents lots of suspects, like "Absolute" versions of Oliver's traditional sidekicks Roy Harper and Mia Dearden, as well as his illegitimate son Connor Hawke. All three of them are archer heroes in the main DC Universe, and therefore are prime Longbow Killer candidates. Dinah is reluctantly working security for evil businessman (and Justice League member) Hector Hammond. Her partner is Malcolm Merlyn, aka Green Arrow's classic "Dark Archer" nemesis. Considering the comic features zombie villain Solomon Grundy, some readers (and Dinah) even suspected the killer was a vengeful, undead Oliver.

But "Absolute Green Arrow" #6 pulled back the Longbow Killer's hood, revealing Merlyn and Connor Hawke. Oliver was not in Connor's life when Connor was growing up, so Malcolm raised Connor instead. The Longbow Killer has been targeting people like Hammond because Connor is avenging his father's death and redeeming Ollie's mistakes.

DC promoted "Absolute Green Arrow" like it was a slasher movie, with Green Arrow himself being described as "a Robin Hood who is less Errol Flynn and more Michael Myers." Except this slasher is targeting corrupt billionaires, not dumb teenagers. During "Absolute Green Arrow," the Longbow Killer becomes a social media hero because many people think his targets deserve it. But Connor and Malcolm aren't killing to spark a revolution.

"Absolute Green Arrow" gradually reveals Hector Hammond is performing illegal human experiments into anti-aging via advanced cellular regeneration. Jubal Slade, Ollie's former business partner and a Jeffrey Epstein-esque child trafficker, was supplying Hammond with test subjects.

It turns out "Malcolm" is actually Arthur King, a mercenary hired to investigate the disappearance of one of Jubal's victims. Once Arthur and Connor got close to the truth, Connor brought it to Oliver; his dad had always resisted actually standing up to Slade, and Connor wanted to shock him into action. It worked, but Oliver moving against Slade and Hammond is why he was was silenced. Cue Arthur going undercover as "Malcolm Merlyn" to investigate Hammond and provide inside protection for Connor's crusade.

There's a classic red herring where, after Connor is introduced in "Absolute Green Arrow" #2, the Longbow Killer seemingly murders him. In reality, that was Connor and Arthur redirecting Dinah's suspicion. But Arthur dies genuinely in "Absolute Green Arrow" #5, leaving Connor as the only living Green Arrow.

Pornsak Pichetshote initially compared "Absolute Green Arrow" to the 1997 slasher "I Know What You Did Last Summer," which is about a group of people with a dark secret being murdered one by one. But the reveal of the Longbow Killer's identity borrows from a different slasher franchise: "Scream," where there is almost always more than one Ghostface killer.

Oliver Queen's legacy influences Connor's choice of weapons. Ollie made his money with a company called Greenarrows Trading (a reference to the real financial app Robinhood Markets). When we first see the Longbow Killer in "Absolute Green Arrow" #1, he pointedly leaves two green arrows in the eyes of Jubal Slade's corpse. His bow is also made from two swords latched together. It's a similar touch to "Absolute Batman" making Batman's chest symbol into an axe; the hero's symbol is a collapsible weapon.

Jubal Slade is a reinvention of a slumlord villain from Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams' "Green Lantern" #76, the beginning of the famous and bitingly political "Hard-Traveling Heroes" arc starring Green Lantern and Green Arrow. The "Longbow Killer" moniker comes from another "Green Arrow" comic, Mike Grell's 1987 "The Longbow Hunters." After Oliver Queen died in 1995's "Green Arrow" #101, Connor Hawke took his father's place as Green Arrow.

Pornsak Pichetshote was also once an executive in DC's TV department, where he helped spearhead TV shows like "Arrow." His previous experience reimagining Green Arrow clearly shaped his latest attempt. In "Arrow" Season 1, Oliver Queen (Stephen Amell) is out to kill or ruin the names of people on a list given to him by his father, Robert Queen (Jamey Sheridan); Robert was once part of this conspiracy and wants his son to enact vengeance. Connor being the Longbow Killer makes "Absolute Green Arrow" into the same story: A son goes out to avenge his father's murder by killing a list of his dad's shady associates. "Absolute Green Arrow" also employs a flashback storyline much like "Arrow" did, and the name "Malcolm Merlyn" comes from "Arrow."

Oliver was presented as a kind of serial killer in "Arrow" Season 1. (Season 2 was even all about him swearing that "I can't be the killer I once was.") "Absolute Green Arrow" embraces that approach, and then some.

I have an annual tradition of watching the best horror movies, and given that Backrooms was so buzzed about earlier this year, I streamed it with my HBO Max subscription. I'd heard some people who saw it found it boring, and while I disagree on that front, I do think it isn't really scary.

The concept of "the backrooms" has existed on the internet for a long time, and I've seen it portrayed across many short films, video games, and horror stories. I wouldn't say I went into this movie with high expectations, but I certainly went in feeling like I'd leave feeling more scared than I was.

The problem, I think, is that I went into Backrooms expecting it to be a horror movie. As mentioned, people generally tackle this premise with a horror bent, typically with weird, deformed monsters and jump scares. This movie has zero jump scares, which bucks the trend of many modern horror movies, but I think it did it no favors.

All this to say, Backrooms is a fascinating thriller, and I really enjoyed the movie. Once I set aside the fact that I expected it to frighten me, I genuinely enjoyed the film and look forward to any future installments. In that way, it reminds me of The Silence Of The Lambs, which is another movie I'd associate with Halloween that isn't really that scary.

A sequel to Backrooms could, and certainly should, be much scarier. Now that the mainstream gets the general idea of how it all works, this is the time for director Kane Parsons to really flesh out how horrifying that concept is and what oddities can come from this space.

I've Been Looking Into Backrooms Theories, And Whoa, There's A Lot More To Unpack Than I Realized

As I mentioned before, we've already seen a lot of other works do this. A lot of what Parsons would need to add to a sequel is sitting there on the internet, and he has the power to make the mythology around it even scarier. It's what made it disappointing that the movie itself was more about being surreal rather than scary.

Without jump scares, Backrooms had me wondering how many people younger than me are genuinely terrified of a generic office layout from the 1990s. Or furniture that's clipped into walls and doors? We saw that all the time in video games growing up! That's not scary to me, that's bad graphics!

The good news is the movie did well and crushed it on streaming, so I think we're going to see the concept further evolve in the coming years. I'm fully on board with showing up for a sequel, but if this next one isn't scary, I don't think I'll stick around for the ride.

#3588. Anker’s New Soundcore Space 2 Headphones Are Already 18% Off

Anker released the noise-cancelling Soundcore Space One headphones a few years ago, and while they were a more budget-friendly alternative to premium models from Bose and Sony, their performance and fit still fell short in several areas. The brand’s updated Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a major upgrade across the board: They’re comfier, have better ANC, and are currently 18% off at $106.49 (originally $129.99), a rare price cut for a still-new release from a popular brand.

Battery life is one of the Soundcore Space 2’s most attractive features: They last up to 50 hours with ANC on and 70 hours with ANC off, and a five-minute charge gives you up to four extra hours. The noise cancellation is strong for the price, blocking out lower-frequency sounds well. Comfort is also a major upgrade from its sparser predecessor, with roomier, more plush memory foam earcups and a padded headband. They’re also travel-friendly, as the earcups rotate and fold.

The Soundcore app allows you to customize EQ and sound presets, giving you added flexibility if you don’t like the default tuning. Instead of touch-sensitive panels, these headphones use conventional buttons, which help prevent accidental commands while adjusting the earcups and are easy to operate. Along with supporting Bluetooth 6.1, they also have a wired-cable option, which isn’t always the case with modern wireless headphones. That said, they don’t support USB-C audio.

If you want over-ear noise-canceling headphones that perform well but don’t have $200 to shell out for a more expensive model, the Anker Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a comfortable, effective, and long-lasting alternative that hover around $100 at the current discounted price.

#3587. Jenna Ortega's Klara And The Sun Movie Set An Unwanted Box Office Record

Things have gone from bad to worse for "Klara and the Sun." Fronted by "Wednesday" star Jenna Ortega and hailing from "Thor: Ragnarok" director Taika Waititi, it's been nothing shy of a crushing disappointment for all involved. Now, the movie has etched its way into the box office history books, but in a very unfortunate way.

Hailing from Sony Pictures, "Klara and the Sun" flopped at the box office on its opening weekend, pulling in just $701,000 in its debut against a $20 million budget. That was bad enough, but in its second weekend, the sci-fi flick dropped a staggering 93.6%, taking in just $45,000 on 880 screens. That means it averaged just $51 per screen. This is just about as bad as it gets for a movie from high-profile filmmakers in Hollywood.

With that, Waititi's latest has etched its way into the history books. This represents the biggest second weekend drop of all time for a new release narrative feature film. The only movie to ever have a worse second weekend drop was the concert film "Stray Kids: The Dominate Experience" (94.9%) earlier this year, according to Box Office Mojo. Concert films are generally more niche and front-loaded. A would-be awards season play like "Klara and the Sun" is designed to hopefully pick up steam, not drop like a rock.

The movie is based on the acclaimed 2021 novel by Kazuo Ishiguro. It focuses on Klara (Ortega), an Artificial Friend who meets a girl named Josie (Mia Tharia). Klara's innocent wonder and loyalty begin to heal Josie's family and bring light to her complicated world. Waititi recently slammed critics after "Klara and the Sun" flopped, taking it all very personally.

There's nothing for Taika Waititi to be happy about. His new movie has made less than $2 million worldwide and is pretty much dead in the water at this point, despite the promising source material and a cast that includes Amy Adams, one of the best actors who has never won an Oscar (though she's been nominated several times). Waititi is also an Oscar winner himself, winning Best Original Screenplay for "Jojo Rabbit."

It doesn't matter at the moment that Waititi directed one of Marvel's most beloved hits, "Thor: Ragnarok" ($855 million worldwide). It doesn't matter that "Thor: Love and Thunder" ($761 million) was also a big hit despite not being as well-liked, broadly speaking. In a "what have you done for me lately?" business, Waititi is floundering. It certainly doesn't help that Waititi's "Next Goal Wins" was also a box office bomb in 2023, even though it was a low stakes one with a low budget.

Jenna Ortega evolved from Disney princess to scream queen, becoming one of Hollywood's most in-demand A-list stars. Right or wrong, she's had enough success in recent years that this probably won't ding her reputation too much. She's also not out there publicly decrying critics for not liking the movie. Waititi, through his own doing, is ensuring that he's going to shoulder the blame.

Big box office flops can put creators in director's jail. This is a lower budget movie, but still, Waititi's on a cold streak and it's very possible that he's either headed for director's jail or is already in it.

"Klara and the Sun" is still in theaters now, but probably won't be for much longer.

Full House might not be hailed as one of the best sitcoms of all time by many, but I have always been a massive fan of the show. I used to watch it every night on Nick at Nite and even own the entire series on DVD. I’ve always adored the Tanners and their extended family and can’t imagine any of them being played by any other actors; but it turns out that Lori Loughlin almost didn’t get to play Aunt Becky.

A majority of the Full House cast reunited at ‘90s Con in Connecticut and appeared on a panel discussing the show. During the panel, John Stamos shared his experience with the show’s creator, Jeff Franklin, when it came to casting Aunt Becky, aka his eventual long-term love interest on the show.

Lori came on at first, and I was like — I think we did some readings together before. I told [series creator] Jeff [Franklin], ‘I don’t know. She’s cute, and she’s adorable. I don’t think she’s tough enough to put Jesse in his place.’

Good casting can make or break a project, especially when it comes to the chemistry between two actors who are playing characters that are romantically linked. At the time, Full House wasn’t considered a hit by any means, so it makes sense that Stamos would want to get the casting right to ensure the show would continue.

While Stamos’ Uncle Jesse and Lori Loughlin’s Aunt Becky eventually became the best couple on the show, their relationship wasn’t always a walk in the park. Jesse was instantly smitten with Becky, as he was with most women on the show, but the same was not true for her character. Thus, it was important that Loughlin be able to play off Stamos’s character in order to build up that will-they, won’t-they tension.

Thankfully, the show’s creator didn’t listen to Stamos and did go on to cast Loughlin in the role. In turn, the When Calls the Heart actress proved Stamos wrong and put him and his character in his place on the first day of set.

Scene one, she came and she put me in my place fast. She had the perfect combination of this adorable, sweet girl. But, when it was time for me to get in trouble, you had no problem [playing] that out.

For those who don’t remember, Jesse meets Becky at the Tanner house and instantly tries to hit on her. Unlike most of the women who swoon at his feet, Becky challenged Jesse’s flirting attempts and even compared him to her baby brother, which gutted him. However, despite Becky’s apprehensions, she did end up falling for Jesse’s charm, and the two got together (for the first time) during the second season’s Christmas episode.

Hiring Loughlin turned out to be one of the best decisions, and the show steadily started to grow its fan base. It’s wild to think that she was initially only hired for six episodes and went on to become a fan favorite character. It turns out Aunt Becky was the missing piece all along.

#3585. 10 Shows Like 'A Different World' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The original A Different World was a groundbreaking sitcom in its era, spending six seasons highlighting Black academic drive among a cast of characters so indelible that we're now checking in on them decades later. Spearheaded by Queen Sugar's Felicia Pride, the update has been a critical and ratings hit for Netflix, earning the rarest prize of all in streaming television: a quick second season renewal. While you're waiting for season two, here are some other smart coming-of-age shows that blend heart and humor with realistic drama.

An easy pairing with A Different World, this show follows Black-ish's Zoey Johnson (Yara Shahidi) as she leaves home to attend a (fictional) California liberal arts college (the last couple of post-graduation seasons shift the focus to her brother Andre, played by Marcus Scribner). The emphasis is on driven young people who are capable of making big mistakes on the path to adulthood. A true comedy-drama, Grown-ish feels real(-ish) in a way that few other college shows have managed. Stream Grown-ish on Hulu.

Adapted from and expanding upon the 2014 movie, this show takes us to a (fictional) Ivy League school for a comedy-drama that tackles campus life and politics from a rather different perspective than that of Rooster. Logan Browning leads the ensemble cast as Sam White, who kind of inadvertently starts the titular radio show following a racially charged incident on campus. Far from the racial screed that some bad-faith YouTubers seem to find it, it's never shy about confronting the complicated and occasionally silly contradictions of campus activism, with each episode approaching life at Winchester University from a different character's perspective. Stream Dear White People on Netflix.

Kimberly (Pauline Chalamet) is an endlessly naïve scholarship student; Bela (Amrit Kaur) is an aspiring comedy writer on the make for the hottest guys; Whitney (Alyah Chanelle Scott) is an overachieving athlete and senator’s daughter; and Leighton (Reneé Rapp) is a closeted sorority girl. They're all randomly assigned to room together as freshmen at the fictional Essex College in Vermont. Created by Mindy Kaling and Justin Noble, this comedy-drama isn't nearly as salacious as its title suggests. There's sex for sure, but mostly it's a funny, queer-friendly show that's a little less about one overarching romance than it is about growing up, and the value of female friendship. Stream The Sex Lives of College Girls on HBO Max.

Even though we're backing up a couple of years to follow teens in their high school years, this British import's setting is a decent match, finding its students living away from home and family for the first time in their lives. At the fictional prestigious boarding school St. Gilbert’s, five Black teens are newly attending on scholarships, but their integration into the existing cliques is less than smooth—especially given that they're there largely as a PR stunt. Boarders blends teen romance, coming-of-age drama, and a delightful willingness to take the piss when it comes to the whole "rich private school" thing. Stream Boarders on Tubi.

Another modern take on a beloved '80s/'90s sitcom, this one's a bit different, serving as a total reimagining with no narrative connection to the original. And while A Different World is a comedy with dramatic heft, this one's more of a straight drama. It’s jarring for fans of the beloved original to tune in to find a serious show with the same premise as the Will Smith original—one that often leans into heavy realism. Jabari Banks plays, er, Will Smith, a 16-year-old from West Philadelphia who moves in with his auntie and uncle in Bel-Air following a gun charge and a run-in with a Philly drug lord. Banks is charismatic and believable, bringing a ton of personality to a show that occasionally veers down dark alleys. Stream Bel-Air on Peacock.

Comedian Benito Skinner plays himself, kinda, in this buzzy comedy that sees a former high school jock facing his freshman year in college while desperately trying to convince himself and everyone else that he's as straight as they come (relatable, except for the jock part). Much of the appeal is in its deft blending of tones: It's both a frequently raunchy college comedy and a sweet coming-of-age story about accepting yourself without worrying about what everyone else thinks. The cast includes Adam DiMarco (The White Lotus) and Rish Shah (Ms. Marvel), and, though it's more a story of one young man's coming of age, there's a strong ensemble backing him up. Stream Overcompensating on Prime Video.

The heart of All American (for most of its run) is Spencer James (Daniel Ezra), based on real-life NFL linebacker Spencer Paysinger. A star player for his high school team in Crenshaw, he's recruited by the coach (Taye Diggs) of a team in Beverly Hills to come and play for them, forcing Spencer to navigate two very different worlds while trying to build a life and potential career. Stream All American on Netflix.

Following a family tragedy, the already awkward 15-year-old Devi Vishwakumar (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) has a pretty terrible freshman year of high school, and decides that she’s going to turn things around the following year, hoping that a nearly academic study of sex will get her the boyfriend(s) her raging hormones have begun to demand. It works, to a point—but getting a surprise yes to sex from her crush leads her to question what she’s really ready for. More about burgeoning sexuality than sex specifically, this Mindy Kaling-produced series is both honest and charming. Stream Never Have I Ever on Netflix.

For realism in a show about the college experience, you could do a lot worse than this docuseries following several students at Gallaudet University, a school for deaf and hard-of-hearing young adults. In one sense, it's a specific setting where perspectives on deafness vary wildly, even in Gallaudet's self-contained world (aside from being a show about academically driven and horny college students, this is also a great primer for hearing people about some of the issues). But even for all of that, the challenges in building a life and future away from home are pretty universally relatable. Stream Deaf U on Netflix.

There's a reason A Different World has returned in 2026, and a lot of that has to do with the fact that there was nothing else on TV quite like it back in the late '80s and early '90s. For all of its sitcom sensibilities, the show tried hard (especially after multi-hyphenate creator Debbie Allen arrived to rework things after its first season) to paint a realistic picture of college life and an HBCU. Of the few shows on TV with largely Black casts, almost none would go so far as to highlight achievement and excellence; A Different World managed to do so while building a cast of characters so memorable that we're more than willing to catch up with them nearly forty years later. Stream A Different World on Netflix.
