#3573. You Should Update Your Garmin Watch's Heart Rate Zones

Zone 2 training is still having a moment—even if no one can agree on what it actually means. Legend has it that your easy, conversational-pace cardio—aka your Zone 2 heart rate—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine, to faster race times, and even to a longer life.

Whether Zone 2 deserves quite this much hype is debatable, but still, there are plenty of good reasons to master heart rate training more broadly. To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you your desired workout. Even if you believe every word of the Zone 2 gospel, it's completely pointless if your watch has the wrong idea of what your Zone 2 is. If you train with a Garmin watch, here’s how—and why—you should reset your heart rate zones now (and periodically).

When you first set up your Garmin, it asked for your age, weight, and a few other details. From there it generated heart rate zones, often using a default formula based on a maximum heart rate estimated from your age (typically some version of 220 minus your age). But these formulas are often wrong, since they give a single number for everybody at the same age, while real maximum heart rates vary from person to person.

Plus, there isn’t one universally agreed-upon heart rate zone system. So if your watch assumed a max of 180 and yours is actually 195, every zone it gave you is shifted. Your "Zone 2" might really, for you, be Zone 1 (AKA a pace so easy it barely feels like a workout). Or your "Zone 2" might actually be a moderate-to-hard effort that's digging you into a hole, while you think you're taking it easy. At every step of the way, there’s a different formula and definition that determines what heart rate zone shows up on your watchface.

To complicate things further, Garmin gives multiple options to set up your zones:

Percent of max heart rate. This is the simplest approach. You enter (or let the watch estimate) your max, and each zone is a slice of that number. It's only as good as your max heart rate figure, which, as noted above, is often a guess.

Percent of heart rate reserve (HRR). This method factors in both your max and your resting heart rate, so zones are based on the range your heart works across rather than just the top of it. It tends to produce more personalized zones, but it means your resting heart rate needs to be current, too.

Percent of lactate threshold heart rate (LTHR). Here, your zones are anchored to the effort level where your body starts producing lactate faster than it can clear it, a point that's closely tied to how you actually perform. Many coaches consider this the most meaningful anchor, because it reflects your real physiology rather than a formula.

That third option raises its own question: Where does your lactate threshold number come from?

In the past, getting a lactate threshold estimate from a Garmin meant wearing a compatible chest strap and doing a guided test, which involved a structured, hard run on your part. On newer models, however, that's no longer the case. Garmin has been rolling out an updated lactate threshold detection that works from the wrist's optical heart rate sensor, with no chest strap and no dedicated test. Instead, the watch estimates your threshold automatically from regular outdoor runs. This feature is typically on by default and generally requires a baseline VO2 max estimate and a run or trail run recorded with heart rate. If you'd rather not leave it up to the algorithm, you can turn auto-detection off and enter your own lactate threshold heart rate manually in the heart rate zone settings. Which watches have this varies by model, so check your specific device.

Even if you set your zones carefully once, they don't stay accurate forever. Several things change over time:

Your fitness changes. As you get fitter, your resting heart rate often drops, and your lactate threshold heart rate can shift. Zones based on where you were a year or two ago may not reflect where you are now.

You age. Your maximum heart rate tends to decline gradually over the years.

You change sports. Running, cycling, and swimming each have different heart rate behavior, and Garmin lets you set sport-specific zones for exactly this reason. If you've never touched them, you may be using running-based numbers on the bike, or vice versa.

You switched watches or imported old data. Zones can carry over from a previous device or a profile you set up years ago.

Your resting heart rate has changed. An outdated resting number could be throwing things off.

None of these have dramatic consequences, but if you’re focused on heart rate training, it’s worth trying to be as accurate and up-to-date as possible. If your zones are set too high, you may not be getting the aerobic stimulus you think you are. You'll also underestimate how hard your harder sessions really are, and your training load and recovery metrics can end up skewed.

On the flip side, if your zones are set too low, your "easy" runs could actually become the classic trap of training in the gray zone: too hard to recover from well, too easy to drive big gains. And because Garmin's training status, recovery time, and load features lean on your heart rate data, bad zones can quietly nudge those numbers off as well.

The good news is that fixing all this should take less than 10 minutes. First, decide whether you want zones based on max heart rate, heart rate reserve, or lactate threshold. There’s a good chance you can trust the lactate threshold your watch gives you, or you can find your actual max heart rate.

The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded. If you want a more deliberate test, a coach or a structured max-effort protocol can help, but only attempt hard testing if you're healthy and your doctor is comfortable with it. Also keep in mind that reading from a wrist-based sensor can also spike unreliably, so a chest strap gives more trustworthy numbers when accuracy matters.

Next, check your recent average resting heart rate in Garmin Connect and make sure the number your zones are using is current.

In your watch's user profile or in Garmin Connect, find the heart rate zone settings. From there you can adjust your max, change how zones are calculated, and set different zones for different sports.

Finally, put these new zones to the test. Go for an easy run or ride at what your watch calls Zone 2. Can you hold a conversation, breathing comfortably in full sentences? Does it feel sustainable for a long time? If it feels either laughably easy or surprisingly taxing, your zones probably need another look.

Maybe Zone 2 is the cornerstone of your training, or maybe you think it's completely overrated. Either way, the principle is the same: You should be able to train by feel, and your watch can only help you do that if the numbers behind it are right.

Garmin gives you more ways to set your zones than most brands do. Spend 10 minutes figuring out which method your zones are using, confirming the number behind it is current, and updating it in your settings. It’ll make every easy run, hard interval, and recovery metric on your wrist more useful.

One of Natalie Portman’s most iconic roles, even twenty years later, is V For Vendetta. How can one forget how great she looked with a shaved head? She just shared her personal takes on what it was like to be without hair for awhile, I didn’t see this recommendation coming from her.

Portman first rocked a buzzcut in 2005 at the premiere of Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith at Cannes Film Festival. It had been freshly shaven on set when she hopped on a plane to go to the glitzy event in between filming. As she recalled about attending the event with the fresh cut in her words:

Everyone was like, ‘Oh wow, she has no hair.’ And then I went back, got on a plane and went back to Berlin and started shooting again on Monday. It was pretty wild to be out in public exposed like a baby bird. I feel like it's something every woman should do at least once in her life. It feels so amazing to have rain on your head for the first time.

Wow, what a glowing review from Natalie Portman about shaving one’s head! While speaking to Harper’s Bazaar, the actress suggested that “every woman” give it a try at some point in their life. She loved it because it felt amazing to feel the rain on her head – which funny enough is the same thing Millie Bobby Brown pointed out about going bald for Stranger Things. Portman had a really positive review for shaving her head, but there is something she didn’t like so much:

I did not love growing it back. I have curly hair, and so when it grows back you just look like a little boy for a very long time.

Another solid point. I guess there’s always a baseball cap for those awkward growing pains? In V for Vendetta, Portman’s character of Evey has her head shaved against her will when she’s captured, imprisoned and tortured in the dystopian thriller. The moment when her head was shaved off had to be captured in one take with three cameras at once. During rehearsals for the scene, Portman said a bunch of men on the crew offered to have their heads shaved in order for it to be tested and ready for Portman.

Portman is one of quite a few actors who’ve left their hair behind for a while for a role. Emma Stone is the most recent example for her film Bugonia, but in her case, she made her director Yorgos Lanthimos do so too “in solidarity”. Though, the pact wasn’t as satisfying as Stone thought it would be. Florence Pugh also shaved her head for We Live In Time, and has talked about how she was worried she might look like “an egg” before officially committing to it, and embracing the haircut wholeheartedly.

You can check out Natalie Portman in V For Vendetta with a Paramount+ subscription. It’s still arguably one of her best movies, so her bold haircut was absolutely worth it.

#3571. Zelda Ocarina of Time release time in your time zone

And what you can get as a pre-order bonus, too

The Zelda Ocarina of Time remake release time is just around the corner, as Nintendo introduces a new generation to one of its classic games. Unlike the 3DS port from 2011, Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 includes a massive visual overhaul, along with several quality-of-life features that weren't present in the original Nintendo 64 release. Pre-orders are still open at some retailers if you're hoping to snag a special bonus, though US-based folks only get one bonus to choose from.

Below, we break down when Zelda Ocarina of Time releases in your time zone.

Nintendo usually doesn't give exact release times for its first-party games, and Ocarina of Time is no different. However, unless stated otherwise, eShop releases launch at midnight in the easternmost time zone of your region. For example, that'd be 12 a.m. on March 5 in New York City, but 9 p.m. PST in San Francisco.

Here's what that looks like around the world:

That means you can play Ocarina of Time early if your Nintendo Account is linked to another region. If you want to play early and haven't linked your account to another region already, however, we recommend just making a new account for that purpose. The process of un-linking and re-registering an existing Nintendo Account is tedious and potentially problematic, since your save data is tied to your account.

Bear in mind that Ocarina of Time is a Switch 2 exclusive. It won't work on the original Switch.

Certain retailers are running a number of Ocarina of Time pre-order bonuses around the world, but if you're in the U.S., you only get one: the game case with a special foil art cover. It's in high demand and has sold out on Amazon, though it's worth checking places like Walmart, as they've had more in stock.

If you're trying to get the Ocarina of Time Switch 2 console and manage to snag one, don't forget it's just the console. It doesn't come with the game.

#3570. A Christmas Horror Movie With A 0% On Rotten Tomatoes Flopped At The Box Office

A new horror comedy film has become both a rare critical disaster and a sizable box office flop. "Christmas at the Kringles" opened over Halloween weekend, though one would be forgiven for not noticing. For starters, Halloween fell on a Saturday which meant most people weren't going to the movies. For another, the weekend's new offerings were a bit lackluster, as evidenced by this newcomer from Briarcliff Entertainment.

"Christmas at the Kringles" opened to just $675,000 on 1,825 screens, giving it a terrible $369 per-screen average and landing it all the way down at number 17 on the charts. The film was directed by Kevin Lewis, the man behind the Nicolas Cage fighting killer animatronics movie "Willy's Wonderland," among others. He's not a terribly high-profile filmmaker, but this isn't going to help his case when it comes to his future.

Perhaps worse than the opening weekend number is the response from critics, as "Christmas at the Kringles" holds a rare 0% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. It's not that horror movies need critics on their side. The recent box office success of "Other Mommy" proved that horror is critic proof to some degree, but this is next level bad. A film like this was always going to lean on VOD and streaming, but the awful response is likely to turn away quite a few would-be viewers.

"Christmas at the Kringles" follows the Seversons as they start fresh in a quiet suburban neighborhood where their neighbors, the Kringles, celebrate Christmas year-round. But what begins as charming quickly turns unsettling, as the Seversons' concerns about their son's growing attachment to the family leads to lots of action-packed holiday chaos. The film's cast includes Ron Livingston ("Office Space"), Rachel Bilson ("The O.C."), Thomas Lennon ("Reno 911"), and Donald Faison ("Scrubs"), among others.

"Christmas at the Kringles" was a big creative swing, as Christmas horror comedy films aren't surefire slam dunks. But if this kind of thing works, it can extend well beyond the box office. To be certain, a Christmas flick can make its way into the annual rotation, meaning money indefinitely. But unless this one becomes an unlikely cult favorite, that's probably not going to pan out.

There are plenty of underrated Christmas horror movies out there. Even ones with a more comedic bend, such as "Krampus" or, most famously, "Gremlins," have found success. But this was a big swing and a bigger miss. The timing didn't help, either, as it's just a touch too early for people to get into the X-mas spirit, while movies like "Clayface" offered a better option for horror fans in theaters.

Briarcliff had reason to believe it might work out, too. "Terrifier 3" killed it at the box office in 2024, pulling in $90 million worldwide. Granted, that was after "Terrifier 2" became a surprise sensation. The "Terrifier" movies have also garnered surprising levels of critical praise, despite the hardcore gore on display.

Even last year's "Silent Night, Deadly Night" was a bloody remake with something new to offer. It wasn't a big hit, but it was received reasonably well. The larger point is that the Christmas horror genre is nothing new and has definitely led to success in recent years. On paper, this one could have worked. But in practice, it's a disaster in every way success is generally measured in Hollywood.

"Christmas at the Kringles" is in theaters now.

#3569. Heat Director Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself at LA Gun Range

Michael Mann was rushed to the hospital Saturday, after the director of films such as Collateral, The Insider, and Ferrari accidentally shot himself at a Los Angeles gun range. According to People, the bullet from Mann's gun struck his leg while the 83-year-old artist was returning the firearm to its holster.

“On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered, resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann. He was treated and is being released,” a spokesperson for Mann said in a statement to media.

In a separate statement that did not name Mann, the Los Angeles Police Department confirmed the incident, which TMZ reports occurred at The Range LA, a members-only shooting club on the Westside region of Los Angeles.

Robert DeNiro, Al Pacino, and Michael Mann at the world premiere of Heat.

“Yesterday at around 4 p.m., officers responded to the 11000 block of Missouri Avenue for a radio call for shots fired at that location," the LAPD statement reads. "Responding units’ investigation determined the shooting to be accidental. The subject was transported to a local hospital in stable condition. An injury report was completed.”

According to Deadline, the incident is not expected to delay work on Heat 2, which is scheduled to begin production in January, 2027. The director, who has been nominated for four Academy Awards and is the winner of two Emmys and a BAFTA, is also responsible for films including Hunter (1986) and The Last of the Mohicans (1992); he is also known for creating the acclaimed television series Miami Vice.

Michael Mann's latest film, the sequel to 1995 crime classic Heat, will explore the origins of the characters played by Al Pacino and Robert De Niro in the original film. Its cast reportedly includes Leonardo DiCaprio, Christian Bale, and Adolescence creator Stephen Graham.

#3568. These Sony Over-Ear Headphones Are Just $88 Right Now

Not everybody needs, wants, or can afford the "best" headphones available, especially when they can easily cost half a grand. If the $450+ Sony XM6s, which I called the best over-ear headphones of 2025 (and 2026 so far), are not in your budget, then perhaps the more affordable Sony WH-CH720Ns could be. While they're not quite as premium, they're significantly cheaper and offer good enough audio quality for most people.

Right now, you can get them for $88 (originally $179.99) on Amazon, their second-lowest price ever according to price tracking tools. Thopugh they've dropped below $100 before, all three colorways have not been available at their current price at the same time until now.

These are Sony's entry-level over-ear headphones, and the company mostly made cuts in the design and build. When you hold them, they might feel hollow and light, but they're still comfortable since the earcups are well-cushioned, as noted in CNET's review. However, Sony did not make as many sacrifices in the audio or ANC department, which, at the end of the day, is what's most important.

These headphones use the same Sony Sound Connect app as the flagship models and share some of the same features, like multipoint technology to connect to up to two devices. They also come with Google Fast Pair and Find My Device support, nice features to have for convenience, especially if you misplace them. You can get 35 hours of battery life with ANC on and 50 hours with ANC off, and the charging is quick, with three minutes giving you three hours of juice.

The ANC is not as good as the latest XM6, but it works great for under $100, according to Mashable's review, and it will block most ambient noise outdoors or indoors. Transparency mode is also great, allowing you to have conversations and hear bikes or cars passing by. The adjustable EQ in the app means you can tweak the crisp and vibrant sound of the WH-CH720N to your liking.

With November here, some people are already making Thanksgiving plans and watching Hallmark Christmas movies. But, I’m personally going to need five business days to mourn the end of spooky season. One of Universal Orlando’s masterminds, Michael Aiello, is totally on my wavelength, as he reflected on making this year’s landmark Halloween Horror Nights happen.

Aiello is the Senior Director of Entertainment Creative Development at Universal Orlando Resort and has over thirty years of experience at the theme park to his name. Since this year was the park’s special 35th anniversary scaring us with Universal’s beloved seasonal festivity, he had a lot to say about bringing it all to life. In his words:

For me, one of the greatest rewards of doing what we do is watching all of you experience the worlds we’ve created. Seeing your excitement, hearing your reactions, and knowing these stories mean as much to you as they do to us is something I’ll never take for granted.

I know HHN has become one of my favorite traditions, and it’s great to hear from the designer that it’s all about our reactions and enjoyment of it. The 2026 edition had a lot of highlights, from the Sinners haunted house, an especially bloody attraction with cannibals and an awesome ode to the Hellraiser franchise. In a post on X, Aiello said creatives like himself only get so many anniversaries in their careers, and doing the one this past season has been really rewarding for himself and his team. He continued:

There’s also something incredibly special about seeing Jack the Clown, Oddfellow and our legendary HHN icons and characters come together to celebrate 35 years of Halloween Horror Nights. These characters represent decades of imagination, artistry, and extraordinary talent, both behind the scenes and in the spotlight. They’ve become so much more than personas in a Halloween event. They’re part of its history, its identity, and the memories of generations of horror fans. Watching audiences embrace them again this year has been an absolute joy.

This year’s event was called Jack & Oddfellow: Chaos & Control. It brought about a crossover between two of HHN’s most popular icons, Jack the Clown and Dr. Oddfellow. Both characters debuted during the tenth Halloween Horror Nights back in 2000. They have become so popular that they’ve made multiple appearances in Orlando. With the season having ended, Aielo took some time to thank everyone involved for basically making it possible.

HHN definitely wouldn’t exist without the many hands and minds that create it every year. Aiello shouted out every division that works on the event including the scareactors and performers "who tirelessly bring the fear night after night”. The Halloween Horror Nights senior director also added this to his message:

I’ve always looked at our anniversary years as a chance to celebrate the stories we’ve told, the characters we’ve created, and the memories we’ve made along the way. Perhaps when the 40th rolls around, we’ll pull that book off the shelf again and discover a few more chapters worth telling. Or perhaps the story takes us somewhere entirely unexpected. That’s part of the magic of what we do. We never really know what the future holds.

The future can indeed be uncertain, but if history is any kind of indicator, the talented creatives at the park will find a way to spook audiences in unexpected ways down the road. Aiello also left fans with this last bit:

As our Infernal Carnival and all horrors within comes to close… Somewhere in the darkness, we direct our focus on the next nightmare… Happy Halloween Horror Nights…Till the fog rolls once again.

Oh, I’m so looking forward to the next nightmare! Before we know it, HHN will be celebrating its 40th anniversary, and we expect even more special surprises. Even though we're heading into the holidays, I feel like I’m already counting down the days for the next scary season!

#3566. God Of War Star Dave Bautista Shows Off Kratos Physique And Beard In Video

After a truly tragic setback for the Prime Video "God of War" series that saw original star Ryan Hurst injured on set, Dave Bautista is set to make his debut as Kratos. It seems the actor is taking his role as seriously as die-hard fans would hope, as a new video reveals Bautista has put on an extra 20 pounds of muscle to play the Spartan warrior-turned-demigod.

Dave Bautista says he's up to 250 pounds after gaining 20 more pounds of muscle to play Kratos in 'GOD OF WAR'. pic.twitter.com/T6dGrqKiAY

— Geek Vibes Nation (@GeekVibesNation) November 1, 2026

The video originated on the actor's Instagram stories on November 1, 2026, and shows him flexing his muscles while sporting a Kratos-like beard and wearing a "God of War" shirt. Text on screen reads "Gained 20lbs for GOW" and "250!", confirming that Bautista has bulked up to 250 pounds ahead of his debut as Kratos. That's a significant gain, especially considering the actor's recent weight changes.

2023's "Knock at the Cabin" proved Bautista is our best wrestler-turned-actor, but it also required him to bulk up to 315 pounds, which he told Chris Van Vliet on the podcast "Insight" was "uncomfortable." "Now, looking back at it I probably overdid it," he added, "I was probably a little too big." After that, Bautitsa noticeably slimmed down. As a former wrestler for the WWE, he weighed 290 pounds, which means he became considerably larger for "Knock at the Cabin." But as the actor told Van Vliet in 2024, he started dropping weight soon after and got down to 240 pounds. "The more I trimmed down the better I felt," he said, "and I also noticed the more I trimmed down, the better I looked on camera."

Now that he's playing Kratos, Bautista has no choice but to bulk back up to believably portray the muscular protagonist, whose namesake in Greek mythology is the divine personification of strength.

In late June 2026, former Kratos actor Ryan Hurst tore his bicep on the "God of War" set. With the actor facing months of recovery time, Prime Video was forced to recast the lead role, and Dave Bautista was quickly drafted in. Given his physicality and well-established acting chops, he was the perfect replacement.

But with the former wrestler having dropped a considerable amount of weight in recent years, he needed to pack on some more muscle ahead of filming. Bautista began weight training for the role immediately after his casting was made official in August 2026. An Instagram video from early September saw the actor showing off his latest gains alongside a caption that read, "3rd week in to weight training again. 2 more months to get to where I need to be. Like ridin a bike! LFG!"

Now, it seems he's close to where he needs to be for filming to start. At this point, Prime Video has yet to confirm when filming will recommence, but based on Bautista's "2 more months" comment in his video from September, it seems cameras will start rolling this month. That means the 250-pound Bautista we see in his latest Instagram Stories post is roughly how he'll look in the show, which will need to reshoot all the scenes featuring Hurst before it forges ahead with new episodes.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. A travel router sounds unnecessary until you run into unreliable hotel wifi, device limits, or a public network you’d rather not use. The TP-Link Roam 6 is built for exactly those situations, and its AX3000 variant is currently down to $69.99 from $79.98 on Amazon, while the cheaper AX1500 is $44.99, down from $59.99, with price trackers showing both at their lowest prices so far.

The AX3000 is the one I would look at if you travel with several devices, work remotely, or simply want more headroom. It can deliver up to 2,402Mbps on the 5GHz band and 574Mbps on 2.4GHz, compared with 1,201 Mbps and 300 Mbps, respectively, on the AX1500, and it can handle up to 80 connected devices instead of 60. You also get a 2.5Gbps WAN port for faster wired internet, plus USB 3.0 for things like phone tethering, a USB modem, or file sharing. None of those upgrades will fix bad hotel internet, but they make the AX3000 better suited to heavier use once you are on a decent connection.

The AX1500, meanwhile, still gives you Wi-Fi 6, Gigabit Ethernet, USB tethering, and the core travel-router features, making it the easier pick if you mostly travel solo or just want a simple way to get a laptop, phone, and a few other devices online.

#3564. Tomi Adeyemi Does Not Want to Talk About the Children of Blood and Bone Movie

“You are a once in a generation talent,” says Tomi Adeyemi, tears in her eyes. The author is not paying me a compliment; she is reading a line from one of her numerous fan letters.

Adeyemi is a New York Times bestselling writer, a feat she accomplished at twenty-four with her 2018 fantasy debut novel Children of Blood and Bone—the first in her Legacy of Orïsha trilogy, which marries old-fashioned American YA with West African mythology. Her new novel, The Siren—released in September—follows Emery, a freshman at Dartmouth desperate to find her place as she undertakes a series of trials to join the titular group of powerful girls on campus.

This is Adeyemi’s first time since childhood not writing fantasy; maybe her first time period, since she says the first book she ever wrote was a Parent Trap fan fiction. But it’s also an attempt to move past the widely successful young-adult fantasy with which she made her name—as well as the drama surrounding the film adaptation of Adeyemi’s debut novel, an experience she has called the worst thing she ever lived through.

In now-deleted TikToks, Adeyemi said that she’s distancing herself from the film, she won’t watch it, and that she blocked one of its leads, Amandla Stenberg, on social media. Sources indicated to VF this summer that Adeyemi got more creative control over the film than most first-time authors do, including a co-screenwriting credit; they also noted that she's switched talent agencies multiple times since striking an initial deal with ICM. “There must be something [going on] because she’s burned every bridge,” one insider who works in the book-to-film space said.

When we meet, Adeyemi says that she doesn’t want to talk about that.

Instead, she talks about how she used to exclusively write fantasy because the world wasn’t safe enough for her to write anything else. Now, though, she no longer feels like she has to hide behind magic. “I’ve become someone who can inhabit it fully,” she says. “When you allow a woman to grow her claws, I am more akin to a jungle cat than I am a house plant.” She breaks into a chorus of Frank Sinatra’s “My Way,” adding a Jackson 5-esque run: “Da-da-da, oh, baby, yeah-yeah.” She tells me that sometimes, when she connects with certain people—like me—she just can’t help herself from singing. “The stars, the moon!” she belts—lines from Florence + the Machine’s “Cosmic Love.”

Adeyemi’s a musical person. She saw Florence play at Lollapalooza: “Somehow, Florence wielded her magic so I was able to get to the very front row, and she’s singing to me. I’m like, Look at this wild woman, howling to the moon.” This reminds her of a scene from her new book: when Roux, the girl Emery idolizes, is introduced. Adeyemi writes Roux dancing on a table, kicking glasses, alive and wild. Emery wants to be like that; so does Adeyemi. She explains this before singing some more: “You woke up like that, you woke up like that.”

Adeyemi’s admiration for Roux is almost tangible. She smiles dreamily when she speaks about her creation, leaving you to wonder if there was a specific person this character was based on.

Though Adeyemi started working on The Siren in 2020, she says the novel’s published version was written entirely last year. She’s gotten used to trying, and trying again; while applying for fiction writing classes in college, Adeyemi says, she was rejected five semesters in a row. One professor actually told her he couldn’t teach her to write, an anecdote she’s happy to relate now: “Hello! So many bestsellers later.” She spent four and a half years writing her first, unpublished novel, which she says was rejected 63 times. Only then did she write Children of Blood and Bone.

Adeyemi says she writes to free herself—and while one can’t be sure exactly what she had to free herself from last year, the film adaptation of Blood and Bone was shot in 2025. That’s also when Adeyemi allegedly fell out with Stenberg. And while they’re spelled differently, it’s notable that Roux—The Siren’s charismatic villain—has the same name as one of Stenberg’s most popular characters, Rue in the first Hunger Games movie.

Female authors are often asked, unfairly, whether they are writing their own lives into a story. Yet it’s also impossible to ignore the parallels between Emery and Adeyemi herself. Both are Ivy-educated writers and self-proclaimed outsiders. Adeyemi also doesn’t shy from comparisons between herself and her most recent main character: she says that all authors write themselves, because doing so is a vehicle for understanding. Reading The Siren is like stepping into her consciousness.

So is interviewing her. Adeyemi has a tendency to go off on tangents about astrology, tarots, mystical energy. “Do you remember how it felt when the entire universe came alive? All these spindles, nerve endings rise,” she asks me at one point, holding out her arms. “If you could feel the stars and taste the wind?”

The novel is wrapped up in themes of belonging, identity, and loneliness—a narrative Adeyemi tells me she relates to. “I think if you don’t belong to yourself, you don’t belong anywhere,” she says—though Adeyemi also thinks that her Aquarius placements mean people like her will never fit in, because they are not designed to. Take “our most iconic Aquarius rising, Audrey Hepburn,” or SZA, who famously wears fairy wings onstage and on red carpets. “How painful must it have been when you were on land?” Adeyemi asks her fellow Aquarius rhetorically. “How painful must it have been to learn how to fly? How painful is it for the butterflies inside before they become their butterflies?”

Adeyemi herself appears on the cover of The Siren—something that “has never been done before,” she says. “But a lot of what I do has never been done before. I remember choosing the image because I saw the darkness, that power in Emery. I’ve never seen that look in anyone else’s eye.”

There was a time where having her books adapted for the screen felt like the epitome of Adeyemi’s work. The author no longer feels that way: “I am the epitome of my work,” she says. And as she said on those now-deleted TikToks, she really would rather not talk about the film adaptation of her first novel at all.

We avoid the topic during our initial conversation. When our time runs out, though, Adeyemi tells me she’d like to talk more at a later date. When I do eventually speak to Adeyemi again—and ask about the Blood and Bone film—she shuts down physically. Her smile drops; the question throws off the energy of the conversation, almost like a betrayal has occurred. I ask another question, and Adeyemi tells me that she is getting a call. She turns off her camera, and I sit in silence for seven minutes.

Eventually, Adeyemi returns and asks if I am still there. She tells me, “The Siren is number three, New York Times.” She’s feeling the hot flash version of goosebumps, she says, like she just finished a marathon.

Adeyemi says that all of this—her career, her work, her writing process—was inspired by extreme fear. She speaks about it in the second person: “An agonizing understanding that you’ve been taught to work so hard to build a better life, [but] you might not get to build that life. It could be snapped away from you like that. I live in that terror.” She’s gone through her own trials: not just the long journey to publishing Blood and Bone, but the internet’s scrutiny over the comments she made about the Blood and Bone adaptation. “I’m exceptionally proud of who I am today,” she says, though “life is terrifying.”

In our first conversation, Adeyemi had said The Siren might be her last book—that she might be finished with writing altogether. “You can depart from all these previous eras of your life with a gentle sort of ruthlessness,” she said, “and then tomorrow can actually be a new day.” Now, she seems reenergized by the idea of work, telling me that she’s met children’s literacy organizations that try to inspire kids with the work of James Baldwin, Octavia Butler, and herself. “I’m proud of writing this from a really hard time and place,” she says, “and I wanna continue Emery’s journey.”

I ask her what changed between that interview and this one. Her smile freezes; she laughs awkwardly before hesitantly replying, “I think it’s interesting talking to you in the summer and then talking to you post this tour. I don’t know how the piece will end up, since you’re getting two very distinct cross sections.”

She takes another beat. “So that quote felt more… there was more of a resonance the first time we spoke. As I’m sitting here with you now, I just have a vision of myself writing deeply.”

The time between our talks seems to have given her space for deep reflection. I remind Adeyemi what she’d told me about feeling more like a jungle cat than a houseplant, and ask if she felt she had to be a jungle cat during her journey with the Blood and Bone film. “I think all women have to be in tune with their power. I think Black women have to be in tune with their power, dark-skinned Black women especially,” she answers. “There’s a sense of gravity that wouldn’t have been there without knowing what it is to step into my power and voice. You owe it to yourself to feel safe, and if you’re the only one there to defend yourself, you have to have the claws.”

As the film’s January release inches closer, one has to wonder if Adeyemi has a desire to retract her claws—and her statements about the movie. Or at least whether everything that’s transpired has changed her relationship with her debut novel. “I think my relationship with myself has changed more than anything,” Adeyemi answers. When narrating the audiobook for The Siren, she noticed that Emery doesn’t recognize her own genius. That broke Adeyemi’s heart, because the character’s insecurities came from a personal place. The difference between her character and her own feelings also shows Adeyemi’s own growth: “You don’t feel that way anymore,” she told herself.

When asked whether she might try to make another movie someday—or adapt The Siren—she answers firmly: “I’ve already done that journey. It’s a lot of work, but it’s not work that is for myself. When you commit to doing something on screen, it’s more about everyone else on the other side of that screen. I think because I have such a directorial and cinematic approach to my writing, I do value having experienced everything.” Selling the rights to your novel means essentially giving it away to other people, she says. That was extremely difficult for her. “I don’t need anyone in this world.”

Maybe Adeyemi’s film future lies instead in front of the camera. She did film a cameo in Blood and Bone, and one in the second Devil Wears Prada film: “At the beginning of the year, I thought, Oh, I would like to try acting,” she laughs now. “By the end of the year, I had a cameo across from Viola Davis and another across from Meryl Streep.” In the future, she’d be interested in voice acting and animation. Or live-action—but maybe only if, say, Jon Chu asked her to star in a Bollywood rom-com with Dev Patel.

“SASUKE!” She yells the name of a Naruto character in a high-pitched voice, then adds in her normal voice, “I’m clearly a very animated person.”

Warning! Spoilers ahead for the Season 3 premiere of St. Denis Medical, “He Ain’t Noah Wyle." If you haven't tuned in for the NBC show, don't fret as this isn't a huge spoiler, but I will talk about the episode in this story.

St. Denis Medical’s third season finally premiered on the 2026 TV schedule, and it was so entertaining. On top of addressing some of the romantic twists left off in the Season 2 finale, the medical mockumentary continued to bring the comedy. This included some fun references to The Pitt, and I had to ask the creator why the direct mentions happened.

Following Ron’s surgery in the Season 2 finale, Damon Wayans guest starred as his temporary replacement, Dr. Highland. While Highland's a good doctor, it’s not hard to see his mannerisms and the way he dresses are similar to that of Dr. Robby from the Emmy-winning drama The Pitt. Alex even makes it a point to say Dr. Highland has a “big performative” energy and thinks he’s in a medical drama. However, “He ain’t Noah Wyle,” as she says (and as the title of the premiere also notes).

Between the way he acts, dresses, and talks, with one speech pulled directly from The Pitt, it was very clear the episode was not attempting to be subtle. St. Denis has in the past had no trouble spoofing other medical shows. That said, references can be tough, and Eric Ledgin told CinemaBlend why it’s easier to mention some shows, like The Pitt, and harder to mention others:

I always feel most connected to the show when the characters are living in the same world I'm living in. So, that gets a little tricky in the sense that they can't be fans of In Living Color because that would cause some kind of time portal warp that would ruin the show, I suppose. But they can know about The Pitt, you know, and they can comment on it, as that's a popular show; it's in the zeitgeist.

I love it when my favorite shows are name-dropped in my other favorite shows, especially when there’s a clear reference, such as Dr. Highland acting like Wyle’s Dr. Robby. It’s understandable why it can get tricky to bring up other shows, particularly ones that have featured the actors on St. Denis Medical themselves, but this time the whole show reference within a show thing worked.

Meanwhile,The Pitt is only two seasons in, but plenty of healthcare workers have praised the drama for its accuracy. It's also one of the most talked-about shows, and that's another reason why Ledgin felt the need to reference it, telling CinemaBlend:

I feel like there probably aren't many hospitals where people are working there and not talking about The Pitt from time to time. And, you know, as I think Alex says, or at least said it in an early draft of the script, it was like, ‘I watch The Pitt, I love The Pitt. But this ain't The Pitt.’ And so it's nice to be swimming in such different waters from them that we can still be fans of that show and comment on it in a fun way.

Since Ron is back at work following his surgery, Dr. Highland seems to have been dismissed (or at least is out of the picture for now). I'm a little sad to be saying goodbye to the St. Denis Medical version of Dr. Robby already. But here's hoping we still get some other shoutouts to The Pitt from time to time. (Especially since Alex has stated she loves Noah Wyle and would leave her husband for him, so I just know she’s gonna be watching Robby's Season 3 return.)

Meanwhile, fans can look forward to more from Season 3 of St. Denis Medical now that it’s finally here. Aside from fun references to other medical shows, there is a lot to look forward to on the plot front. We've got guest stars coming. We've got more chaos coming. So, stay tuned, as new episodes air on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET on NBC, and are streaming the next day with a Peacock subscription.

There’s no shortage of outdoor security cameras, but finding one that balances video quality, battery life, and ease of use without pushing past $100 is rare. Right now, the Tapo MagCam 2K+ is on sale for $59.99 on Amazon, down from $89.99, which is its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. PCMag named it the best security camera of 2024, pointing out that while battery-powered cameras often trade convenience for frequent recharging, the MagCam 2K+ avoids that issue with a 10,000mAh battery rated to last up to 300 days per charge, depending on how often it records.

Charging happens over micro-USB, though there’s an optional Tapo A200 solar panel if you want to avoid manual recharging altogether. As for managing the camera, its companion app is intuitive, offering settings for motion sensitivity, siren activation, spotlight brightness, firmware updates, and more. Overall, the MagCam 2K+ handles the basics well and throws in a few smart features usually reserved for pricier models.

#3561. Avengers: Doomsday Ticket Presales Top Supergirl's Worldwide Box Office Run

Superhero movies have been experiencing troubled times of late. But "Avengers: Doomsday" might just be able to save the flailing genre. Thus far, the upcoming Marvel Cinematic Universe team-up movie has already set box office records with pre-sales, and now, it's just passed another significant milestone. According to a Forbes report from October 31, 2026, "Doomsday" took $125 million in pre-sales by the end of October across all cinema formats. This means that, by now, it has passed the entire box office gross for DC Studios' "Supergirl."

For the most part, DC Studios co-heads James Gunn and Peter Safran have gotten off to a decent start with their DC Universe. The fledgling franchise has delivered such hits as the charming crowd-pleaser "Superman" and the HBO series "Lanterns," proving this latest cinematic enterprise can deliver everything from lighthearted superhero shenanigans to gritty comic book crime dramas. But there has been one glaring misstep thus far: "Supergirl."

Though the movie itself isn't actually all that bad (/Film's review noted that Milly Alcock shines as the self-destructive savior of the DCU in "Supergirl), its box office returns were less than heroic. Indeed, "Supergirl" took in just $126.5 million against a $170-186 million budget, which means "Doomsday" has now matched the film's entire gross before it's even hit theaters.

To be fair, that's more embarrassing for DC Studios than it is encouraging for Marvel Studios, as "Supergirl" isn't a major event movie featuring beloved characters that have been at the forefront of pop culture for the last 20 years. But while a movie that includes everything the MCU has to offer beating "Supergirl" at the box office in pre-sales alone isn't quite as big an accomplishment as it may seem, it's also a reminder that DC can't afford another "Supergirl"-level flop anytime soon.

Back in September 2026, "Avengers: Doomsday" set a major box office record for Marvel when it surpassed $50 million in pre-sales 100 days ahead of its release on December 18, 2026. That was good news for Marvel Studios and fans of the franchise, which has been conspicuously struggling in recent years as mass audiences tire of the interconnected superhero narratives being told by studio head Kevin Feige and his collaborators. As Forbes pointed out, however, "Doomsday" is far from a sure bet for the company.

According to the outlet, pre-sales are almost certainly coming from die-hard fans who want to secure their chance to see the movie as soon as it drops. But 2025's "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" also saw a solid turnout from die-hards before its box office took a hit. That said, it seems unlikely "Doomsday" will suffer a similar fate. Not only is this an Avengers movie, which carries a certain amount of prestige and recognition, Marvel Studios has packed this thing with fan-favorite characters a là 2024's "Deadpool & Wolverine" — which, as it happens, was a major box office success.

With Robert Downey Jr. set to make his MCU return as Victor Von Doom, alongside beloved MCU characters of the past and the 20th Century Fox-era X-Men, it seems likely "Doomsday" will succeed simply by sheer crowd-pleasing power. Meanwhile, there's no getting around the fact that "Supergirl" flopped hard at the box office earlier this year, and DC Studios will want to avoid any similar occurrences with its upcoming slate.

In light of how superhero movies have struggled in recent years, "Supergirl" seemed doomed from the outset. Taking lesser-known characters and turning them into cultural icons worked for Marvel Studios back in the late 2000s and 2010s after 2008's "Iron Man" became the unlikely superhero movie that changed Hollywood forever. But that started yielding diminishing returns by the 2020s, as audiences grew tired of having to keep up with wider developments in the shared universe via middling streaming series and bland, paint-by-numbers movies.

As such, James Gunn's decision to follow up "Superman" with "Supergirl" seemed sort of baffling. We'd seen Milly Alcock's Kryptonian show up briefly in "Superman," but otherwise, this was an unknown iteration of a second-tier DC character who quite clearly had very little box office pull at the time she was given an entire movie. Jason Momoa's Lobo was on-hand to try to increase the appeal, but it was obvious that mass audiences weren't going to turn out. With that in mind, it's not surprising that "Doomsday" has already surpassed the entire box office take of "Supergirl."

Now, the question becomes whether "Doomsday" can, in fact, overcome the issues highlighted by Forbes to establish itself as the true savior of the MCU. The original "Doomsday" teaser trailers were boring, frankly, and RDJ's return as Doctor Doom was met with confusion among fans who remain perplexed as to why the actor is playing a major Marvel villain rather than Tony Stark/Iron Man. But Marvel has clearly managed to increase the hype for this movie since those early days of "Doomsday" promotion. The film matching the box office for "Supergirl" is just the latest sign that things are headed in the right direction.

#3560. 'The Mandalorian' Meets 'Avatar' in Netflix's New Sci-Fi Western Masterpiece

A legendary lawman becomes a cyborg in the Netflix series

Westerns are filled with stories about the toll violence takes on the soul and quests for revenge that begin with digging two graves. Netflix’s new animated Western Bass X Machina leans into those themes on both a personal and societal level, tackling America’s cycles of brutal violence from the Trail of Tears to the Civil War to the outlaws of the Wild West. It also adds in mechs, magic, and one of the best opening themes since Cowboy Bebop. In short, it slaps.

Created by LeSean Thomas and Studio Mir, who both worked on The Legend of Korra, Bass X Machina is a reimagining of the story of Bass Reeves (Brian Tyree Henry), an escaped slave who worked in Indian Territory as a deputy U.S. Marshal. Reeves’ real life was extraordinary, and is said to have inspired the character of the Lone Ranger, but Bass X Machina also gives him a cybernetic arm that shoots magic bullets. The criminals he fights get even bigger upgrades, and the stakes can at times escalate to truly ludicrous levels. Henry does an especially great job expressing exasperation as Bass faces plenty of absurd foes, like an outlaw in a rampaging bull mech that requires complex cooperation to take down.

At the start of Bass X Machina, Bass is a bounty hunter hoping to pull off one last job. Then he’s offered stable employment as a lawman if he can find Eugene Starr (Nick Thurston), a missing engineer capable of building incredible technology. Eugene’s tinkerer niece Dana Starr (Tati Gabrielle of Chilling Adventures of Sabrina and The Last of Us) insists on tagging along. Dana serves as comic relief and an audience surrogate Bass can explain things to, but she also proves herself repeatedly in combat with an endless supply of useful devices. Her goofy Inspector Gadget-like fighting style and constant preaching of nonviolence in a brutal world could easily become grating, but Gabrielle’s earnest delivery and the surprising depth of her character arc make the odd dynamic work.

The Legend of Korra combined steampunk with fantasy, and Bass X Machina does the same, though its TV-MA rating means the fights are far gorier than anything Avatar Korra ever experienced. Bass finds himself at odds with the Holy People, a group of Choctaw Nation women with the power to channel the elements like Avatar’s benders. Battle scenes where they work together to create cyclones and huck icicles demonstrate Studio Mir’s mastery of showy animated choreography, especially when there’s also plenty of gunfire and absurdly powerful war machines in the mix. Unfortunately, the 3D animation Studio Mir leans on for the final two episodes lacks the sharp style of the rest of the work and detracts from the show’s climax.

Another highlight is the music. Janelle Monáe plays Bass’ wife Glory and penned an original theme with a rich intro animation you will never want to skip. Composers Roman GianArthur and Nate Wonder developed a dynamic score that evokes the classic rhythms of Western showdowns while speeding them up to a tempo more fitting for the action-packed anime stylings.

Bass X Machina is only six episodes and probably could have benefited from a bit more time to establish its characters — or even just to do more of the episodic bounty hunting missions that are the focus of the first half of the season. The show is set in the immediate aftermath of the Civil War when Confederate veterans loyal to the twisted General Rivenbark (Currie Graham) pose a major threat, and the story of a bounty hunter pitted against the evil remnant of a defeated army makes this feel like a darker version of the early seasons of The Mandalorian.

The series is tonally more akin to Fullmetal Alchemist in its examination of the horrors of both science and war. Bass X Machina never shies away from portraying racism, whether in the way that white people cheat and demean Bass or the multiple horrific massacres led by U.S. troops against the Five Tribes. Bass X Machina is relentlessly focused on its theme: that it is incredibly hard to forgive the sins of the past, but building a better future is the only way to end the cycle of violence. Bass has been wronged as much as any character in the show, and in classic Western fashion, he both wants vengeance and understands how meting it out would hurt the fragile peace he’s worked so hard to attain.

Bass’ internal struggle is a microcosm of the battle for the soul of America, a plot that can feel a bit trite at times but overall works to make Bass X Machina surprisingly touching. The show tells a satisfying, twisty story in its six episodes, and leaves the door open for plenty more adventures. Bass Reeves spent 30 years as a lawman; Netflix's blend of real history, fantasy, science fiction, and dramatic action feels like it could easily sustain a few more seasons.

#3559. Substack’s Cofounder Might Not Know How to Save the Media—But He Knows How to Outplay It

As recently as a few years ago, Substack was struggling to shed the perception that it was radioactive. “Substack Has a Nazi Problem,” read the headline of a 2023 Atlantic story that surfaced “scores of white-supremacist, neo-Confederate, and explicitly Nazi newsletters” on the platform, which was, in some instances, taking its standard 10% profit from them. Over 200 Substack writers wrote an open letter opposing the company’s hands-off approach to content moderation, and several high-profile writers and publications migrated to competitors.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Charli xcx publish there—Kylie Jenner has said she’d like to—as do new media phenomena like Feed Me and The Free Press. The platform has significant footholds in fashion, AI, politics, literature, celebrity gossip, and most everything in between. In the opening pages of his book, How to Save the Media, McKenzie recalls drinking whiskey at the Chelsea Hotel alongside former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown, who now publishes the popular Fresh Hell newsletter on Substack. The United Kingdom–born Brown, like McKenzie, came to America from abroad, only to rise to the highest rungs of its media world, and she seemed now to see him as a peer.

“You’re a New Zealander, aren’t you?” she asked McKenzie. “There’s something to being an outsider.”

In a recent interview with Vanity Fair, speaking from the Toni Morrison Conference Room at Substack’s San Francisco headquarters, McKenzie appeared uncomfortable with the idea that his book, liberally sprinkled with such encounters with the cream of the Substack crop, amounted to a victory lap. He was, despite a generally mild manner and steadfast earnestness, relentlessly on message. “I’m always going to be like a broken record coming back to the importance of direct relationships,” McKenzie acknowledged. It’s the Substack theory of fixing an ailing media ecosystem: replacing the ad-based chaos sown by the internet with a more nourishing connection between writer and reader, and having consumers pay for the media they want to see in the world rather than subject themselves to the whims of an attention economy controlled by big social media companies. McKenzie admitted his book’s title was a provocation, but “for me, it’s backing up the gospel that I’m trying to preach.”

Still, we could agree that something about the controversies that dogged the platform in recent years now seems quaint—that Substack has achieved some fundamental conquest. Instead of reactively responding to the “Nazi problem,” the company chose to stick with its hands-off approach to content moderation, and the outcry dissipated: Substack remains the go-to home for your established journalists striking out on their own (Jim Acosta, Nate Silver) as well as your upstart media operations repurposing the expertise once best associated with legacy outlets (The Bulwark, The Ankler). I suggested to McKenzie that the platform today is akin to Instagram or Grindr: a tech company, yes, but also an undeniable element of the fabric of contemporary life.

From a writer’s perspective, one knock-on effect of the Substack boom has been the rising cachet around writing itself, despite the spree of recent news stories declaring the end of reading. There are so many—too many?—personal essayists and gift guide impresarios emerging seemingly out of nowhere. (“I’m not snobby about that,” McKenzie said. “I think everyone should try to write and no one should be discouraged through peer pressure from writing.”) And then there is the ever-increasing atomization across media, with political discourse splaying out across countless newsletters that are only intermittently in conversation with one another. Is this new cacophony strictly better than the ones we encountered on Facebook and Twitter? Part of the reason the open letter concerning Nazi Substack newsletters didn’t stick, perhaps, was that no one is reading the same things anyway.

McKenzie is currently chipping away at Anna Karenina. “I honestly think writing is good and reading is good,” he said, echoing the kind of unadorned aphorisms he sometimes issues on X. As far as the purported literacy emergency, he says, “I don’t see many centuries of progress on this fundamental communication form being undone overnight.” Our “cultural crisis,” McKenzie thinks, has more to do with the distribution mechanisms of writing, and “is intrinsically tied to the state of the media system.”

After departing small-town New Zealand to pursue a career in journalism, McKenzie, 44, tried his hand at tech reporting in Hong Kong and San Francisco. Later, while working at the messaging app Kik, he and the company’s chief technology officer Chris Best hatched their plan to reroute the flow of publishing profits away from social media companies and toward writers. (Best is Substack’s CEO, while McKenzie works as its “chief writing officer” and heads up the company’s partnerships and talent acquisition efforts.)

“We had more direct relationships in the traditional media system,” McKenzie said, referring to, for example, a subscription to a print newspaper. “But then it got broken by the internet and replaced by something that corroded the direct relationships and gave all the power to Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg instead.”

As it happens, one of the touchstones in McKenzie’s own writing career is his dust-up with Musk. He worked for a time in communications at Tesla, and Musk, McKenzie writes, threatened to sue to block a book that he wrote about the company after leaving. (Insane Mode was published in 2018. Musk and Tesla didn’t return requests for comment.) Later, McKenzie and Best would turn down acquisition offers from Jack Dorsey’s Twitter and Musk’s X.

It was a choice they made, in McKenzie’s telling, to preserve the company’s independence—to prevent the Substack ecosystem from going the same way as those social platforms, which tend to leave their consumers more exhausted and frustrated than enlightened. I proposed to McKenzie that the company’s endurance in the face of its detractors has something to do with the shifting shape of online discourse, and that Substack itself has had a key role in making the tools of mass censure weaker in the age of media fragmentation. “I wonder if a lesson we are all learning,” he suggested, “is that the heavy-handed censorship approach can often backfire.”

“Did it do any good to kick Trump off Twitter and Facebook for two years?” he asked.

In How to Save the Media, McKenzie reflects on an evening he spent at the Biltmore Hotel in downtown Los Angeles in 2021. He was there to support Bari Weiss, who had struck out on Substack after leaving The New York Times about a year earlier. The schism would go on to shape the future of journalism from the newsletter economy all the way up to the highest echelons of Hollywood and television news after Weiss was appointed editor in chief of CBS News last year. (Of the common criticisms that Weiss has made the network overly Trump-friendly and lacks the requisite TV experience for the role, McKenzie says, “I think for the most part, the media industry is experiencing Bari Weiss as a media gossip story. And I think the more interesting story is the structural story and what it suggests about what’s possible in this emerging media economy. So I’m mostly watching from that perspective and I still think it’s too early to draw grand conclusions about what’s happened so far.”) In her resignation letter from the Times, Weiss wrote that Twitter had become the paper’s “ultimate editor.” On Substack, she built The Free Press, an outlet that has largely defined itself in opposition to what it sees as mainstream media orthodoxies.

That night, the Los Angeles Press Club was honoring Weiss. McKenzie took the accolade, he writes, “as validation of the nascent direct-relationships model”: Despite the ongoing and widespread opposition to her politics, Weiss had identified a journalistic niche that required no traditional media backing. Yet, The Free Press ultimately brought Weiss back to the legacy press—the new Substack class has its eye on some of the old media rewards, to the extent that they remain available.The night served as a sign, McKenzie writes, that “independence can still deliver prestige.”

“I don’t think what we’re going through here,” he told me, “is a moment of change where all the benefits from the old things have to be thrown out.”

#3558. Why the Holidays Are Actually the Best Time of Year to Start Working Out

If you have even the tiniest inkling that you might want to get in shape in the new year—or anytime really—don’t wait until January. This isn't a "winter arc" self-improvement pitch; it's just facts. The best time to start a gym habit is before the holiday season. Heck, in December, you’ll even have the place mostly to yourself.

Sure, technically “right now” is always the best time to start exercising, but the holiday season is special. If you wait until January, gyms will be packed. The first two weeks of the year, everybody thinks they’re at the start of an amazing new fitness habit...and by February, most of them have forgotten all about it. Don’t make life harder for yourself by starting during the big rush. Classes will fill up, you’ll have to fight people for the squat rack, and it will be hard to have any real fun. So start now.

In October and November, gyms and classes are at more or less their normal capacities. This is a good time to feel out the vibe of a new place. But it gets better: Once December rolls around, the fair-weather gymgoers will be off shopping for gifts after work and attending holiday parties on the weekends. They won’t feel like getting out of their warm beds in the morning, either. When you arrive, the squat rack will be free. You’ll have your choice of treadmills. The gym will be your oyster.

If you start now, you'll have about two months to get up to speed before the rush starts in January. And that is a perfect little time frame to set a small goal and keep it. Vow to hit the gym three times a week, and you’ll be able to get in 24 workouts before Christmas, even if you take a few days off for festivities. You can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Or run, if that's the fitness journey you're most excited about. If you start a couch-to-5k running plan now, you’ll be routinely running 30 minutes at a stretch by the time we get to January.

Yes, the holiday season can be busy and stressful, but remember that working out tends to help our brains manage stress. Mark workouts on your calendar, and keep those appointments with yourself.

Don’t worry about missing out on deals. Any gym or studio that offers a January special probably offers sales year-round anyway. And ultimately, if you get into the habit of actually using the gym, you're getting a lot more value for your money than somebody who joins in January and quickly stops showing up.

#3556. One Of 2026's Best Anime Movies Is Based On The Same Book As A Tom Cruise Sci-Fi Classic

In Doug Liman's 2014 sci-fi action movie "Edge of Tomorrow," Tom Cruise plays William Cage, a cowardly public relations officer drafted to fight in the front line of an alien war. Dying due to exposure to an alien's acidic blood traps Cage in a time loop, and with help from decorated soldier Sergeant Rita Vrataski (Emily Blunt), he has to find a way to break the loop and win the war. The movie did not perform especially well at the box office, grossing $381 million against a $178 million budget, but it earned good reviews and, to this day, fans and the creative team remain hopeful about an eventual "Edge of Tomorrow" sequel.

You might assume the nifty premise of "Edge of Tomorrow" is just an action movie riff on "Groundhog Day," but its real origins are more obscure. The movie adapts a 2004 Japanese light novel, "All You Need Is Kill," written by Hiroshi Sakurazaka with illustrations by Yoshitoshi Abe ("Serial Experiments Lain"). The movie and novel share a basic premise, though the movie moves the setting from Japan to Europe. It also turns the novel's hero, a young Japanese man named Keiji Kiriya, into Cruise's William Cage.

Fitting for a story that's all about its characters caught in a loop, "All You Need Is Kill" has been adapted several times. In 2014, Weekly Young Jump serialized a 17 chapter "All You Need Is Kill" manga written by Ryosuke Takeuchi and drawn by Takeshi Obata, artist of "Death Note." Most recently, Japanese studio Studio 4°C turned the story into a mostly 3D-animated film that opened in theaters this past year. The "All You Need Is Kill" anime does justice to the story while making some of the biggest changes to it yet.

The anime "All You Need Is Kill" retains the title of the novel, unlike "Edge of Tomorrow." ("Edge of Tomorrow" was originally titled "All You Need Is Kill," but was then renamed in 2013 ahead of release. Confusingly, it's also since been labeled as "Live Die Repeat" on home media.)

You might expect that the animated "All You Need Is Kill" is a more faithful adaptation, one that strives to tell the real story after Hollywood distorted it. But that's not quite true. While the animated movie retains the Japanese setting, it flips the story in another way: Rita Vrataski is the protagonist. In the novel and "Edge of Tomorrow," she's a soldier who got caught in a previous loop, escaped it, and walked out a hardened battlefield hero distinguished by her large war axe.

In the animated "All You Need Is Kill," we see her stumbling through loop after loop learning to fight. She's more like the novel's Keiji but with Rita's name, and then Keiji being caught in her same loop is the midpoint twist. The movie's ending also echoes "Edge of Tomorrow." The hero (William/Rita) breaks the loop, defeats the aliens, and arrives back at the beginning of the story (but now free of the loop). They then reunite with their partner (Rita/Keiji) with the hope they'll become close again.

The novel and manga's final twist is that, to escape the loop, one of Rita and Keiji has to die. Rita lets Keiji kill her, and he has to carry her sacrifice through to all his tomorrows. Therein lies the meaning of the title, "All You Need Is Kill."

In "Edge of Tomorrow," the soldiers fight with mechanical exoskeletons with guns directly attached to their forearms, while the alien "Mimics" resemble writhing, glowing masses of black tentacles. The manga has a similar aesthetic; Takeshi Obata draws the soldier's uniforms resembling Spartan armor from "Halo" (a vibe also seen in "Edge of Tomorrow" concept art), while the Mimics are also depicted as pure black orbs with large, toothy mouths.

The aesthetics of "All You Need Is Kill" are much stranger and more alien. Rita's armor more resembles an astronaut or a deep sea diver's suit, complete with a transparent bubble helmet. The limbs of the armor are also lanky and exaggerated, with digitigrade legs. The suit looks like it was designed for wider reach than a human can manage, but it doesn't scream "armored" or "intimidating" like the manga or "Edge of Tomorrow" suits do. The aliens are also even weirder, resembling giant, mobile flowers with bright purple-green color schemes.

In an interview with Animation Magazine, "All You Need Is Kill" director Kenichiro Akimoto explained he wanted to depict something a bit different than the "space marines blasting aliens" look of past iterations:

"I wanted to depict a colorful, vibrant hell. The thinking behind that was that this time loop repeats the cycle of life and death. Rita needs to live repeatedly, beautifully, as she faces this inevitable death. I wanted to send the message that life can be beautiful — that's the reason for the film's hypersaturated color palette."

The palette does indeed clash with past iterations' violence and brutality, resembling a landscape of imagination more than a warzone. But at its heart, "All You Need Is Kill" is a romance, and the movie's look grows out of that.

#3555. The Jewelry at the Center of Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall’s On-Set Romance

In many photographs from the 1950s, Lauren Bacall appears alongside Humphrey Bogart with a small golden object between her lips. Curiously, it is a small gold whistle hanging from a bracelet. Not exactly the kind of accessory one would expect to find in a Hollywood star’s jewelry box. Yet, for Bacall, that particular piece held a very special meaning. Bogart himself gave it to her, inspired by a line the actor delivered in the film where the two met and fell in love.

In 1944, Bacall was just 19 years old when she made her film debut alongside Bogart in To Have and Have Not, directed by Howard Hawks. Bogart, 44 at the time, was already one of Hollywood’s most famous actors. On set, their relationship developed into something more than professional. They fell in love, and in May 1945, got married.

It was here that the origin story of the unusual bracelet began, with a line from Bacall that became one of old Hollywood’s most memorable: “You do know how to whistle, don’t you Steve? You just put your lips together and blow.” The scene, a candid moment of trust between the two characters, was a standout in the film, and it was this line that inspired the idea for the bracelet.

The result was a 14-karat-gold bracelet with a small pendant whistle, also made of gold and fully functional. The piece has a rather minimalist look, with smooth, polished surfaces and no particular decorations, except for a few personal engravings.

On one side of the tag are the words “Betty Bacall,” a reference to the actor’s original name, Betty Joan Perske, and on the other, “The Whistler.” On the whistle itself, the initials “B&B”—for Bogart and Bacall—are engraved, along with the number “21,” the meaning of which is still a mystery.

Bacall wore the bracelet in her daily life, carrying with her that small memento of the film that marked the beginning of her relationship with Bogart. In 1954, during a television interview with journalist Edward R. Murrow, the actor herself revealed the meaning of the whistle, explaining its connection to the famous line from To Have and Have Not.

Decades later, in September 2023, the bracelet made headlines again, when it was auctioned by Julien’s Auctions. The initial estimate ranged from $100,000 to $200,000, and on September 8, it sold for $158,750—a substantial sum for a small gold whistle. Though, considering who it belonged to—and especially who gave it to her—it’s not all that surprising.
