#3554. I Tested ChatGPT's New 'Slides' Tool, and Here's How It Compares to Gemini

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

ChatGPT's capabilities continue to expand apace, and the latest feature is a fully capable slideshow creator. Announced a few weeks ago, ChatGPT Slides lets you create PowerPoint-style decks from inside your conversations, and it's now appearing for those on the Pro tier and above (meaning right now, you need to spend at least $100 a month to get it).

If you're on the free ChatGPT plan or the $20-a-month Plus tier, you can still get ChatGPT to generate downloadable PowerPoint files from the content of your conversations. However, they'll be more basic than those made in the full version of ChatGPT Slides, and there are no collaboration or native edit options.

ChatGPT Slides is part of OpenAI's push to give users a complete office suite inside the ChatGPT apps. Pages (the word processor) is already available for Pro tiers and above, while a spreadsheet app is on the way—the idea being that you will soon be able to get all your work done without any help from Google or Microsoft.

While Chatgpt Slides is only available on pricey plans right now, it's likely to come to lower subscription tiers in the future. But for now, how does the tool compare to what's available in the free and Plus tiers, not to mention what you can do with Gemini inside Google Slides? I've taken a detailed look.

When it comes to testing out AI tools, it helps to focus on something you're already knowledgeable about so you can spot any mistakes. To test this, I decided to see what ChatGPT could hoover up from the web about the new iPhone Duo. If you're on the free or Plus plans, you can start a conversation, then ask for a slideshow or PowerPoint about it.

Plus accounts also have access to a specific Presentations add-on, available via the + (plus) menu in the prompt box, though I get the impression this feature is in a state of flux since ChatGPT Slides arrived. In any case, you can begin asking about the iPhone Duo specs and early online reactions, and then say "build me a slideshow on the key features and reviews so far".

What I got back on the $20 Plus account was a fairly competent slideshow on Apple's foldable, with accurate information as far as I could see, and a simple series of layouts. It looked like something you might whip up from a template if you were in a rush and didn't have time to properly align all the bullet points or be very selective about which details you included and which you left out. One neat touch is that ChatGPT was able to drop in an official photo of the iPhone Duo at the start of the slideshow, but I had to specifically ask for one.

You can go back and make specific edits to the slideshow, but you have to describe them in the general prompt box—you can't select individual slide elements and make more precise changes. Still, if all you want to do is occasionally convert your ChatGPT conversations into a rough and ready slideshow, there's no real need to upgrade from the free or Plus accounts for now.

Switching to a Pro account, I gave a similar task to ChatGPT Slides hoping for something more comprehensive. To begin with, Slides gets its own dedicated area in the app, so you can start up a blank presentation from scratch—there are some basic image and text features, but the idea is to use prompts to build your slide deck. It's like a really basic Google Slides, with a prompt box.

Creating a slideshow this way feels rather tedious: Typing out what you want to say and then waiting for ChatGPT to do it isn't as intuitive as just throwing in some graphics and text yourself, as you might do in PowerPoint. It also seems to be a bit buggy, at least during the time I spent testing it, with some requests not properly completing.

Starting a standard conversation with ChatGPT and then turning all the information into a deck is much more useful from my perspective. My iPhone Duo slideshow was longer, laid out better, and more informative than the one I created on the Plus plan—there were even charts of battery life and official photos this time.

However, whether I used the free, Plus, or Pro tools, my presentations didn't come across as particularly well thought through. They don't really flow smoothly, either across individual slides or the slideshow as a whole—it feels very much like an algorithm, rather than a person, has decided what information to include and where on the slides to stick it.

Whether you create presentations in chats or through the ChatGPT Slides space, you're able to click on individual elements and do some basic manual resizing and repositioning. You can also request edits via prompts: "Drop in an image of a cat", "make this pop more", "center all of this information", or whatever it is.

ChatGPT Slides does offer collaborative tools, which I wasn't able to test, and I can see that being useful for teams heavily invested in ChatGPT's ecosystem. I can also imagine ChatGPT Slides coming in handy when you've got a lot of information you need to quickly dump into a slideshow that looks vaguely presentable.

In general though, I think I'd much rather stick to the traditional way of making slideshows for now. These old methods are more precise and more manageable, and give you full control over what's shown and where—even if they do take a bit longer. What's more, modern-day presentation tools come with so many templates and other layout aids that it's not difficult to put together something that's easy on the eyes while including all of the information you think is most critical.

Google is, of course, also all the way in on AI (and then some), and if you pay for Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) or above, you can have Gemini pop up right inside Google Slides to give you some assistance with your presentation-making. To compare the tools, I gave it the same task as I did ChatGPT, asking for a slide deck on the new iPhone Duo.

Gemini actually asked some questions along the way: about wht visual style to use, the audience to aim the slideshow at, and the details to highlight. Though it's always possible to put this sort of information manually into a prompt, this would be a helpful additional to ChatGPT Slides.

What Gemini and Google Slides produced was impressive in terms of the layout and overall vibe of the presentation: It felt much more like a human being had put together the slide deck compared to what ChatGPT had produced, in terms of the information chosen, the way the slides were laid out, and the color picks.

However, Google's result had its faults too: The presentation got the facts on the maximum brightness of the iPhone Duo screen wrong, and produced an "iPhone Duo" graphic that looked like two iPhones from around 2021 stuck together. ChatGPT Slides at least managed to pull official imagery from the Apple website.

You can't attach individual edit prompts to specific parts of your presentation in Google Slides as you can in ChatGPT Slides—you have to mention them in the general prompt box. That said, Google Slides is obviously a much more mature and established slideshow tool compared to the OpenAI equivalent, in terms of its features and layout options (it has been around for a decade, after all).

Given that extra software structure and the lower cost of entry, Gemini and Google Slides is the better option for AI-assisted slideshow making at the moment—though I wouldn't bet against OpenAI catching up. For now, ChatGPT Slides is something that's good to have available if you're already paying a lot for ChatGPT every month, but not a feature that makes it worth your while to swap your AI allegiance.

60 Minutes looked a lot different when it returned to the 2026 TV schedule for its 59th season back in September. That was in great part due to a creative overhaul that took place over the summer and saw several key employees fired from their positions. Since then, a few of those former staffers have spoken out about their oustings and the state of the news magazine under the leadership of CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss. Now, Cecilia Vega is sharing her take and revealing one detail that still bothers her.

Since its season premiere, 60 Minutes has been at the center of various headlines, with a number of those pertaining to low ratings compared to past seasons of the show. On top of that, there have been ongoing claims of editorial interference on Weiss’ part. Vega made such claims in July and alleged that she was pressured to exude what she considered to be bias into her stories. As for her feelings on the show now, Vega said during a talk in Washington D.C. (via The Daily Beast) that she wasn’t pleased:

It pains me. It hurts to watch, from afar. It hurts to talk to my colleagues who are still there. It hurts to see the ratings slump that is happening right now.

Regarding the ratings, it was recently reported that the October 25th broadcast of 60 drew 5.6 million viewers. That marked a notable decrease for the show, which reportedly averaged 9.1 million viewers during Season 58. Weiss recently addressed the concerns during a tech panel and asserted that the show was still doing “tremendously well.” The Free Press founder, who’s denied editorial bias, also said she’d been aiming to block out the backlash against CBS News and her changes on the previously mentioned news program.

The staff firings took place on May 28, 2026, which apparently became known as “Black Thursday” internally. On that day, Vega was fired alongside others like fellow correspondent Sharyn Alfonsi, former 60 Minutes executive producer Tanya Simon and executive editor Draggan Mihailovich. Shortly after, veteran correspondent Scott Pelley was fired as well after accusing Weiss of “murdering” the show. As for Vega, one thing still gives her pause about her exit from the series and the media company as a whole:

I still don’t know why I was fired. I was not given a reason. I was fired without cause. I just find it exceptionally disturbing.

Pelley recalled the staff meeting that was held shortly after his 60 Minutes colleagues and others were fired. The veteran newsman recalled everyone expecting Weiss to be at the meeting but were surprised to find that only series EP Nick Bilton was present. According to Pelley, employees were even more unhappy after Bilton started reading a statement from his phone without looking up at anyone. Months later, Vega seems to have a lot of respect for Pelley and others who have “held the line” or those who are still trying to at CBS:

I held the line, and Scott held the line, and Sharyn held the line, and I think people are still holding the line over there. But what they are having to go through, or what we had to go through, should never happen in a newsroom.

Questions remain in regard to what lies ahead for 60 Minutes and CBS News as a whole under Bari Weiss’ leadership. Additionally, there are more variables to consider following the merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, which has birthed Skydance. Cecilia Vega, for her part, says she’s unaware of the “endgame” and thinks “it’s a real mystery.”

#3552. Idris Elba Almost Played A Different DC Comics Villain In James Gunn's The Suicide Squad

If you're a DC Comics fan, then "The Suicide Squad" casting Idris Elba as Bloodsport and using the character as the leader of the titular team was eyebrow-raising. Bloodsport had no previous association with the Suicide Squad, instead being a minor Superman villain distinguished by using Kryptonite bullets (which gets a brief nod in "The Suicide Squad" as part of Bloodsport's rap sheet).

It makes a lot more sense when you know the behind-the-scenes context. Will Smith, who played Deadshot in 2016's "Suicide Squad," wasn't available to return. So, Elba/Bloodsport took Deadshot's role in the movie. Initial reporting in 2019 even suggested Deadshot had been recast with Elba in "The Suicide Squad." But according to Elba himself, neither he nor director James Gunn wanted to replace Smith or his take on Deadshot. But Bloodsport still functions as essentially a renamed Deadshot. He even has a young daughter, Tyla (Storm Reid), who was clearly meant to be Deadshot's daughter, Zoe Lawton, at some point.

"The Suicide Squad" was made as part of the now-dead DC Extended Universe. With Gunn having since taken over as the co-head of DC Studios and rebooted the franchise via the DC Universe, the movie sits in a limbo of canon. Addressing the issue head-on, DC has now released a one-shot podcast — "The Suicide Squad: Is It Canon?" — featuring Gunn plus actors Jennifer Holland and Steve Agee discussing that exact question.

On said podcast, Gunn discussed how he got from Deadshot to Bloodsport. The change was at Elba's request, with Gunn saying Elba may have seen some "negative reaction" to him replacing Smith. Before settling on Bloodsport, though, Gunn considered having Elba play DC's most infamous mercenary character — Slade Wilson/Deathstroke — as the Squad's leader. Indeed, some "The Suicide Squad" concept art shows Deathstroke leading the team.

According to James Gunn, he decided against using Deathstroke in "The Suicide Squad" at the request of his actor friend Joe Manganiello, who had been previously cast as Deathstroke in the DCEU. Manganiello appears briefly as Slade in a post-credits scene for "Justice League," which was meant to set up Deathstroke as the main villain of Ben Affleck's never-made "Batman" movie. Casting Idris Elba as Slade would've certainly precluded Manganiello from playing Deathstroke again. So, as a favor to a buddy, Gunn dropped the idea of using Slade. Thus, with Deadshot and Deathstroke off the table, he eventually settled on using Bloodsport.

"I like Bloodsport so much. I'd like to see the character return," Gunn said on the podcast. "I also like working with Idris. Idris is a good guy, so I would like to see him return as Bloodsport or even somebody else."

That's definitely not a door closing, but it also sounds like DC Studios doesn't have any active plans to reuse Elba's Bloodsport right now. But one character who DC Studios is focusing on? Deathstroke! In 2024, it was reported that the studio was developing a team-up movie featuring Deathstroke and the infamous Batman villain Bane. As of October 2026, it's been reported that the project (titled "Savage Hunters") is a priority for DC Studios.

(Not for nothing, DC Studios is reportedly working on a "Teen Titans" movie as well. If that goes forward, maybe we can finally get Deathstroke in a film based on the comic where his character originated.)

Should we expect Manganiello to appear as Deathstroke opposite Bane? Not likely. Speaking with ComicBook.com in 2024, Manganiello said that Gunn advised him to "let it go," with "it" being the plans Manganiello had for Deathstroke.

#3551. 'Avatar: Seven Havens' Season 2 Could Return to 'The Last Airbender’s Most Iconic Location

Ba Sing Se once survived a century-long war by pretending the war didn’t exist at all, only to get taken over by the Fire Nation during Avatar: The Last Airbender. Despite ongoing political turmoil extending through The Legend of Korra’s era, the Earth Kingdom’s former capital persisted — and one version of it even survived the Cataclysm. Avatar: Seven Havens revealed the existence of a Haven called New Ba Sing Se during season 1, offering a glimpse of a society still clinging to old traditions while its people go hungry. And based on one specific detail from the season finale, there’s a very good reason to suspect we'll get to see the city of New Ba Sing Se firsthand in season 2.

Spoilers follow for Avatar: Seven Havens season 1.

Avatar: Seven Havens' season 1 finale sends Avatar Pavi (Saheli Khan) on a quest to the Floating Isles to solve that Haven's problems and unlock her second chakra. The show’s creators have confirmed that future seasons will visit more than one Haven each. In an interview with IGN, franchise co-creator Michael Dante DiMartino revealed that while book 1 was set entirely in the fortified city of Ellora, the overarching Seven Havens story is mapped out across four seasons, which means speeding up the journey moving forward.

“We had to split it up a little differently, but we'll get through all the Seven Havens by the end of this series for sure,” DiMartino said. “That’s the full story.”

That’s six more chakras across only three seasons with an average of two per season, so it’s increasingly likely that Pavi and Jae (Major Curda) will visit at least two Havens next season.

Based on what we know about chakras, they have to be opened in order. According to the sequence laid out in Pavi’s cosmic vision, her next destination after the Floating Isles should be the yellow Haven toward the northeastern corner of the world map shown in the series’ opening sequence. We know that the Cataclysm reshaped the world with ongoing storms, but even before New Ba Sing Se was named outright, signs pointed toward the former Earth Kingdom capital as the yellow Haven on that map.

New Ba Sing Se’s representatives arrive at Ellora’s summit on sky bison decorated with an emblem resembling the Earth Kingdom’s square-holed national emblem. An Akashan visitor mockingly calls them “historians” who have ventured out of their “crumbling haven.” Their clothing is also virtually indistinguishable from what the people of Ba Sing Se wore during Aang’s time. When the Haven is properly introduced during episode 8's welcome parade, Nisha (Aishu Devan) remarks from afar that they live as though it’s still ancient times. It’s abundantly clear that New Ba Sing Se clings to the oldest traditions this world knows.

A politician named Kuzon (Eric Bauza) serves as New Ba Sing Se’s envoy at the summit, and his behavior makes it seem like his Haven is protective of its dignity. When Chancellor Kayoko (Jennifer Sun Bell) asks the assembled Havens for benders in exchange for food, Kuzon admits that their own circumstances are desperate.

“New Ba Sing Se has experienced the worst famine in our long history,” he says, offering to trade benders for some of Ellora’s harvest.

Bender birth rates are declining worldwide, presumably because the Anomaly has stagnated the flow of spiritual energy. Pavi’s quest to unblock her own chakras seems intrinsically connected to restoring the flow of spiritual energy in this broken world.

Assuming that New Ba Sing Se was founded in the former location of Ba Sing Se (how could it not be?), then it’s likely associated with the yellow chakra. That’s the third color in the sequence, following Ellora’s red and the Floating Isles’ orange. In The Last Airbender’s season 2 episode called “The Guru,” Guru Pathik explains that this is the fire chakra that deals with willpower and is blocked by shame.

Aang learned some of his most valuable lessons in this Book 2 episode

That sounds like fertile ground for a society struggling to preserve its former greatness while failing to feed its people. Pride isn’t the same thing as shame, but pride can be a way for people to hide their shame. It certainly takes a kind of willpower to cling to old traditions that are probably less suited to survival than embracing more advanced technology used in Havens like Akasha.

The original Ba Sing Se maintained a carefully controlled illusion of security while the Hundred Year War raged beyond its walls. Its successor could be clinging to a different delusion: that neglecting the old ways is what caused the Cataclysm, and preserving them is somehow the antidote to the apocalypse.

The show's creators also told IGN that the relationship between the Havens and chakras is central to the series’ overarching design. DiMartino explained that “The Guru” moved through those ideas quickly, whereas Seven Havens gives the writers room to explore them across an entire story. Co-executive producer Sehaj Sethi described aligning that structure with the characters’ emotional development as one of the production’s greatest challenges.

In other words, the chakra colors offer clues about both Pavi’s itinerary and what she’ll need to confront when she gets there.

Before any potential return to Ba Sing Se, Pavi has to reach the Floating Isles. DiMartino described it as a “more chill place compared to Ellora” with a distinct culture and customs. To be fair, most places would feel chill compared to Chancellor Kayoko’s increasingly authoritarian rule. Guru Pathik calls the second chakra the water chakra (fitting for an archipelago), saying that it deals with pleasure and is blocked by guilt.

What might that look like across an entire society? One possibility is a hedonistic culture devoted to food, revelry, and entertainment where people distract themselves from guilt they refuse to confront. Another is a comparatively comfortable Haven whose inhabitants know people elsewhere are starving.

That's just a theory, but it does draw an interesting contrast with New Ba Sing Se’s famine, which in turn could give season 2 a compelling conflict: one Haven struggling to enjoy what it has and another ashamed of what it can no longer provide.

An Anomaly that amplifies guilt would also offer a disturbing variation on Ellora’s fear-based Affliction. Instead of seeing threats everywhere, its victims might become overwhelmed by memories of everyone they’ve hurt. Whether that would involve orange eyes or another diamond-shaped energy spirit is anyone’s guess. The same could be said of New Ba Sing Se’s third chakra. Season 2 will likely see Pavi confront and overcome the guilt and shame she feels about abandoning Nisha.

In a way, that resonates with the Avatar’s overarching mission of abandoning worldly attachments at the end of their journey. Is it okay for Pavi to find joy and satisfaction in her quest? Does she have the willpower to overcome the shame associated with that? It is therefore fitting that the next chakra (possibly Feather Mountain?) will see her explore love and grief before truth and lies (maybe Akasha?) before she reaches a part of the world we know virtually nothing about. As with Aang, the fate of everything rests in a child’s ability to resolve their trauma.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3550. How Greg Brockman’s Wife Anna Became a Trump and MAGA Mega-Donor

It was weeks before the election and spirits were low in MAGA’s top ranks. The president’s approval ratings had plunged to historic depths. Polling suggested his endorsement had become an albatross for many of his preferred candidates. And so Donald Trump had retreated to the gilded comfort of Mar-a-Lago to attend to “matters of national importance,” including, on October 17, a candlelit dinner with some of his most loyal supporters.

At the head of the table were just four seats: Google cofounder Sergey Brin, President Trump himself, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and his wife, Anna Brockman.

Anna Brockman, Greg Brockman, President Donald Trump, and Sergey Brin during a MAGA Inc. event at Mar-a-Lago. October 16, 2026.

The Brockmans, worth nearly $30 billion, have used their wealth to become the 16th-biggest political mega-donors this midterms cycle: Last year, the couple donated a combined $25 million to MAGA Inc. and $25 million to the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. Greg has said that he and his wife are “single-issue donors,” their lone cause being AI, the technology he’s helped build. “It’s not popular,” he recently acknowledged, so “we really want to support politicians who really lean into [it].” And it has been “we” at each of these turns—the Brockmans working in tandem toward a shared vision of the future.

Yet despite Anna Brockman’s frequent presence amid the backdrop of this pivotal scene in history, next to nothing has previously been reported about her. When The Wall Street Journal profiled Greg Brockman in May, they wrote of his elusive wife, “She is intensely private: almost no information, including her maiden name, is available online.”

Anna Chang has an unlikely past—one that raises some new questions. How did a onetime registered Democrat and ambitious tech worker who “loves everything that positively changes the world” become the retired wife of one of the wealthiest men on earth, Donald Trump’s frequent guest, and one of the single-largest donors seeking to hasten a future where artificial intelligence is developed with minimal regulatory oversight?

Sources close to the Brockmans and to OpenAI suggested that Anna is no bystander, and is worthy of scrutiny as a significant player herself. “She’s not a silent sidekick to Greg,” says one AI industry insider. “She is a force.”

When Greg and Anna met at a Silicon Valley dinner party in 2018, Greg said they “instantly connected.” She was the daughter of Korean immigrants, and he had a long-standing reverence for Korean culture: He has a black belt in tae kwon do, and even attended Korean summer camp as a teenager, picking up some of the language. They had also both worked at the payments-software start-up Stripe in the 2010s, though their tenures never overlapped. (Both Greg and Anna Brockman declined Vanity Fair’s request for comment for this story.)

In 2015, Greg had left his position as Stripe’s chief technology officer to cofound OpenAI with 10 fellow visionaries out of his San Francisco living room. A gifted and relentless coder, he muscled his way through seemingly impossible projects in the hopes of eventually achieving artificial general intelligence, or AGI (the point when the technology can match or exceed human-level capabilities at every possible task). He sometimes clocked 90-hour workweeks. Greg’s colleagues from over the years describe him as fiercely competitive, not just with work projects but also with hobbies like running and weight lifting.

Anna was a quirky and exuberant animal lover from Texas—one source estimates she and her husband live with over 20 animals—who had worked for AmeriCorps mentoring working-class students after graduating from Wesleyan University, well known as an ultraliberal school. (In a total coincidence, I discovered midway through reporting that Anna and I had overlapped there during our college years.) When she became one of the first 100 or so employees at Dropbox, her idealism persisted. In an introduction to her new colleagues, she told them she spent her free time “taking on adventures to help save the world.”

While a source close to Anna said she doesn’t drink alcohol, sources who’ve spent time with her said she has sometimes drawn attention for her juvenile humor and unconventional manner. She “curses like a drunken sailor,” said one. Another described her as “fratty.”

Early in the Brockmans’ relationship, Anna experienced a series of mysterious health mishaps. The couple spent years visiting doctor after doctor, and eventually discovered she had Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS). Greg has also said that she has Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). She believed that with the right AI tools, her arduous investigation might have been made much simpler. “Her whole passion for AI is driven by this medical journey,” said her friend and former colleague Sujay Jaswa.

In her late 30s, Anna was also diagnosed with autism. “Her autism can come at a cost, one of which is requiring a lot of alone time (the fur kids and myself excluded) and downtime to rest and recover,” her husband wrote, referring to their many pets. “A beautiful trait of her autism is her deep connection to animals and attention to understanding their needs,” Greg posted on X.

He, too, required patience from his partner while he focused on his interior life. During their first holiday season together, he decided to teach himself machine learning, scratching out equations in a notebook. “She was there with me no matter how many planned activities it meant skipping,” he wrote on his blog. He described her as “someone who made me feel it was ok if I failed.” Greg said on the Tetragrammaton With Rick Rubin podcast that they even put off having children so that he could focus all his energy on AI.

Anna’s early adoption of AI tools helped her practically float up the corporate ladder, but it also opened the door to loftier visions. In a 2018 blog post, she wrote, “I believe in the power of AI to allow us to become more human, today and in the future, by alleviating monotony and opening the space for creativity and intuition.”

Meanwhile, Greg sounded like he was experiencing vertigo from the progress they were making at OpenAI. His journals from this period, portions of which were later made public as part of discovery for the Musk v. Altman trial, ricochet between self-doubt and megalomania. “No person should have control over what we’re creating,” he wrote in August 2017. Then three months later, he appeared to copy and paste a chat with an unknown correspondent into the journal document. “It is better for us to become increasingly kings of this industry,” one of them wrote. “Being the kings of AI is not so bad.”

In Anna, he found the ultimate support system. According to the WSJ, he took the other side of a bet with his then OpenAI colleague (and later Anthropic cofounder) Daniela Amodei, who wagered $100 that Anna was not the one. He won. As Greg put it, they “have been inseparable ever since.”

At the Musk v. Altman trial, Anna was by her husband’s side almost every day. Some observers noted that she held his hand right up to the last second as she walked him to the witness stand. Sources who know the couple described Anna, 38, as “very devoted” and Greg, 38, as “the ultimate wife guy.”

When Anna and Greg got married in 2019, they held a civil ceremony in OpenAI’s office officiated by fellow OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever. The ring bearer was a robotic hand.

As wife to the “wife guy” at the helm of one of the most powerful companies on earth, Anna has enjoyed a front row seat to scenes of such intrigue that they have inspired multiple books, and the highly anticipated upcoming film Artificial. (Cooper Hoffman, the actor who plays Brockman in the film Artificial, recalls director Luca Guadagnino’s guidance on how to approach the role: “Greg is all-American,” Guadagnino told him. “He’s like a cheeseburger.”)

The Brockmans attended the Met Gala in 2025.

While it isn’t uncommon for spouses and partners to turn up in the offices of start-ups, sources who’ve spent time with the Brockmans noted that by the late 2010s Anna was unusually engaged in his work life, having left her own job at the venture capital firm Basis Set Ventures. While, per The Information, Anna has never been formally employed at OpenAI, over the years she has appeared in live product demos; accompanied executives on trips, like one to South Korea to meet with local start-ups; and even been spotted at high-level meetings at the OpenAI office.

When OpenAI’s top executives were appointed drivers and private security, Anna would sometimes be spotted in the car with Greg, taking him to work, according to former colleagues.

As the money piled up, the relationships between the company’s early team—including Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, Ilya Sutskever, Jakub Pachocki, Mira Murati, and Dario and Daniela Amodei—began to fray. While the imaginations of many of their Bay Area peers ran wild with sci-fi visions of uploaded consciousness and unfathomable abundance, and AI doomsayers warned of extinction events, the Brockmans’ hopes for an AI future felt relatively pedestrian.

Greg was firmly in the pro-commercialization camp, according to OpenAI researchers who’ve worked with him, believing that above all, AI can empower individuals to transform their own lives. Anna, meanwhile, is driven by the “idea that AI for all is gonna take all these major social problems, like the extreme cost of health care and education [and] extreme inequality in access…and it’s gonna democratize all of it,” according to Jaswa.

And to do that, the Brockmans understood that AI leaders needed to win over the policymakers that, in their view, could stand in the way of AGI.

Following the release of ChatGPT in 2022, OpenAI’s founding team found themselves on the other side of overnight fame—at least in the insular tech bubble of the Bay Area. While some of the more socially awkward researchers chafed at the attention, Greg—who’d been promoted to president of the company—and Anna have seemed to bask in it.

The Brockmans have dined with Sylvester Stallone at the Kennedy Center, attended black-tie events at the White House, and even walked the blue carpet at the Met Gala, where Anna wore a black-and-white ruffled gown by Korean designer Ashlynn Park.

The power she’d been quietly amassing by Greg’s side played out in a more significant and dramatic way in November 2023, when the board of OpenAI removed Sam Altman from his position as CEO over concerns that he was untrustworthy. Sutskever, who was on the board, also compiled a memo detailing allegations against Greg, and Greg was removed from his position as chairman of the board (but allowed to stay on as president). When the board called Greg to inform him of their decision, the first thing he did was talk to his wife. He told her, “‘We have to leave.’ And she said, ‘Yes, we do,’” he said on the Tetragrammaton With Rick Rubin podcast. He warned her they would have to be prepared for his equity to disappear if he quit. “‘Still want to do it?’ And she said yes.”

But when the board began to reconsider its decision, Sutskever became the deciding vote. In an oft-repeated piece of OpenAI lore, Anna allegedly begged Sutskever in a tearful encounter to reconsider. (Sources familiar with the events have suggested that the impact of this encounter has been overstated.) According to the WSJ, when Sutskever decided to reverse his decision, Anna left him a cactus as a gift.

After a long negotiation over his place at the company, Sutskever left to start his own venture, Safe Superintelligence. “There were some deep and bitter things” that went down during this period, according to one high-level employee at the time.

After this dramatic inflection point, which has come to be known as the blip, Greg took a three-month leave of absence. This period allowed him to dedicate himself to a project he was passionate about: developing a biological foundation model for genome modeling and design at the Arc Institute—“a domain that’s very personally meaningful to both me and and to my wife,” he has said.

Meanwhile, the company had replaced nearly all the board members who’d risen up against Altman with what one former senior OpenAI employee called a “more loyal and ‘normie’” board who were supportive of the company’s commercial push.

The center of gravity began to shift in Greg’s direction, solidifying his place as Altman’s second in command, soon to be tasked with an even more fraught assignment: building political goodwill. What wouldn’t the billionaire couple do to help the technology that they consider vital to humanity’s future?

“He thinks big, but he is also very practical, kind of a realist,” Peter Welinder, OpenAI’s vice president and general manager, says of Greg. Others felt that his techno-optimism, and subsequent push into Washington to defend those ideals, is “naivete,” says the former high-level employee. “I don’t think he’s very carefully thinking through the political and power implications.”

When Donald Trump was reelected in late 2024, OpenAI found itself facing down a new threat. Elon Musk, an original cofounder of the company who left in 2018, had grown increasingly antagonistic toward his onetime colleagues while also growing close to the incoming administration. According to Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles, OpenAI, and Altman in particular, feared political retribution from Musk, who now had his own competitor company in xAI, if he was allowed to take up all the oxygen in Washington. At the same time, OpenAI’s need for energy and compute had grown so insatiable that the company had no choice but to seek the government’s help. In an administration run on quid pro quo, OpenAI would have to make nice.

Brockman found himself uniquely well-positioned to lead the infrastructure-scaling bonanza, thanks to a preexisting relationship with Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, who hailed from his home state of North Dakota. Greg was also “the most credible” face of the political donations, said one former OpenAI employee.

And so Greg and Anna Brockman became White House mainstays. They have attended state dinners for foreign leaders like Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman and Xi Jinping, and joined top tech executives at a White House event about the future of AI. Brockman, rather than Altman, flanked Trump during the signing of the White House Accord on Super Intelligence in September.

When the political pendulum began to swing back this summer, it began to appear as though whoever had made the call on those political donations might have made a severe miscalculation. Following a steady drumbeat of negative headlines about Leading the Future’s work and significant internal dissent among OpenAI employees, the Brockmans rescinded their second planned $25 million donation to the PAC. Greg wrote in a Slack message, obtained by The New York Times, that Leading the Future had become a “distraction” from OpenAI’s work.

When I reached out to OpenAI to discuss the Brockmans’ political giving, it directed me back to the Brockmans’ team. In an interview this October with Vanity Fair’s global editorial director Mark Guiducci, Altman said, “I did not ask him to donate or stop donating. He can make his own personal decisions.” It seems the Brockmans’ donations are a hot potato no one is eager to catch.

Regardless, their $25 million checks have helped provide the funds to enable a torrent of preelection ads, including warnings like, “This is the final battle” to “liberate America from these villains, once and for all.”

Some observers of the company have come to believe that the plan was “to have Greg be the scapegoat if/when the Democrats come back into power, but to allow OpenAI to privately (with the White House) claim credit for the MAGA PAC donations with the Trump administration while privately (with employees) distance itself from them,” according to the former senior employee. (OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.)

Meanwhile, Greg has returned more of his focus to the product realm, and he and his wife have found a less controversial way to spend their millions. When the couple found out that the Big Bear Valley habitat of two publicly beloved eagles, Jackie and Shadow, was under threat, they donated over $5.5 million to preserve the land this summer. “[Jackie and Shadow] inspire perseverance and a sense of connectedness to something greater,” Anna said of their donation.

“It was clear in talking to her that she loved her husband very much and that she loved the eagles,” says Jenny Voisard, the communications and PR leader for Friends of Big Bear Valley, of her experience working with Anna on the donation. They never talked about politics.

#3549. This New Garmin Feature Is Draining Battery Life, but There's a Quick Fix

Garmin users are taking to the company's support forums with a common grievance: The newly introduced "OK Garmin" hands-free voice feature appears to be eating through battery life. The feature arrived through Garmin’s September software updates, bringing hands-free voice activation to the Fenix 8, Forerunner 570 and 970, Venu 4, and several other models. Here's how to make sure Garmin's new updates aren't slashing your watch's battery life.

Last month's updates for select watches also brought all-day fall detection, a set of new Quick Workouts and Garmin Run Coach plans, as well as that "OK Garmin" hands-free voice command feature. It's exactly what it sounds like: Instead of pressing a button, users can simply say “OK Garmin” to activate voice commands. However, it looks like "OK Garmin" in particular is what causes some watch's projected runtimes to drastically drop, allegedly by roughly 35% to 50% in some cases.

Garmin does acknowledge that enabling these settings shortens battery life, though it doesn't say by how much. The tradeoff makes sense, since the watch has to listen constantly for its wake phrase. Even so, giving up several days of runtime is a steep price for a feature that many people may seldom use. Luckily, the fix is simple: Turning off "OK Garmin" should restore your battery life estimates right away.

If your watch has been draining faster since the update, go to Settings > System > Voice and disable "OK Garmin." If needed, you can also switch off the Phone Assistant wake word from the same area. The good news is that turning this feature off won't even take voice commands away—you can still trigger them manually using the watch's physical controls.

Keep in mind that these numbers are battery estimates rather than independently tested, real-world runtimes. Some of the battery complaints that surfaced after the update may also stem from unrelated issues. Still, trading away as much as half your battery life just to avoid pressing a button is a difficult bargain to defend.

#3548. An Unlikely Frasier Episode Earned Death Threats For Daphne Actor Jane Leeves

The "Frasier" revival probably should have been a one-off special, but  we'll always have 11 seasons of classic comfort sitcom hilarity regardless. "Frasier" ran from 1993 to 2004, maintaining a remarkable consistency over the course of 264 episodes. Kelsey Grammer's lovably snooty Dr. Frasier Crane and his family, friends, and co-workers will remain beloved by a generation raised on the NBC sitcom — unless, that is, you're oddly offended by cruelty against rubber eels. Yes, as Daphne Moon actor Jane Leeves reveals in her book "Daphne & Me: My Life on Frasier (And a Bit More)," her character whacking a rubber eel against a countertop earned her death threats from enraged viewers.

"The Innkeepers" is a fondly remembered episode from "Frasier" Season 2 in which the titular psychiatrist and his brother Niles Crane (David Hyde Pierce) decide to take over a failing restaurant and restore it to glory. Of course, nothing goes to plan, and the boys end up enduring an opening night from hell wherein their family and friends are all recruited to help keep the restaurant running as things fall apart in dramatic fashion.

"Frasier" had already ventured into farce with Season 2's "The Matchmaker." But "The Innkeepers" stands as a farcical triumph — despite, as Leeves points out in her book, some viewers believing it strayed too far from the show's otherwise sophisticated humor. But for other fans of the show, it wasn't the shift of comedic styles that was at issue. Instead, it seems Daphne's treatment of an eel in the kitchen of Les Frères Heureux (The Happy Brothers, as Niles and Frasier christen their culinary venture) was a crime worthy of death.

"The Innkeepers" single-handedly makes Season 2 one of the best seasons of "Frasier." In the episode, as a harried evening in Les Frères Heureux becomes even more fraught, Niles Crane — conscripted to chef duty alongside Daphne Moon — tries to bludgeon a tank of eels so as to not have to handle one of the live creatures. Meanwhile, Daphne's patience wears out. "Oh, for heaven's sakes," she exclaims before marching over to the tank, yanking out an eel, and slamming its head on the countertop. She then hands the lifeless fish to a stunned Niles in one of the episode's many moments of broad slapstick humor.

Turns out, it wasn't just Niles who was stunned. In "Daphne and Me," Jane Leeves reveals that she received threatening letters wishing her a torturous death for this transgression. "What I could never have anticipated were the death threats," she writes. "Yep, you heard me. I got death threats for my mistreatment of the clearly rubber eel. As explained in the scene-opening title card, 'No eels were harmed during the making of this episode.'"

Granted, Daphne gave the thing a good whack, and whoever was in charge of providing the rubber eel certainly delivered a fake fish with some convincing heft to it. But as Leeves goes on to point out, her killing the pretend fish was hardly the most egregious example of small screen violence. "At the time, shows like 'NYPD Blue' and many crime procedurals of the present day got away with, or even overtly endorsed, so much unconscionable carnage and brutality," she writes. "I wonder if they ever got letters?" Just in case you doubt the maliciousness of these missives, Leeves goes on to provide an example.

It might sound unbelievable that Jane Leeves received letters wishing her a painful death simply for clocking a rubber eel with a wooden counter. But in her book, the actor actually provides the text of one such letter. "Miss Leeves," it begins. "Every time I see the 'Frasier' episode where you smash the eel's head for a laugh I wish you'd get an agonizing terminal disease. It doesn't matter if the eel is real or fake. It ain't funny. I pray that you get smashed on the head, too." Bearing in mind this was long before the internet age, which means somebody had to sit down, write the letter, find the correct address, then mail it out. Maybe we were doomed before the internet subsumed our lives after all.

Interestingly enough, "The Innkeepers" was a moderately controversial episode of "Frasier" when it first aired. The show itself had debuted to stellar reviews and outstanding ratings. David Hyde Pierce might have felt the "Frasier" pilot was "terrible" at first, but the series premiere earned Emmy wins for Kelsey Grammer, writers David Angell, Peter Casey, and David Lee, and director James Burrows.

"The Innkeepers," however, prompted what Leeves called "mixed reactions." As the actor writes, "Some thought it strayed from the refined, sophisticated humor that was 'Frasier.' I disagree wholeheartedly. In my mind, 'Frasier' was one of the only shows capable of pulling off an ambitious, expertly-written slapstick comedy with such flair and sophistication, adding another tantalizing flavor to the show." Of course, now "The Innkeepers" is recognized for everything Leeves highlights — though whoever wrote her that letter probably never came around to it.

Season 30 of NBC’s long-running singing competition The Voice, currently airing on the 2026 TV schedule, is heating up with the first ever Cut Week. Due to audience demand, the Live Shows are back with six weeks of live competition, but before the singers could get to that next step, coaches Kelly Clarkson, Queen Latifah, Adam Levine and Riley Green had to make the biggest elimination in one week ever in the history of the show.

To get into the specifics, Cut Week saw each coach send two artists straight through to the Live Shows while the remaining five had to sing their hearts out as they battled for the last remaining spot. That’s three singers for each coach going through to the next round, with one additional pick made by America to round out the Top 13. While some coaches agonized over who to fill their final slot with, The Voice newbie Riley Green had the easiest selection of the night.

This latest episode breezed by, as five singers for each team, 20 in total, gave everything they had to their performances in the attempt to win their individual coach over. The thing that surprised me the most about this new twist that was replacing the Knockouts, also known as Adam Levine’s least favorite part of the competition, was that each artist sang on a level where any of them were deserving of being sent through to the Live Shows. I’ve got to say, Cut Week was painful, with more than half of each team getting dropped all at once and having to say goodbye to truly talented competitors.

For me, the most shocking decision was the Maroon 5 frontman choosing to let Brandon Diaz, his steal from Team Queen, slip through his fingertips. Not to take anything away from Dakota Cohen’s performance of “Hemorrhage (In My Hands),” which was a worthy rock rendition that had Queen Latifah singing along.

However, Brandon’s version of “Dare You to Move” showcased expertly skilled vocals, and they prove he has what it takes to win. Not only that, but performance also ahd the Equalizer star and American Idol winner giving Brandon a standing ovation. That’s why I couldn’t believe Levine didn’t send him through to the next round.

While Riley Green didn’t get every single country singer on Season 30 for his team, he came pretty close, often pulling out all the stops to get them to choose him as their coach. From the beginning, 19-year-old Joe Henley has been a stand-out, so it was surprising when he didn’t get one of the automatic spots for the Live Shows. But his rendition of the Keith Whitley song “Don’t Close Your Eyes” was so heartfelt from the first note to the last that he earned the only four coach standing ovation of the night.

While the Marshals guest star said he thought he knew he was going to pick before Joe took the stage, Kelly Clarkson declared that she would be mind blown if he didn’t make it to the finale. It made Green’s decision to put Joe Henley through an absolute no-brainer, because he really could end up winning the season.

After the craziness of Cut Week, what I’m most curious about with next week’s episode is to learn who America will pick out of everyone the coaches eliminated. Clearly, I’m rooting for Brandon, but there wasn’t one bad performance from the 16 remaining singers. On that note, we’ll see how that turns out.

While we already know the competition series will be shaking things up with Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity, we won’t learn who Season 30’s winner will be until December. So, be sure to keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET until then.

#3546. Dragon Ball Manga Return Hopes Officially Dashed by Shueisha

The status of the Dragon Ball franchise is more complicated than ever

It's almost time for Jump Festa, the annual event where Japanese publisher Shueisha showcases its most important manga and gives fans exciting updates for the future. Except that this year, Shueisha's most famous property, Dragon Ball, will barely be featured at Jump Festa. Fans speculate that the franchise's complicated status could be the reason, and that surprising changes could be on the horizon.

The original Dragon Ball manga by Akira Toriyama ended in 1995. A sequel, Dragon Ball Super, began publication in 2015, with story and supervision by Toriyama and art by Toyotaro. Dragon Ball Super was initially an adaptation of the anime, but it soon took its own original direction, producing story arcs that have yet to appear in anime form, like the much-anticipated Galactic Patrol arc. After Toriyama's sudden death in 2024, the manga went on hiatus, and it still hasn't come back.

After Toriyama's death, the status of the Dragon Ball franchise became quite muddled. The rights to the IP are split between the Toriyama estate, Shueisha (publisher of the manga), Toei Animation (which produces the anime), Bandai Namco (for toys, merchandising, and video games), and Capsule Corporation Tokyo, a company founded by Akio Iyoku, a former Shueisha editor who was Toriyama's right-hand man for many years. Fans speculate that this complex situation is why the manga is still on hiatus, while projects that originated before Toriyama's death, like Dragon Ball Daima, saw the light of day.

In September 2026, fans were surprised to see no Dragon Ball characters in Jump Festa's official visual, which features the protagonists of Shueisha's most popular manga. On Nov. 2, when the full lineup and schedule for the event were updated, Dragon Ball Super was no longer present in the Jump Original Art World zone, a booth that features original art for the most important series. Its spot was taken by Metaphor: ReFantazio, the manga adaptation of Atlus' award-winning RPG, currently published in Shueisha's V Jump magazine (where Dragon Ball Super was serialized).

It's worth noting that the Dragon Ball Super anime will have an exhibition space at Jump Festa 2027 as part of Toei Animation's booth, as the remake Dragon Ball Super: Beerus recently started airing, so it's not like Shueisha is trying to cancel Dragon Ball. However, the absence of the manga, after more than two years of hiatus, looks like the final nail in the coffin for fans who hoped that Toyotaro could pick up the torch and continue the story.

Another recent development adds one more piece to the puzzle and fuels speculation that big changes are coming to the franchise. The building that housed Akira Toriyama's Bird Studio, where the author worked for many years, is due to be demolished soon. Many people have spotted the construction works on the site and shared pictures, even if no official statements have been released. This could be completely unrelated, but some fans are speculating that, in the alleged tug of war for the Dragon Ball rights, Iyoku could soon walk away with the opportunity to publish the manga outside of Shueisha's control, which would explain why the publisher decided to limit Dragon Ball Super's presence at Jump Festa 2027.

The illustrator behind Dragon Ball Super posts a cryptic hint

Among this rampant speculation, one thing is certain: something must be going on behind the scenes to explain why Dragon Ball Super has not returned yet, nor has it been officially canceled. Toyotaro is still at work, producing at least one character illustration every month for V Jump, and he even changed his X bio to: "Everything is for the return of the series." But with the disheartening updates coming from Jump Festa, it's unlikely that this return will happen under Shueisha's banner.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3545. Marshals Season 2 Teases Yellowstone Fans With A Major Character Name-Drop

"Marshals" continues to tease a crossover with "Dutton Ranch," with Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton name-dropping his sister in the latest episode. By this point, however, fans are surely tired of the references and eager to see the "Yellowstone" cast reunited.

With its Season 1 finale, "Dutton Ranch" gave itself the perfect excuse for a "Marshals" crossover. Meanwhile, "Marshals" did the same, ending its debut season by having Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton kidnapped and taken to Texas, where, it just so happens, Kelly Reilly's Beth Dutton and Cole Hauser's Rip Wheeler now live. Meanwhile, Hauser and Reilly spoke positively about a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, suggesting that's exactly what fans would soon be getting — especially considering Reilly referred to the lack of such a thing as a missed opportunity.

Alas, when "Marshals" Season 2 arrived, not only was there no crossover, but Kayce didn't even have to go to Texas, as it turns out Tate was taken to a Wyoming ranch instead. Now, we have the latest example of "Marshals" referencing Beth, which more than anything else serves only to remind us that we're yet to receive the crossover we've been waiting for.

"Marshals" Season 2, Episode 5, "Secret Weapon" picks up in the aftermath of Rudy Carpenter (Braxton Hale) exploding a bomb and taking himself out in the process. After the Marshals track down his accomplice, Derek McCoy, Kayce chases Derek's brother, Will McCoy (Keean Johnson), into a barn that collapses, trapping the pair below ground. It's here that Kayce decides to bring up his family and once again tease audiences with a crossover that is yet to materialize.

In "Secret Weapon," after the barn floor collapses, Will McCoy's leg is badly injured. While trying to find a way out of their predicament, Kayce tries to convince Will to give up details about his brother, who evidently treats Will like a "punching bag." Kayce takes the opportunity to talk about his own brother, Jamie Dutton (played by Wes Bentley on "Yellowstone), and his sister, Beth Dutton, who also treated Jamie like a punching bag. Of course, Beth ultimately kills Jamie Dutton in the final season of "Yellowstone," but Kayce stops short of mentioning that still buried crime.

"You remind me of my middle brother," he tells Will. "Never quite fit in, always on the bad end of a beatdown. My sister made his life hell." Will replies with antagonism. "Picked on by his sister? I'm not that pathetic." But as Kayce quite rightfully points out, "She'd eat you for lunch," adding, "Meaner than any of your brothers, guaranteed."

It's true that Beth Dutton is a force of nature, and that only makes it even more frustrating that she hasn't shown up in "Marshals," which could do with a jolt of energy at this point. Beth and Rip are too busy setting up shop in Rio Paloma, Texas, in the far superior "Dutton Ranch." But this brief mention of Kayce's sister and how she'd eat Will for lunch is a reminder of just how good we once had it with "Yellowstone," and how much "Marshals" is struggling to match the excitement of its predecessor. Of course, "Yellowstone" lost its way at one point, but Beth was never anything less than electrifying, and "Marshals" would benefit from having anyone in its cast with half as much charisma.

For now, these brief references in "Marshals" to beloved "Yellowstone" characters aren't doing the CBS procedural any favors. In "Secret Weapon," Kayce Dutton recalls how fighting wasn't in Jamie Dutton's nature. "He had to be smarter, more cunning," he says, "And eventually he broke from the family, forged his own path." Of course, that path ultimately ended in his death, with Beth taking a knife to the middle Dutton brother's stomach and exacting revenge for the controversial death of Kevin Costner's John Dutton earlier in "Yellowstone" Season 5.

The thing is, being reminded of the "Yellowstone" years is bad enough on a show that clearly struggles to match the quality of Taylor Sheridan's original neo-Western. But when you take into account the anticipation for a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, it's just downright frustrating.

The "Marshals" Season 1 finale seemed to set up a perfect crossover with "Dutton Ranch," but in the end we got nothing of the sort. We could still see Beth show up later in the season, but for now all we know is that another "Yellowstone" fan-favorite character will be appearing in "Marshals" when Jefferson White's Jimmy Hurdstrom makes his return to the Montana plains. In the meantime, let's hope the show finds a way to keep the "Yellowstone" connection alive without reminding us of what we're missing out on.

I’ve been thriving off Marvel nostalgia thanks to repeated trips back to the age of Iron Man. First with VisionQuest, and now with some hilarious trivia. I’m always up for some fun BTS stories about the shared universe, but even I couldn’t have predicted how the MCU connects to spy guinea pigs. Yes, you read that correctly. So imagine my reaction when I heard the wild (guinea pig-related) story behind Jon Favreau casting one star for Iron Man 2.

Turns out, we have a family-friendly spy movie to thank for Sam Rockwell’s role as Justin Hammer. For those of you who don’t remember (or hasn’t strayed from the MCU re-watch list for Doomsday), back in 2010 Tony Stark dealt with two villains: Ivan Vanko (played by Mickey Rourke) and Hammer who was Vanko’s benefactor in his crusade against Iron Man. While the second movie doesn’t get as much love, it’s clear that the Galaxy Quest actor enjoyed playing the cheeky bad guy, and even has a connection to Justin Theroux who penned the script. He dished to Esquire on the unique way he landed the part while sharing BTS stories behind some of his popular roles:

Justin and I were friends, and I was dating Leslie Bibb and she had done the first Iron Man. And I went over to Theroux’s apartment just to get coffee, and he's packing a bag. And I'm like, ‘Where are you going?’ He's [like,] ‘I'm going to LA. I'm going to write Iron Man 2.’ I'm like, ‘Get the fuck out of here. I want to be in that. What's the part?’ said, ‘I want to be the bad guy. Let me be the bad guy.’ And he goes, ‘Yeah, yeah, OK, whatever.’

While he’s not involved in any upcoming Marvel projects, I’m glad he got to live out his dream. Not only did he get a part in the movie, he also got to play a bad guy. Justin Hammer has everything you love about Bond villains (plus Sam Rockwell’s cheekiness), and was the perfect charismatic foil to play off of Robert Downey Jr. Though what exactly do guinea pigs have to do with him landing the role? Well, Rockwell explains:

And then, like, six months later, a few months later, I’m doing G-Force, and Jon Favreau and I are in a room playing guinea pigs, and we’re like wrestling around with each other in the sound studio, and he says, ‘Hey, there’s this thing Theroux’s writing.’ I said, ‘Oh, is it Iron Man?’ So he said, ‘I got the Marvel guy coming. We're going to take the villain. We're going to split it in two and we're going to make one the fast talking guy and then sort of alpha. So they got me and Mickey to sort of do both do the villain sort of as two parts.

I shouldn’t be surprised by this story and yet I didn’t expect the two to connect while pretending to be guinea pigs. Am I the only one who can’t stop picturing Happy and Hammer running around pretending to be adorable rodents? Though Favreau has a gift when it comes to picking actors, as he ignored the pushback against RDJ and chose to back him as Iron Man anyway. At the time, he explained that he “just saw it” regarding RDJ in what would be his most famous role. Clearly something about Rockwell’s performance as Darwin (the no-nonsense leader of G-Force) that was perfect to play Hammer.

The actor gave a shout out to a memorable moment. Before you guess, it’s not when he’s fine-dining while interviewing Vanko. Turns out, when Hammer gave the gun demonstration, the actor had to use an earwig as they changed up the props right before filming. What apparently stood out most in the interview was Rockwell’s willingness to return to the MCU if asked. He’s just waiting to get the call. Although Hammer’s return would be the least surprising thing after VisionQuest Episode 6 blasted us back to 2008 with Faran Tahir reprising his Iron Man 1 character. Somehow I missed that casting news prior to watching.

At this point, Justin Hammer could easily come out of the wood works, and I wouldn’t be shocked to learn that he escaped from prison. This would be relatively simple to achieve, especially since our characters keep making trips to the island of Madripoor and it’d be believable that he’d hide out there. Plus, Tony’s rival would easily fit in with the lawless chaos.

So why not include a Benefactor that can face off against the Power Broker?

#3543. This Is the Robot Vacuum I Use Every Day, and It's 50% Off Right Now

I live in a 1,600-square-foot home, and vacuuming and mopping it by hand takes a considerable chunk of time. Passing that labor off to a robot vacuum was a great decision. I decided to go with the Roborock Qrevo CurvX since it seemed like a great fit for my circumstances. If you also have a dog, a mix of different floor types, and a gym with a workout mat, this robot vacuum might work for you, too. Amazon currently has it for $749.99 (originally $1,499.99), a 50% discount, and the lowest price it has ever been, according to price-tracking tools.

One of the main things I was looking for in a robot vacuum was suction power. The Qrevo CurvX has 22,000 Pa, which is stronger than most options at its price and is powerful enough to pick up anything that needs vacuuming in my house. I like that it has a self-lifting chassis so it can climb over my workout mat, rugs, obstacles like cables, or anything else that might be in the way, so I don't have to babysit it while it's doing its job. I also like the extendable mop pads and side brushes that allow it to reach corners and crevices it might not be slim enough to fit into. (Speaking of which, it's only 3.14 inches tall, so it can fit under most couches and beds without issue.)

My experience with the Roborock app has been great. It's easy to use and gives me enough control to clean my house how I want without a hassle. "No Go Zones" are easy to set up, as is the schedule. The main issue I've had is the size of the internal dust bin: It's small, so it needs to be cleaned after basically every scheduled use (though that shouldn't be as bad if you don't have a pet that sheds a lot).

Take it from me: If you're looking for a reliable hybrid robot vacuum that can clean multiple types of floors, mop, and comes with a great app, the Qrevo CurvX makes a compelling case at the current $750 discount.

#3542. Ta-Nehisi Coates on Haley Stevens, Abdul El-Sayed, and the Right’s “Campaign of Hate”

When Michigan congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers yesterday, she offered a curious framing. “I’m choosing country over hate,” Stevens claimed. “This is not anti-Muslim at all.”

Rogers, for his part, invoked Martin Luther King Jr.: “You cannot solve darkness with darkness; you have to solve it with light. You can’t solve hate with hate; you have to solve it with love.” For the site of their hard launch, the odd couple chose Perfecting Church, a Black church in Detroit, evidently seeking to exploit the aura of social justice implicit in the Black faith tradition.

Aura farming aside, it is very hard to square the claims of patriotism and love with the actual campaign that Stevens now supports. Indeed, since the moment Abdul El-Sayed triumphed in the Democratic Senate primary, Rogers has made his views of his opponent clear. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice,” he claimed the morning after El-Sayed won. “Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” (Never mind that Hasan Piker, not El-Sayed, said the 9/11 quote, which El-Sayed has disavowed.)

Indeed, a consistent theme of Rogers’s campaign has been the implication that El-Sayed is a tool for shadowy forces originating in the East. “The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year,” Rogers claimed. “Abdul El-Sayed’s.” As a factual matter, the attack is highly dubious. But facts are not the point, so much as the deployment of “Muslim” as a slur.

To understand this, one need only look to the overlord of the Rogers campaign, President Donald Trump. As is his wont, Trump delights in mangling El-Sayed’s name, referring to him as “Abduladadalalalala” or simply “Mohamed.” “Somebody said his name isn’t Mohamed,” Trump told attendees at a rally. “I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he’s Mohamed.”

The Trump theory of El-Sayed holds that his ascendance is being facilitated by the machinations of Wayne County, a “strictly Third World” jurisdiction that seeks to elevate to Congress a “jihadist” who shouldn’t even be eligible for “a seat on an airplane.” If seated in the world’s greatest deliberative body, El-Sayed, the theory holds, would execute his dastardly plan to ban Christmas and—you guessed it—impose Sharia law.

Trump’s attacks have been echoed and amplified by right-wing news outlets like Newsmax, which has lambasted El-Sayed as an “anti-Israel Muslim,” an “immigrant from another Muslim country,” and a Midwest variant of that other alien, Zohran Mamdani, the “socialist Muslim who’s always smiling.” For those too dense to catch the message, the Newsmax chyrons have helpfully driven home the point—“THE LEFT IS FORGETTING THE HEINOUS ATTACKS OF 9/11,” “DEMOCRATS DROOL OVER NON-WHITE SOCIALISTS,” “MUSLIMS TELL US THEY’RE TAKING OVER, AND THEY ARE.”

Lest one think that this bigotry is merely limited to the crude ramblings of unlettered ogres, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has stepped in to offer some intellectual heft to the attack. The Muslim Brotherhood, according to Kennedy, is responsible for not just the menace that is El-Sayed, but also the dark age that has fallen over the entirety of the Arabdom. “There’s 500 million Arabs in the world,” Kennedy claimed, “and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Field[s] prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce the literature they used to produce.”

Again, facts aren’t really the point here, and there is no wisdom in debating a quack whose brain has literally been infected by a worm. Nonetheless, it is worth noting the particular history at work. During both his run for president and his time in the White House, Barack Obama endured his share of racist attacks. To Rush Limbaugh, Obama was “Barack the Magic Negro.” To Newt Gingrich, he was America’s “food stamp president.” At the Value Voters Summit, a vendor hawked “Obama Waffles,” a product featuring a racist caricature of the president on the packaging. The tagline was: “Point box toward Mecca for tastier waffles.” That last line deserves particular attention. Indeed, by 2016, the political scientist Philip Klinkner would find that the best way to discern whom a voter would support in the upcoming election was to pose a simple question—“Is Barack Obama a Muslim?”

Stevens, in joining Rogers, has allied herself with this odious culture war, one that is itself tied to a very real war. The campaign of hate, of which El-Sayed is the latest victim, has a simple goal: to render Muslims and Arabs more killable. The latter does not require the former. In 1953 the CIA backed a coup that overthrew a democracy in Iran. In 1965 it supported a coup in Indonesia, the country with the largest Muslim population in the world, that killed between 500,000 and a million people. During the Cold War, the justification for this death toll was the threat of communism; post-9/11, it is racism. In 2008, John McCain confronted a supporter and disputed the claim that Obama was Arab. “No, ma’am,” McCain told his supporter. “He’s a decent family man.” This moment is often referenced as an act of patriotism, and perhaps it was one. But the notion that “decent” people exist in one place, while Arabs exist in another, is the major premise for a syllogism of violent, chauvinist power—wedding parties droned, governments overthrown, schoolgirls bombed, and inconvenient people eliminated.

This long war on the Muslim and Arab world has reached its apogee in the concentration camp of Gaza, where every single bomb was dropped from a plane of American extraction. And the genocide is but the latest chapter in a book authored by Israel, a state whose own basic laws reserve full rights for its “decent” people and something less for everyone else. This is the state that Haley Stevens has claimed to literally see in her dreams. And it is ultimately the defense of this state that drove Stevens into the arms of Mike Rogers. From this perspective, Stevens’s defection isn’t a story about party intrigue. It is a story about Stevens waking up and choosing violence.

#3541. The Garmin Cirqa Finally Got a Much-Needed Feature

This week Garmin's screenless Cirqa smart band received a firmware update that fixes one of its most obvious gaps: the lack of alerts from your phone. With Version 4.20, you can now set up your smart band to buzz your wrist for texts, calls, and other smart notifications from your phone. The addition is listed on Garmin's forums as "Support vibration for smart notifications/incoming calls." Reaction has been upbeat, too—users on the Garmin subreddit have been glad to see the feature arrive.

Amusingly, Garmin's own FAQ still states that the Cirqa does not vibrate for text messages, phone calls, or other smartphone notifications. Clearly that page is now out of date, so Garmin will want to correct it. Since Garmin doesn't yet have step-by-step instructions, I tested the text-message vibrations myself. Here's how you can set up your Cirqa smart band to vibrate for calls and texts, in addition to a number of other promising updates to check out.

To receive these alerts, your band must be running firmware 4.20 or later. Here is how to get everything configured.

Update the firmware. Open your Garmin Connect app and sync your Cirqa, so the app can check for and install version 4.20 or newer.

Grant the necessary phone permissions. In your phone's settings, make sure Garmin Connect has permission to access SMS, Contacts, and Phone.

Configure notifications in Garmin Connect. Back in Garmin Connect, tap the Menu (or More) tab. Select Garmin Devices, then choose your Cirqa Smart Band. Go to Notifications & Alerts (or Smart Notifications) and turn on text and call alerts.

Troubleshooting tip: If alerts aren't coming through, check that Do Not Disturb, Sleep Mode, and any aggressive Battery Saver settings are turned off on both your phone and the band.

For most a lot of Cirqa fans, the phone alerts are the headline, but the 4.20 update carries a solid list of other improvements and bug fixes:

Trail Run: Run/Walk detection is now available for Trail Run activities.

Timestamp fix: Resolved a problem where an activity's recorded time didn't match the time on your phone.

Distance calibration: You can now calibrate distance for Treadmill Run, Indoor Rowing, and Indoor Cycling before saving the activity on the device.

Duration alerts: Duration time alerts for speaking out now accumulate.

Stress alerts: Stress alerts are now blocked while Auto Activity Detection is recording.

Bedtime reminders: Fixed an issue where the bedtime approaching notification sometimes failed to trigger.

Live Activity: Heart rate now appears on the Live Activity screen before recording begins.

Pinned activity bug: Fixed an issue where the pinned activity reverted to Timed Activity after changing the phone's language.

Workout editing: Fixed a problem that prevented editing reps during a workout.

Stability: General system stability improvements.
