#3540. Cillian Murphy's Overlooked 2024 Drama With A 94% Rotten Tomatoes Score Is A Must-Watch

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Many of Cillian Murphy's best characters are either American, like J. Robert Oppenheimer or Jonathan Crane, or British, like Jim from "28 Weeks Later" or the immortal (?) Thomas Shelby from "Peaky Blinders." But as Murphy himself will remind you, he's Irish, and one of his most recent films tackles a dark part of his country's history.

That would be 2024's "Small Things Like These" by "Peaky Blinders" Season 3 director Tim Mielants, adapted from author Claire Keegan's 2021 novella. The movie received strong reviews and more than made its modest $3 million budget back with a $15 million gross in theaters, but it's still under-discussed. Sadly, that makes sense, as it's a quiet character study not really designed for a wide audience.

Murphy (who produced the film) plays Bill Furlong, a coal merchant in the Irish town New Ross during the 1980s. He's a moderately successful man, with his own business plus a wife and five daughters. But he remains troubled by his childhood, having been born out of wedlock and never known his father. If not for the kindness of his mother's employer, the widowed Mrs. Wilson (Michelle Fairley), who sheltered Bill and his mother, Sarah (Agnes O'Casey), like her own family, Bill would've likely been put up for adoption and Sarah sentenced to a Magdalene Laundry. What's that?

Until 1996, the Catholic Church in Ireland operated "Magdalene Asylums" for "fallen women" (unmarried women caught having sex or becoming pregnant, even if through sexual assault). These women were put to work to cleanse their supposed sins and basically enslaved. One of these laundries exists in Bill's own town, where everyone keeps their head down and doesn't peek too closely. But Bill, knowing he only has the life he does because of charity, can't look the other way.

Spoilers for "Small Things Like These" ahead.

In the opening shots of "Small Things Like These," church buildings loom over New Ross as their bells ring out. The Church's power is baked into the town and personified by the convent's Mother Superior (Emily Watson). Watson plays the soft-spoken nun as being so powerful that she doesn't have to be loud. Bill can't even meet her gaze as she makes subtle threats behind her niceties.

Bill's work in coal means that he comes home and cleans his hands every night, i.e. exactly the spiritually symbolic labor that the "fallen women" of the laundries are tasked to do. But a small kindness cleans Bill's hands: He saves an imprisoned girl locked in a shed, wrapping her in a coat and taking her to his home. Bill is particularly suited to break this social norm because of his background. The girl Bill saves, Sarah Redmond (Zara Devlin), literally has the same name as his late mother. As Bill walks with Sarah through New Ross, everyone around them looks on in shock and judgment. Yet, they're all out of focus, as if Bill is finally tuning them out.

"The fact was that he would pay for [taking Sarah], but never once in his whole and unremarkable life had he known happiness akin to this," reads one of the novel's closing lines. Speaking to GQ in 2024, Cillian Murphy even said Bill saving Sarah is "not a classically heroic act."

"Small Things Like These" came about in part due to Murphy's work on "Oppenheimer" and not just via his post-Oscar win clout. During that production, Murphy passed along the script to his co-star Matt Damon, who had recently founded the new studio Artists Equity with Ben Affleck.

"[Artists Equity] really let us make the film we wanted to make, because they're filmmakers themselves and writers, and they really understand it," Cillian Murphy told GQ. Indeed, "Small Things Like These" is extremely faithful to its somber source book and trusts its audience to weather the slow pace with Murphy's quiet but steely performance as an anchor.

Actor Eileen Walsh plays Bill's wife, Eileen Furlong, who advises him: "If you want to get on in this life, there are things you have to ignore." Walsh's casting rings hard because she previously appeared in Peter Mullan's 2002 film "The Magdalene Sisters" as Crispina, a woman imprisoned in one of those laundries. One of the greatest Irish films of the 21st Century, "The Magdalene Sisters" brought new attention to the real-life atrocities of the Magdalene Laundries (and was unsurprisingly condemned by the Catholic Church).

That "national reckoning" continues to this day, Murphy told GQ. "There's government commissions and government reports and academic papers on all of these things that you can get your hands on, but the public doesn't really read them. They will consume books and films, and I think it's a gentler way to confront it," he added. After all, "Small Things Like These" has as realistic a happy ending as one could hope for in this story.

In December 2024, shortly after the movie's theatrical release, the "Small Things Like These" novel was selected by Oprah's Book Club. That publicity is another win for civil education about the real history the novel dramatizes, at least the "gentler way." The book is only about 120 pages, and like the movie, it's easy enough to absorb in a single sitting if you set your stomach right for the cruelty inside.

In the weeks since You Can See Everything hit the 2026 movie schedule and started tearing up the box office, it's no surprise that some of those tickets have been sold to former Theranos employees. Whistleblower Tyler Schultz spoke out shortly after the Nathan Fielder/Lance Oppenheim-directed documentary about the company’s founder, Elizabeth Holmes, was released, and now more employees are speaking out about their takeaways from the movie. Two of them recently spoke to The Times about it. Here’s what they have to say.

According to the article, former Theranos creative director Gage Clegg and former chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill saw the movie together, and they described their complicated feelings to the paper. O’Neill is glad that people are finally seeing the real Holmes, in his estimation, telling the paper:

No one’s asking me any more how I could possibly work for someone like that; people now understand it … I’m excited that the world is going to experience Elizabeth in the way that I did. People will finally understand her ability to persuade and to connect, and how that gave her such enormous power. [Fielder] fell for it, too.

Much has been said of Holmes’ ability to manipulate people, and some have said Fielder fell under her spell while living with her and her partner, Billy Evans, while he and Oppenheim shot the movie. Personally, I’m not sure he did, but it's easy to see how people fall for it when watching You Can See Everything. Clegg was more direct, saying the documentary:

Sees her as being kind of on the spectrum, a person who doesn’t understand regular people, as a way to garner sympathy and to make people think that maybe she didn’t really understand that what she was doing was wrong. That is crazy. The person I knew was smart, capable and decisive. She walked into the room and owned the room. She is a night and day different person from who was in Fielder’s movie.

As to whether or not they think people should believe the Holmes they saw in the movie, Clegg’s answer was clear: No. He told the paper:

Hearing her say that she didn’t know she was lying made me want to jump out of my seat in the cinema.

Clegg and O’Neill were not alone in pointing out both the deception and the role-playing they see in Holmes. A former in-house lawyer for Theranos (yikes!), Brad Arington, summed up seeing the movie the same way.

She’s always performing. She’s very convincing. I wasn’t going to fall for it again.

Whether or not Fielder fell under Holmes’ spell is one of the big questions the movie leaves audiences wondering. It’s even brought up in the movie itself when he is questioned by another star in the movie over whether he’d gotten too close to his subject.

In fact, the last scene in the movie, with Fielder and Holmes swimming together in the ocean, harkens back to an earlier scene when Holmes tried to convince Fielder to go on a swim with her. Fielder demurs, saying he doesn’t want to, but obviously did swim with her at some point. Was that Fielder reinforcing the notion that Holmes can sell anything to anyone? The film doesn’t answer that for us.

Like so much in the movie, we’re really just stuck asking more questions than getting answers, and for me, that is part of what makes the movie an Oscar contender, and one of the best movies of the year.

#3538. Even Pierce Brosnan Is “Eagerly” Awaiting News of the Next James Bond

Like the rest of us, Pierce Brosnan has been following the seemingly endless and exhaustive search for the next James Bond. Having played 007 across four films, Brosnan says he admires all the actors in the running, but Callum Turner, who played his angsty Manhattanite son in The Only Living Boy in New York, gets a particularly warm mention. “Callum is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. As for Dune director Denis Villeneuve’s vision for the franchise, Brosnan is already sold. “I think we are going to be blown away.”

Away from Hollywood, the Irish actor stars in Burberry’s new holiday campaign, celebrating 170 years of the luxury fashion house, alongside actor Fiona Shaw, his son Dylan Thomas Brosnan, and a cast of characters including Dwyane Wade, Cara Delevingne, Gabrielle Union, Nico Parker, and more. Set at the cinematic Longleat House in Wiltshire, England, it’s a festive British Christmas, complete with Burberry’s signature checks and partygoers draped in classic garments. On set, Brosnan found a kindred spirit in Shaw. The two bonded over their shared love of art—though he wishes they had much more time to chat, “It was all too brief with Fiona,” he muses.

Pierce Brosnan in the Burberry Festive 2026 Campaign video.

Pierce Brosnan and Fiona Shaw in the Burberry Festive 2026 Campaign video.

Brosnan is no stranger to good style. Having spent a career playing some of the most impeccably dressed men on screen, from James Bond to Thomas Crown, Brosnan has come to re-embrace the joys of good tailoring after an era of rebelling against the gentlemanly image he created for himself. Now, he’s looking forward to seeing a new generation of leading men step into some of those familiar roles, including Michael B. Jordan, whose upcoming take on Thomas Crown he’s cheering on.

In conversation with Vanity Fair, the former 007 talks favorite Christmas traditions, the Burberry Mac he’s kept for years, the art of playing it cool, how filming MobLand shaped his personal style, and the paintings waiting for him in London.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: The new Burberry campaign celebrates 170 years of the fashion house with a festive Christmas party in the English countryside. How was your time on the campaign set?

Pierce Brosnan: I was with my son, Dylan Thomas Brosnan, which was just absolutely wonderful, and we had the most magnificent time. I’d never seen so many people on a set in all my days for such an event. Everybody was very charming.

Do you typically go all-in on Christmas? What’s your favorite holiday tradition?

I think it starts with the Christmas tree, and my wife really decks the halls, as it were. She loves decorating the tree, and that becomes a great ritual. The boys are much older now, but we do have grandchildren joining us for Christmas. My son Sean Brosnan and his family will be coming down. My wife is a wonderful cook; she’ll make a feast for us all.

Midnight Mass is a tradition and a great joy if we’re in London. Friends, family, and reflection on the year past. Having been brought up within the Catholic religion, the season and all of those traditions are very much ingrained in me.

Harmony Korine (Gummo, Kids, Spring Breakers) directing a holiday campaign feels like such an inspired choice, given how experimental his films can be. What was it like working with him?

I thought he was charming! Very charming. It moved very fast. He was busy and deep in the workload of the day. The highlight was meeting and being with Fiona Shaw. That was just absolutely magnificent. I’m such a huge fan of the lady’s work.

The Burberry trench is such a cornerstone of British style. Is there a clothing item in your wardrobe that holds that kind of status for you?

Oh, dear. There are so many beautiful items in my closet. One of my favorite suits has become a workhorse because it’s so durable. The cloth is wool, and it’s just a two-piece, beautifully tailored suit by Anglo-Italian. I’m very partial to my shoes and belts by Bottega Veneta. And of course, a Burberry Mac, which I’ve had for many, many years. It is the classic, dream trench coat of anyone who has grown up on the movies.

It was wonderful to celebrate such a garment of classic time, and to be in the company of Fiona Shaw. [She’s] someone who I would adore to work with again on any level, really. We had a wonderful time talking about art. We’re both painters, and art is very much part of the tapestry of our lives now.

Pierce Brosnan in The Thomas Crown Affair, 1999.

Speaking of art, I wanted to ask you about playing Thomas Crown in The Thomas Crown Affair. Michael B. Jordan is stepping into that role now, in a new version of the film, which he’s also directing.

I love Michael B. Jordan. I think he’s an outstanding actor and artist, and I wish him every great success with his vision of Thomas Crown. There’s something just beautifully cinematic about the character. He was brought onto the stage by one of the great actors, Steve McQueen, who was so gifted in the art of film acting, stillness, and inner life. For me, the romance with the film came from his body of work as an actor and has always been with me since I was a young lad in Ireland. These characters are very hard to really understand, but they create a sensation.

He was so cool, Steve McQueen. How do you play cool? You play it with sincerity. You play it with stillness, with just the knowingness—and hopefully some humanity and humility, and a kind of inner knowing of being the actor you are.

What do you think makes Thomas Crown such an enduring character?

When I made my rendition and produced it with my late dear friend Beau St. Clair, I wanted to steal art. I didn’t want to steal diamonds or money. I wanted to steal paintings. It was against all the political correctness of his time and space. Thomas Crown was a man who had everything in life: wealth, fortune, intellect. But he didn’t have love. So it was a love story for me.

When we were looking for the film’s art, I suggested René Magritte: the bowler hats, the red tie, the great coat. Magritte is someone I find spellbinding, captivating, and always has a narrative which is almost cinematic. So that’s where the bowler hats came from. The visible and the invisible: Visible with an apple in front of a face, but you don’t see the face. And I thought that translated well to the enigma of Thomas Crown.

Pierce Brosnan and Callum Turner, The Only Living Boy In New York, 2017.

Having played James Bond yourself, I’m curious how you’re following the conversation around this upcoming chapter.

[Laughs.] Oh, I’m just an audience member now. I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history. All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire. Callum, Callum Turner is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong. They all have a voice and a physique, and a presence on film. They all have longevity as actors, all of these young men.

Pierce Brosnan as 007 in The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

What would you say to the next actor stepping into 007?

Whoever plays the role, I wish him the very best of life and strength and courage. You know, it’s hard to tell who it would be, but I eagerly await to hear the news and the celebration of the next James Bond.

Martin Campbell gave your era such a memorable introduction with GoldenEye. Now, with Denis Villeneuve taking on the franchise, what are you most curious to see him bring to Bond?

I think we are going to be blown away. I really do. [Villeneuve] is such an iconoclastic director. His work is visionary, and his stealth and imagination of camera work and storytelling is so visceral and sensuous. It’s going to be great. It’s going to be truly magnificent. Of course, we all get sentimental and nostalgic, and you have to give it time and be patient, and it’s always such a delightful game. But Villeneuve is someone who I have great admiration for, and I look forward to seeing the work.

Pierce Brosnan as Remington Steele, 1986.

Pierce Brosnan as Remington Steele, 1986.

You’ve played some of cinema’s most impeccably dressed men! Have those characters influenced the way you dress in your own life?

I have always been, I suppose, a clothes horse. When I played Remington Steele, I delved into the work of Cary Grant, another emblem of cinema that I’ve admired. Bob Butler, who directed it, said, “We’re making an old movie,” so I styled myself and had the joy of wearing beautiful suits every week. That continues through my life.

As I’ve gotten older, I used to try to rebel against the look, character, and style of actor I had created for myself. Now I embrace it more because it excites me. I love the elegance of tailored clothes and dressing up, and fitting into the season, the gale of emotion, the world around you.

You’ve got some great hunting coats in MobLand too.

Rebecca Hale, the costume designer, has brought so many great ingredients to the world of Conrad. He’s an Irishman from a hard part of Irish life, the Troubles, a mangled life of abuse and violence. He wants to fit into the world of the Cotswolds and be the gentleman. There’s this magnificent coat in MobLand, where Conrad has a shootout, and they made a magnificent overcoat, which I managed to keep from last season. And, of course, I step back and just revel at what Dame Helen Mirren does. She is such an empress of fashion herself.

When Vanity Fair last caught up with you, around your first solo exhibition, you’d already been painting and curating work for years. How has your relationship with art evolved since then?

I had, yes. I had the exhibition three years ago, and it was a great success in the sense that I had the courage to step out and show the work. I have a body of work now that has progressed, and hopefully I will have another showing here, maybe in London.

Do you find that painting gives you something different from acting, or do the two creative practices feed into each other?

Both are essential to my life. Acting is how I make my living and provide for my family. And to be able to have a lifestyle that is not only creative but productive, and then is hopefully entertaining, because you’re working towards an audience.

The practice of my art is a constant exploration of inner life, inner thoughts, inner emotions expressed through color and form. Having lived in Kauai for 25 years, there’s a wonderful artist there who’s become my teacher, Saim Caglayan. Both are necessary to my life. They soothe me and frustrate me and challenge me and exhilarate me—sometimes all in the same space of day and time.

Yes! I was sketching when I was doing Burberry. There was a lovely landscape down there, and I have my sketchbook with me at all times. I wanted so much to be an artist, to be a writer, a poet, to live a creative life. I have no real head for figures or the abstraction of figures, but I certainly have a great love for art and the power of art on the wall.

With the holidays coming up, and hopefully a little time to slow down, is there anything you’re hoping to make more time for, creatively or personally?

I have a little time left before I go back to London with my wife, Keely. London is home, and my mother of 94 is there, so I’m looking forward to seeing her. In my studio, I have a number of paintings that I’m quite pleased with, and I’d like to finish a couple more. And I’m really excited to jump into season three of MobLand. I have no idea where the story is going. Conrad is slowly, slowly going bonkers. But the thing is, he’s aware of it, and the love story of Maeve and Conrad lives on. It’s very exciting.

#3536. Behaviour Interactive Addresses Dead by Daylight Controversy

Behaviour Interactive is under fire for supporting VTuber TheBurntPeanut following a Halloween stream. Many community members dislike the controversial streamer due to repeated accusations of offensive behavior, alleged viewbotting, and the use of racial and homophobic slurs. This caused dozens of players to uninstall Dead by Daylight and voice their discontent on social media. Behaviour Interactive is doing damage control and has issued a statement addressing the matter.

TheBurntPeanut is one of the most popular streamers on Twitch right now. To celebrate Halloween, he played Dead by Daylight, an online multiplayer game featuring several horror icons, for the first time. The official Dead by Daylight account tuned into the stream and granted the streamer all paid DLC packs. TheBurntPeanut is a rather divisive streamer in the gaming community, which is why this sparked such a heated discussion online. When the streamer apparently refused the gift, citing the controversy that would follow, the DeadbyDaylight Twitch account answered with "We can take the heat!"

According to the statement, Behaviour Interactive gifted free items to TheBurntPeanut after noticing a "very large" audience tuning into a Dead by Daylight stream to watch someone who had never played the game before. The post explains that even though it is not unusual for the dev team to grant content creators in-game content to help promote Dead by Daylight to a new audience, it failed to do its due diligence, analyze the streamer's past content, and verify whether he represented the team's values.

The content has now been removed from TheBurntPeanut's account. Approval methods for granting free content are being reviewed and updated to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future. Behaviour Interactive underlines that it values respect and diversity. Its goal is for Dead by Daylight to be a welcoming space where players feel safe being themselves.

According to the official statement, the choice to gift the items was hastily made by an unnamed member of the team rather than being pondered and discussed by the team as a group. Behaviour Interactive promises that action will be taken internally against those involved, but no further details will be shared, as it is a confidential matter. Despite the company's attempt to make amends with the community, the comments section was filled with angry fans. Many players felt that its justification was lacking, and the consequences felt minimal for the disorderly team.

#3535. The Martian Author Andy Weir Explains The One Thing He Would Change About The Story [Exclusive]

Looking back at the success of 2015's "The Martian," it's remarkable to realize just how influential this crowd-pleasing blockbuster really was. It helped launch author Andy Weir to the upper echelon of sci-fi writers, paving the way for even bigger box office hits like 2026's "Project Hail Mary." Alongside Christopher Nolan's "Interstellar" in 2014 and Alfonso Cuarón's "Gravity" the year before, Ridley Scott's adaptation also served as a bellwether for the mid-2010s "space race" in film. And, for those of a certain age, there's something genuinely nostalgic about the tone struck by both the source material and the movie — a last gasp of the sense of optimism and unity that defined the Obama-era U.S.

So, when I had the chance to speak with Weir over a Zoom interview, as he's promoting his newest original project as an executive producer on Audible's "Exoplanet" series (due later this month), I jumped at the chance to revisit the whirlwind experience of "The Martian." Has over a decade of hindsight given Weir a different perspective on his game-changing book, now that he's more established as a novelist? In response, the science-abiding author maintained he wouldn't change anything ... except for the natural disaster that sets the plot in motion in the first place on the surface of Mars:

"If I had it to do over again, there's a few minor changes I'd make. I'd probably make the initial problem not be a windstorm, because that windstorm was not physics-accurate. I'd probably have it be — well, I've since learned that there's lightning strikes on Mars, and that could be something. Lightning strikes something, it causes overload here, that causes an explosion there, and then [the other astronauts have] all got to bail, something like that."

When things just happen to fall into place perfectly, you count your blessings and don't look back. That's more or less the mindset Andy Weir has with "The Martian." Unlike his hands-on role with "Project Hail Mary," Weir notes in our conversation, he was much more of a passenger on this first adaptation of his work. As a result, he simply sat back and let director Ridley Scott and screenwriter Drew Goddard do their thing along with some of the best and most talented actors in the world.

Sure, the part of his brain obsessed with making things as realistic and scientifically-accurate as can be may have some corrections or two. In the book, everything goes haywire when astronaut Mark Watney is separated from his fellow crew during a hellish windstorm and is left behind on the surface of Mars, presumed dead. But while there are dust storms on the surface of Mars, Weir is correct to note that the atmosphere and gravity of the planet couldn't sustain one of this magnitude. "But other than that," he tells me, "I don't think I'd change anything."

He goes on to compare the success of "The Martian" to, well, I'll let Weir's quirky sense of humor speak for itself:

"It's like, have you ever been casually talking to a beautiful woman and then you realize she's interested in you, and you have no idea what you did right, but you don't want to jinx it? That's kind of what happened to me with 'The Martian.' I'm like, 'I don't know what I did right, but I'm sure as hell not going to change anything.' [laughs]"

For those interested in more sci-fi approved by Weir, "Exoplanet" hits Audible on November 5, 2026.

#3534. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Is 'Ballhog'?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's zeitgeist snapshot explains what ballhog means, how a video of someone wrapping a burger led to a new meme format, and the dangers of Benny tripping. So strap in, and let's go.

Ballhog or ball hog is a streetwear fashion style growing in popularity among younger people. The cool ones, anyway. The idea is to wear vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique. Like the best youth trends, it's an insider vs. outsider thing that takes connoisseurship to understand. Some examples: If you're wearing a late 1990s Helmut Lang denim jacket, most people will think "thrifted," but a ballhog-enjoyer would recognize it as a seminal piece of streetwear history. If you want to be ballhog, rocking a pair of skinny jeans isn't going to cut it unless they're from Dior Homme or at least Cheap Monday.

The style is named after the Ball Hog Collective, a group of rappers, Twitch streamers, and content creators founded by the Atlanta-based indie record label Ballhog. It was popularized by streamer Brady Goodwin, seen below looking quite ballhog:

The #ballhog hashtag is blowing up (as people used to say) lately with a growing collection of kids posting videos to show off their ballhog fits, like so:

The popularity of the style comes down to, I think, how difficult it is to commodify. Most truly organic trends are recognized quickly by culture vulture types, and in a few months, there's a line of clothes at Target, but you can't do that with ballhog. There's no way to make "new" ballhog gear, as that would mark it as inauthentic immediately. Gotta hand it to the kids for adopting a style that is at once exclusionary and impossible to rip off.

On the opposite edge of the spectrum from ballhog fashion is the "while they're out partying btw" meme, videos made to show off the strange, specific, and usually useless talent one develops while others are out wearing cool clothes and socializing. The phrase has been kicking around since last year, when TikToker @tacobella posted this video

but it's taken off more recently, thanks to the huge number of views on this video showing off some truly mind-blowing burger wrapping skills:

This led to an influx of videos of people showing off what they were doing instead of partying. Like this mechanic:

This is the second youth trend I support wholeheartedly. We can't all be cool ballhoggers and we don't all have talent, but we can all learn to do a thing really well through brute force and repetition.

The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

As for "scuba," it now describes something that is very smelly, which might be because the word conjures the dead air of unventilated, underwater spaces. But it's often accompanied by a pinch-your-nose gesture, which looks like the gesture in the Scuba Dance that was popular on TikTok a few months ago, so that's a more likely origin for the term.

There has been a steady stream of news stories about kids overdosing on Benadryl over the last few years. They call it "Benny tripping," and it's achieved by taking too much of the allergy medicine, like 10 times the amount recommended. Among the active ingredients in Benadryl is Diphenhydramine, and it's a particularly nasty drug. Unlike most recreational substances, tripping on Benadryl is not fun. It's a deliriant, and taking too much results in hallucinations that are usually described as terrifying—swarms of spiders, shadow people, whispering voices, etc. Benadryl overdoses can result in loss of short term memory, displacement from time and space, and panic attacks that last for hours or even days. Or you die from tachycardia. Here's how Reddit user Reasonable-County971 described their experience,

I lost access to my memories. I couldn’t recognize my mom—I mistook her for a 'pretty nurse'. Early in the trip, before you lose yourself, you develop tremendous anxiety, far far beyond anything else I can compare it to. Also, you have motor skills affected, including losing access to your bladder.

So yeah, it's a bad drug. And it's easy to get—just pop down to CVS. On the plus side, despite sometimes overly hysterical reporting on Benadryl as an "online trend" or challenge, tripping on Benadryl is such a harrowing, not-at-all-fun experience, its use isn't particularly popular among young people. But if you want to scare yourself, read some trip reports, watch this YouTube video, and imagine someone you love going through this.

This week's viral video is very meta, and it's hilarious to anyone who follows the trajectory of viral internet sensations. Brought to us by the great @ariisaysso, this video lays out the history of the fictional Cheezit Girl as she becomes an internet sensation, quits her job, sells merch, releases a rap single, releases a remix, reheats the nachos, and falls into obscurity, all in about two and a half minutes. We've seen this story before with the Hawk Tuah Girl, Dah Bih Gah Kid, and many more future members of the "remember that thing" club, and we'll no doubt see it all again soon. Such is the circle of life.

#3533. 50 Years Ago Today: John Carpenter Directed A Gritty Action Thriller That Became A Cult Classic

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Retired filmmaker John Carpenter is best known for his horror films. After all, we don't have the modern slasher film without "Halloween." But before Michael Myers returned to Haddonfield on Halloween night 1978, Carpenter tried his hand at an action-exploitation film: 1976's "Assault on Precinct 13," which opened in theaters 50 years ago today.

Carpenter was born in 1948, the perfect age to grow up on cowboy movies. He dreamed of going to Hollywood to make Westerns, not horror films. But, by the time he enrolled in University of South California film school in 1968, Westerns had already faded as Hollywood's biggest genre. Throughout his decades-long filmmaking career, Carpenter never directed a Western — but you can see that longing in "Assault on Precinct 13." The movie has a courageous lawman who has to hold his ground against the black hat gangs. The catch? The movie is set in contemporary Los Angeles, not the Wild West.

Lieutenant Ethan Bishop (Austin Stoker) is overseeing the closure of the LAPD's Precinct 13. A prison bus, carrying convicted murderer Napoleon Wilson (Darwin Joston), also stops at the precinct for a respite. Before long, the building is under siege by bloodthirsty gang members. Bishop, Wilson, and surviving secretary Leigh (Laurie Zimmer) are in a literal fight for their lives as unlikely allies.

Made on a meager budget of $100,000, "Assault on Precinct 13" wasn't an instant mega-hit. Reviews weren't too enthusiastic either. Whitney Williams of Variety was ambivalent, writing backhanded praise like, "some exciting action in second half packs enough interest to keep this entry alive for the violence market." Ellen Edwards of The Miami Herald condemned the film for its "hideous, unmotivated violence." But "Assault on Precinct 13" found its audience. It even got a remake in 2005, starring Laurence Fishburne and Ethan Hawke.

One of John Carpenter's acknowledged influences for "Assault on Precinct 13" is one of the most beloved Westerns ever: Howard Hawks' "Rio Bravo," about a sheriff (John Wayne) and his deputies trying to keep a murderer with a rich brother and many hired guns locked up. But "Rio Bravo" is not a tense thriller; often called a hangout movie, it's leisurely paced with only bursts of gun violence.

In "Assault on Precinct 13," the threat is everywhere. There's not even a reason for the siege beyond violence for its own sake; there's nothing of value inside the precinct besides more lives to end. That leads into one of the other movies that inspired Carpenter: George Romero's 1968 "Night of the Living Dead," the first modern zombie movie. When asked if "Night of the Living Dead" inspired "Assault on Precinct 13," Carpenter said, half-seriously, "Everybody who made a low-budget film was inspired by ['Night of the Living Dead']."

The comparison rings even more true here. Both movies are about people trapped inside a small building, surrounded by a horde outside that wants to break in and kill them. Both films also cast a Black man as their hero: Stoker as Lt. Bishop in "Precinct 13" and Duane Jones as Ben in "Night of the Living Dead." That was a bigger deal in the 1960s and '70s than it is now, and one spot where Carpenter's exploitation movie is rather progressive. "Living Dead" ends on a famously cynical note, with Ben shot by white men who mistook him as a threat. In "Precinct 13," Bishop and Napoleon Wilson achieve mutual respect; at the end of the movie, they walk out of the basement together as equals.

After its U.S. theatrical release in 1976, "Assault on Precinct 13" played along the European festival circuit, including the Cannes Film Festival and the London Film Festival. (At the latter, it received "deafening applause" per a contemporary review by The Guardian's Derek Malcolm.) Seeing the movie at Cannes, George Romero paid forward the compliment of Carpenter modeling his movie after "Night of the Living Dead."

The most shocking scene in "Assault on Precinct 13" is when a little girl, Kathy (future reality TV star Kim Richards), is shot in the chest after buying an ice cream cone. It's a jaw-dropping scene, and the movie is clearly having perverse fun turning such a taboo of violence against children into a spectacle and sick joke.

Quoted in Jason Zinoman's "Shock Value: How a Few Eccentric Outsiders Gave Us Nightmares, Conquered Hollywood, and Invented Modern Horror," Romero testified to this scene's impact: "John Carpenter at Cannes wiped us off the face of the earth with 'Precinct 13.' Right from the scene when the little girl gets blown away, I was blown away." (The same book reports that, to get an R instead of an X rating, Carpenter cut the girl's death from the rating review board then added it back in before the film went to theaters.)

This sort of gang violence is echoed in Carpenter's later "Escape From New York," which is all about a future where the gangs like those in "Precinct 13" have taken over the Big Apple. Like "Escape from New York" and many of his other movies, Carpenter also composed the score for "Precinct 13." The title sequence theme, a synthesized anthem of droning dread, is still the most perfect mood setter for an action thriller even 50 years later.

#3532. The Fitbit Edge Is Everything the Charge 6 Should Have Been

I’ve been using the new Fitbit Edge for a little over a week, and am happy to report that it’s quite good at its job. It shipped with more features than I expected (Google Maps directions were there from the jump) and corrects the missteps that Google made with the Fitbit Charge 6. After running the Fitbit Edge through its paces, here’s my breakdown of what works well, what doesn’t, and what I think of the device overall.

When I reviewed it in May 2025, I liked a lot about the Charge 6, but found it had a few serious flaws. Tightening the strap messed up its GPS readings (weird but true), and some of its features required a subscription (like the music controls that only worked with YouTube Music). Its promised side button wasn’t really a button, and didn’t even always work.

I’m happy to report that all of my biggest gripes have been fixed in the Fitbit Edge. Or to put it another way: the Edge is what the Charge should have been in the first place.

Accuracy tests are always one of my top priorities in testing, but honestly I wasn’t expecting much from this device. A Fitbit can still be successful in my eyes even if its heart rate sensor is only “good enough.” Nobody should expect lab-level precision from a Fitbit.

But I was pleasantly surprised by just how capable the Edge is in this regard. It sometimes takes a few minutes to lock on to a heart rate signal (as most optical devices do), but after it does, it is spot-on—I think it might be in the running alongside the Apple Watch and high-end Garmins as one of the better heart rate wearables on the market. The Edge’s accuracy is notably better than the Fitbit Air's, even though they seem to share the same sensor hardware.

Location accuracy is also quite good, only deviating slightly from a Garmin I tested alongside the Edge. It may not be the best out there, but it’s miles ahead of what the Charge 6 was able to do.

The Fitbit Edge has real music controls, unlike the Charge 6. I can play something in Spotify or in Castro (my favorite podcast app) on my phone, and then control the audio from my wrist—and you no longer need to use YouTube Music or have a subscription to get this feature.

When the Fitbit Air and the Google Health app first launched, it was possible to pair both a Fitbit and a Pixel Watch to the same phone, but not two Fitbits. That has finally changed: I was able to connect the Edge to my phone without losing my connection to the Air. It also works to swap seamlessly between the two Fitbits. For example, one night the Edge was low on battery, so I slept with the Air on, and then swapped back in the morning once the Edge was charged. The app happily showed my sleep data from the Air and my activity data from the Edge without my having to do mess around in the app.

As a nice bonus, the charger for the Fitbit Edge is the same as for the Fitbit Air. (The chargers for the Pixel Watch and for the Fitbit Charge 6 are not compatible with the Edge.)

The Fitbit Edge is a similar size as the old Charge 6, but with noticeably more screen real estate. The strap fits pretty much the same way as a Pixel watch band—that is to say, normally, not with the strange hang-off-the-wrist stiffness of the Charge 6.

The Fitbit Edge also has a physical button—not a haptic nub like the Charge 6, but an actual, physical button. And it even works (to return you to the home screen) nearly every time I press it. The Charge 6’s nub was not as reliable.

Overall, I’m quite happy with the Fitbit Edge. It’s much better than the Charge 6, and adds accuracy and a screen to the things I already liked about the Fitbit Air. But there are a few things I don’t totally love.

One is that there is no NFC chipset, which means no option to use Google Pay. I don’t mind using my phone or card at checkouts (and I always carry my phone), so this isn’t a big deal for me, but I know a lot of folks love a wrist-based payment, and that’s missing from the Fitbit Edge. (Google reportedly said most Fitbit users didn’t actually use Google Pay, so they removed the functionality—presumably to fit in the other components while keeping the device small.)

The other downside is, I hate to say it, the Google Health app. It’s OK, but I still find myself arguing with the AI when it assigns me workouts I never asked for, and I have to agree with the redditors who are commiserating about the lack of a “yesterday” view. (On the bright side, Google recently added a feature that lets you turn off the AI insights, which helps a lot.)

Overall, the Fitbit Edge is a great fitness tracker. It measures heart rate and running/walking mileage accurately; it can control music in a sensible way; and it looks good, feels good to wear, and works smoothly. The price also tracks: It’s definitely worth the $20 premium over the Charge 6, and it’s not quite double the price of the Air, which I think is fair. For anyone who doesn’t want a smartwatch or a running watch and will be satisfied with just “a Fitbit,” this one is pretty much perfect.

#3531. As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually

Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing expanding California’s current film and television tax credit program from $750 million to at least $1 billion annually as the state is struggling to attract entertainment industry jobs. The move comes as a report last month by FilmLA found that production levels fell 3.7 percent in the third quarter even as California has continued to enhance its tax credits. Many of the major studios and streamers are headquartered in Los Angeles, which makes the contraction in production jobs more painful.

Last year, Gov. Newsom pushed to increase California’s film and TV incentive from $330 million to $750 million annually, and the state’s film commission saw an initial rise in applications before the number of productions began falling again. California is not only grappling with increased competition from states like New Jersey, New York, and Georgia that offer richer incentives, but they are also facing off against foreign production hubs such as the United Kingdom and Hungary. Related Stories ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them

In a press release, Gov. Newsom said the proposed expansion would include credits for above-the-line talent, as well as rewards for companies that commit to fielding more than one production in California. If enacted, the tax credit will be extended through 2040, which would give companies more certainty about the incentives they can access. The previous incentives were scheduled to last through 2030. It would also increase independent film funding to $100 million annually, up $26 million from the current program.

“California created the modern entertainment industry; we’re the capital of entertainment and we’re going to keep it here,” Newsom said in a statement. “At least $1 billion in tax credits means more investment flowing into our economy and more opportunity across the industry. Through this expansion, we will maintain the momentum and success of our historic expansion last year.”

The governor also urged national lawmakers to pass a federal film and television incentive, which could augment states’ efforts to bolster local production.

“States can’t shoulder the cost alone, which is why I am calling on Congress to back up an expanded tax credit by passing national film and TV tax credit legislation already on the table,” Newsom said.

#3530. WoW: Forever Makes Every Class More Powerful in Last-Minute Change

Blizzard said it had learned from the beta that it hadn't given itself enough 'headroom' to make changes to the classic-style MMO

Blizzard has detailed a final round of fixes and balance changes that it's making to World of Warcraft: Forever, based on feedback from the recent beta, before the retro MMO launches this week. The headline change is both simple and pretty dramatic: every class will do more damage.

In patch notes published on the official WoW forums, the developers explained that they had realized that sticking to the original game's power budgets for each class "meant that every new element we added needed to come at the expense of something else. Those reductions left some iconic abilities feeling lackluster, and closed the door to other potentially exciting design options."

The solution, Blizzard has decided, is to raise damage across every class and increase the health of high-level creatures to compensate. "This additional 'headroom' has allowed us to tune things to a place that we hope feels better overall," the developers said.

The patch notes also include a raft of tuning for a wide range of classes and specs, which Blizzard said was aimed at distinguishing Forever's changes to classic WoW from those made in early expansions The Burning Crusade and Wrath of the Lich King. "Our aim in class design is not perfect numerical equality, but rather for every class to feel valuable to the groups they join, with powerful, unforgettable moments brought on by mastering them," Blizzard said.

The developer said that it would now leave balance alone until Forever's raids open a month after launch, on Dec. 9. Then it will make a "large tuning pass" based on data gathered from the live game, including on players leveling past 30 (the level cap in the beta).

The grassroots reimagining of classic World of Warcraft seems huge, but the team wants to stay small

Other changes in the patch notes include increased creature respawn rates in lower-level zones, to support the "large player volumes" Blizzard expects at launch, and a huge update to WoW: Forever's official gamepad support, which Blizzard reckons has now "entered a complete functional state" in which "all major gameplay and core user interface experiences can be played with a controller."

World of Warcraft: Forever, a reimagined version of classic WoW as it was in 2004 with updates and new content, launches on Nov. 4 (or Nov. 5, depending on your time zone). If the beta is any indication, it's going to be extremely popular.

#3529. Marshals Season 2 Episode 5 Exposes A Major Problem With The Yellowstone Spin-Off

"Marshals" Season 2 Episode 4 ended on a deadly cliffhanger that left the fate of Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Ash Santos' Andrea Cruz unclear. Caught in an explosion, the pair were flung through the air just before the episode cut to black. What would become of Kayce and the character with whom he's clearly developing deep feelings? Well, nothing. The latest "Marshals" installment quickly establishes that they were both fine in what is the latest example of one of the show's most frustrating problems.

It's no secret that Grimes' procedural has struggled to live up to "Yellowstone" and its fellow spin-off "Dutton Ranch." There are many reasons why. For one, "Marshals" Season 1 had no idea what it was about, with the show jumping from premise to premise in an attempt to find its footing and ultimately never succeeding. But there are several other issues with this show, and one of them is its proclivity for building things up only to disappoint viewers in the most unnecessary ways.

Consider the Season 2 premiere. "Marshals" Season 1 ended by having Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton taken captive by investor turned rancher Tom Weaver (Chris Mulkey). Tate was supposedly being shuttled to Texas, where it seemed we might get the first official crossover between "Dutton Ranch" and "Marshals." But in the Season 2 premiere we learned that Tate was having a grand old time fishing on a Wyoming ranch. By the end of the episode, Tom Weaver had been apprehended and Tate was back to barely featuring in the series. Now, we've had yet another cliffhanger undermined and it's starting to get ridiculous.

"Marshals" Season 1 seemed to introduce a love triangle between Kayce Dutton, Andrea Cruz, and Dolly Weaver (Ellyn Jameson). Now that Dolly's out of the picture, however (she died in that disappointing "Marshals" Season 2 premiere), Andrea and Kayce are free to embrace their attraction.

Season 2, Episode 4, "Blast Radius," saw the pair growing closer than ever. Turns out this duo have been executing warrants as an extra-curricular activity to distract them from their sleepless nights. But it's clear there's also a slow-burn romance developing between the two. As such, when they were seemingly blown sky high in the episode's closing moments it looked as though the writers were about to leverage this burgeoning love affair for some dramatic tension. There was no way Kayce was going to die, but perhaps his new love interest's life would be left hanging in the balance?

Nope, they're both fine. Season 2, Episode 5, "Secret Weapon" opens in the immediate aftermath of Rudy Carpenter (Braxton Hale) exploding his bomb in range of Kayce and Andrea. We see the former lying unconscious on the floor, before he wakes up and crawls over to Andrea, who's also coming to. Meanwhile, their fellow Marshals do a sweep of the barn, determine Rudy's gone for good, and after that everything's back to normal. It's a frustrating opening as it calls to mind all the previous "Marshals" cliffhanger moments that have similarly come to nothing.

"Marshals" is a CBS procedural in the vein of "SEAL Team" — the show from which its showrunner Spencer Hudnut hails. As such, we know there's a case-of-the-week format, and we know that a network show isn't necessarily beholden to the production values of, say, an HBO drama. But is there any rule that states the show has to be made with the dimmest possible audience members in mind?

"Marshals" keeps reiterating the plot of each episode in the simplest terms possible, with the latest example coming in "Secret Weapon." After the team finds tire tracks near the barn where Rudy Carpenter died, it becomes clear that someone other than Carpenter is transporting missing bombs elsewhere. Pete Calvin (Logan Marshall-Green) then announces, "Someone's driving this bomb around right now and we got no idea what the target is." Is this like the Netflix thing where they assume people are on their phones and aren't paying close enough attention?

These frequent consequence-free cliffhangers are another aspect of "Marshals" that gives the sense of a show doing an impression of a better show. It's like the writers know cliffhangers can be compelling, but don't want to cause any actual distress to an audience they evidently assume is made up of phone-addicted simpletons barely following the plot. So, we get these half-baked moments of tension, after which nothing changes. Remember when "Marshals" Season 1 introduced a powerful Dutton family rival who'd apparently been at odds with Kayce's family for generations, only for that same rival to be arrested several episodes later, never to be heard from again? It's the same thing. A threat arises, then it's neutralized. I get that "Marshals" isn't "Yellowstone." But does that mean it has to be bad?

#3528. If You Loved 'Crystal Lake,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Peacock’s Crystal Lake is an unexpected treat in a lot of ways, taking one of horror’s most iconic figures—Jason Voorhees of the Friday the 13th franchise—and digging into the universe’s background by focusing on his mother, Pamela. Famously the actual serial killer in the original film, Pamela’s development into a psychotic killer who inspired her son to become the psychotic killer of all time is the engine that drives Crystal Lake, finding the damaged humanity behind the terror. If you’ve burned through all eight episodes of Crystal Lake’s first season, and you’ve worked through the streamalike series with similar DNA, it’s time to check out some movies—starting with the perfect companion film, 2022’s Pearl.

The second film in Ti West’s X trilogy (starting with X and concluding with 2024’s MaXXXine) is the ideal film to watch after Crystal Lake. Like the series, it explores a female serial killer’s backstory and recontextualizes your understanding of their motives and psychology. It also requires that you be familiar with the original story—while you can certainly watch Crystal Lake or Pearl without having seen the Friday the 13th films or X, you’ll be missing out on a lot if you do.

In X, a group of young people descends on a dilapidated old farm to film an adult movie in Texas in 1979, and by the end of the film most of them are dead, killed by the farm’s elderly couple Howard (Stephen Ure) and Pearl (Mia Goth), with Pearl presented as the most deranged and dangerous of the two. It’s a riveting update to the classic splatter movie template, and Goth nails her dual role as the Final Girl Maxine and the psychotic, murderous Pearl. The prequel, Pearl, jumps back to 1918, when Pearl (Goth again) was a young woman living with her strict mother and paralyzed father. Pearl has big dreams of being an entertainer, but her mother tries to trap her to ensure she’s there to care for her parents and work the farm. Pearl’s lonely unhappiness and frustration (both mental and, er, physical) inspire a slow boil of tension as her grip on sanity frays, and her anger toward her parents curdles into something frightening.

Like Crystal Lake, Pearl takes a killer who seems fairly one-dimensional in their original presentation and gives them a deeper back story and psychological framing. Pamela Voorhees wasn’t just crazy—she was driven to madness by the horrible things that happened to her and her son, and the awful way she’s treated by her fellow humans. Similarly, Pearl is a hopeful and innocent young woman who is slowly molded into a killer by the events of her life. Both the series and the film serve as reminders that monsters are rarely born—they’re made. And it’s usually the casual cruelty of the people around them that does the making. If you loved Crystal Lake’s fresh take on Pamela, Pearl is the perfect choice for a movie night. Stream Pearl on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Need more serial killer movies that hit the Crystal Lake vibe? Never fear—here are some other excellent choices to pair with the series.

If you’ve never actually seen the original Friday the 13th (or if it’s been a while), this is a must-watch for fans of Crystal Lake. Although the series takes some liberties to update the timeline, it’s still intended as a glimpse into the events that shaped both Pamela and Jason Voorhees into inhuman (and somewhat supernatural) monsters. Initially given savagely bad reviews, the film was a surprise blockbuster and is now regarded as a classic of a genre it helped to create in the first place; rewatching it today not only helps contextualize Crystal Lake, it puts the entire slasher genre into perspective. Stream Friday the 13th on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

The success of Friday the 13th led to a rush of copycat films, of course. Most of those weren’t particularly good or even interesting, but Sleepaway Camp is an exception (although it was similarly savaged by critics at the time). Now a cult classic, Sleepaway Camp has two things that recommend it to fans of Crystal Lake and Friday the 13th: a weird sensibility that gives it an otherworldly atmosphere that enhances the sense of dread, and what is probably the most unexpected twist ending in the history of slasher films (and it’s probably a Top 10 twist in general). Stream Sleepaway Camp on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

One reason Crystal Lake exists is the enduring power and influence of slasher films in general and Friday the 13th specifically. Few recent films have tapped into that dreamy nightmare feel like Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. As with most of Schoenbrun’s work, the film delves into themes of identity, subverting queer tropes, and the malleable nature of reality itself. If you’re looking for a slasher story that’s less straightforward than Crystal Lake while dealing with some similar themes of transformation and destiny, this is it. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

If you’ve seen all the Friday the 13th movies and want more slasher horror with a bit more edge, check out The Burning. Is it a great film? Not really. Combining the straightforward slasher thrills of Friday with some of the villain motivations of fellow classic franchise A Nightmare on Elm Street, The Burning dials the blood and guts up to 11 (and beyond) and remains notoriously gory even by today’s standards. But if your fave part of Crystal Lake is the frequently over-the-top gore and violence, this is an ideal movie choice. Stream The Burning on The Roku Channel or Kanopy.

Want a slasher film that explores the psyche of a female killer the way Crystal Lake deconstructs Pamela Voorhees? Check out May. A fragile young woman, May struggles to find connection with the people around her, and slowly descends into a fantasy world that inspires her to literally make her own ideal friend. What makes May so interesting is the depth of the exploration of May’s personality that’s similar to how Pamela is handled in Crystal Lake, tracing each step of her stumble into a bloody hell. Stream May on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

#3527. Netflix Will Give Joel Coen’s Gothic Mystery ‘Jack of Spades’ a Theatrical Release in 2027

Joel Coen is heading back to Netflix. After taking his 2021 “The Tragedy of Macbeth” to A24, the filmmaker is bringing his latest solo directorial outing back to Netflix, where he last teamed with brother Ethan Coen on the 2018 release “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.” Rest assured, however, while Ethan is not sharing directing duties with his big brother again, he did co-write the film‘s script alongside Joel, novelist and screenwriter Eleanor Catton, and playwright and screenwriter Conor McPherson.

The new film is called “Jack of Spades,” and the streamer will give it a theatrical release in the fall of 2027 ahead of its debut on Netflix. The film is based on Frances Frederica Montrésor’s 1901 novel “The Alien: A Story of Middle Age” and its official logline reads: “A sinister gothic mystery filled with intrigue and betrayal set in the atmospheric Scottish Highlands.” Related Stories ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them

The film will star Olivier Award winner Patsy Ferran, BAFTA nominee and Golden Globe winner Josh O’Connor, BAFTA nominee and Golden Globe winner Damian Lewis, and Oscar nominee Lesley Manville.

The book itself is billed as “a thoughtful pick for readers who enjoy character-driven fiction with a touch of wanderlust and a battle between integrity and longing.” Montrésor’s novel follows Esther Mordaunt, “now well into her thirties by the story’s start” and “follows her evolving bond with Jasper, a traveler with a vivid past and a talent for storytelling. Through his tales of sailing, revolutions, and distant lands, the book explores how a single life can stretch across time, risk, and longing without losing its humanity.”

Coen will also reunite with Oscar-nominated cinematographer Bruno Delbonnel (“Inside Llewyn Davis”) and composer Carter Burwell (“Fargo,” “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs”). The film will be produced by Robert Graf, Frances McDormand, Coen, Steven Rales, Graham Broadbent, and Pete Czernin, and executive produced by Donald MacKinnon.

#3526. The Greatest Crime Epic's Final Line Officially Changed the Genre

After nearly three and a half hours of bloodshed, betrayal, and thorny interpersonal relationships, Killers of the Flower Moon ended with a bang, but not in the traditional sense one would typically expect from a crime epic. Martin Scorsese's historical saga about a coordinated genocide of members of the Osage nation in Oklahoma is a complex, dense, and aggressively challenging film that forces the viewer to reckon with the director's beloved filmography. Everyone who adores Taxi Driver and Goodfellas may find themselves the subject of criticism in Killers of the Flower Moon's ending, which features a stunning cameo by none other than Scorsese himself, who plays a presenter in a radio play years after the events of the movie. In a film ripe with stellar performances by Leonardo DiCaprio, Robert De Niro, and breakout star Lily Gladstone, Scorsese's final line, in which he reveals that "there was no mention of the murders," is its most powerful line delivery and a damning indictment of the glorification of crime on the big screen, especially by Scorsese himself.

The cheery pomp and circumstance of Killers of the Flower Moon's final set piece is a jarring sight to see, as it's capping off roughly 200 minutes of existential dread and dour confrontations with death. With a huge portion of the Osage nation being wiped out and deprived of their family fortune by William Hale (De Niro), the ailing health of the film's heart, Mollie Burkhart (Gladstone), and the extreme guilt harbored by Ernest Burkhart (DiCaprio), the events are simply too morose for a lively radio play to adapt straightforwardly.

This epilogue, which tracks how our major characters lived out the rest of their lives, takes a stark turn when an older presenter, played by Scorsese, reads Mollie's obituary. There is one staggering omission, which Scorsese reveals to the crowd and sends shockwaves through the audience. "There was no mention of the murders," he announces, referring to the tragic slayings of Mollie's family and loved ones carried out by Hale and his team of assassins. The film ultimately concludes with an unbroken overhead shot of a present-day Osage gathering, where they perform a song and dance ritual. The profundity of Scorsese's performance and the magnitude of the final shot combine to make Killers of the Flower Moon perhaps the director's most emotionally sweeping movie yet.

Martin Scorsese's cameo in Killers of the Flower Moon, from a formalist perspective, is one of the director's most audacious moves to date. Blending the line between narrative and documentary, the choice reflects the director and co-writer Eric Roth's decision to shift the story away from the FBI's investigation, the primary focus of David Grann's true crime book of the same name, and towards the interpersonal dynamics between Ernest, Mollie, and Hale. By focusing on the investigation of the murders, a mystery that's hardly cryptic when watching the film's banality of evil, you lose sight of the people who had their lives cut short by greed and power. In turn, more focus (leading to inherent glorification) is given to the heinous murderers rather than the victims, who, like the Osage people, were rich with values, culture, tradition, and economic prosperity that America supposedly celebrates. Considering the relative obscurity of the Osage murders before Flower Moon, it's no surprise that Mollie's obituary would omit the harsh truth of her family’s mass execution by greedy white settlers.

Many would argue that Scorsese's condemnation of our densensitized relationship to crime is throwing stones from a glass house, as the filmmaker's seven-decade career has been partly defined by his intoxicating and captivating depiction of the criminal underworld. Even though his films underline the dark side of crime in the third act, he argues that the often fun and rewarding nature of being a wiseguy is why everyday human beings commit grave sins. However, in the most personal and self-reflective moment of his career, Flower Moon's final line indirectly suggests that Scorsese has some culpability in this media climate of romanticizing and forgiving criminals and neglecting victims, a moment that wouldn't carry the same punch without the director appearing on-screen. The somber conclusion, leading to the Osage ritual, is perhaps a wake-up call to the industry, as Flower Moon should probably be the last time a white filmmaker tackles stories about Indigenous people and their history.

Martin Scorsese has another movie (and hopefully more) in production, but the final line in Killers of the Flower Moon is a perfect capstone to his career that addresses his recurring themes and engages with criticisms he's faced going back to Taxi Driver. Unfortunately, no matter how hard he reminds us to remember the murders of the Osage Nation, the legend continues to be printed, and legends cover up America's dark history.
