#3525. ‘Loser Core,’ ‘EBK,’ and Other Gen Z and Gen Alpha Slang You Might Need Help Decoding

If constantly being mogged by sigmas has you feeling like a fuhuhluhtoogan, and you have no idea what any of that means, you've come to the right place. This glossary aims to define and explain popular slang words and phrases of Generation Z (usually defined as people born between 1997 and 2012) and Generation A (anyone born between 2012 and now) so you'll know what the hell people are talking about.

A word of warning: If you aren't of those generations, and/or you need an online list to know what slang words mean, you should not say them aloud unless you're trying to be embarrassing.

Ballhog: A fashion trend among Gen Z and Gen A characterized by wearing vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique retro clothing.

Benny tripping: Intentionally overdosing on Benadryl to experience an (almost always unpleasant) "trip."

Crunged: The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

EBK: stands for "Extreme Baller Knowledge." It goes beyond the sports reference to apply to to anyone who has deep knowledge of a subject. It's usually used ironically.

GiGis: Good game. Pronounced like the name Gigi. The post game pleasantry "good game" has been a staple in sports since forever. Gamers adopted it and shortened it to "GG" in text. So GiGis is a way of saying "good game."

Glass skin: Describes skin that is so smooth, luminous, and clear, it seems to shine.

Loser core: A youth sub-culture/musical sub-genre categorized by listening to depressing, alternative-inspired music and dressing in drab, oversize clothing.

304: Hoe. (Type "304" on a calculator and turn it upside down.)

4+4: Ate. Four plus four is eight, or "ate." (See "ate.")

6-7 (or 67): This piece of Generation Alpha brainrot slang doesn't mean anything. It's just funny to some people to say "6-7," especially in answer to any question involving numbers. Ex: "Q: What time is it? A: six-seveeen."

6-7 weekend: A weekend in which Saturday falls on the 6th day of the month and Sunday on the 7th.

7x7=49: Often refers to a man who is attractive in a self-evident way. Based on the belief that the equation 7x7=49 makes intuitive sense in a way other equations do not.

80/20 rule: An axiom in online incel spaces, the 80/20 is the idea that 80% of women only date the "top" 20% of men.

Algo speak: Coded language used to bypass online content moderation. Examples: "regarded" used instead of "retarded" and "unalive" instead of "kill."

Alpha male: Taken from animal ethology, an alpha male is the dominant member of a group of males, or just a male who is in charge. (See "beta male" and "sigma male.")

Alpine divorce: An alpine divorce is when a man takes his wife or girlfriend on a hike, usually in the mountains, and then just leaves her there to fend for herself.

ASAP (or A$AP): When a rapper has ASAP or A$AP in front of their name, it indicates affiliation with the ASAP Mob, a New York hip-hop collective.

Ate/eat: Done very well, often regarding clothing. e.g.: "You ate that outfit." See also: "serving."

Aura: Someone who is mysterious and cool is said to "have aura."

Aura battle: Aura is coolness or charisma ("rizz" if you prefer). An "aura battle" is a public contest in which the person with the most aura, as determined by the crowd and/or comment section reaction, wins. (See "Aura")

Aura farming: Depending on the context, “aura farming” can refer to a person who does something cool without trying or someone who is trying too hard to appear cool.

Baby Boo syndrome: A joking reference to people who are very into the Baby Boo memes popular on TikTok.

Baddie: A bad/wild girl. Meant as a compliment.

Baka: Japanese word meaning “crazy" or “foolish.” Used mainly in the anime community.

Bed-rotting: Staying in bed all day. You may know it as “lazing around.” (See "Hurkle-durkle.")

Beez: Popularized in Nicki Minaj's 2012 track "Beez in the Trap," beez means something like "I am always." So "beez in the trap" means "I am always in the trap." (See "Trap.")

Beta male: A beta male, or just "beta," is a weaker, subservient male. (See "alpha male" and "sigma male.")

Boombayah: A euphemism for having sex. It’s used mostly online, often to defeat censorship algorithms.

Bop: A girl who sleeps around. Also: a great song.

Boy aquarium: TikTok slang that describes hockey games.

Boy kibble: The male response to "girl dinner," boy kibble is food boys eat. It usually consists of rice and ground beef, often served without spices or vegetables.

Boysober: Someone who has sworn off sex, relationships, and/or dating.

Brain-rot: A description of the overuse of stupid slang. See also: “Skibidi.” Also used to describe the effects of being overly online.

Brat: The contemporary meaning of "brat" is an adjective describing a person who is edgy, imperfect, and confident. It was coined by pop star Charli XCX who defined it as "that girl who is a little messy and likes to party and maybe says some dumb things sometimes. Who feels herself but maybe also has a breakdown."

Bruzz: Bros. Part of the -uzz family of slang words. See "Huzz" and "-uzz."

Bubba truck: A lifted or otherwise modified pick-up truck.

Catch a fade: To have a fight. (See "fade.")

Chad: An attractive man; an “alpha male.” See "Giga-Chad."

Chat: A reference to streamers addressing their chat windows aloud. Saying “chat” in real life is an ironic joke.

Cheesin': The slang word "cheesin'" refers to smiling, particularly a big, goofy smile. It comes from the common exhortation to "say cheese!" before a photo is taken. The word "cheesing," with a "g" at the end, often means the same thing, but it can also refer to the trend of throwing slices of cheese at cars and/or people.

Chopped: Ugly. Chopped is often applied to someone's face or outfit, but anything that isn't aesthetically pleasing could be called "chopped," as could anything that is generally not good, like an awkward situation.

Choppelganger: A portmanteau of "chopped" and "doppelgänger," a choppelganger is someone who looks like another person, but worse. (See "chopped.")

Chud: A physically unappealing person. Sometimes used for a man who holds right-wing views.

Clanker: A slur aimed at robots and AI agents pretending to be human.

Clock that: "I understand and agree." Not to be confused with older slang, where "clock" meant to see, or even older slang where "clock" meant "to hit or punch."

Corn: “Corn” is algo-speak that means “porn.” Used in online spaces where the word might cause your account to be flagged or banned.

Cortisol-coded: Describes something that's meant to be relaxing but is actually stressful, like watching a video of the 5 a.m. yoga routine of an influencer surrounded by $400 candles.

Coworker-core: A catch-all description for things that are unfunny or uninteresting in a way that appeals to older people.

Cracked: This slang term has two meanings: to have sex, as in "I got cracked last night," and to be really good at something, like "he’s cracked at Fortnite."

Crashout: To have an intense emotional outburst, usually accompanied by impulsive behavior. Crashing out is often due to being overwhelmed or overly frustrated.

D1 Crashout: An epic, elite level, extreme crashout. (See "crashout.)

Dah Bih Gah: "That bitch good," ie: "I like that thing." Usually used to describe food.

Dah Bih Tah: "That bitch tough," ie: "I like that thing." Usually used to describe food.

Dead: Past tense of having died laughing. If someone responds to a joke with "dead" or a skull emoji, they find it funny.

Deadass: Seriously. Used like, "I am deadass not lying."

Deriod: A combination of "dick" and "period," deriod refers to men seeming to experience the mood swings commonly associated with women's menstrual cycles.

Dih: Algo speak for “dick.” (See "Algo speak.")

Doi doi doi: This piece of brain-rot slang doesn't mean anything. It's correctly pronounced by putting your hand up to your mouth and saying "doi doi doi" in a way that sounds funny.

Doomer: A person who is overly negative and/or cynical.

Dwerking: A male-centric variation of twerking. A sexually suggestive dancing characterized by rapid, repeated hip thrusts and shaking of the dick. Other variants include "pwerking" and "bwerking" where the "p" and "b" stand for pussy and boobs.

Edgar: A variation of the Caesar haircut worn especially among Hispanic males. Also refers to the kind of person who wears the haircut.

Fambushing: A combination of "family" and "ambushing," fambushing refers to young people checking where their parents are on location-sharing apps so they can get free food—if you see mom at Chipotle, you ask for a burrito.

Fanum tax: The theft of food between friends. Named for streamer Fanum, known for “taxing” his friends by taking bites of their meals or stealing fries.

Fax, no printer: Telling the truth. Since "fax" and "facts" are pronounced the same, this is a colorful way of saying "facts, no cap."

Fent-fold: A description of the bent-over posture of people nodding on heavy drugs.

Fuhuhluhtoogan: Supposedly from Baltimore slang, this is a nonsense word used so people will ask what it means but never receive an answer. Often paired with "Jittleyang."

Fujoshing: The verb form of the Japanese slang term "fujoshi," fujoshing describes women/girls enjoying media that depicts romantic relationships between men. This word is used almost exclusively in online fandom communities.

Gamer dent: The temporary indentation left on someone’s hair or skin after wearing headphones for too long.

Glaze: To overly praise someone, often insincerely, or with the hope of getting something in return.

Gleek: An older slang term that is gaining prominence lately, gleeking describes squirting saliva from under the tongue.

Glizzy: Hot dog. "Glizzy" was originally slang for Glock or gun, but came to mean hot dog based on the hot dog shape of a Glock's magazine.

Green fn: An interjection one might used when someone does something cool or impressive. Often used ironically.

Goonbait: (See "gooning") Goonbait is, essentially, media that exists to inspiring gooning.

Gooner: A man who goons. (See "gooning.")

Goonette: A woman who goons. (See "gooning.")

Gooning: Extended masturbation without orgasm done for the purpose of entering an altered state of consciousness. (See "gooner," "goonette.")

Gyatt or Gyat: Once an interjection used when seeing someone sexy, like “god-DAMN,” “gyatt” has come to mean “attractive booty.”

Heavy soda: Pop with extra syrup. Some gas station soda machines have settings that control the ratio of syrup to carbonated water. A heavy soda is a soda with the syrup level set very high.

Hewwo: An overly cute way of saying "hello." Usually used online, and often ironically.

HGS: Abbreviation for "home girls" used in comment sections.

Hiplet: Derogatory slang for a woman who has "hip dips," i.e. inward curves on their outer thighs just below the hip bone.

Hozier yell: Named for singer/songwriter Andrew Hozier, a "Hozier yell" refers to the sound one makes when experiencing a peak, climactic, and/or awe-inspiring moment.

HTN: This acronym comes from the online incel community, where fairly good-looking men are described as "high-tier normies" or "HTN." (See "normie.")

Hurkle-durkle: Based on an archaic Scottish word, “hurkle-durkle” means to lounge in bed after it is time to get up. See also: “bed-rotting."

Huzz: -uzz slang for "hoes." See "bruzz" and "-uzz."

"It's giving": Used to convey that something has a specific vibe. Example: "That dude texts you every 10 minutes; it's giving desperate."

"It's so over": The situation is hopeless. The opposite of "we're so back." See also: "Doomer."

IWEL: This comment-section acronym is short for "I wouldn't even lie." Sometimes written as "IWL."

Jelqing: The use of stretching or weights in an attempt to increase penis size.

Jittleyang: Supposedly from Baltimore slang, this is a nonsense word used so people will ask what it means but never receive an answer. See also: "Fuhuhluhtoogan."

JOMO: A play on FOMO (fear of missing out) JOMO is an acronym that stands for “joy of missing out.”

"Learn Chinese": Sports slang directed at failing players. They are in danger of being sent to play in China, so they should "learn Chinese."

Loaded water: Water enhanced with something—a flavor boost, fruit juice, electrolytes, carbonation, and even vitamins or prebiotics. The idea is to increase hydration by making water more palatable.

Looksmaxxing: Maximizing one’s physical attractiveness through personal grooming, working out, and dressing stylishly. See also: “-maxxing.”

🪫 (low battery emoji): The low battery emoji means "I am experiencing emotional depletion, heartbreak, or a general feeling of 'I can't anymore.'"

Lowkenuinely: This mash-up of "low key" and "genuinely" expresses sincerity but in a way that says "let's not make a big deal about it."

Lucky Scoops: Lucky Scoops are a kind of TikTok or Instagram video where buyers purchase a scoop that represents a chance to win merchandise. These videos are very popular with children; critics feel like they are a form of gambling.

Mason (or Mason 6-7 kid): A "Mason 6-7 Kid" or "Mason" is a stereotypical male member of Generation Alpha. Mason kids are known for their love of baseball-inspired fashion (caps and shorts), their "ice cream" haircut, and for repeating brainrot slang like "6-7."

-maxxing: A suffix used with any word to indicate trying to improve. Seeing your friends could be called "friendmaxxing," working out could be called "gymmaxxing," making jokes could be called "jestermaxxing," etc.

Mewing: A facial exercise meant to strengthen the jawline.

Mirror sex: Using a mirror to watch yourself have sex.

Misery girl: A young woman with piercings, a penchant for the darkly dramatic, and highly stylized makeup that makes them appear to have a skinny, pointy nose and huge eyes and lips.

Mog: To be more attractive than someone, usually in an intentional or aggressive way. Example: "I was rizzing up this girl, but he walked in and totally mogged me."

"My 90 in a 30": A song played while driving that inspires speeding.

"My steak is too juicy": The phrase "my steak is too juicy" and other variants like "my lobster is too buttery," are online insults that suggest someone is complaining about something they should be grateful for.

Neurospicy: A different way of saying “neuro-divergent.”

Normie: A person who is considered normal or average. It's sometimes an insult suggesting someone is boring and witless. (see also, "mid.")

NPC: Non-player character. Originally describing video game characters, NPC is now used on the internet to mean people who don't think for themselves.

Opp: Short for "opposition." Someone who is out to get you. An enemy.

Performative male: An insult for young men whose tastes, hobbies, and lifestyle are seen as a performance aimed at obtaining societal approval, especially the approval of young women.

Pheromone maxxing: Trying to influence the behaviors of others through your stink. Supposedly, young men in the "looksmaxxing" community are skipping showers and not washing their clothing in an attempt to make young women like them more. (See "-maxxing").

Phonk: The word phonk can refer to one of two musical sub-genres. It originally referred to throwback '90s hip-hop categorized by slow-tempo "chopped and screwed" production and vintage Memphis rap vocals. It now more commonly describes the heavily distorted, up-tempo EDM used in brainrot videos.

Pink cocaine: Also known as "pink snow," pink cocaine is slang for a powdered drug mixture that usually contains some combination of ketamine, MDMA, meth, opioids, and other substances.

"Press F for respect:" In 2014 video game Call of Duty: Advanced Warfighter, the player attends a funeral and a prompt is given that reads "Press F to pay respects." Now, a singular "F" in a chat window indicates respect. It's usually ironic.

Quiet on the creek: A fishing-inspired way to say "keep it on the down low" or "be cool."

Rawdogging boredom: Rawdogging is "doing something with no safeguards or support," so "rawdogging boredom" is consciously doing nothing.

Regarded: “Regarded” is algo-speak for “retarded."

RegencyCore: A fashion and design aesthetic that springs from the popularity of the fantasy-regency era look of the Netflix show Bridgerton, RegencyCore combines the opulent style of the British Regency era of the early 1800s with fantasy elements like pastel colors and gold accents.

"Reheating your own nachos:" This slang phrase comes from cultural critics in online fandom communities. It refers to performers and/or artists whose new works are seen as trying to recapture what was good about their previous artistic output. It's not always negative; it's possible to successfully reheat your own nachos.

Rizz: As a noun, "rizz" means charisma. As a verb, "rizz" or "rizz up" means attracting someone with your charisma.

Scientology speedrun: Young people running into a Scientology building and acting foolish until they are ejected.

Scorigami: A slang term among football fans for when the final score of an NFL game has never happened before in the league's history. The most recent scorigami was on September 28, 2025, when the Green Bay Packers and Dallas Cowboys tied 40 to 40.

SDIYBT: An acronym for "start digging in your butt, twin," this brainrot phrase doesn't mean anything. Some people just think it's funny to say.

Sendy and “Let’s get sendy": Sendy is an adjective based on the older rock-climbing and extreme sports slang phrase "send it." A shortened version of "ascend it," "send it" is said right before one is about to do something challenging. "Sendy" describes a person who is prone to doing bold things. "Let's get sendy" means something like "Let's get wild." It's been adopted by brainrot fans, so it's often repeated with no meaning meant to be attached.

Serve: Wearing a particularly stylish outfit. See also: "ate."

Serve cunt: To act in a powerfully and unapologetically feminine way; to slay.

Sharking: Looking for people to hook up with.

Side quest: A side quest in a video game is a quest that is not necessary to complete the game's main objective. In slang, a side quest is anything you do in life just for the experience of doing it.

Sigma male: An internet-created male classification, a "sigma male" is as dominant as an alpha male, but is outside the male hierarchy, i.e.: a lone wolf. Originally used seriously, the concept was so widely derided it's now almost always used ironically. (See "Alpha male" and "Beta male.")

Skibidi: Named after “Skibidi Toilet,” a popular series of YouTube videos, “skibidi” itself has no specific meaning, beyond ridiculing the overuse of slang itself. See “brain-rot.”

Skrt: Onomatopoetic word for the sound of tires squealing upon acceleration.

Slopcore: This term describes the countless 100s of millions of cheesy-looking, unsettling, AI-generated images, videos, and songs that have hit the internet since AI was given to the masses a couple of years ago.

Slopper: Insult directed at people who use AI programs too much, people who takes conversations with LLMs too seriously, and people who have basically offloaded their thinking to an algorithm.

Snatched: Very attractive and/or flawlessly styled.

Spawn point: Mother. Based on the spot you start in a video game.

Surf Dracula: A hyper-specific phrase that describes "prestige" television series. The joke is that if there were an older TV show called "Surf Dracula," Dracula would be surfing in every episode, but modern shows would make the whole first season about how Dracula got his surfboard.

Sweat: A person who tries too hard, usually used in reference to video games. The adjective form is "sweaty."

SYBAU: An online acronym that stands for “shut your bitch ass up.”

That's AI: "I don't believe you" or "I doubt it," even when not connected to artificial intelligence.

TLPUR: This supposed acronym section has no meaning. The joke is to tell people it means something like "True Love Pills Until Rope" or "Too Late for Puberty."

Tradwife: Believer in traditional married gender roles.

Trap: Once used to refer to a house where drugs are sold, trap has come to describe both a form of music and any place where one works or hustles.

Treatler (and Treatlerite): "Treatler" and "Treatlerite" are online insults that combine "treat" and "Hitler" to refer to entitled users of services like Doordash or Uber Eats who regard luxury delivery services as a human right, and don't consider the hardships of the people who do the work that makes "private taxis for burritos" possible.

TS: TS originally was AAVE shorthand for "this shit," but it is often used to just mean "this."

Turnt: Excited or intoxicated, or excitedly intoxicated.

Tweaking: In older slang, "tweaking" referred to the nervous and erratic actions of someone on drugs, specifically, speed. Generations A and Z have expanded the definition to refer to any actions that are erratic, or even just mildly energetic, not necessarily related to drug use.

Tylenol baby: After President Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a scientifically dubious link between the active ingredient in Tylenol and autism, kids have been calling each other "Tylenol babies."

Unc: Short for "uncle," used to describe slightly older people. Example: "The class of 2024 are unc-status to the class of 2028." See "yunc."

-uzz: -uzz slang words use "uzz" at the end of any word, so "bros" becomes "bruzz," "hoes" becomes "huzz," "granny" becomes "gruzz," etc.

"We're so back": Opposite of "it's so over."

Venus tummy: When a woman's belly is a little fat, but not too fat, she is said to have a Venus tummy. Named for ancient Greek statues of Venus and Aphrodite who were a little fleshy.

Viking rap: A musical sub-genre consisting of AI-generated Vikings rapping about longboats, raiding, and other Viking things.

Wojack: The name of a style of internet drawings used to quickly stereotype someone. See this post for a full explanation of the Wojak universe.

Yapping: Describes a presentational style often seen on online streams of talking a lot and/or quickly while not saying anything worthwhile.

You the birthday: A phrase that means "you're awesome" or "you're great" in the way a birthday is great: fun, exciting, extra, etc.

Young ho: "Young ho" is both a reclamation of the word "ho" and an expression of youth-based solidarity. Young women are posting videos of themselves defining what makes them "young hos," noting things like "Getting up at 7:50 to be at work at 8," and air-frying chicken nuggets.

Yunc: Yunc is a variation of "unc." In AAVE, a "yn" is a "young n-word." So "yunc" means something like "young uncle," or a person who may be young but has uncle vibes or unc status.

Zoomer Perm: A curly on top, short on the sides haircut popular among young people.

#3524. ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year

When I first thought, “Is ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ the funniest show on television?”, I worried saying as much would be damning the uproarious NBC sitcom with faint praise. After all, the modern TV landscape is awash with crime shows, genre mash-ups, and I.P. brand extensions. Bad comedies abound (and tend to be mercifully easy to spot), but great ones? Hmm. At least the most recent Emmy winner for Best Comedy Series is an actual comedy, but the nominees (including a feel-good weeper, a rom-com heavy on the rom, and that cooking drama) were still emblematic of a Hollywood era when laughs aren’t the top priority. Related Stories As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually ‘Who Killed Alex Odeh?’ Review: A Scattered but Searing Documentary Examines America’s Tacit Acceptance of Anti-Arab Discrimination

So, returning to the original question, how many funny funny shows actually came out this year?

Turns out, quite a few. “Adults” jumps to mind among recent releases for its successful Season 2 evolution into a hang-worthy Gen-Z hangout sitcom. “Colin From Accounts” capped a three-year run that saw the Aussie romantic-comedy get stronger every season. “Youth” has Sharon Horgan back at the top of her game (let’s not speak of “Bad Sisters” Season 2), and “The Comeback” did the impossible by delivering a worthy successor to one of HBO’s greatest-ever TV seasons. Then there’s trusty comedy staples like “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia” and “Abbott Elementary,” which don’t need another crossover to keep us laughing, as well as the half-comedies that feel full to anyone with the same funny bone, like “The Lowdown” (a noir comedy), “The Audacity” (a black-comic drama), and “Trying” (a family comedy). I didn’t even mention the final season of “Hacks” (which is great) or the first (and hopefully final) season of “The Hawk” (which is not).

Following fallen NFL running back Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan), decades after he’s ousted from the league for gambling, Season 2 picks up amid incremental progress toward his crowning redemption: making the Pro Football Hall of Fame. His documentarian, Arthur Tobin (Daniel Radcliffe), is still searching for the right angle to support their comeback film (Arthur needs it as much as Reggie wants it), while Reggie’s agent and ex-wife Monica (Erika Alexander) tries to build on the little momentum they gained at the end of last season (when Reggie earned his first votes ever).

The irresistible ensemble doesn’t have a weak link. The staging is vibrant. The writing is as happy to delve into topical subject matter (like documentary subjects paying their documentarians) as it is to revel in carefree absurdity (like a harebrained murder-conspiracy or calamitous Thanksgiving gathering). And every element of it is always focused on being funny. Not only is Robert Carlock and Sam Means’ NBC sitcom designed to squeeze in as many jokes as the human brain can process in 21-minute chunks, it’s also carefully paced and polished to keep those jokes as superb and surprising as possible.

Take a check-your-phone-and-you’ll-miss-it gag from the Season 2 premiere: Monica is struggling to keep up with the media landscape’s sprawling marketing opportunities and admits she booked Reggie on the wrong show: She mixed up Pablo Torres’ sports podcast with Julio Torres’ “something.” Quick cut to Julio (as himself) interviewing Reggie about “the color clear.” There’s a laugh in recognizing Monica’s mistake, another laugh in Julio’s question (“What do you think about the color clear?”), and another laugh in Reggie’s response (“A lot!”).

But rather than one joke stepping on the next, they amplify one another. Monica’s explanation is given the most space to land, since technically it’s setting up the cutaway jokes to come. Those jokes hit one after the next, but in a rhythm that makes them easy to process independently. They’re calibrated to keep you laughing all the way through, but they’re not so rushed that you feel overwhelmed instead of entertained.

That’s the magic (or maybe the math) behind what’s recognized as Tina Fey (an EP on “Dinkins”) and Robert Carlock’s comedy style, as established by their landmark sitcom, “30 Rock” and extended more successfully than not in comedies like “Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt” (where they picked up Radcliffe), “Great News,” “Mr. Mayor,” and “Girls5Eva.” Carlock continues it here with Means, who worked on all those shows, while relying on their proven bonds with Morgan, Radcliffe, and stealth MVP Bobby Moynihan to maintain the right balance. (Moynihan’s understanding of tone and timing is impeccable, and he’s such a joyful presence it’s hard not to smile whenever Rusty surfaces.)

The Season 2 premiere illustrates the trust the writers’ have in their entire acting company. The story still pivots around Morgan’s lovable doofus, but the emphasis is elsewhere. Arthur is dying for the family to find out about Reggie’s son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall) and his secret relationship with Delilah Basmati (Arica Himmel), daughter of Reggie’s nemesis, Jerry Basmati (Craig Robinson). Brina (Precious Way) gets close, while Monica is busy hiring a new assistant “head of publicity” to help her tap into younger markets with a broader reach. Moynihan’s Rusty is everywhere, chipping in enough quips, reaction shots, and physical comedy to convey his supportive yet integral presence in each character’s life.

By the time our original dynamic duo gets a cathartic moment near the episode’s end, it’s hard not to notice that Reggie and Arthur almost feel like an afterthought — and that’s just fine. They take back control in the ensuing episodes, after “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” proves it can thrive no matter who gets to press the most buttons. The joke-delivery machine is operating at peak volume, and it needs every capable hand to keep its performance at the same incredible sweep.

With only four episodes screened for review, there’s plenty of time for Season 2 to break down. The charming vibe could fade, the sharp jokes could soften, the elastic performances could calcify. But not only does Carlock and co.’s lengthy track record suggest the opposite trajectory, so does the excitement shown in creating this specific project. You can feel it in the ideas, big and small, throughout “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins,” and their cumulative impact makes the series special — not because of a general dearth in great comedies, or even because it harkens back to an era of Must-See TV, when multiple classic sitcoms airing on the same night spoiled viewers with an abundance of laughs. It’s just because laughing this hard, this often, is a gift. And there’s nothing faint about it.

“The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” Season 2 premieres Monday, November 2 at 8:30 p.m. ET on NBC. New episodes will be released weekly and made available on Peacock the next day.

#3523. 'VisionQuest' Star Officially Breaks Silence on Her Character's Avengers Movie Future

Will Lisa Molinari eventually become the anti-hero Coat of Arms?

Six episodes into VisionQuest, it's clear Marvel’s latest show has a lot going on. In addition to seeing the evolution of characters like Vision (Paul Bettany) and Ultron (James Spader), we saw the death of J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), and the rebirth of Tommy Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The show is also giving us the origins of Jocasta (T’Nia Miller), Paladin (Todd Stashwick), and Lisa Molinari (Lauren Morais), the latter becomes the character Coat of Arms in Marvel Comics.

In the comic books, Lisa Molinari is also linked to Tommy Maximoff, having spent time with him in a juvenile detention center. Once released, she struggles to adjust to life in the real world until she discovers a magical cloak named Tiboro's Coat, which grants her the ability to fly and, more notably, four extra arms. Adopting the identity Coat of Arms, Lisa joins the villain team the Young Masters, though her allegiance is often shifting in the comics from good to evil to somewhere in between. Part of the reason for her ambiguous loyalties is that she views the hero/villain struggle as a kind of performance art, which makes her very unpredictable.

In VisionQuest, we have yet to see Lisa Molinari with any extra appendages, but in one of the trailers, she is shown with two extra robotic arms coming out of what looks like a high-tech backpack. This means Coat of Arms, or at least some early version of her, is coming. And, when Lauren Morais sat down with Polygon, that’s precisely what we wanted to talk about.

Polygon: When you got cast as Lisa Molinari, what kind of research did you do?

It’s mostly the comics, but then getting to know Ruaridh while doing the scenes helped. Lisa and Tommy were getting to know each other, that was the start of it, and I think it was a very appropriate and useful start to the whole process.

Lisa is a character that’s been a villain, a hero, and an anti-hero. I’m curious what you’d like to see happen with the character in the future.

I would definitely love to see her wrestle with villainy and superheroism, and what happens to her relationship to Tommy as she does that, because she's been through so much with Tommy in VisionQuest. It'd be interesting to see how she gets to that point and why she starts questioning what it all means. I think the Young Masters route is a really cool route as well. That would be sick.

What was it like for you doing your first fight scene with those extra arms?

It was so fun. We did a lot of rehearsals and fight choreography and some boxing. They were like, “You need to picture where this arm is going to hit,” which was really funny. As an actress, you have to be like, “Okay, I think it's gonna hit your face, so I'm going to have to angle my shoulder this way.”

Paul [Bettany] was like, “You're going to feel really silly doing it, but if you commit to it, it will look amazing afterwards,” and he was right.

I'd never done fight scenes of that caliber before, having fake hands and extra arms. You're not going to get more Marvel than having two extra fake robotic arms, so that was a really cool moment for me.

What was your reaction to the fight scenes with the extra arms when you first saw them?

I saw them first in post. I had to do a bit of ADR and I saw a rough version of it. I was so gagged by it. I was like, “You are kidding,” because you have a picture of it in your head, but it looks a thousand times better when you see it in person. You spend so much time with this character and so much time imagining the arms, that seeing them in real life was such a surreal experience.

Then I saw it properly, with all the effects afterwards and I so chuffed. Paul Bettany was right; you do have to commit and then it looks really cool.

So joyous. So funny. We have so many jokes on set. He was very welcoming and he understood that it was my first massive job. I think I was one of the last ones to be cast of the main cast and he really took me under his wing. He had a good balance of being really fun and funny to work with, but also, you can see that he had a deep commitment and regard for Vision's story. It was lovely seeing that passion, while also being an amazing number one on set. I think that's a real testimony to him. Everyone in the crew and the actors had so much fun working with him.

My last question for you is if we can expect to see you in maybe Avengers: Doomsday or Secret Wars.

Wow, I think we should concentrate on VisionQuest first. We've got two episodes left. We've got an amazing finale ahead. I think we've got enough going on.

VisionQuest is streaming now on Disney Plus.

#3522. IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’

IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace is officially an Emmy winner.

Wallace won the Editing for a Daytime Studio Program category at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys for his work on Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables.” He accepted the award during the ceremony at the Hollywood Palladium on Friday, October 30.

IndieWire was also nominated for a Daytime Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Daytime Studio Non-Fiction Series for IndieWire executive producer Mary Pelloni’s work on the show. The two nominations and one win, in categories that also included broadcast talk shows, reflect IndieWire’s increasing presence in the traditional video spaces in addition to our written coverage. Related Stories ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year Netflix Will Give Joel Coen’s Gothic Mystery ‘Jack of Spades’ a Theatrical Release in 2027

Wallace works on IndieWire’s staff as a video producer, where he also produces and edits video content across brands like Filmmaker Toolkit, Future of Filmmaking, and other editorial and sponsored projects.

Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables” highlighted the below-the-line artisans on many of the biggest films of the season. Hosted by IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill, the season consisted of four episodes, each centered around a different filmmaking department: cinematography, editing, production design, and casting. Each episode aired on PBS SoCal and streamed on the PBS App in addition to editorial coverage on IndieWire.com.

Wallace won for the editing roundtable episode, which featured included editors Kirk Baxter (“A House of Dynamite”), Affonso Goncalves (“Hamnet”), Michael P. Shawver (“Sinners”), Andy Jurgensen (“One Battle After Another”), Pamela Martin (“Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere”), Saar Klein (“Dead Man’s Wire”), and Luke Lynch (“BLKNWS: Terms & Conditions”).

The cinematography roundtable featured Adolpho Veloso (“Train Dreams”), Malik Hassan Sayeed (“After the Hunt”), Michael Bauman (“One Battle After Another”), and William Rexer (“The Testament of Ann Lee”).The production design roundtable featured conversations with Cara Brower (“Hedda”), Sam Bader (“The Testament of Ann Lee”), Alexandra Schaller (“Train Dreams”), Scott Chambliss (“Kiss of the Spider Woman”), and Dylan Cole and Ben Procter (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”).

The casting roundtable also featured casting directors Nina Gold (“Jay Kelly”), Margery Simkin (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”), and Jessica Ronane (“After the Hunt”).

“IndieWire Craft Roundtables” returned for Season 2 in June 2026, with six episodes devoted to the biggest TV shows of the year.

#3521. What I Love (and What I Don't) About the New Una Fitness Watch

I’ve reviewed every type of fitness watch and thought I had seen it all, but my first glimpse of an Una watch had my jaw on the floor: There is a USB-C port on the side of the watch. Not a set of pins for a magnetic charger, or a socket that requires a proprietary cable—just a hole you can stick a regular old USB-C cable into. This is what watches have been missing.

The Una watch started popping up on my feed about two years ago, and finally started shipping this summer. I’ve been wearing a review unit for a few weeks. The Una watch is advertised as repairable and upgradable, with open source software. There are little screws that I can see around the watch face, and on the back panel. The Una website sells a replacement battery for $40 and a replacement screen for $50. They also sell the tiny screwdriver that you’ll need to make repairs, but if you’re the kind of person who gets excited about a repairable watch, you may already have your own.

Overall, I like it. The Una watch has an MIP screen (an older tech that is a cult favorite) and an app that's simple but effective. Not everything lived up to my expectations in testing, but no features failed outright. This feels like a solid start to the concept of “one watch for life” and I’m excited to see how the hardware and software offerings evolve over time.

Most wearables these days try to do as many jobs as possible, whether they’re the right tool for those jobs or not. I am honestly fine with a running watch measuring time, distance, and heart rate while I run, and not trying to score my sleep or pretend it can tell how fast I’m aging.

The Una watch app shows my steps, activity, and floors climbed for the day, as well as my average and resting heart rates. When I go for a run, it tracks my pace, distance, and heart rate during the run and gives me a nice page of data afterward. It reliably uploads this data to Strava, and can make little bar graphs of how these numbers vary from day to day.

There is a “store” (everything is free, as far as I can tell) where you can download extra watch faces and features. One I’m trying out is a habit tracker called HabitLab: It asks you every evening whether you had alcohol, cigarettes, a late meal, and so on. Every morning, it asks how you’re feeling. And then, even though the watch doesn’t normally track your sleep, the app takes note of your overnight HRV and resting heart rate. Over time, it will correlate the answers to those questions with the sleep data, to hopefully give results that are similar to Whoop’s journal analysis. (I haven’t been using it long enough to judge how well it works, but stay tuned.)

HabitLab appears in one area of the watch as a standalone app; another, called Gym Sets, gives me a strength training activity type, which the watch did not otherwise have. I just select Gym Sets instead of “Run” or “Workout,” and the app tracks my heart rate while also giving me a set timer.

The store is small, and the apps are simple, without many of the features that you can find on the apps for Apple Watch or other more fully featured devices. But the Una watch has only been out for a few months, so it’s not surprising that users haven’t created a plethora of apps yet. The company’s software development kit, and even its circuit board designs, are free for people to download and develop from.

I was worried that the emphasis on repairability, and the affordable price, meant that the Una watch would be made with components that maybe aren’t fully up to date. Heart rate sensors have been getting better over the years, so Una’s will have to be pretty good if it wants to even sit in the middle of the pack. Garmin, Apple, and now Fitbit have raised the bar quite a bit.

I will say the GPS track was reasonably good; on trail runs and road runs, it accurately followed the path I actually took. (It doesn’t seem to do quite as well as a new Garmin, but it’s still perfectly usable and its distance totals added up to reasonably accurate numbers.)

Heart rate accuracy disappointed me, though. When I first got the watch, the heart rate tracking was abysmal. I sent a few emails to my contact at Una, and almost had to publish this review with very bad news about the watch’s accuracy, but then a firmware update for the Una watch popped up on my phone. I installed it, and then tried another test run or two, and the heart rate accuracy is much better. If you get the watch, make sure it’s updated to at least 1.6.0.

That said, the update brought the heart rate accuracy to a level where I’d say it’s adequate, but it’s not good (and definitely not great). Its graph follows the ups and downs of my heart rate as measured by a chest strap, but sometimes the Una will spike and show a reading that’s significantly higher than my heart is actually beating. In the graph below, note the spike to around 165 when the true value was 155, and then later in the workout the Una watch detects another spike around 160 when my heart rate was actually around 145 and decreasing. (I saw similar anomalies in multiple workouts.)

In my time with the Una watch, many things made me happy. I still love the USB-C charging, and it was a delight to just plug it in to the same nightstand cable I normally use with my phone, no need to go looking for an adapter or dongle.

I like the MIP screen, which was brilliant in the sunlight and had a serviceable backlight for use indoors or in the dark. The small number of workout profiles and the small number of glances and apps is just fine if you’re not asking for much from a watch, and I wasn’t. It’s minimalist, low-distraction, and there isn’t a single AI-based feature anywhere. A true breath of fresh air.

And at $199, you’re not paying extra for these privileges. The price is just a little more than the new Fitbit Edge ($179.99), but less than a Coros Pace 4 ($249) or a Garmin 70 (also $249). The Una watch doesn’t have as many features or activities as these watches, but perhaps those pluses I mentioned make up for it.

The Una watch would be a good pick for someone who is excited about developing apps, wants a repairable watch, always loses charging adapters, or appreciates a minimalist approach. But would I recommend it for the average person who just wants a basic fitness watch? I’m not so sure.

The flaky heart rate sensor disqualifies it for a wearer who wants a more accurate, modern watch. The MIP screen is going to look old and weird to people who have gotten used to brighter, clearer AMOLED screens. The lack of sleep tracking or other convenience metrics may be hard to take when plenty of watches have these features.

So I like this watch today, with reservations, and I have high hopes for the future. If Una lives up to its vision, it’s going to be great to see replaceable components become available—perhaps there will be an option for an AMOLED screen for those who want it, and maybe there’s room for heart rate accuracy improvement in future firmware updates.

But a lot depends on the company itself. “One watch for life” implies that the company stays around long enough to make more than one model. I’m also hopeful that the future offerings will match what people want, and that the watch and app will stay uncluttered and subscription-free. But surely there will be competing interests that the company has to balance as they grow (if they grow), so time will tell whether the reality lives up to the vision. That said, I am liking the vision a lot.

#3520. ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 13, 2026 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.]

You’re going to see the hits coming with this one. When Anthony Ippolito first utters the title of Peter Farrelly‘s “I Play Rocky” — it’s an admission and an ask, a demand and a plea — the moment is primed for stand-up-and-cheer crowd-pleasing. Such is the case with Farrelly’s entire film, which tracks Sylvester Stallone’s wild, improbable Hollywood success story through the lens of his creation of “Rocky,” often functioning as its own version of that underdog story, presumably because “Rocky” proper isn’t available to be remade and Stallone was not formally involved with the production of this one. Related Stories IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’ ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year

Stallone has long mythologized his rise to greatness, and that’s no knock on him; his rise to Hollywood royalty was crazy and filled with eye-popping twists and turns. The guy sold his dog when he didn’t have enough money! But Peter Gamble’s script sands down those hard edges into something much more made-for-the-movies, a distinctly knotty treatment for a movie that is meant to be about how hard it is to get original movies made.

While the lightness of the film — including an awkward dinner in which Frank Stallone, Jr. (Matt Dillon) giddily admits to beating his kid, mostly played for chuckles — can detract from the much darker stuff that really happened to Stallone, it’s hard to deny the power of a feature so genuinely built to delight. You can see the strings being pulled (the ropes being strung?), but that means it works more often than not. With a big crowd — a man behind me at the film’s second public screening at TIFF guffawed and hooted with such abandon throughout the film that I could only embrace his joy — “I Play Rocky” does exactly what it’s trying to do.

Stallone’s life story has been threaded through the period just before he started writing scripts and the opening night of “Rocky,” an essential time in the career of a man so dedicated to acting and his craft that it could have ruined him forever. And there’s some light ruin here, including a short stint sleeping on the street (we see literally one night), bonkers financial decisions, and grievous financial choices. Embodied to an almost disarming degree by actor Anthony Ippolito — most people are probably going to get hung up on his impersonation of Stallone’s signature voice, but I’ve never seen anyone make their cheekbones look like Sly’s unexpectedly sunken ones — what feels most real about the film exists because he’s so fully committed to the bit.

And it’s very much to the breakout star’s credit that it doesn’t feel like a bit. While Gamble’s script doesn’t get much further than “this dude just really loved acting,” Ippolito gets pretty soulful here. His Sly (or, as we first meet him during a run of demeaning auditions, “Mike”) is a striver who would likely never call himself “ambitious.” Self-taught, self-educated, and self-aware to a fault, Sly knows he’s not the ideal Hollywood star, but he’s hellbent on showing the world what he’s got.

When his eventual first wife Sasha (a wonderfully calm AnnaSophia Robb) encourages him to just “write a fricking script” worthy of his talents, he does. The first is not “Rocky.” Neither are the seven that follow, but Sly and Sasha still pull up stakes for Hollywood and to chase his dream. No one is buying what he’s selling, though, and even some promising meetings (including one with Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff, both played to the absolute hilt by P.J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell, respectively) end nowhere. A chance encounter — the film’s script lives and dies by those — with a seminal boxing match gives him fresh inspiration, and after just three days, the kid has “Rocky.”

But is he going to be Rocky? Of course, everyone on Earth who sees this film (and plenty who don’t) knows that answer, but what the film lacks in tension, it makes up for in pure grit. Sly learns all about Hollywood negotiations, blustery studio men (a role Tracy Letts was born to play; no one has more fun yelling “Fuck Paramount!” than this guy), and holding fast to seriously deluded dreams. And while the film can flag as we chug through those paces, once “Rocky” is greenlit with Sly in the lead role (and a mess of stipulations, all of them seemingly designed to trip him up), things really start zipping along.

Part of that is due to smart casting. Jay Duplass is a stellar pick for director John G. Avildsen, though anyone who knows anything about Stallone’s on-set approach will chuckle at how much these two seemed to get along (Stephan James should get his own Carl Weathers film now). But more of it comes from the film’s eventual bent toward the mechanics of moviemaking. Come for the high jinks involving beating back union reps (but also, ew?), stay for a subplot about the genius of the Steadicam that is genuinely moving to observe.

That “Rocky” will be a hit is a given — and a fricking huge one at that! — but “I Play Rocky” is far more invested in getting the audience on board with the road it took to get there. And while Farrelly’s approach to this material, extremely glossy and built to delight a wide array of audience members, doesn’t quite speak to the real pain that went into the making of “Rocky,” there’s still plenty here that will make people stand up and cheer. It would, however, be nice if this Hollywood story didn’t feel quite so, well, Hollywood.

“I Play Rocky” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide later in the month.

#3519. Frank Herbert's Dune Saga Gets Stunning New Release Today

When Frank Herbert published Dune in 1965, he forever changed the landscape of science fiction, introducing readers to a sprawling universe filled with political intrigue, cryptic and mysterious religious prophecy, and some of the most ambitious world-building the genre had ever seen. More than six decades later, Herbert's influence remains undeniable, with the franchise enjoying a massive resurgence thanks to Denis Villeneuve's blockbuster film adaptations.

Herbert ultimately wrote six novels in the original Dune saga, beginning with Dune, Dune Messiah, and Children of Dune. These earlier stories have received renewed attention thanks to the movies, particularly Dune Messiah, which serves as the foundation for the upcoming third film. However, the latter half of Herbert's original series is arguably just as impressive, if not more so.

God Emperor of Dune, Heretics of Dune, and Chapterhouse: Dune explore some of the saga's most fascinating ideas, yet remain criminally underrated compared to their predecessors. Fortunately, these three novels are finally getting some much-deserved attention with a stunning new Dune release arriving today, November 3.

Frank Herbert's legendary science fiction saga is getting a gorgeous new release today, November 3, 2026, with the arrival of Frank Herbert's Dune Saga Books 4-6 Deluxe Hardcover Boxed Set. Published by Ace, an imprint of Penguin Random House, the collection brings together the final three novels in Herbert's original series in stunning new hardcover editions, complete with exclusive artwork and several premium features.

The collection includes God Emperor of Dune, Heretics of Dune, and Chapterhouse: Dune, spanning an impressive 1,520 pages. Priced at $150, the boxed set is officially available starting today through retailers including Amazon and Barnes & Noble.

Each hardcover features brand-new cover artwork by Matt Griffin, along with stained page edges, illustrated endpapers, and stamped and foiled covers featuring memorable quotations from the novels. Each dust jacket also contains an illustrated poster on its interior, while all three books come packaged inside a beautifully illustrated slipcase.

Beyond these being stunning new designs with vivid art styles, these novels represent some of Herbert's most ambitious storytelling. God Emperor of Dune takes place thousands of years after the original trilogy, following Leto II Atreides and his extraordinary transformation into a human-sandworm hybrid. The novel explores the consequences of his millennia-long reign and the future he envisions for humanity.

Heretics of Dune jumps another 1,500 years into the future, exploring a galaxy transformed by Leto II's legacy, while Chapterhouse: Dune continues the story with the Bene Gesserit facing an existential threat from the Honored Matres.

You can order Frank Herbert's Dune Saga Books 4-6 Deluxe Hardcover Boxed Set via Amazon here.

Of course, this isn't the first deluxe hardcover collection released for Herbert's original novels. Penguin Random House previously published a companion boxed set featuring Dune, Dune Messiah, and Children of Dune, also featuring premium finishes, illustrated covers, and additional artwork, so collectors and longtime fans who already have the first set will definitely want to grab this one ASAP.

With today's release, fans can finally display all six of Herbert's original Dune novels in matching deluxe hardcover collections. Although the upcoming films have understandably brought renewed attention to the earlier books, this new collection offers a fantastic opportunity to rediscover the remarkable second half of Herbert's original saga.

#3518. This 'Nothing' Fitness Smartwatch Is on Sale for $59

If you haven't heard of the upstart tech brand Nothing, it's a UK-based company that aims to make products like cellphones and headphones with innovative features and designs—but at a lower price point than tech giants like Apple and Samsung. Last summer, the company released its newest smartwatch, the CMF Watch 3 Pro, which incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT, and you can currently pick it up at a major discount.

Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $59 at Amazon. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been, according to price-tracking tools.

According to Nothing, the CMF Watch 3 Pro is designed for "everyday users and casual fitness explorers." It quickly earned a reputation as one of the best budget smartwatch/fitness trackers of 2025. If you have a Nothing phone, the most noteworthy feature is its direct ChatGPT integration: You can use voice prompts to ask the chatbot questions or set reminders, among other things. Another neat feature, regardless of whether you have a Nothing phone or not, is its ability to record voices and auto-transcribe conversations or notes with the Nothing X app, which is great for work meetings or class.

If you've used the CMF Watch 2 Pro, you'll already be familiar with the design, which hasn't changed much. It still has a round display with a rotating crown on the top right, though the display is a bit bigger—1.43 inches compared to the Watch 2 Pro's 1.32 inches. Nothing has also kept the auto brightness adjustment, which is determined by a built-in sensor, and dual-band GPS support with access to five satellite systems, providing greater accuracy when tracking your outdoor activities.

The real upgrades come mainly from the software: The Watch 3 Pro has over 130 sport modes, compared to 120 on the older model. There's also AI tracking with personalized workout recommendations in real time. The battery now lasts 13 days on a single charge, which is two days longer than before. It's certainly in the running for the best sub-$100 fitness watch you can buy right now.

#3517. Alan Ritchson’s 98-Minute Action Disappointment Officially Hits Hulu in 3 Weeks

Action heroes are a staple feature of the entertainment industry. From icons like Sylvester Stallone and Dolph Lundgren to more modern figures like Tom Cruise and Vin Diesel, they all share the ability to spike our collective adrenaline levels while watching them perform. Alan Ritchson has since put himself firmly in that conversation thanks mainly to the Prime Video action-thriller Reacher. The hard-hitting show is based on the bestselling novel series by Lee Child, and recently completed its fourth season with a fifth season in the works.

Prior to his role as Jack Reacher, Ritchson made his acting debut as Aquaman in Smallville, with more exposure in other roles, including as Raphael in Michael Bay's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles reboot and director Guy Ritchie's WW2 epic The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare, which co-starred Henry Cavill. However, the success of the Prime Video series truly established him, even as he headlined the Netflix sci-fi action movie War Machine, which released earlier this year on the streaming service. It would be as though whatever Ritchson touches turns to gold, given that War Machine holds the title of the most-watched Netflix original of the year with more than 150 million views.

In September 2026, Ritchson hoped to continue his success story when he starred as Hank Malone, a former soldier and current medical courier in the Brisbane-set action thriller, Runner. Produced on a reported $45 million budget, Runner ultimately disappointed at the box office, grossing just over $15 million. The action thriller, which also stars Owen Wilson in the lead role, will be hoping to find some redemption on streaming as it makes its way onto Hulu on November 27. Runner will become the first series featuring Wilson to stream on Hulu. More importantly, the streaming service will be hoping Ritchson brings home some of his streaming star power as other action movies starring Ritchson have climbed streaming charts throughout 2026.

Directed by Scott Waugh, Runner holds an 89% audience score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, in addition to a rather solid 78% critics' score on the platform. The chemistry between Ritchson and Wilson is top-notch and helps bring a story that also stars Rodrigo Santoro, Leila George, Scarlett Crabtree, among others, together. Runner follows a Good Samaritan who teams up with a courier to deliver a liver to a dying girl while being chased by gangsters who are also interested in said liver. Runner will be part of a host of new additions to Hulu this month. They include The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader, Ridley Scott's The Last Duel, Jason Statham's The Meg movies, both seasons of Percy Jackson and the Olympians, among others.

Runner arrives on Hulu on November 27, 2026. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3516. Zach Cregger's Resident Evil Is Officially Coming Home

One of the best movies of 2026 finally arrives on digital

Director Zach Cregger, known for Barbarian and Weapons, proved he was ready to tackle the behemoth task of taking on a franchise when he took on the latest adaptation of Capcom’s Resident Evil video game series. In just the first week alone, Cregger’s Resident Evil raked in $60 million at the domestic box office. That number kept growing, making it the most successful Resident Evil film to hit the silver screen.

Fans of the 2026 film are in luck — Resident Evil is now available to rent or purchase digitally on services such as Prime Video for $24.99 US dollars. It is currently unknown when it will come to streaming services, but when it does, it will likely land on Netflix because of Netflix's exclusive deal with Sony Pictures.

Resident Evil fans would be the first to tell you that most adaptations of the video game franchise have been disappointing. They either stray wildly from established video game canon or rehash stories fans have already played through — only much worse.

Mixed-to-negative feelings about Cregger’s adaptation, however, are nowhere to be found. Not only has Resident Evil continued to break box office records long after its debut, but fan opinion also leans positively toward Cregger’s adaptation as being true and authentic to the Resident Evil experience. Simply put: Cregger’s Resident Evil isn’t just the most successful adaptation of the franchise, but the most beloved too.

Cregger’s Resident Evil is a soft reboot of the franchise, but rather than following an epic, scrappy hero like Leon Kennedy, it centers on Bryan, an exhausted, put-upon medical courier played by Austin Abrams. After agreeing to deliver a last-minute package to Raccoon City, Bryan soon discovers that a virus has infected people in the surrounding area and that his package is, in fact, the cure to stop it from spreading.

Despite being far from prepared to take on a city full of the infected, Bryan has little choice but to do just that. What follows is a mix of the terrifying and the gut-bustlingly funny, perfectly capturing the range Cregger has shown in his previous films.

This schlocky gore-fest is officially coming home. So whether you haven’t seen the movie yet and want to, or have been patiently waiting for it to arrive digitally after catching it on the silver screen, now’s the perfect time to check out Resident Evil.

#3515. ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on February 13, 2026 at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. IFC Films will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6.]

For the final 20 or so minutes of an early screening of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson‘s Berlin-bound “Mouse” that I recently attended, the woman sitting behind me in one of NYC’s smallest screening rooms sobbed. Like, really sobbed. I could hear her gasps in between her cries. Yes, I thought to myself, one of my people.

While I’m not sure there’s yet a cult assembled around the deeply empathetic and uniquely humane cinema of O’Sullivan and Thompson (partners in both film and life), God willing, there will be after more audiences see the pair’s third effort. I’ve been banging the drum on their wondrous output since 2020’s “Saint Frances” (which Thompson directed and O’Sullivan wrote and starred in) and their deep-feeling follow-up, 2024’s “Ghostlight” (written by O’Sullivan, who also joined Thompson in co-directing duties). Around these parts, any O’Sullivan and Thompson joint is an event. Related Stories ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’

“Mouse” is no exception, and their best effort yet.

As is typically the case with the pair’s films, its logline does not quite do it justice. “Saint Frances” was about a disaffected nanny who bonds with her young charge. “Ghostlight” followed a fractured family as they found unexpected healing in live theater. “Mouse” is about a shy high school senior looking for ballast after the sudden end of her lifelong BFF-ship. These are all “small” stories, but they are also crucially about people, and thus contain the wild multitudes of humanity itself.

O’Sullivan and Thompson reunite with their “Ghostlight” star, Katherine Mallen Kupferer (whose own parents starred alongside her in the previous feature), who is cast here as our titular Mouse. Well, sort of. Her name is Minnie, but her shyness leans toward the mousy, though no one would ever say that to her, least of all her beloved and extremely outgoing best friend, Callie (Chloe Coleman). But when Minnie’s itchy nickname is (wrongly, it turns out) attributed to the flashy Callie, it’s hard for her to shake its deeper meanings.

When the film opens, Minnie and Callie are wrapping their final day as high school juniors in the early summer of 2002 (cue the Michelle Branch soundtrack, perfect). The stage is being set for their senior year — and, quite literally, for the very talented Callie’s next big high school musical moment and her eventual plans to attend Juilliard — and it’s obvious that they’re not about to have the same experience. Callie is popular and vivacious, perpetually surrounded by admirers and various hangers-on (Audrey Grace Marshall’s Cara is hellbent on usurping Minnie’s place in Callie’s life, while her himbo-esque boyfriend Brad is given wonderful dimension through Beck Nolan’s sneaky-good performance).

Minnie? She’s much more reserved, orbiting around Callie and company, not quite ever the star of her own show. But this is not a story about two best friends who break up because of the vagaries of popularity, and Coleman’s Callie is not a villain who breaks Minnie’s delicate heart. Well, not on purpose.

It’s clear that Minnie is out of touch with lots about her life — though not her affection for Callie — including her own sexuality (Iman Vellani as cute local video store clerk Kat happily cracks through that) and her fraught relationship with her overworked mother (Mallen Kupferer’s own mom and “Ghostlight” co-star, Tara Mallen). Callie’s friendship and trust are the best things in her life. Her nice house with a fully stocked kitchen is a bonus, as is Callie’s very-put-together mom Helen (a heartbreaking Sophie Okonedo), who wisely seems to like the steady Minnie a whole heck of a lot more than the rest of Callie’s coterie.

That will prove to be the one saving grace of what comes next. When Minnie and Callie’s friendship comes to a sudden end, it’s only through bonding with Helen that Minnie finds any sort of ballast in her life. But as point-A-to-point-B as that might sound, O’Sullivan and Thompson remain uniquely attuned to the ebbs and flows of real life and how real people respond to it. Mallen Kupferer, so outspoken in “Ghostlight” and so wonderfully goofy in “Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret,” here sinks into the far harder-to-crack Minnie. That’s not to say that Minnie isn’t prone to the emotional wilds of any teenage girl, but the young actress’ finely tuned performance is never broad or silly.

Instead, we get to know Minnie during one of the worst times of her life. So too does Helen, who handles her own feelings about Callie through her own coping mechanisms, some of which work, most of which don’t, and many of which center on building her own friendship with Minnie. The pair of them has a lot in common beyond Callie, including a general sense of wisdom beyond their years that has not always been beneficial to them.

Early in the film, Cara insists that Callie’s group of friends (including both Cara and Minnie) partake in a horrific little parlor game she likens to “Personal Feedback.” Mostly, it’s an excuse for the teenagers to say terrible things about each other under the guise of honesty and friendship. Even our golden girl, Callie, doesn’t escape unharmed, though Minnie almost does, because Cara simply can’t be bothered to remember she exists.

“Mouse” is, at its heart, a wonderful rebuttal to just that sort of cruel thinking — for all the Minnies out there — and a reminder that everyone matters and everyone deserves to be seen. Lofty as that might sound, it’s one of the most basic tenets of humanity, and the kind of thing too often forgotten on the big screen. O’Sullivan and Thompson never forget, however, and their films reflect exactly that. Our only request: more, please, our people need this.

“Mouse” premiered at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival.

#3514. These High-End Marshall Headphones Are Under $200 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Marshall’s Monitor III ANC headphones have the kind of design that makes you want to show them off. The textured earcups and gold logo lean fully into the amp-inspired look, and at $199.99 (down from $379.99 at launch), they’re finally priced in a way that feels competitive. It's their lowest price ever, according to price trackers.

These are over-ear Bluetooth headphones with active noise cancellation, and they’re clearly aimed at people cross-shopping Bose and Sony. The difference is that Marshall is selling a vibe along with the sound. The build feels sturdy, and small details like replaceable ear cushions and a swappable silicone headband strap suggest they’re made to last longer than most. They fold down neatly into a compact hard case (included), but they’re not water-resistant, so they’re better suited for travel and home listening than sweaty workouts.

Living with them day to day is mostly smooth. The small gold joystick handles volume and track controls in a way that feels intuitive after a few minutes. There’s a separate button to toggle noise cancellation and transparency, plus a customizable shortcut button you can set up in the Marshall app. The app itself is simple, with a five-band EQ and a few presets, though it’s not especially deep if you like fine-tuning every frequency. Bluetooth 5.3 keeps connections stable, but you’re limited to AAC and SBC codecs, so there’s no hi-res audio support. You also can’t charge and listen through a traditional 3.5mm cable at the same time, since the single USB-C port handles both charging and wired playback.

Battery life is where these headphones truly stand out. Up to 70 hours with ANC on is more than enough for long trips, and turning ANC off stretches that to an almost excessive 100 hours. As for sound, they deliver strong bass and crisp highs, with enough punch to make hip-hop and electronic tracks feel lively. Noise cancellation reduces plane engine rumble and city noise well, but it does not match leaders like Bose in blocking midrange chatter, notes this PCMag review.

#3513. The John Wick Franchise Is Officially Bringing Back Keanu Reeves

The John Wick franchise has become one of the most influential action series of the modern era, but it's difficult to imagine the films being so successful without Keanu Reeves. His portrayal of the legendary assassin has become inseparable from the character, and it's clear in every film he fully commits, both physically and emotionally, performing his own incredible stunts and fight sequences that have taken a relatively modest 2014 thriller into a billion-dollar franchise.

Although John Wick has since expanded through various spin-offs, including The Continental and Ballerina, there's a strong argument that the larger franchise would struggle to survive without Reeves. After all, the actor remains its biggest draw, and replacing him would be an almost impossible task, especially considering how beloved his performance has become and how inseparable his face is from the franchise itself.

Fortunately, fans haven't seen the last of the Baba Yaga. In an exciting announcement, Reeves is officially returning to his iconic role for an upcoming prequel story that promises to explore an entirely different chapter of John Wick's life.

Keanu Reeves is officially returning as John Wick, although this time, fans will actually get to step into the legendary assassin's shoes. The actor is lending both his likeness and voice to an upcoming AAA John Wick game from Saber Interactive, the studio behind Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 and the recently released Hellraiser: Revival, which turned out to be a huge success among fans. Franchise director Chad Stahelski is also directly involved in the project, collaborating with Saber and Lionsgate to bring the Baba Yaga to life.

The currently untitled game was officially unveiled on February 12, 2026, during Sony's State of Play presentation, where fans were treated to an impressive reveal trailer. Although Lionsgate had expressed interest in developing a major John Wick game as far back as 2022, this marked the first proper announcement of Saber's ambitious adaptation.

Interestingly, the game will serve as a prequel to the original 2014 film, taking place years before Wick's legendary Impossible Task, which ultimately allowed him to retire from his life as an assassin. The original storyline will explore an earlier chapter of his career, introducing familiar faces alongside completely new characters created specifically for the game.

As for gameplay, Saber is developing a single-player, third-person action experience built around the franchise's iconic gun-fu combat. Players can expect intense hand-to-hand fighting, brutal shootouts, cinematic camera work, and driving sequences, with an entirely new combat system designed to recreate the movies' distinctive choreography. Saber has also suggested that this younger version of Wick will fight with a rougher, less polished style than audiences have come to recognize.

Based on Saber's success with the recent Hellraiser release, it seems they're tapped into what fans of a given franchise are expecting out of their video game adaptations, which is a great sign for John Wick fans, assuming the studio can stick the landing.

Unfortunately, there's still no official release date, although 2028 has emerged as a possible launch window. In July 2026, Saber executive Steve Allison referenced the John Wick project while discussing the company's 2028 lineup, alongside Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 3 and the Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic remake. However, Saber subsequently clarified that these remarks weren't intended as an official release announcement.

For now, the game remains in development for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC, with its final title and launch date still awaiting confirmation. Nevertheless, with Reeves and Stahelski both involved, this could become the definitive John Wick video game fans have wanted for years.

#3512. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses

Lionsgate‘s “Hunger Games” prequel “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” will be available in 3D when it opens in theaters on November 20. That on its own isn’t strictly news, but the 3D conversion on the film is coming from a new and unlikely place: Facebook parent company Meta.

Meta is partnering with Lionsgate to convert “Sunrise on the Reaping” to 3D, with director Francis Lawrence working to adapt the film for 3D viewing. Meta worked with VFX giant DNEG and their internal 3D conversion branch Stereo. This is the first time Meta has partnered with a Hollywood film studio on such an undertaking, and it also won’t be the last Lionsgate movie that will get the 3D treatment down the road (other titles will be announced at a later date). Related Stories ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser

In addition to “Sunrise on the Reaping” being in 3D in theaters, the movie will eventually be available on Meta VR Glasses when those VR devices hit the shelves in spring 2027. IndieWire got to demo those recently, and they’re designed to be lighter and less obtrusive than other VR headsets that can be tougher on the eyes while not sacrificing any of the immersive qualities (they feel and look like slightly larger sunglasses that you might get at the dentist rather than a bulky, wraparound headset that weighs on your face).

The demo we saw included a snippet of the Billie Eilish concert doc co-directed by James Cameron, as well as a clip from “Avengers: Endgame” that added an extra expanded screen effect to fill your line of sight. It’s clear that Meta wants to expand into the entertainment space and compete with the likes of YouTube and Google and other tech giants, and they need premium content like a new “Hunger Games” movie in order to do that.

“From the beginning, we wanted ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ to feel visceral and immersive, pulling audiences deep into Haymitch’s experience,” Lawrence said in a statement. “Adapting the film for 3D gave us another creative tool to bring audiences even closer to his perspective. I’m excited for people to see the film on the big screen and ultimately experience it in an entirely new way on Meta’s VR glasses.”

“As we continue to explore new ways for audiences to experience ‘The Hunger Games,’ we’re thrilled to partner with Meta on this first-of-its-kind collaboration,” said Jim Packer, Chief Revenue Officer, Lionsgate. “Francis Lawrence has created an incredible 3D experience for ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ and we’re excited for audiences to experience it in theaters and then on Meta VR Glasses. This is a compelling example of how technology can transform existing formats to create fresh, new experiences.”

“With our upcoming VR Glasses, we’re proud to create premium entertainment the way it’s meant to be felt, and Lionsgate is an ideal partner because of the artistic strength and global appeal of its franchises,” said Sarah Malkin, Head of Entertainment for Meta’s Reality Labs. “’The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ is exactly the kind of cinematic experience that will be phenomenal in theaters, and also showcases what this technology makes possible at home. We’re delighted to work with Lionsgate and Francis Lawrence to bring the film in 3D to audiences around the world.”

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is the sixth “Hunger Games” film and the second prequel after “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” from 2023, which brought in $363 million at the worldwide box office. This film stars Joseph Zada as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy, who is the District 12 character portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original series of films. The film also stars McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., and Ben Wang.
