#3511. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

#3510. 2026’s Best RPG Is Finally on Consoles Just in Time for GOTY Season

Disco Elysium follow-up Zero Parades has serious staying power

I’ve played close to 150 new video games in 2026, but few of them have stuck in my mind quite like Zero Parades: For Dead Spies. What I thought might land with me as a pale follow-up to the sensational Disco Elysium has only cut deeper as I’ve spent time with a story of personal failure in a world built on betrayal. Every day, I feel more like Hershel Wilk, a disgraced spy who can’t seem to do right by anyone.

If you’re as much of a glutton for self-loathing as me, you’re in luck: Zero Parades is finally available on more platforms today. A new Director’s Cut brings the formerly PC-only RPG to Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X with new content in tow. Despite carrying the baggage of a turbulent development cycle that ended in post-launch layoffs, Zero Parades is still very much worth playing to discover a sharply-written espionage RPG that has a way of getting under your fingernails.

Zero Parades very much follows Disco Elysium’s playbook to the letter. It’s a narrative-driven RPG built on tabletop rules, complete with dice rolls and skill checks. There’s a narrator who gives voice to the clashing personality traits in your head, a cast of eccentric townies, and painterly art that makes it clear that’s consistent with developer ZA/UM’s breakthrough success. Those elements were almost a burden when the game first released earlier this year, as some worried that Zero Parades would be a desperate imitation of Disco Elysium made without many of the key creatives behind that game.

I had the same concerns when I first tried it, but it’s a testament to Zero Parades’ quality that it overcomes the baggage. That’s thanks to its brilliant writing, which is on par with Disco Elysium — if not better in moments. The star of the show is Hershel, aka Cascade, a spy who is shipped off to the town of Portofiro for one last job. Genre conventions would have you believe that Cascade is some kind of super spy who is a master of deception, but that’s not exactly the case: She’s a total screw-up.

The story’s power comes from the fact that Hershel’s last big job ended in disaster. Unfortunately, she can’t get her new mission done without regaining the trust of several of the spies who she betrayed in that operation. That premise takes a traditional spy tale and turns it into a personal reckoning. You’re on an apology tour as you explore Portofiro, trying to make things right with the people you hurt while also getting them on board for another risky mission with major political ramifications.

Some manipulation is required to pull that off, and that’s what makes Zero Parades’ such a tragic comedy of errors. As much as Hershel wants to sincerely apologize, that noble desire for forgiveness is hampered by a job that demands she deceive the very people she’s trying to apologize to. Every successful dice roll stings as you lie your way into redemption; and every failed dice roll is a hilarious reminder that Hershel is no James Bond.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

With an emotionally complicated story driven by high-stakes RPG risk-taking, every decision you face in Zero Parades will stick with you. I’m still thinking about my playthrough, which — if I’m being honest — ended in total disaster. I keep thinking back to every choice I made and questioning where it all went wrong. And as I do that, I can’t help but ask the same questions about my life outside the screen. What decisions do I wish I could take back? I can think of a few.

Zero Parades: Director’s Cut is now available on Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.

#3509. 6 Franchises Based on Books Where Every Movie Is Perfect

130 years ago, in 1896, the American Mutoscope Company produced Trilby and the Little Billee, a 45-second short that depicts a scene from George du Maurier’s Victorian novel “Trilby.” This achievement is widely considered the first-ever film adaptation of a novel. Suffice to say, books have been a powerful inspiration for filmmakers since the very earliest days of cinema. Adapting a single novel well is one thing, but to bring an entire franchise to the screen while staying true to the source material and maintaining consistent perfection is another thing entirely.

To illustrate just how almighty a feat it is to accomplish, it is worth noting that The Godfather, Jurassic Park, Shrek, and the James Bond franchise are just some of the pop-culture-defining film franchises based on novels that don’t deliver perfection across the entirety of their runs. The film series do range from blockbuster fantasy epics to animated classics, sci-fi spectaculars, and even superhero sensations.

The superhero genre has dominated the 21st century so far, with modern technology allowing for such stories to be brought to life on the big screen with a gravitas and high-octane entertainment befitting of the comic books that established the genre. Christopher Nolan’s The Dark Knight trilogy still stands as the pinnacle of this monumental pop-culture movement some 14 years on from its conclusion in 2012. Its thematic depth, astonishing practical action sequences, mesmerizing performances, and pervasive sense of grounded grit all work beautifully in tandem across the three films.

Based on characters created by Bob Kane and Bill Finger for DC Comics, the trilogy follows Gotham billionaire Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale) as he becomes Batman, a crime-fighting vigilante determined to decimate the influence of the city’s criminal infrastructure and protect citizens. Among his main enemies are the anarchistic terrorist known as The Joker (Heath Ledger) and the destructive mercenary Bane (Tom Hardy). While 2008’s The Dark Knight is an obvious standout, as well as one of the defining films of the century so far, the whole trilogy is a treat of blockbuster spectacle. It combines the genre’s penchant for thrilling action set pieces with compelling explorations of such ideas as fear, chaos, resilience, and the importance of symbols of strength and humanity in society.

It may be debatable if two feature films constitute a cinematic franchise, but with three short films and an anime miniseries bolstering its stocks, as well as a live-action miniseries arriving on Amazon Prime Video in November, it is hard to knock Blade Runner’s pedigree as a multiplatform saga. Despite its variety, there is no doubt the two full-length movies stand as the defining pillars of the franchise. Ridley Scott’s classic is one of the greatest sci-fi movies of all time, and Denis Villeneuve’s bold legacy sequel stands tall among the best movies of the 21st century thus far.

Based on Philip K. Dick’s Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, the original Blade Runner excels at combining Dick’s thought-provoking story of humanity with a stunning visual aesthetic of stark shadows, neon glow, and dystopian industry. For its part, Blade Runner 2049 expands the story world brilliantly, cleverly twisting the exploration of human nature and android morality while recapturing and reinventing its predecessor’s breathtaking display. The two films as a whole serve as a faultless feat of science-fiction cinema, genre-defining classics that exemplify dystopian drama at its most enthralling.

Based on Cressida Cowell’s children’s book series, the DreamWorks Animation’s How to Train Your Dragon movies mark a joyous highlight of family animated cinema in the 2010s. Set in a Viking realm where the village of Berk is frequently attacked by dragons, the first film revolves around the unlikely friendship that blooms between the young prince Hiccup (Jay Baruchel) and Toothless, a rare Night Fury dragon. The next two films follow the duo’s efforts to defend both Berk and the dragon race from their fierce and powerful adversaries.

The three acclaimed animated films don’t strive to adapt the narrative of Cowell’s books. Still, they excel at bringing the author’s characters and story world to life with the same infectious charm that underlines Cowell’s 12-part series while shifting the tone from delightfully wacky satire to epic, cinematic grandiosity. The result isn’t only a dazzling animated adventure, but a modern gem of fantasy fun as well, especially as all three movies work so perfectly in tandem while delivering important and evocative messages of emotional growth, self-belief, and empathy.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

While young adult fiction had been a staple of modern literature prior to its release, Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel series was something of a pioneer in establishing the genre in widespread pop culture. The film adaptations only heightened this interest in the form. With Collins herself co-writing the screenplay for three of the four initial films, The Hunger Games franchise at large stands as one of the best and most culturally impactful of the 21st century thus far.

Set in a dystopian future where a region of North America has become Panem, it revolves around The Hunger Games, an annual event in which two child champions from each of the 12 districts compete in a fight-to-the-death tournament at the behest of The Capitol. The original four-part film series—following Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) as she participates in the games before igniting a rebellion against The Capitol—is a masterful mix of social commentary, escapist adventure, teen drama, and bleak action. The 2023 spin-off, The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, is a brilliant expansion on the story world, while the soon-to-be-released The Hunger Games: Sunrise of the Reaping is an eagerly anticipated exploration of the 50th Hunger Games.

Based on J. K. Rowling’s “Harry Potter” novels—which remain the bestselling book series of all time—the Harry Potter movies are outstanding at bringing the wonder and magic of the wizarding world to the screen. What is so brilliant about them is how they evolve with the audience, with the earlier movies exhibiting a sense of adventurous awe and childlike charm as Harry Potter (Daniel Radcliffe) begins his education in magic at Hogwarts. Then, the series grows gradually darker as the evil Lord Voldemort (Ralph Fiennes) returns hell-bent on killing Potter and establishing the supremacy of pure-blood wizards over the rest of the world.

All elements of the movies are handled magnificently. Indeed, the franchise flaunts everything from immersive visuals and worldbuilding to John Williams’ mesmerizing score, marvelous practical filmmaking, and a litany of iconic performances from emerging young stars and Hollywood legends alike. The Harry Potter movies are a quintessential pillar of fantasy blockbuster cinema. The Fantastic Beasts spin-off films expand the “Potterverse,” particularly pertaining to the world’s many magical creatures and the exploration of the global wizarding world in a 1920s setting, but they're not half as good as the core series.

As the greatest movie trilogy of all time, the defining triumph of fantasy cinema, and a masterclass in adaptation, The Lord of the Rings is the epitome of cinematic perfection. Based on J. R. R. Tolkien’s books, it follows Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood) as he journeys across Middle-earth to destroy a ring of terrible power in the fires of Mount Doom. Meanwhile, other members of the Fellowship of the Ring rally the forces of Middle-earth to stand against the forces of Mordor.

It is impossible to find a single aspect of the movies that isn’t utterly perfect. Practical filmmaking and astonishing cinematography work with New Zealand’s natural beauty to bring Middle-earth to the screen in spellbinding fashion. Howard Shore’s sweeping score brings depth and tonal precision to every kingdom and character, while every single actor plays their part to perfection. If one watches the extended editions of the films, The Lord of the Rings trilogy delivers over 11 hours of astounding cinematic mastery and absorbing, rousing, and emotionally overwhelming storytelling that balances triumph and tragedy with impeccable skill.

#3508. Google Is Using Data From Gmail and Drive to Target Ads, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

Emily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City.

#3507. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 26, 2026 at the 2026 New York Film Festival. GKIDS will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Asked to explain the goofy title he gave to his globally successful 2023 kaiju smash “Godzilla Minus One,” writer-director Takashi Yamazaki explained that it was meant to convey two co-equal things: 1.) That the movie took place before Ishirō Honda’s original “Godzilla,” and 2.) That “people rise up from a postwar Japan that is at zero, and then Godzilla arrives, making the situation even worse and more tragic.”

Continuing the story of its Oscar-winning predecessor while also doubling down on everything that made it the most acclaimed film in its franchise since the King of the Monsters first lumbered out of the Pacific Ocean in 1954, Yamazaki’s thunderously loud and frequently spectacular direct sequel has in turn been saddled with an even sillier title: “Godzilla Minus Zero.” To paraphrase the scene from “Sideways” where Paul Giamatti’s character reveals that his novel is called “The Day After Yesterday”: Isn’t that just… “Godzilla?” Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale

Yes and no. Sure, the title is absurd on its face, but — in keeping with Yamazaki’s logic — it also rather eloquently speaks to the premise of a film about a fragile people who are struggling to maintain (and build upon) the new equilibrium they’ve fought so hard to achieve in the years since their country became the epicenter of Earth’s nuclear era. Another mid-century melodrama with very occasional monster sightings, the more thematically coherent and emotionally affecting “Godzilla Minus Zero” expands on the naive grassroots nationalism of its predecessor by reframing that movie’s characters from victims to survivors, an emphasis that forces ex-kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) and his friends to confront a series of impossible questions. How do you balance grief with growth? Vengeance with peace? Self-sacrifice with self-preservation?

By way of answering those questions (or at least asking them in a variety of increasingly anguished ways), “Godzilla Minus Zero” also forces Shikishima and co. to confront a flying, IMAX-sized, three-headed asshole they come to know as King Ghidorah. Possibly the single most hateable kaiju who’s ever eaten innocent civilians on screen before, King Ghidorah is a real piece of work even before he earns his crown. He first rears his ugly dragon head in Matsumoto circa 1949, which is two years after the events of “Godzilla Minus One,” and maybe two weeks after this scaly destroyer of worlds crash-landed into the mountains of Japan on the back of a meteorite (an arbitrary point of origin that feels like a missed opportunity to freight Ghidora with more human-facing pathos). Seeing as how Godzilla was obliterated and left to rot at the bottom of the sea at the end of the previous film, Ghidora is free to terrorize the countryside whenever he isn’t taking cute little naps in the Nagano hills.

Lucky for Japan, and for all of the other nations that are still living under the delusion that none of this monster business will ever be their problem, at least one of the key heroes who “defeated” Godzilla in 1947 has been preparing his people for the possibility of another kaiju attack. Government higher-ups are still nowhere to be seen, but Einstein-haired Naval engineer Noda (a sweet and eccentrically professorial Hidetaka Yoshioka) has been appointed to the head of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, where he’s joined by newcomer Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a preternaturally gifted meteorologist whose ability to predict the weather proves crucial in the fight against Ghidorah, and also embittered biologist Kanji Murakami (“Twilight Samurai” star Min Tanaka), who survived the bombing of Hiroshima, the attack on Ginza in “Godzilla Minus One,” and the assault on Matsumoto that opens this film — a detail that evokes the terribly remarkable story of Tsutomo Yamaguchi.

Thanks to Noda’s hard-earned wisdom, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is able to skip over the part where everyone has to discover that kaiju like Ghidorah are immune to conventional weapons — if not also strengthened by them. That ignorance is reserved for the occupying Americans, who were entirely absent from the previous movie (which nostalgically privileged the self-reliance of Japan’s civilian population at the expense of a more historical view of the post-war struggle). Here, the U.S. Army is represented by a unit of square-jawed, power-hungry jerks who are only interested in helping Japan so far as it helps themselves. They don’t bear the wounds of nuclear devastation, and so they see kaiju as more of an opportunity than a threat.

The opposite is true for our pal Shikishima, who has absolutely no interest in ever climbing back into the cockpit of a fight plane. Now married to the angelic Noriko — Minami Hamabe, who miraculously escaped “Godzilla Minus One” with a new eyepatch and some big secrets — and embracing his role as adoptive father to the devastatingly cute Akiko (returning champion Sae Nagatani), Shikishima just wants to wear his cool brown leather jacket and messenger bag combo in peace.

If only it were that simple. If only Shikishima were convinced, as he tries to convince himself, that staying out of the fight is the best way to protect the women he loves. If only Noda’s plan of electrocuting Ghidorah to death in the skies above Matsumoto were as successful at killing the kaiju as it is at blowing our hair back.

There are only two sustained monster sequences in “Minus Zero,” which adheres to a similar cadence as its predecessor, but they’re both among the most gripping setpieces of their kind in all of moviedom; they match the grandeur — if not the majesty — of those from Gareth Edwards’ “Godzilla,” and eclipse their violent intensity. The ridiculously thrilling aerial sequence above Matsumoto is lifted by the Wagnerian strings of Naoki Satō’s visceral score, kept aloft by special effects that exponentially improve upon the resourceful but weightless CGI from “Minus One,” and seared into your retinas by IMAX razzledazzle of the highest magnitude. And while the final showdown between Ghidorah and Godzilla is slightly weakened by grayscale atmospherics and a few missing beats (one of them very bizarre), it goes without saying that the climatic brawl is one for the ages, as Yamazaki earns the franchise’s first “R” rating with an elegantly choreographed monster mash that rattles with Darwinian force.

Oh yeah, I suppose it also goes without saying that Godzilla is (eventually) in this Godzilla movie. Somehow, the King of the Monsters has returned — if Palpatine had infinitely regenerative flesh, perhaps his resurrection would have been similarly unsurprising. But fans of Honda’s original film, Yamazaki’s previous one, and/or Edwards’ failed 2014 reboot have come to expect and appreciate that Godzilla is most effective when framed as more of a recurring weather phenomenon than a dramatic engine in his own right, and “Godzilla Minus Zero” doesn’t suffer from its title kaiju’s limited screentime.

On the contrary, his absences are crucial to the construction of a florid tear-jerker about a traumatized country trying to move forward in the atomic shadow of a world that will never feel safe again. While a cursed biologist like Murakami might see vengeance as his only path towards peace, a former kamikaze like Shikishima — the guilt he once felt over not killing himself for Japan now bent towards the responsibility he feels towards living for Noriko and their daughter — is left to wrestle over the best way to protect his family: fighting the monsters, or fleeing from them.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is hardly the most nuanced or effective film to explore its country’s post-war despair (the original “Godzilla” still towers above it in that regard, to say nothing of “Drunken Angel,” “The Human Condition,” “An Inn at Osaka,” or any number of other cornerstones of Japanese cinema), but the anger it assigns to Murakami is provocative on its own terms, and the path that it contrives for Shikishima is considerably more nuanced and well-earned than the one he stumbled through before. While the future is still uncertain by the end of this latest Godzilla movie (which feels very much like the middle chapter of a trilogy), “Minus Zero” makes rewarding sense of why the series’ numbers are starting to add up.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” premiered at the 2026 New York Film Festival. GKIDS will release it in U.S. theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3506. Need For Speed Underground 2 Is Playable For Free In Your Browser Now

AI coding is a bit of a weird one because, while the technology is clearly going to be an overall net negative in many respects, it has enabled individuals to produce some fun projects that otherwise wouldn't have been possible. Most obviously, recent months have seen a ton of classic games brought back in a whole new format, which is actually quite a good thing for those titles that are hard to play in 2026.

Now, beloved racer Need for Speed Underground 2 is the next target in their sights, and a new release allows players to enjoy it from the comfort of their chosen browser. The fun doesn't stop there, though, so here's everything you need to know about why the 2004 release is retruning in a big way.

As first reported by Tech PowerUp, a new fan project called Underground 2 Revived lets you play Need for Speed: Underground 2 in a web browser. While it is obviously going to be vibe coded in many instances, the game seems to be running well for players at the time of writing, and its nice to see the classic release return to the fore once again.

Not only that, the developer, who goes by th0mk, has also included an online free roam, essentially turning the racing game into a pseudo-MMO for the first time. The project came about because the creator played the game with their brother about 20 years ago and they wanted to easily recapture that magic and play together again.

At the time of writing, it has been confirmed to be working in Chrome and Firefox using WebAssembly and WebGPU, though it will likely also work in other advanced browsers. There are also a shocking number of players online right now, with the project clearly striking a chord with those who grew up playing it.

It might also be the best way to play old Need For Speed games without digging out all the old hardware and booting up the CRT TV. EA is showing no signs of bringing back their older titles in the franchise with remasters and remakes, so the old visuals will have to do in this case.

At the same time, the sale of EA to an investment consortium based in Saudi Arabia has seemingly done nothing to brighten the company's future on the development front either.

We all heard the news that legendary developer Bioware was set to close, and the upcoming fifth game in the Mass Effect series cancelled. That came about after those in charge supposedly made the choice to pursue Battlefront 3 in earnest, with that presented as a straight choice between the two.

That likely means that EA has little intention of investing significant money elsewhere, particularly on franchises that don't have a track record over the last few years. Unfortunately, that will leave Need For Speed out in the cold for some time to come yet, if we ever get a new game in the series again.

#3502. 5 Thriller Books That Need to Be Turned Into a Miniseries

If there’s one foolproof idea for a TV show, it’s adapting a thriller book for the screen. However, not all books make great source material for a must-watch miniseries. Whether it’s Netflix’s His & Hers, Prime Video’s The Night Manager, or HBO’s Sharp Objects, streaming platforms have found major success thanks to these book-to-screen adaptations. However, while television can hook audiences with jaw-dropping visuals and A-list stars, it ultimately boils down to how suspenseful the book is.

Both the book and the TV show must keep audiences glued to the mystery from start to finish, not letting them rest for a second until they get the answers. Even when audiences finally get the full picture, the answer should be something beyond their wildest deductions. From a plagiarism and identity case gone wrong to a battle between what your mind tells you and what other people say, here are five thriller books that need to be turned into a miniseries.

Granted, Lionsgate TV has technically optioned R. F. Kuang’s Yellowface as a scripted series. But since the announcement back in 2024, there haven’t been any confirmed updates about the project. Still, Yellowface has all the more reason to be adapted into a television series. Raising uncomfortable truths about race-based privilege, the novel follows ambitious novelist June Hayward, who has a hard time generating any hype around her work. Compared to Athena Liu, a successful Chinese-American author, June pales in comparison. But when Athena suddenly dies, June discovers her unpublished manuscript and sees an opportunity to finally get the recognition she wants.

Stealing another person’s work is a cardinal sin, especially when you're a writer. But even more atrocious is the fact that June, a white woman, steals the work of a writer of color who is not only dead but has written about experiences June could never relate to. But there’s another twist to this novel: Athena seems to “come back from the dead.” And so begins this twisty psychological thriller, where June is hunted by an anonymous person who knows about her plagiarism. A Yellowface adaptation could see June backed into one moral dilemma after another, and more often than not, she makes the least favorable choice just to save what remains of her struggling career. As her lies pile up, watching June desperately try to keep everything together could make for one seriously tense TV thriller.

It’s tough having a sister, especially when she has a thirst for blood. Oyinkan Braithwaite’s My Sister, the Serial Killer is set in Lagos, where Korede works as a dedicated nurse. But when her younger sister Ayoola keeps showing up with a corpse, usually a guy she’s dated, it becomes Korede’s job to clean up the mess. It’s an unlikely siblinghood, but when you’re bound by blood, it’s hard not to save your sister from her own misgivings. Things get even more complicated when Korede develops feelings for Tade, a handsome doctor who also happens to catch Ayoola’s attention.

As seen in hits like The White Lotus and Beef, audiences love watching twisted premises play out through dark comedy. There’s something absurd about seeing people take situations that would otherwise be considered serious crimes a little too lightly. My Sister, the Serial Killer is no exception. Korede and Ayoola repeat their cycle of murder and cleanup as if it’s just another part of their daily routine. But even with a dead body in the mix, the heart of the book lies in how far Korede is willing to go to protect her sister. With the sisters’ ordinary lives and their increasingly messy secrets, it’s only a matter of time before their bond snaps when their hearts get in the way.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

John le Carré, the author behind The Night Manager (adapted for Prime Video and starring Tom Hiddleston), is also best known for his equally riveting work, The Spy Who Came in from the Cold. Set during the bleak Cold War of the late 1950s and early 1960s, the novel follows Alec Leamas, a disillusioned British intelligence agent stationed in divided Berlin. He has watched his agents get killed one by one by Hans-Dieter Mundt, a ruthless East German intelligence chief. But when Leamas is tasked with taking Mundt down himself, he must face one final mission despite being worn out by years of espionage.

Forget the James Bond and Jason Bourne tropes — Leamas is the definition of an exhausted spy, worn down by years of working during one of the most politically tense periods in history. He lives a lonely life and drinks to numb his pain, far from the glamorous image people often associate with espionage. Once Leamas enters East Germany, he’s surrounded by enemies, and even the smallest mistake could put him in serious trouble. But there's more going on than Leamas realizes. He's caught up in a much bigger plan, with the agency willing to keep him in the dark to serve its own interests and those of the nation.

TikTok book recommendations often make the most sought-after shows, and Alex Michaelides' The Silent Patient became a BookTok sensation for good reason. Alicia Berenson seems to have the perfect life as a successful painter married to Gabriel, but everything changes when she shoots him five times. After his death, Alicia stops speaking and is admitted to a psychiatric facility, where years of treatment fail to uncover the reason behind her silence. Six years later, psychotherapist Theo Faber takes on her case, convinced he can finally get her to talk. But figuring out what happened proves much harder than he expects.

One of the thriller genre's most effective tricks is the unreliable narrator, and The Silent Patient uses two. Through Theo's investigation and Alicia's diary entries, readers get different perspectives on the events leading up to Gabriel's death. However, neither account necessarily tells the whole story. As Theo digs into Alicia's past, he discovers troubling relationships and painful memories that only make the mystery harder to solve. With short chapters and carefully timed revelations, Michaelides keeps readers guessing about whom they can actually trust. After all, the murder is only part of the mystery; figuring out the truth behind Alicia's silence is what makes the story so compelling.

If Stephen King's Carrie can get the modern TV treatment, the same can go for Misery. The psychological thriller feels especially relevant today, when stan culture can turn a harmless obsession into something much darker. Bestselling author Paul Sheldon finds this out the hard way after crashing his car during a Colorado snowstorm. He wakes up in the home of Annie Wilkes, his self-proclaimed number one fan, who claims to have saved his life. But Annie isn't the sweet, caring fan Paul expects. With two broken legs and no way to escape, Paul is stuck writing a new Misery novel to keep her happy.

Fans can get pretty intense about the people they idolize, and the internet has made stan culture a regular part of everyday life. But Misery takes things much further by showing what happens when a fan gets the chance to control the person she's obsessed with. Most of the story takes place inside a remote cabin, where Paul has nowhere to run and must deal with Annie's unpredictable demands. She gives him enough medication to keep him alive and writing, but she's also willing to torture him when he doesn't do what she wants. Each episode would see Paul struggle to escape a toxic fan who believes her loyalty to him gives her the right to own his life.

#3501. How Charlize Theron's John Wick Replacement Was Key To Nicholas Hoult's New Heist Thriller

EXCLUSIVE: Charlize Theron's movie has echoes in an upcoming release.

Director David Leitch has explained how Charlize Theron's John Wick replacement movie was key to developing Nicholas Hoult's new heist thriller, How to Rob a Bank. The forthcoming heist film sees Hoult take on the role of Ryan, leader of a group of bank robbers who livestream their heists and communicate with fans across social media. This leads to a police investigation and high-octane thrills, with Hoult's character at the forefront of the film. The movie arrives in theaters on November 13, 2026.

In an interview with ScreenRant's Brandon Zachary about the upcoming film, Leitch explained how his work directing the Theron-led 2017 thriller Atomic Blonde informed the way he approached How to Rob a Bank almost a decade later. He explained how Atomic Blonde had a number of ongoing, evolving changes during its production due to factors like "budgets and locations and size." This helped inform his approach to How to Rob a Bank, which also had a particular budget and worked with similar limitations.

David Leitch: [Of my movies] as a director, Atomic Blonde and How to Rob a Bank are probably the closest siblings, right? In terms of the drama that takes place. The thing I took away from Atomic Blonde — I learned a lot of lessons on that set. You have to focus on what you can change and really take the best of what's given to you in the scene and then move on. I think I learned a lot about the flexibility of filmmaking because that was such a twisty plot, and there were a lot of things changing in real time because of budget and locations and size. Because we had to do [How to Rob a Bank] at a price point, we had similar constraints at times. But having learned those lessons in the past on John Wick and Atomic Blonde, coming into How to Rob a Bank, I was feeling really confident. The decisions that you're making on the day on the battlefield.

Atomic Blonde follows MI6 field agent Lorraine Broughton in the 1980s, sent on a mission to find a list of agents being smuggled into the West ahead of the Berlin Wall's collapse. The action film had a budget of just $30 million, despite also featuring a twisty story and other notable actors like James McAvoy, John Goodman, Sofia Boutella, and Toby Jones in vital roles. Reviews for Atomic Blonde were mostly positive, and the movie managed to earn $100 million at the global box office during its run.

Based on Leitch's statement, production of the action movie required diligence and a flexible working schedule, something that would be vital to the way it was developed. The movie was also the filmmakers directorial debut, leading to him taking the reins on other big-budget projects, including Deadpool 2, Bullet Train, and The Fall Guy. It's clear Atomic Blonde had a major impact across his career, though, with How to Rob a Bank taking note of Leitch's directorial debut in the way its production was approached.

How to Rob a Bank is just one of Leitch's forthcoming projects. The director is also in charge of the upcoming action comedy Jason Statham Stole My Bike, starring Statham as a fictionalized version of himself. Leitch is also the founder of 87North Productions, under which the franchises Nobody and Violent Night have been produced. Needless to say, the director has plenty of experience in producing action movies, which makes the importance of Atomic Blonde to his latest release hold all the more potency.

With Hoult's movie just a few weeks away from arriving in theaters, How to Rob a Bank is shaping up to be another memorable installment amongst Leitch's movies. Since his approach to the film has echoes of Atomic Blonde, it remains to be seen how close the pair will feel in tone and in filmmaking approach. But, since he's proven himself with plenty of high-budget action movies already, his latest film seems poised to impress on a similar scale.

#3500. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

#3499. The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

When long-time producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped away from the James Bond franchise last year and Daniel Craig made it clear that he was finished playing agent 007, new producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman were faced with an unenviable task: finding a new actor to step into one of the most iconic roles in all of cinema. In the last few weeks, it’s been reported that Pascal, Heyman, and new Bond director Denis Villeneuve have zeroed in on a few final contenders including Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

Whoever the filmmakers choose, it’s likely to be controversial; Bond fans are very loyal to their particular favorites, and have been ever since Sean Connery was first replaced in the role back in 1969. The general consensus seems to be that Connery was the best Bond (though Craig runs a close second in most polls), but often one’s preference depends on which Bond was one’s first; as someone who grew up with Roger Moore, he’s always been my favorite, and I argued for his supremacy in an earlier IndieWire piece. Related Stories ‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Is Lured Into Lily James’ Cult in a Gut-Wrenching Drama ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

The casting of a new James Bond has always set off a media furor, even in the days long before social media and Letterboxd. When Connery decided he had had enough as 007 after shooting the fifth James Bond movie, “You Only Live Twice,” the press followed producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman’s talent search with bated breath. Once the role was cast, they scrutinized the choice with an intensity that no actor could have survived — certainly not a male model whose only screen credit was a series of chocolate commercials.

After Connery quit, Broccoli, Saltzman, and director Peter Hunt spent over a year interviewing, auditioning, and screen testing hundreds of actors — including a young Shakespearean thespian named Timothy Dalton, who would go on to play Bond nearly 20 years later — to play Bond in “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” Anthony Rogers (“Camelot”), John Richardson (“Black Sunday”), and stage actor Roy Marsden were considered before the filmmakers landed on George Lazenby, whose previous acting experience was limited to those chocolate commercials.

Lazenby lied at his initial meeting and said he had been acting in movies in Germany and Hong Kong, figuring the producers wouldn’t be able to check, but came clean to Hunt the next day. Hunt and the producers were concerned about Lazenby’s chops but loved his look, so they took a chance on the newcomer and put him through hours of voice coaching (to lose his Australian accent) and stunt training before deciding to pull the trigger a few weeks before production was scheduled to begin.

The question then became how to frame Lazenby’s onscreen introduction to make the transition as seamless as possible for audiences. One of screenwriter Richard Maibaum’s drafts began with Bond surviving an explosion that required him to undergo reconstructive surgery, but this was scrapped in favor of a more conventional prologue involving Bond encountering love interest Diana Rigg and fighting foes on the beach and in the water. When Rigg leaves Bond behind instead of making love to him as was customary for Bond’s leading ladies, Lazenby looks in the camera and says, “This never happened to the other fellow.”

It’s a very funny and very efficient way of acknowledging the change in personnel and then moving on, and the opening credit sequence further eases the transition by utilizing clips from earlier Bond movies. It also helps that the creative team on the movie consisted of Bond veterans including Maibaum, production designer Syd Cain, composer John Barry, and Hunt, who made his directorial debut with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had been an editor and second unit director on earlier Bond films.

As a result, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” still looks and sounds so much like a Bond film that the introduction of Lazenby is less jarring than it might have been, though what’s interesting about the movie is how much better it is in just about every way than the previous Connery pictures. One can argue about the relative merits of Connery vs. Lazenby, but there’s no debating the visual elegance of “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” which eschews the somewhat bland high-key lighting of the earlier Bond films in favor of something more atmospheric and glamorous.

Audiences at the time might not have appreciated Hunt and cinematographer Michael Reed’s efforts, being distracted by debates over Lazenby, but contemporary directors like Steven Soderbergh and Christopher Nolan have referenced “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” as an influence and made a case for it as the best of all James Bond movies. On his website, Soderbergh wrote that “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was cinematically “the best Bond film and the only one worth watching repeatedly for reasons other than pure entertainment (certainly it’s the only Bond film I look at and think: I’m stealing that shit).”

Aside from containing several of the series’ best set pieces (including some awe-inspiring ski chases that inspired Nolan when he made “Inception”), “On Her Majesty’s Service” is also the most emotionally resonant Bond film to be made before the Daniel Craig era, with a genuinely moving love story between Lazenby and Rigg. Although composer John Barry scored a lot of 007 movies, his talents were never put to better use than in this film, which fully took advantage of Barry’s skill for sweeping, romantic themes that would later win him an Oscar for “Out of Africa.”

Lazenby gets some of the credit here too; he may lack Connery’s icy charm, but he’s a more human Bond. Displaying a slightly goofier sense of humor than Connery, he’s a transitional figure between the original 007 and the more overtly comic one Roger Moore would introduce in “Live and Let Die” four years later. According to Lazenby, he could have expressed even more emotion had Peter Hunt allowed it; when the actor played one particularly devastating scene with tears in his eyes, Hunt ordered a second take, arguing that Bond shouldn’t cry.

As good as he is in the part, Lazenby’s experience shooting “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” doesn’t seem to have been pleasurable, though whether or not the blame rests on his shoulders depends on who’s telling the story. According to Lazenby, Hunt went cold toward him early in shooting over a misunderstanding and was too preoccupied with the technical side of things to give him much attention; Cubby Broccoli, on the other hand, said Lazenby was spoiled and entitled and alienated many of his colleagues.

Although Broccoli was ultimately happy with Lazenby’s performance, by the time the movie opened, there were a lot of lingering hard feelings — a situation that wasn’t helped by the fairly lukewarm reviews Lazenby received, or by one of his representatives making a statement that Lazenby would not be returning to the role of James Bond. This was the first Broccoli or Harry Saltzman heard of any plans for Lazenby to abandon the part, and they quickly announced that Lazenby had been fired to make it seem as though his departure was their decision, not his.

Although Lazenby later stressed that he wasn’t the one who made the announcement he was quitting, he also clearly didn’t have any great desire to stay on as Bond. His contract was for seven years and had multiple clauses that he felt would restrict his career and lifestyle, and he still hadn’t signed it when “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” wrapped. Lazenby figured he could make more money doing one film in Italy than he could in five years on his Bond contract; he also, in one of the great errors in judgment in movie history, assumed that the James Bond franchise was dying in the era of “Easy Rider” and wouldn’t last much longer anyway.

In fact, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was a sizable hit, grossing $82 million on a production budget of $8 million. It wasn’t as popular as the last Connery film, however, and the mixed reviews gave it the aura of a failure. Broccoli and Saltzman began another worldwide search for a new Bond, considering American stars like Clint Eastwood, Burt Reynolds, and Adam West before convincing Connery to return. The result, “Diamonds Are Forever,” was a monster hit, and Lazenby went on to scattered work around Europe, acknowledging years later that his decision to quit Bond was a major mistake.

Lazenby didn’t completely leave 007 behind, however. After “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” he played a James Bond-esque character in the “Alfred Hitchcock Presents” episode “Diamonds Aren’t Forever” and, in 1983, Lazenby appeared in the TV movie “Return of the Man from U.N.C.L.E.” as a spy with the initials J.B. (who drove an Aston Martin, no less). The actor made a handful of interesting films after he played Bond, most notably Brian Trenchard-Smith’s great action film “The Man from Hong Kong” and Peter Bogdanovich’s exquisite Paul Theroux adaptation “Saint Jack.”

Lazenby was never more memorable than he was as James Bond, however, and it’s a shame he didn’t play the character in more pictures and further develop his variations on the persona. It remains to be seen where Villeneuve’s selection will place in the pantheon of Bonds, but whoever is cast would best be advised to ignore the inevitable social media firestorm that’s coming their way.

Lazenby’s saga proves that no matter how capable an actor is stepping into Bond’s shoes, it takes a while for history to render a fair assessment. 57 years after critics dismissed it, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” has stood the test of time — it’s Soderbergh and Nolan’s verdicts, not those of the contemporary press, that have proven correct.

#3495. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3493. Denzel Washington's 122-Minute Thriller Masterpiece Is Officially Streaming For Free

Denzel Washington’s absolute greatest performance is a thriller masterpiece that’s available to stream right now. Denzel Washington has built one of Hollywood's most acclaimed careers, moving effortlessly between gripping dramas, high-octane action movies and Shakespearean adaptations. With a truly illustrious career, the two-time Academy Award winner has repeatedly demonstrated why he remains one of the industry's most compelling leading men.

Some of Denzel Washington's most memorable performances come when he steps outside the familiar territory of the heroic protagonist. The actor has a particular talent for playing characters whose charm conceals something considerably more sinister, making audiences question just how much they should trust the person standing at the center of the story.

His collaborations with director Antoine Fuqua have produced some particularly memorable results, including The Equalizer franchise that has kept audiences entertained across multiple installments. Yet their most celebrated collaboration remains a much grittier affair, one that gave Washington an opportunity to embrace his darker instincts while sharing the screen with another exceptional actor.

Released in 2001, Training Day is a crime thriller that boasts terrific performances, an increasingly nerve-racking story and an uncompromising portrayal of police corruption. It barely gives audiences time to catch their breath, and its central performances remain just as compelling more than two decades later. Training Day is available to watch for free on Tubi from November 1, 2026, making it a particularly tempting addition to the free streaming catalog.

Antoine Fuqua's Training Day benefits enormously from the chemistry between Washington and Ethan Hawke, whose contrasting performances provide its dramatic backbone. Washington plays Alonzo Harris, a veteran Los Angeles Police Department narcotics detective who takes rookie officer Jake Hoyt (Hawke) under his wing for an eventful first day with the department's narcotics division.

Alonzo initially presents himself as an experienced officer who understands the realities of working in dangerous neighborhoods. However, Jake quickly discovers that his new partner's methods are considerably more questionable than he anticipated. Alonzo operates according to his own rules, manipulating situations, intimidating suspects and demonstrating an alarming willingness to disregard the law.

Washington is magnificent as Alonzo, bringing an extraordinary amount of charisma to a character who is fundamentally terrifying. His confidence makes it easy to understand why people follow him, even when his behavior becomes increasingly indefensible. The actor also clearly relishes the opportunity to abandon his traditionally heroic screen persona, delivering a performance packed with swagger, menace and unpredictable energy.

Hawke is an equally important part of the equation. His Jake begins as an ambitious but relatively inexperienced police officer, and his growing discomfort provides the audience with an increasingly desperate perspective on Alonzo's behavior. Rather than simply playing the straight man opposite Washington, Hawke gives Jake a convincing progression as his character begins to recognize the danger surrounding him.

There is a reason Training Day continues to feature prominently in conversations about Washington's finest performances. Alonzo Harris is a character who genuinely believes his methods are justified, even when his actions become increasingly criminal. That conviction makes him considerably more interesting than a straightforward cinematic villain.

Screenwriter David Ayer builds the story around a single day in Los Angeles, allowing the relationship between Alonzo and Jake to deteriorate as the rookie discovers what his new partner is really doing. The escalating tension comes from Jake's increasingly difficult decision whether to follow the instructions of an experienced detective or trust his own moral instincts.

Snoop Dogg's appearance as wheelchair-using drug dealer Blue, Dr. Dre's role as Paul and Macy Gray's appearance as Sandman's wife give Training Day a particularly distinctive supporting ensemble. Scott Glenn and Tom Berenger also help establish the wider network of relationships surrounding Alonzo.

Training Day was not without its critics, particularly regarding its increasingly exaggerated violence and final act. Nevertheless, Training Day remains a fascinating examination of authority, corruption and the seductive nature of power.

Warner Bros. first announced plans for a Training Day prequel in October 2019, with the proposed movie focusing on a younger version of Alonzo Harris. Titled Training Day: Day of the Riot, the project would take place in late April 1992, two days before the verdict in the Rodney King trial. The acquittal of the four Los Angeles police officers charged in connection with King's beating sparked the infamous Los Angeles riots, providing a historically significant backdrop for the story.

The project was subsequently expected to begin production in California in February 2022, although that proposed filming date came and went without the movie entering production. Antoine Fuqua later provided a more encouraging update in 2023, confirming that the project remained in development and that the filmmakers were still working on the script while looking for another director. Fuqua also made clear that he did not intend to direct it himself.

In March 2025, Fuqua again confirmed that the prequel was still being developed, although the screenplay remained under revision. He was not attached to direct, meaning the project still had considerable creative hurdles to overcome.

There is certainly an interesting story to explore in Alonzo's earlier years, particularly given the historical circumstances surrounding the 1992 Los Angeles riots. However, Washington's performance established such a distinctive screen presence that casting a younger actor will be a considerable challenge.

The prequel will need to give audiences a convincing portrayal of how Alonzo became the charismatic, ruthless detective they encountered in the original film. For now, Day of the Riot remains a development project rather than an imminent release.

Washington has continued to deliver acclaimed performances since Training Day, but his portrayal of Alonzo Harris is one of the defining achievements of his career. It also represents the last time he won an Academy Award for acting, despite receiving several nominations in the years that followed.

The actor previously won Best Supporting Actor for his performance as Private Silas Trip in Edward Zwick's Glory (1989). However, his Best Actor win for Training Day was a particularly significant achievement, as he became only the second Black actor to win the Academy Award for Best Actor, following Sidney Poitier.

Washington has hardly disappeared from the Academy's radar since then. He received Best Actor nominations for Flight (2012), his adaptation of Fences (2016), Roman J. Israel, Esq. (2017) and The Tragedy of Macbeth (2021). He also received a Best Picture nomination as a producer of Fences.

More recently, Washington delivered another memorable performance as Macrinus in Ridley Scott's Gladiator II (2024), earning nominations at several major awards ceremonies, although he missed out on an Oscar nomination. His subsequent work demonstrates that there is considerably more to his career than one extraordinary crime thriller. However, his performance in Training Day.
