#3491. ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement

The Kasato Maru ferried 325 Okinawans to Brazil in 1908, making it the first immigrant ship from Japan to do so. That history is highlighted by the opening of the documentary “Okinawa Saudade,” (“saudade” being a Portuguese word for bittersweet longing, typically around a memory or place). The film looks at the results a century later, now that an estimated 200,000 Brazilians of Okinawan descent are living in Brazil today, and director and cinematographer Yoju Matsubayashi finds a specific and emotionally straightforward route into complicated history. The director has covered the subject to some extent before in 2020’s “Okinawa / Santos,” a film which collected testimony on the forced deportation and even internment of Japanese immigrants in Brazil in the 1940s.””Okinawa Saudade”” narrows that focus to the families of two third-generation Okinawan-Brazilians, specifically ones with an interest in — and a longing towards — the island their families came from, something partially explored through the arts. Related Stories AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

A visual motif of waves viewed from above punctuates different segments of the film, typically as its subject reflect on the previous movements of their families. In the first instance of the shot, a dissolve to a young girl practicing a traditional Japanese dance on her family’s farm in Brazil immediately communicates that feeling of “saudade,” a soft and gently expressed shadow hanging over much of the film. That feeling of “saudade” is seen in the incidental details the director chooses to include, like how one subject’s grandfather grew dragonfruit with Okinawan seeds, as well as his capturing of more outwardly emotional moments, like a tearful reaction to photos not seen in a long time.

The teenage girl Yumi practices Ryukyu Buyo, while a man named Everton practices Eisa, an Okinawan folk dance involving drums. By unspooling their enthusiasm for the history of such Okinawan heritage arts and the history of their families, Matsubayashi also orbits a history of displacement. This emerges in an accumulation of lots of small personal stories, like how one characters recounts their family’s war-motivated exile from Santos. Yumi and Everton also learn more of these details for themselves, the film following them on their travels to Okinawa through exchange programs and traineeships. (In some delightful cases, the learning cuts both ways, as Everton reunites with estranged family, and Yumi’s Okinawan relative marvels at the dialect being preserved halfway around the world.)

Capturing their subjects’ respective journeys with occasional and mostly spontaneous interviews, Matsubayashi prioritizes personal histories over the big picture,as the assembly of the footage and the occasional interjection of archival material makes the relationship of this diaspora a bit clearer. Some of these families left Okinawa to avoid the military draft as well as starvation. Others were divided because of land seizures by the US military in the wake of the war (“I’ve learned that this is a sad place,” Yumi reflects, a quote placed over footage of lingering American military bases on the island). Some viewers might be dissatisfied with how Matsubayashi never quite engages with World War II and the full history of Okinawan annexation directly, but the context feels like plenty for the stories which he is telling, choosing instead to focus on the feelings which all children of immigrant backgrounds have felt: an uncertainty about their connection with the homeland of their parents and grandparents, and a yearning to understand it. The glimpses are enough, as “Okinawa Saudade”gradually paints a picture of how the historical struggles of the island have translated to the diaspora.

Everton outright says why he engages in Eisa drumming, saying that “we are Brazilians, but we don’t look like Brazilians, so we are always looking for belonging,” and his engagement with these traditional artforms becomes a part of this. Both learn the different nuances of their respective practices at home compared to in Okinawa, though both are graced with teachers who refuse to be super didactic about what is “authentic” (“We are always adjusting,” Yumi’s teacher says, “there is no such thing as perfection”). It’s also simply moving seeing, through Matsubayashi’s rather unvarnished camerawork, how the connections and feelings embodied in performing arts can have such far reach across time and place, highlighting the community found by the Brazilian Okinawans who preserved a little piece of the island for themselves.

“Okinawa Saudade” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3490. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3489. Johnny Depp Officially Confirms 'Pirates of the Caribbean' Return Chances

Some franchises just wouldn't be right without certain stars, and it's fair to say that Disney's multi-billion dollar seafaring franchise is one of them. Johnny Depp and Captain Jack Sparrow are undoubtedly, and intrinsically, linked and it may well end up being his defining role at the end of the day but it seemed like, after five movies, billions of dollars at the box office, and a rather spectacular amount of controversy, Captain Jack's days were numbered. Not so.

Depp has confirmed that he's open to returning as Captain Jack Sparrow in Disney's Pirates of the Caribbean franchise, but he's got his own. Speaking with Entertainment Tonight while promoting his new movie Ebenezer, Depp said he would happily reunite with longtime franchise producer Jerry Bruckheimer, although his involvement would depend on the direction of the story.

If things are exactly where they need to be with regard to how they are going to top off the ‘Pirates’ franchise… the only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note. I will go to work with [Jerry] Bruckheimer tomorrow for anything. Doesn’t matter… if it’s Jerry, i trust him. We have a deep friendship.

Depp originally debuted as Sparrow in 2003's Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl, delivering a performance that earned him an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor. He subsequently returned for Dead Man's Chest, At World's End, On Stranger Tides, and Dead Men Tell No Tales, with the five movies collectively earning more than $4.5 billion worldwide.

Bruckheimer has remained enthusiastic about bringing Depp back, previously confirming that he'd spoken with the actor about returning for a sixth movie. Speaking with Entertainment Weekly in 2025, the producer explained that the decision would ultimately depend on the quality of the screenplay.

If he likes the way the part’s written, I think he would do it. It’s all about what’s on the page, as we all know… We are still working on a screenplay. We want to make it. We just got to get the right screenplay. We haven’t quite gotten there yet, but we’re close.

The next installment has been in development for several years, with Jeff Nathanson, who previously wrote Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, working on the screenplay. Bruckheimer previously revealed that Nathanson had made significant progress on the movie, particularly its conclusion.

He’s cracked it. He’s got an amazing third act. We just gotta clean up the first and second and then we’ll get there. But he wrote a great, great third act.

Bruckheimer has also made no secret of his admiration for Depp, previously explaining why he believes the actor remains such an important part of the franchise.

It’s a reboot, but if it was up to me, [Johnny] would be in it. I love him. He’s a good friend. He’s an amazing artist and he’s a unique look. He created Captain Jack. That was not on the page, that was him doing a little Pepé Le Pew and Keith Richards. That was his interpretation of Jack Sparrow.

Disney has not officially confirmed Johnny Depp's return or announced a release date for Pirates of the Caribbean 6. All five previous installments are streaming now on Disney+.

#3488. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3487. Apple TV's 8-Part 'Prison Break Meets The Night Manager' Thriller Is Just 2 Months Away

Thriller fans should buckle up because Apple TV is starting 2027 off with a bang. When the streaming platform first launched in 2019 (back when it was known as Apple TV+), it didn't make much of a splash. Though flagship series like The Morning Show and See boasted starry casts, they received tepid reviews, and without a back catalog to speak of, Apple TV initially seemed like an easy subscriptionto pass on.

However, with such a wealthy parent company behind it, Apple TV could take its time finding its footing. Slowly but surely, the platform became more known for its top-tier programming, from Emmy-winning comedies like Widow's Bay, The Studio, and Ted Lasso to groundbreaking sci-fi shows like For All Mankind, Severance, and Pluribus. While other streamers prioritize feeding the almighty algorithm, Apple TV has become the new HBO in its commitment to producing innovative, risk-taking television.

Though Apple TV's sci-fi shows are its most popular, the platform is also upping its thriller game. In just four years, it's released six seasons of the popular spy thriller series Slow Horses, while miniseries such as Presumed Innocent, Disclaimer, and Lucky became hits just as famous for their water-cooler plot twists as their A-list stars. In January 2027, the streamer will premiere The Wanted Man, a "Prison Break meets The Night Manager" thriller series with one of the most phenomenal casts of any Apple TV show to date.

Created by George Kay, the writer behind Netflix's best thriller series Lupin and HBO's buzzy new legal thriller War​​​​​​, The Wanted Man premieres on Apple TV on January 6, 2027. The series stars Hugh Laurie as Felix Carmichael, Britain's most powerful crime boss, who is incarcerated after a shocking betrayal. Eager to take revenge and reclaim his empire, Felix devises an elaborate prison-break plan.

Laurie isn't the only veteran actor in the Wanted Man cast, as he's joined by Thandiwe Newton, who won an Emmy for her work in Westworld, and Stephen Dillane, who delivered one of Game of Thrones' most underrated performances as Stannis Baratheon.

The upcoming Apple TV series also has an incredible younger cast, including Dunkirk star Fionn Whitehead and Sanctuary: A Witch's Tale breakout Hazel Doupe. British character actress Gina McKee (The Borgias) and child actor Elliott Heffernan (Blitz) round out The Wanted Man's main cast. While not a sprawling ensemble, it's an excellent mix of talented British performers at different stages in their careers.

Based on its premise, The Wanted Man promises to take the high-octane, master-escape-plan thrills of Prison Break and give them a British, elite-crime polish à la The Night Manager. Even more exciting, the new show will feature Hugh Laurie playing another underworld kingpin. The key difference, however, is that unlike Laurie's acclaimed role as arms dealer Richard Roper in The Night Manager, Felix Carmichael is the underdogas the titular "wanted man".

Choose the movie with the higher Rotten Tomatoes score.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

By swapping The Night Manager's glamour for Prison Break's grit, The Wanted Man can't hide behind vibes. It has to be smart, psychological, and twisty, but it can't be too far-fetched because, as Prison Break fans know, that's how the whole story can fall apart. Fortunately, with a masterful storyteller in George Kay and a talented, Laurie-led cast, 2027 may get its best thriller very early on.

#3486. Apple announces all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen Mac

Apple has officially announced the all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen laptop.

The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser. Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well.

Read on for all the details about the new high-end laptop…

The new machine features a light-up Apple logo, tandem OLED, and touch input on the display.

It runs on the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, like the existing MacBook Pro models without OLED touch displays.

John Ternus, who is rocking a new profile picture with the new Mac, shared the first look at the new machine on X:

We’re glowing with excitement over the new MacBook Pro. You’ve gotta touch it to believe it. pic.twitter.com/BLiGkGaefL

Apple previously used a glowing Apple logo on its notebook hardware for years until the 12-inch MacBook and 2016 MacBook Pro.

Pricing for the new laptop starts at $2899 for the 14-inch model. The 16-inch version starts at $3399.

Pre-orders are available starting today with deliveries starting November 6. You can find the product page for the new MacBook Pro here. The new machines are also available on Amazon.

Colors include silver or space black options with standard or nano-texture display configurations.

Beyond the new high-end laptop, Apple also announced the redesigned iPad mini, M6 iMac, and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro this week. Back in March, Apple upgraded the standard 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops to the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple calls the new design both thinner and lighter than the standard MacBook Pro models in the same size configuration.

The new MacBook Pros look awesome with glowing Apple logos. We’re so back. pic.twitter.com/Ce6G8EIVQF

The new MacBook Pro is the first to use what Apple calls a PROLED XDR display, replacing Mini-LED as the MacBook Pro display technology.

While Apple has innovated with multi-touch on the iPhone and iPad, the Mac has been resistant to touch input for years. The new MacBook Pro changes that with the first touchscreen Mac display. Here’s what Apple says about touch on the Mac.

MacBook Pro features Touch for the first time, bringing pros a whole new way to interact with their content. Crafted specifically for the Mac, every touch interaction feels incredibly responsive and refined. Everyday tasks are simple and intuitive, allowing users to scroll through a webpage with a natural swipe; pinch to zoom in on a photo; drag and drop slides from one presentation to another; and double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick to tile it into place. And the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it — reducing latency so users feel like they’re touching the content itself.

Apple also touts the use of a new hinge technology in the MacBook Pro, in part to support touch input without compromising on stability:

Touch also introduces entirely new ways of working for pro users. Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing; musicians can play software instruments right onscreen; and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display. And these new ways to interact with MacBook Pro work in tandem with the keyboard shortcuts and trackpad gestures pros know and love. In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.

In addition to touch as an additional input method, the new MacBook Pro also adopts the Dynamic Island in favor of the notch.

The Dynamic Island now comes to Mac, serving as the home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Not interested in touch? The existing MacBook Pro configurations from March stick around at the same prices. You just lose OLED, the glowing Apple logo, and the thinner and lighter design. Performance, however, is pretty much on par between versions as both offer M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

The new laptops can be configured with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of solid state drive storage.

Peak display brightness jumps from 1600 nits to 2000 nits for HDR content.

I honestly think this is a downgrade. Remember when Apple introduced the Touch Bar? It was supposed to be a big deal, but eventually Apple removed it. Now they’re adding a touchscreen to the MacBook. What’s the actual point?

If it supported the Apple Pencil, I could understand the appeal, especially for designers. But without it, I honestly don’t see much use for it. Maybe I’m wrong, but I’ve used touchscreen Windows laptops before, and I never really found it useful.

I can’t help wondering whether Steve Jobs would have approved of this direction. Apple needs a better marketing team that understands what people actually want, rather than adding a touchscreen that, in my opinion, offers very little practical use.

The 14-inch model is half a pound lighter at just 3 pounds even compared to 3.5 pounds for the same version of the previous design. The overall footprint is reduced as well with 0.59 x 12.24 x 8.52 inch dimensions compared to 0.61 x 12.31 x 8.71 inch dimensions when comparing 14-inch models.

The 16-inch model is notably lighter as well. The new design weighs in at 4 pounds even compared to 4.7 pounds for the previous design. Dimensions change to 0.63 x 14 x 9.62 inches compared to 0.66 x 14.01 x 9.77 inches between designs.

Playing piano on the touchscreen MacBook Pro pic.twitter.com/lDlwIeqErd

The new machines still use Touch ID with no Face ID support. Apple also doesn’t offer built-in cellular models of the new MacBook Pro. We’ll have to keep waiting for Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity.

#3485. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3483. 'Scream 8' Officially Confirmed by Original Star

Lade Omotade is a News and Features Author at Collider, covering everything from casting announcements and streaming trends to behind-the-scenes stories and the cultural impact of today's biggest film and TV franchises. Since joining the team in 2024, she has written more than 1,000 news stories, with her work also cited by outlets like AOL and IMDb.

One of this century's biggest horror franchises has just confirmed that a veteran star will be back for its planned sequel. As reported earlier in March, Scream is set to return for its eighth installment, following the commercial success of Scream 7, despite its critical misfire. Released in theaters on February 27, 2026, Scream 7 debuted with a 43% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes, which has since fallen to 29% from 228 reviews. Still, it became the franchise's highest-grossing film, earning $214 million worldwide against a $45 million production budget.

An official release date for Scream 8 has yet to be announced, but the film appears to be in active development, with no director on board yet. Meanwhile, writing duo Lilla and Nora Zuckerman have been tapped to write the screenplay. The sisters most recently served as showrunners for the hit Peacock series Poker Face and have also worked as writers and co-executive producers on popular shows including Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., Suits, Fringe, and Prodigal Son.

As the horror sequel moves forward, Neve Campbell, who has been part of the franchise since its inception in 1996, has officially announced her return, per Deadline. While promoting her role in the Netflix series Black Doves, Campbell confirmed her involvement in Scream 8, naming it one of her two upcoming projects in an interview with the Associated Press. "Scream 8. That's in the pipeline as well," she said. However, when pressed for further details about the upcoming film, she said, "You know I can't tell you anything about Scream 8," before adding, "I'll be in it."

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Campbell has starred in six of the seven Scream films so far, taking a break from the franchise for 2023's Scream VI after a contract dispute. She returned for Scream 7 after reportedly receiving a $7 million salary to play Sidney Prescott (now Evans) again, which supposedly helped the movie achieve its biggest box office success, with $63.6 million in its opening weekend alone.

In Scream 7, Sidney has built a new life: she's married to police chief Mark Evans, runs a coffeehouse, and raises her children, including her teenage daughter Tatum, named after Sidney's late best friend, Tatum Riley. Soon, her life is turned upside down when a new Ghostface killer emerges and targets her daughter. Franchise actors Courteney Cox and Matthew Lillard also returned in Scream 7.

#3480. Chris Hemsworth's Netflix Action Franchise Is Already Huge, But It's About To Become So Much Bigger

Chris Hemsworth’s gripping action franchise is dominating Netflix, and it’s only going to get bigger. Chris Hemsworth has become one of Hollywood's most recognizable action stars, largely thanks to his decade-long run as Thor in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. However, the Australian actor’s appeal extends well beyond wielding Mjolnir, with increasingly ambitious roles establishing him as an impeccable action star.

Netflix has been particularly successful in recognizing that potential. While the streaming giant has invested heavily in established properties and familiar intellectual property, some of its biggest original hits have come from relatively straightforward action concepts. A charismatic leading actor, spectacular stunt work and an international setting can go a surprisingly long way, especially when the resulting movie attracts an enormous global audience.

Hemsworth has already enjoyed considerable success with one such property, delivering two hugely popular installments that have established a compelling alternative to his superhero work.

With another major sequel on the way and two separate spin-offs expanding the fictional universe, Extraction is rapidly becoming one of Netflix's most ambitious action franchises. And Tyler Rake might soon have plenty of company.

When Extraction dropped on Netflix in April 2020, it immediately became one of the platform's biggest action releases. Directed by Sam Hargrave and produced by Anthony and Joe Russo's AGBO, Extraction stars Chris Hemsworth as Tyler Rake, an Australian black-ops mercenary hired to rescue the kidnapped son of an imprisoned Indian crime lord.

The premise is hardly complicated, but that's part of its appeal. Rake is an exceptionally capable operative thrown into an increasingly dangerous situation, and Extraction gives Hargrave plenty of opportunities to capitalize on his background as a stunt coordinator. One standout sequence is an extraordinary 12-minute apparent single take involving street fights, car chases and rooftop pursuits.

It's the sort of action filmmaking that makes just watching somebody reload a weapon feel exciting. The 2023 sequel, Extraction 2, raised the stakes considerably, giving Hargrave an even bigger canvas for his elaborate action sequences. Its celebrated prison-break sequence features another ambitious continuous-shot illusion, lasting more than 20 minutes when its various components are combined.

Both movies reached number one on Netflix's global charts and entered the streamer's all-time most popular English-language film rankings (via Netflix).

The franchise also benefits from Hemsworth's convincing action-star credentials. Although audiences will always associate him with Thor, Tyler Rake gives the actor a considerably more grounded character, one whose physical abilities are impressive but whose personal vulnerabilities provide an emotional foundation.

Netflix officially confirmed Extraction 3 in April 2026, with Hemsworth returning alongside Idris Elba. Hargrave is also back in the director's chair, while David Weil, known for Hunters and Citadel, is writing the screenplay.

The third installment has already begun production, with filming getting underway in New South Wales in July 2026. The production subsequently moved to Thailand, with reports indicating that filming wrapped in late October. Netflix has yet to announce an official release date, although a 2027 arrival is anticipated (via Variety).

Plot details remain firmly under wraps, but the returning cast offers some interesting possibilities. Elba's mysterious character was introduced towards the end of Extraction 2, offering Rake an opportunity to work for a powerful new employer. His return suggests that the relationship between the two characters could become increasingly important.

Pierce Brosnan is also joining the third movie, alongside franchise newcomer Don Lee, whose casting provides another exciting indication of the series' expanding ambitions. Lee is particularly well suited to this kind of physical action filmmaking, having established himself as a formidable screen presence in South Korea's The Roundup franchise.

Hargrave has promised to push the boundaries of action filmmaking again, describing the third installment as the franchise's biggest undertaking yet. Considering what he achieved with the previous two Extraction movies, that's a fairly exciting prospect.

Perhaps the most exciting development is that Netflix isn't relying exclusively on Tyler Rake to keep the franchise alive. Two separate spin-offs are expanding the property into different countries and formats, introducing new characters who can carry their own action-packed adventures.

The first is Tygo, a South Korean spin-off starring Don Lee, best known internationally for Train to Busan, Eternals and The Roundup franchise. Lee plays Tygo, a former child soldier turned mercenary who embarks on a revenge mission against Korea's criminal underworld after an operation goes wrong.

Directed by Lee Sang-yong, Tygo also stars Lee Jin-uk (Squid Game, Sweet Home). It's an intriguing combination of international talent, particularly given Lee's reputation for delivering wonderfully physical action performances. It also gives the franchise an opportunity to embrace South Korean action cinema rather than simply transplanting its established formula into another country. Production wrapped in March 2026.

Netflix is also developing Mercenary: An Extraction Series, an eight-episode television project starring Omar Sy. The Lupin actor plays a soldier-for-hire attempting to rescue hostages in Libya while navigating competing factions, ruthless killers and increasingly difficult moral decisions. Filming took place in Ireland and Morocco, with production wrapping in March 2026. These projects expand Extraction into a much more ambitious franchise.

Vitally, the Extraction franchise doesn't necessarily require every story to revolve around the same protagonist. Mercenaries undertaking dangerous rescue operations provide an exceptionally flexible foundation for storytelling, particularly when each assignment can introduce a different country, criminal organization and set of personal complications.

That's an advantage the franchise's creative team appears to understand. Rather than making every installment dependent on Tyler Rake, the filmmakers are establishing a broader world in which different operatives can operate independently while sharing the same general universe. Tygo and Mercenary are already demonstrating how that approach can work.

There are plenty of possibilities beyond the projects currently in development. A future installment could follow another international extraction team, explore the organizations employing these mercenaries or introduce an entirely different corner of the global criminal underworld. There's also room for the individual projects to develop their own identities.

A South Korean action thriller should feel different from an African-set mercenary television drama, even if both share the same fundamental DNA. That creative flexibility could prevent the Extraction franchise from becoming repetitive, something that inevitably becomes a problem when action sequels just try to make everything bigger and louder.

#3479. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR vs MacBook Pro: Here’s every difference

Apple unveiled its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR this week (pre-order here), which joins the lineup alongside the existing MacBook Pro using the same M5 Pro and Max chips. Here’s an in-depth comparison of the two models.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has an all-new industrial design. It’s the first design overhaul for the MacBook Pro since 2021.

You still get a 14.2-inch regardless of whether you choose PROLED XDR or not. On the 16-inch model, PROLED XDR is 16.3 inches, slightly larger than the standard 16.2-inch.

Apple’s new design is a bit sleeker and significantly lighter-weight. It also brings back the glowing Apple logo on the lid that was an iconic element in previous generations. Additionally, the PROLED XDR has a newly designed hinge that provides greater stability.

Here’s a breakdown of how each model compares in size and weight:

As the numbers show, the overall size difference is fairly minor, but the reduced weight should be obvious to anyone who upgrades.

The new MacBook Pro’s display technology is so important, Apple put it in the branding. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR features a tandem OLED that Apple says is “the world’s best laptop display.”

Again, it’s available in 14.2-inch or 16.3-inch sizes that are nearly identical to the standard MacBook Pro.

The PROLED XDR display is touch-enabled, with macOS 27 introducing a variety of optimizations for touch input. So if you want a touchscreen on your Mac, that’s a big advantage.

Tandem OLED means you’ll get deeper blacks, true-to-life color, and also a new max peak brightness of 2,000 nits (up from 1,600). And Adobe RGB is now supported, along with a host of industry-standard reference modes.

There’s also a Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro. It replaces the notch and serves as the home to software features like Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Apple is using the exact same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips in its two MacBook Pros, so performance should in theory be the same across models.

That said, real-world testing will reveal whether the new MacBook Pro design has an impact on sustained performance—for better or worse.

Memory options are also identical with the PROLED XDR model and standard MacBook Pro. That means:

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR largely retains the same storage options as the standard MacBook Pro, with one exception.

The only change here is that there’s now a high-end 16TB option when you choose M5 Max. Previously, 8TB was the most storage available in any MacBook Pro.

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers identical battery life and fast charging features as the standard MacBook Pro. That means:

All MacBook Pro models can fast charge up to 50 percent battery in 30 minutes.

Apple’s MacBook Pro models all feature the same 12MP Center Stage camera with support for Desk View, 1080p HD video recording, and an advanced image signal processor with computational video.

However, because of touchscreen support, the PROLED XDR model adds one new feature: Advanced Video Stabilization.

Essentially, this exists so that if you’re touching your display during a video call, it won’t have an impact on your camera feed.

The MacBook Pro PROLED XDR features largely the same speaker system as the standard model, but with a pair of key upgrades. Per Apple Newsroom:

The industry-leading six-speaker audio system in the new MacBook Pro features an all-new woofer design that provides 50 percent deeper bass and all-new tweeters that shape sound dispersion for remarkable clarity…And for the first time, dedicated audio tuning for closed-lid use delivers exceptional sound quality when MacBook Pro is connected to an external display, so users can enjoy a premium audio experience however they work.

Apple clearly learned from past mistakes of removing ports from pro users. With the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, you get all the same ports as on the standard MacBook Pro. Ports include:

One upgrade that will benefit some users is that Genlock is now supported by the Thunderbolt 5 ports as well.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. That’s a $400 premium over the standard MacBook Pro.

Apple’s standard MacBook Pro starts at $2,499 for the 14-inch size and $2,999 for the larger 16-inch.

Warm fuzzies for the return of the glowing Apple logo but I won't need the other features so it's not worth the extra $400 to me.

Overall, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers a lot of upgrades over the standard model, but with the same basic performance and battery life. If you want a better display, touch support, a Dynamic Island, and various other smaller improvements, PROLED XDR is the way to go.

You can pre-order MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display here for launch-day delivery.

#3474. 'Victorian Psycho' Officially Reveals the Most Shocking Popcorn Bucket Ever Made

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

After the Dune: Part Two sandworm bucket became everybody’s favorite inappropriate conversation starter, it was only a matter of time before another movie made us question what we were willing to stick our hands into for popcorn. Collectible concessions have become a competition, and horror fans are an easy audience for anything disgusting enough to make the person sitting next to them uncomfortable. Speaking as one of those people, it takes quite a bit to make me reconsider a snack.

Victorian Psycho has apparently taken that as a challenge. Maika Monroe’s new movie is heading to theaters on Friday the 13th, a perfectly lovely date to watch a governess make an English household regret hiring her. Its promotional campaign would also like to ruin the refreshments.

The movie's newly revealed popcorn bucket is a baby with an open, bloodied torso that you eat out of. Dressed in cream-colored lace and a bonnet, the little nightmare comes nestled in an ornate wooden-style cradle. The promotional photos include a helpful demonstration of someone holding it like an actual infant while eating handfuls of popcorn from its abdomen. Check out the popcorn bucket below!

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Directed by Zachary Wigon, Victorian Psycho stars Monroe as Winifred Notty, a governess who arrives at Ensor House in 1858. She’s supposed to educate the children and teach them manners while concealing her psychopathic tendencies, which feels like something the family should have caught during the interview. Staff members begin disappearing, and suspicions about the new hire follow. Thomasin McKenzie and Jason Isaacs also star.

After being stalked through It Follows, Watcher, and Longlegs, Monroe getting to be the problem is an appealing change of pace. Winifred’s name appears on the bucket’s promotional artwork, which attributes your new cinematic companion to her “demonic impulses.” Without having seen the movie, it's probably safe to bet that leaving children in her care is a bad idea. The supplied announcement doesn’t include a price, purchase link, or participating theater chains, so we’re still waiting to learn how fans can acquire their own popcorn baby. The artwork does invite people to procure one, though, which gives collectors something deeply unpleasant to look forward to.

Personally, I need to know what happens after the movie. Do you wash it in the sink? Put it in a cabinet? Bring it out when guests ask if you have a serving bowl? Buying this bucket means making several more decisions about the baby in your home, and none of them are going to sound good out loud.

Victorian Psycho opens in theaters Friday, November 13.

#3469. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. Anything that you can plug an AUX cable, USB, or USB-C port into can stream high-quality, 24-bit audio wirelessly to the Tour One M3. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

As the official synopsis teases, Secret Service follows Kate Henderson, a senior MI6 officer and head of the Russia Desk, as a covert investigation uncovers evidence that a high-ranking U.K. politician may be a Russian asset. #3464. You Can Get These 'Nothing' Over-Ear Headphones for $55 Right Now

Nothing, the upstart U.K. brand that makes products like phones, smartwatches, and headphones, has quickly become one of my favorite players in tech. Its products offer unique features and designs, and the prices are competitive. For example, right now, Nothing's latest budget over-ear headphones, which were released in October 2025, the CMF Headphone Pros, are just $55 (originally $99). This is a great option for anyone looking to get reasonably priced over-the-ear headphones that punch above their weight when it comes to performance.

Much like Nothing's CMF Buds Pro 2 earbuds, the CMF Headphone Pros are budget headphones that don't feel like it. They're an affordable alternative to the popular Headphone 1 (currently $199), and seamlessly integrate into the Nothing/CMF ecosystem, which includes smartphones, watches, and other audio products. There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). On the other side, you'll find an "Energy Slider," which tunes your sound in real-time, instantly adjusting the treble and bass balance.

You'll get an impressive 100 hours of playback on a single charge (reduced to up to 50 hours with ANC turned on) as well as AAC, SBC, and LDAC support. They have an IPX2 rating for resistance against sweat, and there is a 3.5mm audio jack for wired listening.

Nothing is known for its minimalistic design, but these headphones do a bit more by allowing you to mix and match the earcups with different colors (sold separately for $25). These are a good option for those looking for stylish, budget over-ear headphones that have great battery life and excellent audio quality for their price point.

#3463. Ex-Ohio State Professor Kills Wife, Tries to Stab Dog After Nude Photo Blackmail Threats

A former Ohio State University professor has been sentenced to life in prison after admitting he stabbed his wife to death in a shocking murder he claims was triggered by an online sextortion scheme.

77-year-old James Hill, a retired Ohio State music professor, confessed to killing his wife, attempting to stab his dog, and then plunging a knife into his own chest after a woman he met online allegedly threatened to release his nude photos unless he paid her $15,000 in Apple gift cards.

According to court documents, Hill told investigators he believed the only way out of the situation was to kill his entire family.

On November 9, 2025, Hill says he received a threatening message from a woman he'd been communicating with online. He'd previously sent her nude photos. The woman allegedly demanded $15,000 in Apple gift cards, threatening to expose his explicit photos if he didn't pay up.

Hill claimed he felt trapped and saw no other way out.

He told investigators he initially went looking for his gun, but couldn't find it, claiming his 64-year-old wife, Mary, had hidden the firearm years earlier. So, instead, he grabbed a knife.

Hill told local authorities that Mary was sitting at her computer in the couple's den when he approached her from behind and began rubbing her shoulders.

She reportedly told him it felt "good" ... but what happened next was horrifying.

Hill says he pulled a knife from his belt and stabbed his wife once in the chest. He told investigators Mary looked directly at him as he stabbed her, and he apologized while holding her as she died.

He told authorities he then walked into the living room and attempted to stab the couple's dog. According to court documents, the dog was struck but managed to escape before Hill could do anything more.

And before calling for help, Hill allegedly logged onto his computer and deleted several photos and documents.

Around 2:30 PM that afternoon, Hill finally called 911, telling the dispatcher, "We need police and an ambulance."

But when the dispatcher asked what was happening, the call abruptly disconnected.

Hill then unlocked his front door, sat down on his couch, and stabbed himself in the chest.

According to WBNS, he remained on the couch until officers arrived just four minutes later.

Court documents obtained by TMZ show Hill initially pleaded not guilty to his wife's murder. However, on October 28, 2026, he withdrew that plea and pleaded guilty to felony murder and cruelty to a companion animal.

Hill was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 15 years.

That means the 77-year-old could potentially be eligible for parole in his early 90s.

#3461. Henry Cavill & Mike Flanagan's Sci-Fi Prime Video Series Warhammer Hits Major Milestone

Henry Cavill and Mike Flanagan's Warhammer 40,000 just hit a major milestone.

Flanagan has provided a key update to the sci-fi Prime Video series, offering a new information about the show as its development continues. The upcoming, live-action Warhammer 40,000 TV show is being led by Cavill and Flanagan, both of whom are working on bringing the dark sci-fi universe to life on the small screen. Development of the series has received general updates since December 2024, when Amazon MGM Studios finalized a deal with Games Workshop on the adaptation rights to the universe. Flanagan joined the project in July 2026.

Now, speaking with Deadline about his future projects, including Carrie season 2, Flanagan offered a major update on him and Cavill's approach to Warhammer 40,000 onscreen. The filmmaker explained the challenge of adapting a universe that has hundreds of novels and other pieces of media, any of which could be used as a launchpad for an adaptation. However, he confirmed that he and Cavill have officially found a starting point for the franchise's live-action debut, expressing his excitement without revealing what to expect.

Check out what Flanagan had to say below:

Henry Cavill would be furious if I divulged anything about what we’re working on. All I can say is that Warhammer is a fascinating world. The challenge, as anyone familiar with it knows, is finding a way in – it’s so big. There are 700 novels, discounting the [table top] game, the interactive elements and so much of the rest of the lore.

[We found] a very cool and unexpected on-ramp into it, which I think is very exciting. I’m sworn to secrecy on all of it, but I’m having the time of my life working on it.

The new Warhammer 40,000 TV show is expected to star Cavill in the leading role, while he also serves as an executive producer on the series. It's also planned to be the start of a larger expansion of the franchise, with its onscreen presence under Amazon's umbrella getting developed into a shared universe. Since story details have yet to be revealed, it's unclear how the show will play out, and from where it's story will derive. But with a starting point now in place, Flanagan's update is a positive one for the new series.

Warhammer 40,000's debut on an Amazon-owned platform has already happened, too, priming audiences for the upcoming series. This came in the form of an episode of Secret Level, an anthology series with episodes derivative of various video games. For the sci-fi universe, its episode takes place after Space Marine 2, a third-person shooter released in 2024. An animated series based on the episode is in development as of August 2026, with Cavill serving as executive producer alongside creators John Orloff and Dave Wilson.

As for the live-action series, there's no word yet on when production will begin, nor how long it'll take for the series to see the light of day. But the franchise is still plotting plenty of other major releases in the meantime, including the upcoming Total War: Warhammer 40,000, which will take the franchise into the world of real-time strategy. The universe isn't going anywhere anytime soon, which means whatever Flanagan and Cavill have been planning, it's something that'll stay relevant no matter what.

Although there's still no official word on where Cavill and Flanagan have decided to start the show, it's clear the pair have a distinct vision for what Warhammer 40,000 will look like on the small screen. Since there's now a plan in place, details are likely to be revealed sooner rather than later. Flanagan has been sworn to secrecy for now, but whatever grand plan is in place, it sounds like it'll be the beginning of something grand for the franchise as a whole.

#3459. Ternus addresses Apple breaking touchscreen Mac taboo: ‘Who knew?’

In an interview with WIRED, Apple executives including CEO John Ternus, hardware chief Johny Srouji, and marketing chief Greg “Joz” Joswiak discussed the company’s decision to bring touch to the Mac. Here are the details.

For years, online commenters countered rumors of touchscreen Macs with quotes from Steve Jobs and other Apple executives, including Phil Schiller, arguing that touchscreens had no place on the Mac.

Shortly after Apple announced the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, journalist Steven Levy published an interview with Apple executives in WIRED discussing the company’s decision to reverse its longstanding stance on touchscreen Macs.

I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.

In the interview, Ternus notes that while indirect input through the trackpad and keyboard remains central to the Mac experience, “there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”

He also stresses that Apple sees touch as an add-on, rather than a feature that should require compromises to the MacBook Pro’s design.

Throughout the interview, much of Apple’s reasoning for finally bringing touch to the Mac revolves around the fact that it reworked and developed several hardware and software components to make touch possible without compromising the Mac experience.

“We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”

As for Srouji, he argued that advances in technology over the past decade had finally made it possible for Apple to meet its standards for a touchscreen Mac.

Thank God the touch support is very basic and limited to specific situations, and there’s no redesign of macOS that would make it something like a hybrid device. I'm fine using it occasionally for very specific tasks, but the Mac should remain a touchpad/mouse device.

That included custom silicon, a redesigned thermal system to keep the display from feeling hot to the touch, and a reworked hinge to minimize screen wobble when users interact with it.

“Ten years is a very, very long time,” says Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer. “Many things have changed, whether it’s the display technology, the custom silicon, et cetera.” Eventually, he told me, the confluence of chips, display tech, and software architecture “met our bar.” “I like my engineers to be gated by physics, not imagination or timelines,” he says.

Joz, in turn, noted that part of Apple’s decision was driven by a new generation of touch-first users who expect to interact directly with their screens:

“Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone,” Joswiak says. “So this is something that they’re natural with. There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.”

He added that professional users, including “engineers, scientists, software developers, and media creators,” had also been asking Apple to bring touch to the Mac.

The full interview also touches on (no pun intended) how Apple adapted macOS for touchscreen interactions, the new gestures for Dynamic Island, and whether touch might eventually make its way to other Macs. You can read it in full here.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

#3456. The new MacBook Pro has everything I wanted, minus one thing

Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is an exciting upgrade that delivers nearly every feature I was hoping for, with just one exception.

I’ve been waiting a long time for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR. I haven’t used a Mac as my primary computer in years, but rumors about this new model made me think that might finally change.

The iPad Pro has been my main computer of choice since 2015, but lately I’ve grown increasingly curious about revisiting the Mac full-time.

This is largely due to Apple making the Mac, to me at least, a lot more exciting than it was in 2015. The Mac’s hardware and software are advancing in compelling new ways, and today’s new MacBook Pro brings an especially big leap.

As a longtime iPad Pro user, I’ve come to expect features like touch support and OLED in a relatively thin, lightweight device. I also love how iPadOS tends to advance in lockstep with iOS, a trend that has recently started extending to macOS too.

Until recently, it seemed like Apple’s latest and greatest tech—with the exception of pro-focused chips—has been in the iPad and iPhone.

I don’t need an extremely powerful chip, as my computing needs are pretty basic. But I do value having a great display, touch support, and modern OS features like the Dynamic Island.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR delivers those things. I’ve ordered one and can’t wait to give it a legitimate shot to be my full-time computer. But my biggest hesitation is the lack of cellular.

I use cellular all the time on my iPad Pro. I tend to work from coffee shops and random outdoor spots for at least a few hours every day. And in my experience, public Wi-Fi options aren’t reliable enough for my needs.

Having a persistent cellular connection on my iPad is a killer feature. I very much wish Apple provided the option of cellular on the MacBook Pro too.

I’m hoping that personal hotspot has become a lot more reliable since I last tried it. Apple does say its N1 wireless chip makes the feature better.

I’m very surprised that they didn’t include cellular. They can fit it in an Apple Watch, so why not a laptop computer? I think more buyers would want it than not want it. And given the price of the machine, nobody’s going to not buy it because it has a cellular modem that they’re not going to use.

I’ll stick with my MacBook Air and 13" iPad Pro.

Additionally, I wonder if the need for cellular will be mitigated some by having a tablet-sized iPhone Duo in my pocket soon. So if I need to stop in the middle of nowhere and get work done quickly, maybe the Duo will suffice.

In any case, the MacBook Pro looks like a fantastic product regardless. It’s not for everyone, and the high price hurts, but I’m excited to give it a try.

What are your thoughts on the new MacBook Pro? Would you use cellular if it was offered? Let us know in the comments.
