#3455. 10 Disney Films That Are Perfect From Start to Finish

There is something simply magical about Disney. You've likely grown up with the films as a child, shared them with your own kiddos, and, for some, remained a Disney kid at heart through your adult years. Whether Disney was simply part of your past or still in your present, there's no denying how incredible the Disney vault of films truly is. While we cherish so many movies, only a handful of Disney films are perfect from start to finish. These ten titles are among them.

From brilliant animated features that defined the Disney Renaissance to live-action masterpieces that continue to spark joy, these ten films captured the magic of Disney the entire way through. These films are so good, you can't help but think about them long after the final credits roll! They may even be on repeat in your own home! For this list, we will consider films under the Pixar umbrella as well since they are so ingrained into the Disney world. Are there any Disney classics not on this list that you consider practically perfect in every way?

Bringing a theme park ride to the big screen, Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl is a little thrill ride. Directed by Gore Verbinski, eccentric pirate Captain Jack Sparrow (Johnny Depp) teams up with blacksmith Will Turner (Orlando Bloom) to rescue the governor's daughter, Elizabeth Swann (Keira Knightley). They pursue the cursed, skeleton-transforming crew of the Black Pearl, led by Captain Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush), who need Elizabeth's blood to break an ancient Aztec gold curse. Proving that a fun, original story is the recipe for success, the first chapter in the storied franchise blends tight, multi-functional writing, iconic character introductions, and a rare mix of practical and supernatural spectacle.

Right from the jump, the film wastes no time establishing the world as the dominance of the British Royal Navy and the apparent death of piracy. From there, Captain Jack is introduced, and a legendary character is born. Standing atop the mast of a sinking, micro-sized boat and stepping off onto the dock just as it slips completely underwater, he communicates his entire philosophy: he is wildly incompetent-looking, endlessly lucky, deeply dignified on his own terms, and completely unpredictable. The film works as a self-contained story, yet allows just enough rope for a future. And a future followed. Verbinski infused the film with a kinetic, swashbuckling energy reminiscent of classic Hollywood adventures, paired with a grim horror edge courtesy of the moonlight-revealed skeleton crew. With a stellar score by Klaus Badelt and Hans Zimmer, the movie balances genuine dread, physical comedy, and grand romance without ever taking itself too seriously.

After a rough start to the 21st century, Disney animation found its footing once again. One of the very best entries is the magical Encanto. The film tells the story of Mirabel Madrigal (Stephanie Beatriz), the only member of an extraordinary Colombian family who has not been blessed with a magical power. When she discovers that her family's enchanted home is in danger, she realizes that she might be their last hope to save the magic. Encanto is praised as a masterpiece because it flawlessly subverts traditional fairy tale tropes, delivers an emotionally complex narrative about generational trauma, and features a perfectly integrated soundtrack.

Encanto is a celebration of family told through the eyes of a previously underrepresented culture in animation. Yet the characters are brilliantly accessible and relatable. Every character represents a specific, recognizable family role, from the overburdened eldest sibling in Luisa (Jessica Darrow) to the seemingly perfect golden child in Isabela (Diane Guerrero) and the scapegoat Bruno (John Leguizamo). Encanto transcends typical fairy-tale storytelling because it is not a typical good-versus-evil story. The "antagonist" is actually the crushing weight of perfectionism, expectation, and unresolved generational trauma embodied by Abuela Alma (María Cecilia Botero). Through visual brilliance, Encanto leans heavily into Colombian culture, utilizing magical realism, authentic regional clothing, diverse Afro-Latino representation, and localized flora and fauna to ground its fantasy in real-world beauty. Add in an addictive score by Lin-Manuel Miranda, and we all talked about Bruno because it was the ultimate earworm. Disney is all about magic, but Encanto reminds us that the gift of empathy is just as powerful. ​​​​​​​

We saw a whole new world through the brilliance of Aladdin. The iconic film tells the tale of Aladdin (Scott Weinger), a street-smart young man, who frees a powerful, wish-granting Genie (Robin Williams) from a magic lamp and disguises himself as a wealthy prince to win the heart of Princess Jasmine (Linda Larkin). Along the way, he must thwart the evil royal vizier, Jafar (Jonathan Freeman), who seeks the lamp to take over the kingdom. Blending breakneck comedy, rich hand-drawn art, and a timeless heart-versus-facade theme, Aladdin continued to prove why the Disney Renaissance was a landmark moment for animation.

Beneath the magic, Aladdin's arc is a classic tale of self-worth, proving that true value comes from being honest about who you are rather than hiding behind a royal disguise. With that profound theme at its core, the film works as a fun, flashy romp of identity. A buddy comedy at its core, the film moves at a brisk, energetic pace that never drags between action, romance, and comedy. Williams’ vocal performance as the Genie shattered the boundaries of traditional animation, bringing a rapid-fire, pop-culture-riffing energy that adults and kids alike adore. Animator Eric Goldberg matched Williams' voice with fluid, limitless metamorphosis that kept every second on screen unpredictable. Alan Menken, Howard Ashman, and Tim Rice crafted a powerhouse musical lineup of hits, both comedic and romantic. A beautifully animated feature, Aladdin remains a heartfelt classic. ​​​​​​​

Arriving before the rise of superhero blockbusters, The Incredibles served as the blueprint for how to master the genre. The Incredibles follows Bob Parr (Craig T. Nelson), known as Mr. Incredible, and his wife Helen (Holly Hunter), also known as Elastigirl, undercover superheroes forced into mundane suburban lives after masks are banned. When Bob secretly accepts a rogue mission, his entire family must unite to save him and the world from a vengeful former fan. The Incredibles seamlessly blends a mid-century spy aesthetic, mature family dynamics, and a sharp deconstruction of the superhero genre long before modern cinematic universes dominated the box office.

The Incredibles explores the cost of heroism. The movie immediately addresses the legal and social consequences of collateral damage, showing citizens suing superheroes and forcing them into a government relocation program. By showcasing that weight, when it moves toward learning about the family, The Incredibles focuses on universal human problems like midlife crises, marital tension, sibling rivalry, and the awkwardness of growing up. Each family member, though they may resemble another fantastic quartet, has a power that reflects their psychological state: Bob carries the heavy burden of the past, Helen tries to pull everything in different directions, Violet (Sarah Vowell) hides behind her force fields, and Dash (Spencer Fox) bursts with restless energy. With a compelling villain in Syndrome (Jason Lee), the narrative moves beyond simple superhero tropes. A technical and artistic wonder, the retro-futuristic style is remarkably crisp. Launching a franchise, The Incredibles is exactly that. ​​​​​​​

While we have great reverence for the classics, only one is genuinely perfect: Pinocchio. It tells the story of a wooden puppet named Pinocchio (Dickie Jones), brought to life by a fairy and told he can become a real boy if he proves himself brave, truthful, and unselfish. With the help of his conscience, Jiminy Cricket (Cliff Edwards), he must navigate dangerous temptations and treacherous con artists to reunite with his creator, Geppetto (Christian Rub). Pinocchio pairs groundbreaking hand-drawn animation with a bold, emotionally resonant story about temptation, morality, and growing up.

For the time, Pinocchio was a stroke of animation genius. The film was pioneering, achieving hyper-realistic water effects, swirling smoke, rain, lightning, and natural lighting. Multiplane layers gave 2D backgrounds stunning, three-dimensional depth, making Geppetto's cluttered, cozy workshop and the open ocean feel tactile and alive. Backgrounds used gouache and oil paintings that deliberately kept visible brushstrokes and paper textures, making every frame look like a living painting. The story is one that was meant to bring a bit of fear to young viewers. The story shifts smoothly from the charming, homey warmth of Geppetto's clock-filled cottage into genuinely dark, high-stakes territory as a means to teach. Sequences like the transformation on Pleasure Island and the frantic escape from Monstro the Whale are visceral and frightening, making Pinocchio's moral choices actually matter. A truly timeless tale, perhaps having the song that became the company’s official theme song proves why this film has such a brilliant reputation. ​​​​​​​

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Though we had experienced life under the sea before, it took Finding Nemo to truly make us completely enamored with the creatures that populate the ocean. After a diver captures his young son, Nemo (Alexander Gould), and takes him to a Sydney dentist's office, an overprotective clownfish named Marlin (Albert Brooks) embarks on a perilous ocean rescue mission. Accompanied by a forgetful blue tang named Dory (Ellen DeGeneres), Marlin learns to overcome his fears and let go, while Nemo plots his own escape from a fish tank. A modern animated classic, Finding Nemo blends tight, dual-narrative pacing, deep emotional stakes about letting go, and groundbreaking underwater visuals that still hold up today.

Like many Disney films do, trauma sets the tone for the story. The film starts with a devastating, high-stakes prologue that immediately grounds the story in real parental grief and fear. It’s an accessible entry that then moves into the heart of the film. Marlin’s nervous overprotectiveness isn't a simple character flaw; it is a trauma response that makes his painful journey across the ocean feel earned. While Marlin learns to loosen his grip and trust the world, his son Nemo learns to be brave, act independently, and step up when it counts. Finding Nemo is a masterclass in character. Every encounter, from the vegetarian sharks to the East Australian Current with Crush the sea turtle (Andrew Stanton), builds high-energy comedic relief while subtly forcing Marlin to adapt, surrender control, and change his worldview. Pixar studied marine biology, underwater lighting physics, and limb-less animation to craft a vivid, luminous digital ocean that revolutionized 3D animated design. With brilliant world-building, extraordinary characters, and a high-stakes adventure, Finding Nemo leaves you wanting more in all the right ways. ​​​​​​​

The fact that a hybrid film from 1964 still feels so timeless proves just how magical Mary Poppins is. Based on P. L. Travers' book series, the live-action-animated musical comedy follows Mary Poppins (Julie Andrews), a magical nanny, who visits a dysfunctional family in Edwardian London to help reconcile a preoccupied father and his children. Using music, whimsical adventures, and a touch of magic, she teaches the family how to love and appreciate one another again. Mary Poppins blends a transformative family redemption arc, unforgettable Sherman Brothers music, and a seamless fusion of live-action and hand-drawn animation into a cohesive masterpiece that taps into every human emotion.

Mary Poppins thrives on its bold storytelling risks. The fusion of styles became a magical touchstone that simply worked wonders. By combining live actors with hand-drawn animation, matte paintings, and practical stage tricks, Mary Poppins created a tactile, storybook London that still enchants audiences today. Between the dynamic performances from Andrews and Dick Van Dyke and the sensational score, the film takes on great heights that fly as high as a kite. Every single song is memorable, doing double duty by advancing the plot and defining character psychology. The heart of the story is Mary’s mission to wake up George Banks (David Tomlinson), who is emotionally detached, rigid, and consumed by his bank work. The family starts the film fractured and ends it together in emotional unity. The film brings the laughs with just enough emotion to provide a practically perfect film. ​​​​​​​

Through the Magic of Toy Story, we were reminded that we will always have a friend in our toys. In this groundbreaking Pixar classic, a group of living toys has their secret world disrupted when an old-fashioned cowboy doll, Woody (Tom Hanks), becomes jealous of Andy's (John Morris) sleek new space action figure, Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen). After getting lost and captured together by a destructive neighbor, Woody and Buzz must set aside their rivalry and work together to return home to their owner. Toy Story matches era-defining technical ambition with a razor-sharp, economical script that treats toys and human emotions with equal dignity, igniting our imaginations in brand-new ways.

We all pondered what our toys do while we’re away, and Toy Story gave us that answer. The core anxiety of whether I’ll still matter when someone new comes along is an ugly, universal human emotion disguised as a toy story. It becomes a universal theme that is presented accessibly. Woody starts out petty, insecure, and genuinely jealous of Buzz Lightyear, making his eventual growth and redemption feel earned. Buzz’s delusional belief that he is a real space ranger isn't just a running gag; it's a genuine identity crisis that mirrors the human struggle of finding out you aren't the center of the universe. The film is a masterclass in voice acting, with a top-notch ensemble bringing each character to life. Limiting the world to tactile, everyday locations creates high-stakes tension out of small, relatable spaces. The brilliance of its computer-generated animation comes from its attention to object textures. In turn, it creates a timeless visual that still looks dazzling today. ​​​​​​​

It’s safe to say that Beauty and the Beast is a tale as old as time. This game-changing animated classic tells the story of an arrogant prince (Robby Benson) cursed to remain a hideous beast until he learns to love another and earn her love in return before an enchanted rose loses its final petal. When a spirited young woman named Belle (Paige O’Hara) trades her freedom for her father's, she and the Beast gradually grow close and discover true love. Beauty and the Beast blends a Broadway-caliber musical score, a progressive heroine, and a groundbreaking visual style into a tight, emotionally earned romance.

Beauty and the Beast changed how we look at the princess archetype. Inspired by independent archetypes, Belle is intelligent, book-loving, and unimpressed by traditional vanity or handsome men who lack substance. Instead of a generic monster, the Beast undergoes a painful, gradual redemption arc defined by learning empathy, self-sacrifice, and patience. With an iconic supporting cast, Lumiere (Jerry Orbach), Cogsworth (David Ogden Stiers), and Mrs. Potts (Angela Lansbury) provide warmth, humor, and a rich, lived-in feel to the enchanted castle. The film functions like a classic Broadway musical, where every song moves the plot forward or defines a character. From toe-tapping production numbers to one of the greatest love songs ever written, Howard Ashman and Alan Menken wrote a genuine masterpiece. The film pioneered the Computer Animation Production System, culminating in the sweeping, multidimensional CGI ballroom dance that set a new benchmark for animated cinema. Earning a Best Picture nomination at the Oscars, Beauty and the Beast became the benchmark for animation. ​​​​​​​

Truly one of the greatest films ever made, The Lion King is peak Disney. The animated musical follows a young lion prince named Simba (Matthew Broderick and Jonathan Taylor Thomas), who is tricked into exile by his treacherous uncle, Scar (Jeremy Irons), after his father, Mufasa (James Earl Jones), is murdered. After growing up away from his kingdom, Simba must face his past and return home to reclaim his rightful throne. A masterpiece from start to finish, The Lion King blends a timeless Shakespearean drama, groundbreaking animation, and an unforgettable musical score into a tight, universal coming-of-age story that celebrates the circle of life.

The film kicks off in perfect fashion. The first four minutes of "The Circle of Life" set a hypnotic tone without needing a single line of exposition, gathering the animals of the Pride Lands as baby Simba is presented. From there, the world is painted with pristine realism. Animators studied live African wildlife and landscapes to give the hand-drawn savanna a mythic, breathing scale. The story is not light by any means. It tackles heavy, adult concepts like grief, betrayal, legacy, and identity in a way that remains digestible for children while hitting home for adults. Simba’s journey reflects stages of human growth in a relatable manner. Hans Zimmer's score and Elton John and Tim Rice's songs do more than entertain; they act as a secondary narrator that deepens the emotional weight of every scene. The film brilliantly balances high-stakes drama with necessary comic relief. A beautifully animated film, The Lion King defined a generation.

#3453. Apple fined $15.5 million as South Korea orders changes to App Store rules

Apple and Google were fined today in South Korea over their app payment practices, with regulators also ordering both companies to change several policies. Here are the details.

South Korea’s Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) announced today a series of fines and corrective orders against Apple and Google over violations of the country’s Telecommunications Business Act.

Specifically for Apple, the KMCC imposed a fine of 20.81 billion won (approximately $15.5 million) and ordered the company to revise its App Store policies regarding payment methods and app review procedures, as well as prevent what it referred to as “discriminatory commission” practices from recurring.

This is the first enforcement case under the 2021 amendment to the Telecommunications Business Act, which introduced prohibited acts for app market operators, such as forcing specific payment methods and unfairly delaying app reviews.

In essence, the decision centers around three violations: forcing specific payment methods, unfairly delaying app reviews, and imposing discriminatory commissions.

On the payment methods front, the KMCC said Apple and Google “effectively forced” developers to use their own in-app payment systems by imposing a 26% commission and additional restrictions on third-party alternatives.

“This constitutes an act in which an app market operator unfairly uses its position in transactions to force mobile content providers and others to use a specific payment method,” the KMCC said.

As a result, Apple and Google must revise their policies to allow external payment methods and address restrictions imposed on developers using alternative payment systems.

As for the app review process, the KMCC found that Apple and Google “delayed app reviews, for example by not providing specific reasons when reviews were delayed or not clearly responding to individual inquiries about the reasons for delays and expected timelines.”

Accordingly, Apple and Google must revise their app review procedures to address these issues.

Finally, on the discriminatory commissions, which applied only to Apple, the KMCC found that between July 2015 and January 2023, the company calculated its 30% commission differently for South Korean and overseas developers. While overseas developers were charged based on prices excluding value-added tax (VAT), South Korean developers were charged based on prices including VAT.

“KMCC determined that this constituted an act of unfairly providing rates, numbers, telecommunications facilities, or other economic benefits for telecommunications services or bundled services in a discriminatory manner compared to other users […].”

The KMCC said Apple will also have to take measures to prevent discriminatory commission practices between South Korean and overseas developers from recurring.

According to Reuters, Apple said it “‌disagreed ⁠with the decision and was evaluating options in accordance with South Korean ​laws.” ​Apple added that “⁠it has worked with outside developers ​to enable innovation ​through ⁠its App Store.”

Today’s decision comes on the heels of similar regulatory pressure in other markets, including Brazil and Japan, where Apple has introduced alternative app distribution and payment options in response to local competition rules.

The company has also faced years of scrutiny in the European Union, where it recently overhauled its App Store fees and business terms to address concerns raised by the European Commission.

#3451. Hideo Kojima Brutally Rejected Anime Adaptation Of His Most Iconic Game

As Hideo Kojima's iconic Death Stranding gets an anime spin-off in Death Stranding: Isolations, fans learn that not only was Kojima pitched on a similar adaptation for Metal Gear Solid, but he laughed the idea out of the room.

Launching in 1987, the Metal Gear franchise follows the adventures of Solid Snake as he opposes his clone father Big Boss and the shadowy, Illuminati-esque group known as the Patriots. The franchise reached international acclaim with its move to 3D in 1998's Metal Gear Solid.

Boasting six mainline games and over a dozen spin-offs, Metal Gear Solid is known for its lengthy cinematics and byzantine lore, with each game taking a radical new approach to its supposed protagonist, whose clone origins allow his likeness to be used in creative and misleading ways (for example, none of the images in this article depict the same person.)

As recently reported by ComicBook.com, Toonami co-founder Jason DeMarco shared a (now deleted) post on X detailing a failed attempt to pitch Hideo Kojima on a Metal Gear anime. According to ComicBook.com, the post read:

About a year after Metal Gear Solid came out, I met with Kojima and discussed the idea of making a Metal Gear anime. I talked about how much I loved the games and what the anime might be like. He paused, looked at his producer, pointed at me and said “Otaku.” and laughed.

In this context, 'otaku' is Japanese slang for a person with an overly intense, nerdy interest, often used to dismiss fans of manga or anime. A later (also deleted) tweet makes it clear that DeMarco found the response funny rather than insulting, but the pitch was nevertheless turned down.

Kojima's use of 'otaku' as an insult isn't surprising to fans of Metal Gear Solid, since the franchise includes a character named for and dedicated to mocking this archetype. Hal "Otacon" Emmerich is Solid Snake's closest ally, but is often depicted as the cowardly butt of the joke, especially unlucky in love.

The character has given many fans the mistaken impression that Kojima has a disdainful attitude to anime, though that isn't the full picture. While Kojima appears to have a joking dislike for those who obsess exclusively about the format, he has frequently shared his enjoyment of anime including Chainsaw Man and Blue Eye Samurai, albeit in the context of a more overarching enjoyment of television and cinema (indeed, Kojima recently reviewed James Watkins' Clayface.)

Kojima's jibes at 'otaku' seem to be relatively light-hearted, with potentially a note of genuine criticism for those who obsess over a specific facet of pop culture rather than pursuing a broader experience.

With the launch of Death Stranding: Isolations, fans are understandably speculating about whether Metal Gear Solid could get a similar treatment. The answer is yes, but with a major catch.

As a franchise, Metal Gear Solid is owned by Konami Group Corporation, the publisher of the Metal Gear games. However, Kojima underwent an acrimonious split with the company in 2015, establishing his own indie studio Kojima Productions in the aftermath. Kojima has seemingly directed veiled barbs at Konami since, leaving fans with the impression that he has no desire to partner with them again.

For that reason, if a Metal Gear Solid anime adaptation or spin-off does ever appear, it will likely be without the involvement of Hideo Kojima, and - judging by how the corporation handled marketing around Metal Gear Solid V and the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Volume 1 - may not even bear his name.

Death Stranding: Isolations is coming 2027 from Disney+.

#3449. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3447. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3444. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3441. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3438. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3437. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

#3436. Apple and OpenAI trade secrets lawsuit now has an official trial date

Judge Edward Davila today formally established the schedule for Apple’s trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, including a trial date. Here are the details.

A couple of weeks ago, during an October 14 case management conference, Judge Edward Davila instructed Apple and the defendants to agree on a proposed schedule for the lawsuit, working toward a tentative trial date of July 19, 2027.

The parties were given until October 23 to submit their proposed schedule, which the judge has now formally established.

As we’ve been covering since July, Apple filed this lawsuit accusing the defendants of improperly accessing or using confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts.

In recent days, Apple scored two procedural wins in its efforts to obtain expedited discovery, with Judge Davila granting the company access to additional documents and information from the defendants ahead of the normal discovery process.

In a case management order issued today, Davila established July 19, 2027, at 9 a.m. as the official trial date, with additional deadlines for discovery, motions, and pretrial proceedings in the meantime.

Notably, the schedule includes a June 1 deadline for the lead attorneys on both sides to meet and discuss a potential settlement.

To be clear, this is a common procedural step in federal civil lawsuits and does not necessarily indicate that Apple and OpenAI are considering settling the case.

#3434. How AI Will Change Chip Design

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3433. Russia now requires Apple to store user communications and hand them over if requested

As Bloomberg reported today, Apple and Microsoft are now subject to Russian regulations requiring companies to store users’ communications and provide them to security agencies if requested. Here are the details.

Apple and Microsoft are now in Russia’s state surveillance registry, joining companies and services such as Google Meet, WhatsApp, Telegram, Snapchat, Cloudflare, and Blizzard Entertainment, all of which are required to store users’ messages, audio and video communications, and provide them to Russian security agencies if requested.

According to Bloomberg, Apple and Microsoft were added on October 2 to the “organizers of information dissemination” registry, which is maintained by Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor.

Companies on the list are required under Russian law to store local users’ correspondence, audio and video messages and turn that data over to security services if asked. They must also store in Russia information about users and the transmission of their communications for three years.

Companies that fail to comply can face fines and ultimately have access to their services restricted in Russia. Google and its Google Meet video-calling service were added to the same registry in January.

The move comes as Russia continues to tighten restrictions on foreign messaging services, having already blocked or limited access to platforms such as WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, and Apple’s FaceTime.

Specific to Apple, the company’s relationship with Russia has become increasingly complicated since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, prompting Apple to suspend product sales and exports while limiting services such as Apple Pay.

However, Apple continued operating the App Store in Russia, which has led to several disputes with local authorities.

In April, Russian users lost the ability to make new App Store purchases or renew subscriptions without an existing Apple Account balance, following government-imposed payment restrictions.

Apple might get away with it by simply exit Russia's market. It won't impact its economy much, afterall.

But what will happen when China will ask to do the same?

In June, the Kremlin demanded an explanation after Apple removed several apps developed by Russian state-controlled company VK from the App Store. Around the same time, Apple also removed banking apps linked to sanctioned Russian financial institutions.

More recently, in August, Russia’s antitrust regulator opened formal proceedings against Apple over its failure to preinstall the state-backed MAX messaging app and the RuStore app marketplace on its devices.

All of that said, neither Apple nor Microsoft has publicly commented on its inclusion in the registry or indicated whether it intends to comply with the requirements.

#3429. Apple seems to have the right approach to the first touchscreen Mac

Steve Jobs famously dismissed the idea of a touchscreen Mac back in 2010 when he said that it “gives great demo” but turns out to be “ergonomically terrible” in real-life use.

It was inevitable that eyebrows would be raised when the company did a U-turn on this by launching the first touchscreen Mac. But while I have no interest myself, I do think the company’s counterargument some 16 years later makes sense …

We thought about this years ago. We’ve done tons of user testing on this and it turns out it doesn’t work. Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical. It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue – and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off. It doesn’t work, it’s ergonomically terrible. Touch surfaces want to be horizontal […] that’s why we’ve perfected our multi-touch trackpads over the years.

Current CEO John Ternus addressed this change of heart directly. Specifically, he said that touch was intended to be a supplementary way of interacting with the machine rather than a primary one.

The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.

He suggested that it isn’t the headline feature of the new model.

All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.

I’m a Mac guy through and through, right from the original Macintosh back in 1984. I’m also a massive trackpad fan, using the Magic Trackpad on my desk setup rather than a mouse. To me, it’s just the perfect way to control a Mac.

There was a period when I quite frequently used a 12.9-inch iPad with Magic Keyboard as a mobile alternative. Like the new MacBook Pro, that setup offered the choice of using the trackpad built into the keyboard or the touchscreen.

What I noticed about my own usage in this laptop-like configuration is that I almost exclusively used the trackpad. The only time I used the touchscreen was for scrolling, especially when I wanted to scroll a significant way down a page. That absolutely tracks with Ternus’ perspective of trackpad first, touchscreen sometimes.

However, when an M1 MacBook Air replaced my iPad with a Magic Keyboard, I didn’t miss the touchscreen at all.

One of the many things that’s changed over the years, in large part because of Apple’s launch of the iPhone way back in 2007, is that almost an entire generation has grown up with a touch interface. For them, the idea of a laptop without a touchscreen seems somewhat archaic.

However, I do very much suspect that even this generation will still use the trackpad as the primary control mechanism for the very reasons Steve outlined 16 years ago.

I use a 2 in 1 Yoga for years and loved it. So, I’d prefer that the MacBook had a hinge like the Yoga to allow it to fully fold into a “tablet” or “tent” mode. But a touchscreen Mac, even only being allowed to use vertical, is a Giant Leap for mankind! 😄

The nightmare scenario for Mac users was Apple compromising the interface in order to support touch. None of us wanted to lose the high resolution UI elements and see them replaced with giant cartoon-like equivalents. None of us wanted to lose the precise control we get from a trackpad. Thankfully, that hasn’t happened.

So no, I won’t be buying one personally, but I can see why Apple added the feature, and I do think the company has the right attitude to it.

Do you agree, or have a different view? Please share your own take in the comments.
