#3424. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

#3417. Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback

Comedian Dane Cook’s house sits perched above Hollywood like a fortress, or a prison. A $7 million modernist hillside oasis with a baby-blue pool and a view stretching halfway across the Pacific, the house is Cook’s prized possession. He bought it back in 2008, in the boom years, when he was at the height of his career: selling out arenas, breaking chart records — and still a few months away from learning that his brother had stolen nearly every cent he’d earned. But we’ll get to that.

If “Dane Cook” is a name you haven’t thought about for a couple of decades, you wouldn’t be alone. For a period in the mid-2000s, Cook was the pinnacle of the comedy world. His résumé is like an aughts time capsule: one of the first comics to predict the power of social media, who harnessed millions of fans via MySpace; headliner of big Hollywood comedies opposite Jessicas Alba and Simpson; star of an HBO documentary series that aired after Entourage. In one 18-month stretch, Cook released an HBO special, dropped the highest-charting comedy album in 28 years (which eventually went double-platinum), hosted Saturday Night Live — twice — and sold out two shows at Madison Square Garden on the same night. “I had a great run,” he says with a grin.

Yet even at his apex, Cook was often the punch line — his very name a synonym for “overrated douchebag hack.” Other comics couldn’t stand him — partly for artistic reasons, and partly because they were jealous of his success. As a performer, he was always more energy than craft — cannonballing around the stage with his spiky hair and pre-distressed jeans, consonants popping like they were on creatine, sprinkling his Seinfeld-style observational bits on parking garages and mini golf with punchlines about blowjobs and tits. (Sample joke: “When you’re with somebody awful — I call that a relationshit!”) And no one could touch him.

Comedian Nikki Glaser was a huge Cook fan who once planned a girls’ trip to Las Vegas in college just to see him perform. “He was the biggest comedian in the world when I was starting out, so his influence was undeniable,” Glaser says. “There are still so many comics today who remind me of Dane, whether or not people remember him for it. He presented like a dumb frat bro, but he would sprinkle in phrases and new groupings of words that illustrated his point almost poetically. His comedy was almost musical — people would put it on at parties to just hang out to. To this day, I don’t know a comedian my friends listen to like we listened to Dane.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

But even as Cook stood astride show business, his life was secretly being dismantled under his feet. What he didn’t know was that his half-brother, Darryl McCauley — who’d served as Cook’s business manager since before he was famous — had been embezzling from him for years, possibly decades. It all came crashing down in 2008, when Cook got suspicious and started asking questions, and McCauley went on the run before being arrested. When the Massachusetts attorney general’s office finished their forensic audit, they put the total theft around $12 million. And that’s just what they could prove. Cook thinks it might be double that.

Cook avoided talking about it in public for years, for a variety of reasons. He was devastated, he was ashamed, he couldn’t figure out how to make it entertaining. But now he has a documentary — Funny Money, streaming on Netflix starting Nov. 6 — that details the whole sordid tale for the first time. “There was a hope and a concern,” Cook says of the film. “The hope was that this was a true-crime story that’s funny. The concern was that I’m a sad clown. I cried more [doing the film] than I did in therapy. So there’s really some anxiety that you see me like this.” Related Content Dane Cook’s Brother Stole $12 Million, Then Disappeared After Prison Release The Best Tech and Home Audio Gifts From Marshall and Google The Wait Is Over: Parke's NYC Mocknecks & Big Apple Merch Are Finally Here Steel Guitars by the Dozen: A Cultish Concert Pays Tribute to the Most Country Instrument of All

Cook, 54, is sitting in his home office, full of platinum records and framed magazine covers — a shrine to his fiveish-year peak. He’s wearing Earth-tone Nikes and a fitted brown polo, his highlighted hair both thicker and more kempt than it used to be. The shelves behind his desk are filled with fun nerd memorabilia, like an Obi-Wan Kenobi toy and a still-unboxed Wolverine.

As a kid, Cook used to spend hours playing with these toys — Stormtroopers battling G.I. Joes, Chewbacca fighting Doctor Doom. “But it was never ‘evil and bad’ for me,” he says. “It was always ‘misunderstood.’” What was Darth Vader’s trauma? What if Cobra Commander just needed a friend? “I was the only person watching Die Hard like: ‘But what happened to Hans?’”

For the past two decades, he’s been trying to figure out the same things about his brother. “Sometimes I sit and wonder, ‘Who is Darryl?’” he says. He shakes his head. “I don’t know.”

COOK GREW UP IN Arlington, Massachusetts, a working-class suburb of Boston. “I was very much a wallflower introvert,” he says. “A lot of anxiety. Mama’s boy.” He had cystic acne that left deep scars on his face. This is why he always moved around so much onstage — what he calls “the whirling-dervish thing.” “I just didn’t want you to look at me,” he says. “If I don’t stay still, then you won’t key in and go, ‘You’re ugly.’”

Darryl was seven years older — his half-brother from his mom’s first marriage. They were never extremely close on account of the age difference, but they did share a bedroom, and they did hang out — playing R.B.I. Baseball on Nintendo, or raking the leaves while the other held the bag. Darryl was a manager at Burger King and hired Cook to work the drive-thru.

To this day, Cook has never had a drink or done a drug in his life. That’s probably because his dad was a violent alcoholic. The house was “a place of mayhem,” he says: shouting matches, wall-shaking fights, and one harrowing incident when he was 14 involving a kitchen knife that ended with his father being arrested and leaving the house. Cook says he was never a target of the abuse per se, so Darryl didn’t protect him. But just his presence helped Cook feel safe. “I remember so many nights, looking over at him as I was going to sleep,” Cook says. “Just happy he was there.”

Not long after his 18th birthday, Cook started doing standup around Boston. From there it was a long slog to overnight success: six years of living at home, doing shitty gigs at laundromats, Chinese restaurants, and open mics. “I’d spend more on gas driving my mom’s 1978 Lincoln to Maine and back than I’d even make,” he says. “A Tuesday night meant hoping you’d get up at Nick’s Comedy Stop next to the Combat Zone, where maybe I can make a couple prostitutes laugh on the way out.” Eventually he got successful enough to move to New York, and later L.A., where he landed such glamorous jobs as half a season on an ABC sitcom starring Betty White and a Dennis Rodman movie that grossed $292,000 worldwide.

Meanwhile, Darryl — who’d dreamed of being a state trooper but failed the test — was working as a corrections officer at Walpole State Prison (now called MCI-Cedar Junction), a maximum-security facility near Boston. (You might know it from The Town.) “It was a scary place,” Cook says. “I hated that he worked there.” He started plotting how to get Darryl out. “I’m incorporated now,” he recalls thinking. “Maybe at some point I can turn this into a regular around-the-clock job for us.” Then a month later, Darryl was viciously attacked by an inmate. “Some old guy put a can of corn niblets in a pillowcase and boom — cracked Darryl’s head open,” says Cook. “I go see him in the hospital. My mom is terrified. We’re all terrified. That’s when I said, ‘I want you to quit and come work for me.’”

In the beginning, Darryl was more like an assistant: paying the car insurance, boxing up CDs to ship out, selling merch at shows. But as the checks started getting more zeros, the job got bigger. Darryl became Cook’s business manager, handling operations at his company, Great Dane Enterprises, complete with a $150,000 salary. Cook says he had no reservations about giving control of his finances to someone relatively unqualified. “I felt like, he’d believed in me,” he says. “We’d gone through a lot of crazy shit together, we got out of that house, we have some normalcy and an income now. We would sit at dinner and be like, ‘This feels good. Cook-McCauley brothers for life.’

“And there was a certain safety,” he says. “Me already seeing some of the piranhas in this town, and the bad language in the contracts, I’m like: ‘But I’ve got my brother looking out for me.’”

Darryl didn’t show Cook his financial statements. Instead he would create Excel spreadsheets with “summaries” of everything going in and out. Cook says he never questioned them. For one thing, he has “dyscalculia,” the numerical version of dyslexia. (“I see numbers and they just spin around.”) Darryl also kept it low-key. “Same pair of dirty sneakers. No frills,” Cook says. “Anytime I would say to him, ‘Is there anything you want or need?’ he was like, ‘No.’” (In hindsight, that’s probably because he was stealing all Cook’s money.)

And ultimately, Cook says, he never really cared about the money. “I just love the game,” he says. “I can’t tell you how many times I’d leave a gig and they’d call me at home and go, ‘You know you forgot your check?’ So no, I didn’t ask. I believed the statements.”

‘FUNNY MONEY’ TAKES A WHILE to get going, with its first third chronicling Cook’s long rise, but when it finally drops into gear, it’s compelling — especially as it catalogues the breadth and depth of Darryl’s deceit. Cook still isn’t sure when it started, but it grew exponentially. In 2004, Darryl was writing himself checks for $22,000 here, $31,000 there. Two years later — Cook’s commercial zenith — Darryl was making deposits as flagrant as $780,000 and $995,000. As Cook’s (legit, later-hired) business manager says in the film: “There wasn’t even an attempt to hide it.”

By the fall of 2008, Cook decided to transfer all his business dealings to a more established firm. The new business manager kept asking Darryl for his files; Darryl kept ducking him. Soon he stopped returning the manager’s calls. Then he stopped returning Cook’s.

In a joke from his 2003 album, Harmful If Swallowed, a girl tells Cook that all men want is sex. Not true, he says: “Any guy here — if they had the choice — would rather be part of a heist.” The Darryl story also ends with a heist — this one in broad daylight.

In December of 2008, McCauley walked into a Bank of America in downtown Boston with a check from Cook’s company made out to himself for $3 million. It also had Cook’s forged signature. Incredibly, the bank cashed the check, and McCauley stuffed the cash into literal duffel bags, which he loaded into a rented Escalade and drove away. A final $3 million fuck-you.

Increasingly frantic that he couldn’t reach Darryl, Cook went to a bank branch near his house. A sympathetic employee pulled up his accounts. One had $110,000 in it. Another was empty.

“I’ve never been in a plane crash,” Cook says. “But I imagine when everything’s rattling, and you start to hear unusual sounds, and things are tearing apart — that’s kind of how I felt. My legs go out from under me. I’m howling with sadness. Because I know my best friend in the world has done this.”

“It was a shattering unlike I ever imagined,” he continues. “I’ve had a couple of bad panic attacks in my life — like, catatonic. Nothing compared to what I felt that day. I could cry right now thinking of it.”

Cook called the cops, who brought in the FBI. Darryl went on the run — a wild sequence in the doc — and was arrested by Massachusetts State Police a few weeks later. His wife, Erika, was also arrested; when police searched the couple’s home near Boston, they found $800,000 in cash stashed in a wall safe. A separate search of their beach house in Maine turned up hundreds of thousands more: bricks of cash in Tupperware tubs of tomato sauce hidden in the freezer; $90,000 in a box of Bagel Bites; $150,000 buried in the dirt of a potted plant.

Investigators later found that the couple had spent $5 million on real estate and investments and $500,000 on jewelry. There were also vacations in Ireland, a time-share in St. Kitts, and his-and-hers Cadillacs, along with $2.7 million in cashier’s checks that were never accounted for. “I think it’s way more than the $12 million,” Cook says today. “I’m thinking $17 to $22 million is really the number.”

McCauley pled guilty to 27 counts of larceny, three counts of forgery and one count of embezzlement. He was sentenced to six years in Walpole — the very same prison where he’d worked as a guard. Cook, meanwhile, was very fucked. Not only was all his money gone. He also owed the IRS for the taxes Darryl hadn’t paid — a staggering $6 million with interest.

What Cook did next was truly impressive. He still had about $300,000 in stocks that Darryl somehow hadn’t touched. He used the money to book himself an arena tour, renting the venues out of his own pocket. “I take the door, they take the food, I sell my merch,” he says. “If I’m renting a $35,000 dollar arena, there’s nights where I’m walking out with $350,000. I was like, ‘I’m gonna go down maybe. But not because of you.’” He spent the next two years crisscrossing the country, playing a hundred-plus shows, often back to back to back. And by the end, “I’d made everything back that they told me he took.”

That was the financial hole. The emotional hole took much longer.

“The humiliation was way more damaging than the theft,” says Cook. “All my childhood stuff I thought I’d overcome, all the insecurity that was still there but shielded by success, all the self-loathing I felt as a kid — it all came back. I’m on the school playground that I thought I got away from, and everyone’s looking at me going, ‘This fucking idiot. What a moron.’”

He couldn’t write any jokes or get onstage for a year. “I was bad, man. The ruminating was really bad. All through the night. I was trying to find girls to spend time with — just unhealthy. Sex. Trauma dumping. It’s love, and it’s temporary, and then it’s rinse and repeat, another night.”

To make matters worse, this was all going down when Cook was grappling with multiple other catastrophes, both personal and professional. A couple of years earlier, he’d lost both parents to cancer within a span of nine months — a double dose of tragedy that initially brought him and Darryl closer, but ultimately made their estrangement even more painful. Around the same time, Cook was famously (and, in hindsight, unfairly) accused of joke-stealing by a pre-disgraced Louis C.K., leading to a pile-on of haters and internet stand-up police. Not to mention the normal backlash and decline he was already facing from overexposure and his defiantly un-P.C. shtick.

“I’m just spinning,” Cook recalls of this time. “I’m no longer in vogue. Also my parents have passed, and I’m probably ignoring that and not grieving. I’m doing sets at night because it’s alleviating the sadness of the day.”

One of his first shows back was a disastrous, rambling set at the Hollywood Improv, where other comics described him as “spiraling” as he reportedly told “jokes” like: “Go fuck a dirty whore. That’s the best therapy.” Eventually he realized he needed actual therapy. “It was like a year of twice a week,” he says. “Brick by brick. Figuring out again how to move in the world.”

It’s hard not to notice that Cook’s trajectory changed drastically after Darryl’s betrayal. Since 2009, he’s done just two stand-up specials and only a handful of acting gigs (including four episodes of a sitcom that got canceled before it aired). It’s been seven years since he appeared on TV or film at all. From the outside, it looks like his life got derailed and he never got it back on track.

Was it just the natural cycle of fame? The more intellectual turn stand-up took in the 2010s? Or does he blame his brother for that?

“I did blame him for a while,” Cook says. “I knew I was at the end of a run in my career — I’m cooling off. At that point where the pendulum naturally swings and everything slows down, I didn’t have the bandwidth to untangle the knots. But also, being realistic,” he adds, “I wasn’t putting up, like, Sandler $100 million movies. I was hitting doubles.”

For years, Cook struggled with how to tell the story. He wrote a few bad jokes about it. (“My brother was a prison guard. I hired him to protect my money, not help it escape!”) He even tried some material out on his therapist. (“Man. Worst audience. The stonewalling I took on some of my gems…”) For a while he thought about doing a one-man show. But he could never figure out how to get into it all while still delivering for his fans. “They’re there to see me do what I do,” he says. “I wasn’t ready to bum them out.”

Then in 2019, he talked about it on a podcast for the first time, and it unlocked something. Soon after, he got a call from the documentary’s producer offering him a million dollars.

There is, of course, one big, Darryl-sized hole in the film. McCauley turned down multiple requests to be interviewed by the filmmakers. Cook even offered to drop his $12 million restitution claim in exchange for a face-to-face sit-down; Darryl declined. According to Darryl’s LinkedIn page, after his release from prison, he worked for six months at a Home Depot, three years at a grocery store, and five years as a driver for FedEx, before entering “semi-retirement” in 2024. His bio says he “possess[es] strong judgement and decision making skills.” And in the “Skills” section, he lists one: “Finance.”

Cook says he’s never tried to reach out to his brother. He seems to be waiting for Darryl to make the first move. Even 17 years later, he sounds freshly wounded, yet surprisingly open to reconciliation. “Even in this doc, there’s some version of a love letter to my brother,” he says. “Like: ‘You did a lot for me. We did a lot together. Why are you dumb?’”

Cook claims — incredibly  — that if he could go back, he wouldn’t change a thing. “I feel like it’s all brought me to the best of my life,” he insists. “Where I’m at right now is way more interesting than anything that would have happened, had nothing happened.”

“But I do miss my brother sometimes,” he adds. “I miss that guy I game-planned with. That I made those first flyers with back in the day. A million memories of high-fives and bad fast food and driving to gigs. It was cool having an older brother. If I had a time machine, I’d probably go back and throw one more hug on him.”

Just a few months ago, his younger sister Courtney got a DM from Darryl. It was the first time any of them had heard from him in decades. The message, says Cook:

“‘Everybody’s wrong. It was $12.8 million.’ With a money bag emoji.”

LATER THAT NIGHT, COOK rolls into a theater in Santa Monica for the documentary’s premiere — the first time he’s seen it with strangers. Friars Club roastmaster Jeff Ross is in the house; Cook’s pal Dave Chappelle was going to come, too, but he had to bail last-minute. Seated next to Cook is his wife of three years, Kelsi. She’s 26 years his junior — they started dating when she was 18 and he was 42 — but at least Cook jokes about it. (Goes one bit: “People are like, You’re robbing the cradle. I’m like, Relax. She hasn’t slept in a cradle in nine years.”)

The audience is admittedly full of friends and fans, but the movie goes over great. People laugh and gasp in all the right spots. Ross uncorks a few nice heckles. Afterward, Cook is beaming. “Putting up a win with the worst moment of your life is fucking awesome,” he says. “I have regained the narrative that was hijacked from me.”

Earlier, in his office, Cook talked about the future. He hopes the documentary will be a “catalyst” for his career. He’s been inspired by seeing Chappelle and Chris Rock still touring and directing films, and says he’s hungry to get back to that level. “I belong there,” he says. “That’s the class I put myself in.”

He’s been getting in shape — preparing his mind and body. Kelsi is a certified Pilates trainer and fitness instructor, and she has him on a strict 2,000-calorie diet, doing an hour of Pilates and swimming every morning and in bed by 8 every night. He sounds like a prizefighter training for a comeback.

Can he make one? Who’s to say? Flip phones are cool again — why not Dane Cook?

“I have always been rooting for Dane,” says Nikki Glaser. “I’m sure his downfall was schadenfreude for a lot of comedians, but I think the comics at the top now owe him a lot. There’s been a stand-up boom since he showed up on the scene that hasn’t really dropped off. He made it popular, he made it sexy, and he changed the scale at which it could be done. And he’s still got it.”

Lately Cook has been taking meetings, trying to get some momentum back. He says he recently landed a role on a prestige drama from “one of the greatest producers of all time.” He wrote a book about his story and has a new hour of stand-up that he calls the best he’s ever done. His misfortune is already opening doors.

Cook is almost heartbreakingly earnest when he talks about getting back to work. “Permission to speak freely?” he says. “I’d love to work more. I’m so ready. I hope this reminds people, if you have forgotten: I’m a workhorse. I love to show up on time. I love to create an environment for the cast and crew where they go, ‘I want to work with Dane again.’ Trending Stories Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Andy Garcia, David Foster, Paul Anka Lead Kennedy Center Honors Yes, Matt Damon and David Letterman Were Background Actors on ‘The Gilded Age’ Season Premiere Britney Spears Says Kevin Federline and Jamie Lynn Spears Made Her ‘Feel Like a Slave’

“I didn’t work for a long time,” he says. “I hate being on the bench. I’m OK with whatever it is. I just want to be working.”

In some ways, he sounds like a kid still looking for approval. From an audience, a dad… or maybe a big brother. “When I’m on set and hitting the mark, and I get the arm around me walking out of the studio saying, ‘You brought it today’?” he says. “That’s all I want. I think I’ve got a little bit of that left.”

As a fitness expert in my 40s, my priorities have definitely changed. Yes, I still want to build muscle and feel strong, but I'm increasingly interested in exercises that challenge my balance, test my coordination and help me stay agile for the long haul.

I want to move well, in as many different directions as possible, for as long as possible. Because for me, it's no longer just about lifting heavy weights. It's about building a body that can move well and cope with life. And it turns out celebrity trainer Simone De La Rue thinks along similar lines.

The former professional dancer and founder of Body By Simone has worked with an impressive list of A-listers, including Taylor Swift, Jennifer Garner and Gigi Hadid, and recently shared a full-body compound exercise designed to challenge strength, balance and coordination in one go.

There’s quite a lot going on, but that’s exactly why I like it.

You’re strengthening your glutes, quads and hamstrings as you lunge, working your shoulders and arms as you press the weights overhead, then challenging the stabilizing muscles around your hips as you move laterally.

Your core has to work throughout to keep you stable and controlled, while the little hop to the side adds another challenge, asking the muscles around your hips, knees and ankles to power you up, then help you land safely again.

It also gets your balance and coordination involved: two things that become increasingly important as you get older.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Want to give it a go? Grab a pair of dumbbells and follow the steps below.

A post shared by Lucy Miller (@lucycmiller_)

The trick here is to break the move down and practice each part separately. There are several movements to coordinate, so start with lighter weights until you can move smoothly from the split squat into the press and lateral hop without losing your balance or letting your knees collapse inward.

Aim for two sets of six to eight repetitions on each side, using light dumbbells until you've mastered the move.

There’s a lot packed into one move. Here’s why I’ve added it to my strength workouts:

This is the big one. Rather than isolating a single muscle group, you’re asking several to work together.

The split squat targets your glutes, quads and hamstrings, while the overhead press works your shoulders and arms. Your core has to stabilize your torso as you move between the two.

For me, that makes it a great option when I want to get more from one exercise rather than spending hours in the gym.

Split squats already reduce your base of support compared with a regular squat. Add an overhead press and lateral movement, and your body has a lot more to deal with.

You need to stay stable as your weight shifts and your arms move overhead, which makes this as much a balance and coordination challenge as a strength exercise.

It’s a known fact that balance can decline as we get older, so exercises that challenge balance alongside strength are becoming a regular and important part of my own workouts.

It works your body in more than one direction

Most of us spend plenty of time moving forward and backward, whether that’s walking, running, or doing exercises such as squats and lunges.

Moving sideways recruits the muscles responsible for stabilizing your hips, including your gluteus medius. Strong hip stabilizers are important for controlling the pelvis and keeping the lower body stable when you walk, run, or stand on one leg.

You’ll find that the hop to the side takes a little effort to start with; your foot almost doesn’t want to jump out to the side, but it doesn’t take long to click, and you just really have to think about it, which I like when training. It's challenging. Think deep mind-muscle connection.

It makes your core work harder than you might think

You know those standing abs moves that we often talk about? Well, this is a great example. Your core is active throughout because it has to work to keep your torso stable during the split squat, stop you wobbling as you change direction and hop and provide a solid base as you press the dumbbells overhead. There’s a lot going on here.

You’ll probably notice it even more as you fatigue, which is why I started with a lighter pair of dumbbells and kept the entire movement controlled rather than overloading my body and losing form.

There’s no shortage of exercises to keep you strong as you get older, but I like this one because it combines so many things I want from my training in one sequence: strength, balance, coordination and mobility.

It’s also surprisingly challenging. You don't need particularly heavy dumbbells to feel your shoulders and legs working, and adding the overhead press and lateral step means your core rarely gets a chance to switch off.

Would I replace my squats and deadlifts with it? No. Those big compound lifts allow me to go heavier, which is crucial for building and maintaining strength as I get older. But as an accessory exercise in a full-body strength session, this is definitely one I’ll be keeping in my repertoire.

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

Mariah Carey season is officially underway as the Queen of Christmas makes her first holiday appearance of 2026 with a new Gucci campaign.

The “All I Want for Christmas Is You” singer stars in Gucci’s new holiday video, showing off her new Butterfly collection, inspired by her 1997 album of the same name, and designed in collaboration with the Italian fashion house. Directed by Harmony Korine, the clip finds hotel workers and guests scurrying about as they prepare a party in Carey’s honor. Christmas trees are dressed, lights are strung, and candles are lit, just in time for the singer’s arrival (to the sounds of her signature seasonal song, natch).

Gucci says the campaign celebrates Carey’s “role as a cultural icon and a fixture of the holiday season,” while capturing the “festive excitement of one of the most anticipated moments of the year.”

Of course there are plenty of presents to go around, too, with the campaign showing off the Italian fashion house’s collection of luxe handbags, shoes, and accessories for the season, all “offering inspiration for celebrations, winter escapes, and the many moments shared during the holidays,” per a release.

Carey’s Butterfly collection, meantime, includes jackets, dresses, T-shirts, shoes, and jewelry, many of which feature a custom Gucci butterfly print with crystals.

This sequined jersey top features the butterfly print against a lightweight viscose material. Gucci says the glittery piece “illuminates the holidays,” making it a festive piece to throw on for Christmas parties and New Year’s Eve gatherings alike.

This bag features Gucci’s iconic GG canvas monogram with crystal embellishments throughout. The bag comes with a chain strap and a leather strap, along with leather trim in Carey’s signature lavender colorway.

Carey fans and fashion fans alike will also want to pick up this limited-edition pendant necklace, which features a crystal-embellished GG charm, along with a crystal butterfly charm, both set on a palladium-toned chain.Butterflies, have long been associated with the singer, ever since she released her autobiographical song and album of the same name.

Carey officially kicked off the holiday season on Sunday, with her annual “It’s Time” video, marking the transition from Halloween to Christmas. This year’s video, created in collaboration with beauty brand Sol de Janeiro, has already amassed more than 4.5 million views and counting on YouTube.

Carey is also picking up streams online for her seasonal hit: According to Spotify, “All I Want for Christmas Is You” re-entered the charts at Number 37, with more than 1.8 million streams on Nov. 1.

The Queen of Christmas will also be looking to reclaim her throne at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, after Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” replaced “All I Want for Christmas Is You” as the biggest hit in Hot 100 history, at 25 weeks and counting. Carey’s song had spent a cumulative 22 weeks at the top of the charts.

#3414. The Ice Where It Happens: Watch U.S. Figure Skating Pair’s New ‘Hamilton’-Inspired Routine

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

The Tony-winning Broadway hit Hamilton is moving from the Great White Way to the bright white ice.

The official X account for the musical posted a clip Sunday of U.S. ice dancers Caroline Green and Michael Parsons rehearsing their new rhythm dance to the Broadway show’s hit soundtrack. The two-time U.S. medalists debuted their Hamilton-themed routine at Skate Canada over the weekend, the second stop in figure skating‘s prestigious Grand Prix series of events.

Green and Parsons posted a score of 74.24 points for their Skate Canada rhythm dance (formerly known as the “short dance” or “short program”) on their way to a third-place finish overall. The couple’s two-minute-and-50-second routine uses three songs from the Hamilton soundtrack: “Ten Duel Commandments,” “Your Obedient Servant,” and “The Room Where It Happens.” All three tracks were written by Lin-Manuel Miranda for the original Broadway show.

As Green explained in a backstage interview, “It’s Hamilton versus Burr. It’s taken from the opening, where Burr’s in the red and pretty much the entire cast is in the white and the cream. But it’s sort of like a modern Hamilton meets figure skating, because unfortunately, we can’t wear really long coats and colonial dress.”

Dag! They amaze and astonish.🎥: Caroline Green & Michael Parsons pic.twitter.com/Yzk4WtAjBC

While Skate Canada marked the Hamilton program’s Grand Prix debut, Green and Parsons actually tested it out on audiences at two smaller “Senior B” events earlier this fall: the Denis Ten Memorial Challenge, where the couple finished third, and the CS Nepela Memorial Trophy, where they finished in fifth place.

The figure skating routine comes on the heels of a 10th-anniversary box set released in September. Titled Rise Up! Hamilton, the seven-LP set includes the original Broadway cast recording, the 2016 Hamilton Mixtape recording (featuring Kelly Clarkson, Alicia Keys, and others), plus the first-ever vinyl pressing of Hamildrops: The Complete Collection, Miranda’s sequel to the Hamilton Mixtape. The box set also includes previous unreleased songs, plus an 80-page book with behind-the-scenes photos, as well as a poster, custom slipmat, and other collectibles.

Each box is numbered and released in extremely limited-edition, and it’s almost sold out online.You can stream or purchase a physical copy of the original Broadway recording, meantime, here.

The Hamilton soundtrack topped Billboard’s Broadway albums chart and has been certified diamond. It also took home the Grammy for Best Musical Theater Album in 2016.

This isn’t the first time a figure skater has performed to the Hamilton soundtrack. U.S. men’s star Jason Brown skated to “The Room Where It Happens” for his short program in the 2017-2018 season.

#3413. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

Learning about the factors that could lead to a crash for the AI industry

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With the ongoing “RAMageddon”, the rapid development of data centers and the pure vitriol brought against “AI slop” these days, I can see why AI skeptics are hoping for an AI industry market crash.

Once the news of China’s AI sector suffering a massive market crash that wiped out $480 billion reached my timeline, I started thinking about the possibility of that event coming to fruition in the US. There’s been so much speculation over the very existence of an AI bubble, when it could finally burst and what could happen to the several US sector & the tech itself if a crash took place.

Since I’m so prone to asking the likes of ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity hot-button questions, I knew it was time for me to see what they thought about those three topics. So I brought this loaded set of questions to their attention: “Is there really an AI bubble? If so, when is it going to burst and what will happen if it does?

Here are some of the most intriguing responses each chatbot gave me, with one of them even drawing comparisons between a possible AI market crash and the infamous dot-com crash from 2000 to 2002.

OpenAI’s chatbot was first up at bat for my latest inquisitive session about AI. It made sure to point out that there are clear signs that there is an AI bubble and that parts of it may be on the verge of popping. But it also noted that an AI crash isn’t such a sure bet:

Yes, there are credible reasons to worry that parts of the AI industry are in a bubble — but that doesn't mean AI itself is a fad, or that a crash is inevitable. The most useful way to think about it is to separate two questions:

- Is AI valuable? AI tools can already help people write, code, analyze information, automate tasks and create content.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

- Are investors paying too much for AI? Potentially. Companies can be building genuinely useful technology while investors simultaneously overestimate how quickly it will generate profits.

That distinction is important because the dot-com boom of the late 1990s offers a useful comparison: the internet transformed the economy, but many internet companies still failed when their valuations outran their businesses. The AI industry could experience something similar — a correction in investment and valuations even as the technology continues to improve.

As for when the AI bubble could burst, ChatGPT stated that no one can reliably predict its occurrence. The main scenario it alluded to as the worst one was set from 2027 through 2029, as it explained how a serious reckoning could come to pass if its revenue for the AI industry fails to keep up with the infrastructure spending from private sectors going into it. Or if customers discover that AI delivered less measurable value than they originally expected.

To wrap up its investigation into the matter, ChatGPT stated that the central question at the heart of the AI bubble-bursting topic is whether the money it generates can eventually justify the money that’s being spent on it. If yes, then it noted that this current AI investment boom will be looked back on as an expensive yet productive period of technological development. If no, then AI investors, startups, lenders and workers could be dealt a very bad hand while the technology itself continues to advance in some way.

As I went through Gemini’s detailed breakdowns of its explanations to my questions, its comparisons to the dot-com crash and the AI bubble possibly bursting caught my attention the most. It pointed to three ways in which both events share striking similarities:

Gemini also made sure to point out a key difference between the fallout of the dot-com crash and the possible AI bubble finally bursting. It acknowledged that several dot-com firms ceased to exist after the dot-com crash, while the AI bubble bursting wouldn’t be too catastrophic for some of the tech leaders backing the tech, since they have other worthy investments (Amazon with e-commerce and Microsoft with software as a service, for example).

While those companies would face some financial struggles from the AI bubble bursting, Gemini noted that a complete shutdown of their businesses due to it happening wouldn’t likely occur.

Anthropic’s chatbot dived into the possibilities of an AI bubble existing by detailing why everyone’s so worried about it bursting, why an AI bubble may not fully exist at the moment and a possible timeline for when it could burst:

Perplexity’s response to my questions stated that there are notable signs of an AI bubble bursting, but those same signs don’t fully paint the picture of the AI industry being close to a crash:

There are credible signs of an AI investment bubble, especially in parts of startup funding and infrastructure spending—but that does not establish that the entire industry is overvalued or that a crash is imminent. Nobody can reliably tell you when it will burst, or whether it will end in a sudden crash rather than a long, uneven adjustment. The biggest distinction is between a stock-market bust and a debt crisis: both could hurt, but the latter would spread much further through the economy.

To back up its reasoning, Perplexity brought up a report from The Olympian that offers debates about the existence of an AI bubble. It also mentioned a report from a prominent management consulting firm to provide an assessment of when the possible AI bubble could burst:

With shocking news hitting my timeline about AI investments going bad, it’s easy to envision a world where the AI bubble finally bursting comes to pass.

With Google’s recent massive loss of $500 billion due to its AI search feature disrupting ad sales, the odds of that aforementioned event taking place are getting higher and higher. All four chatbots do agree that there are sectors of the AI industry that are in danger of collapsing, while Gemini highlighted the clear comparisons between the AI bubble bursting and the 2000s dot-com crash.

After comparing ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity, I walked away from my latest chatbot questionnaire session knowing that the AI industry shows signs of plunging badly. But as for when that moment could take place, no one truly knows.

#3410. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3409. Apple says it’s ‘only getting started’ updating macOS for touchscreens

Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (pre-order here) includes a variety of software optimizations for touch input. But Apple says it’s “only getting started” making macOS more touch-friendly.

The new touchscreen-equipped MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR will ship with macOS 27.2, software that includes a variety of touch-centric optimizations that only impact PROLED XDR users.

Early feedback from hands-on testers, including our own Chance Miller, appears very positive.

Bloomberg’s Chris Welch reassuringly says that Apple is “taking a measured approach as it introduces touch capabilities.” This echoes comments from John Gruber, who says his concerns about touch “adversely affecting the Mac UI” have all been allayed.

But it sounds like Apple plans to roll out even more macOS optimizations for touch in the future.

An Apple employee answering press questions at Wednesday’s event said the company is only getting started optimizing macOS for a touch screen. I’d expect a slew of refinements to arrive alongside macOS 28 next year, much in the way the iPhone Duo’s user experience will inevitably evolve with iOS 28.

Overall, this isn’t necessarily reason for alarm if you’re worried about touch having a negative impact on macOS.

How about, spitballing here, a tablet device that takes advantage of MacOS’s new found touch capabilities? 🙄

Even though Apple has prepared an initial set of macOS changes to support touch input, it’s only natural for the company to continue refining the touch experience in response to early adopter feedback and usage patterns. My assumption is that the same “measured approach” we’re seeing right now will continue guiding these future macOS enhancements.

You can pre-order MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR on Amazon for day-one delivery.

Timberlake and Jackson’s Super Bowl XXXVIII halftime show has gone done in history as one of the most controversial performances on live television. The network and Timberlake were quick to apologize, with Timberlake later calling the incident a “wardrobe malfunction” and distancing himself from the controversy as Jackson received the majority of the crushing blowback — the star was blacklisted from radio and her career was momentarily derailed following the incident. At the time, Timberlake received little repercussion, and even returned to the Super Bowl halftime show as a solo artist in 2017.

In 2021, following the recent release of the documentary Framing Britney Spears, the past was rehashed and Timberlake was criticized for his role amid the backlash against Jackson following the “Nipplegate” scandal. Timberlake publicly apologized to both Britney Spears and Janet Jackson. “I specifically want to apologize to Britney Spears and Janet Jackson both individually, because I care for and respect these women and I know I failed,” Timberlake said. “The industry is flawed. It sets men, especially white men, up for success. It’s designed this way. As a man in a privileged position, I have to be vocal about this. Because of my ignorance, I didn’t recognize it for all that it was while it was happening in my own life but I do not want to ever benefit from others being pulled down again.”

Unfortunately, rats don't hibernate in the cold

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’ve ever had a rat problem, then you'll know there are many ways you can prevent these pesky creatures from entering your home — especially in the fall and winter.

Yes, the National Pest Management Association (NPMA) recently released a statistic showing that 45% of all annual rodent infestations happen during the fall and winter months.

So if you haven't thought about it before, here's what to do in October to keep rats from coming to life in November or December.

Not only is the thought of a rat living in your house spine-crawling, but we all know that they can carry diseases. And they eat anything in sight — wires, wood, and food.

They also don't need an open invitation to come inside; a large hole or an open window is enough to encourage them in. They're the opposite of escape artists; let's call them entrance assassins.

The two main culprits in the U.S. are Norway rats and Roof rats, and in cold weather, their survival depends on where they live and feed. So when the temperature drops, rats head closer to the heat — if not indoors, they may go toward the insulation beneath your subfloor, up into your roof (because heat rises), or into a cozy garage.

Did you know?Rats can squeeze through a gap that’s the size of a quarter; for mice, it’s the size of a dime.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Lawns and hedgingLet's start outside because yes, it all makes a huge difference. This might be music to your ears, or you may roll your eyes, but a trimmed lawn is an easy, quick way to deter rats.

The same goes for any foliage: if you cut it back, it won't attract rats, but the problem starts when it becomes overgrown. While English Ivy looks amazing, in winter it becomes the perfect climbing ladder for these creatures, especially if it’s attached to your house wall. Therefore, check the gap between your hedging and any greenery near an open window.

Open trashAs for your trash cans, cracked or warped containers may attract rats, which can quickly become a huge problem. It's time to replace them with new ones. Worse still, is if you keep your trash bags outside instead of in a can.

Feeding the birds, and the ratsLove to feed the birds? You might soon change your mind. Bird feeders attract rats this season, which is a shame for the birds, but realistically, you may need to wait until spring. Otherwise, you can feed them huskless seed and use a squirrel guard instead.

A game-changer for safe bird feeding in the winter, this also means that those pesky squirrels can't take any of their food. Easy to install and currently on sale, get it now or regret it later.

Rats don't hibernate. They try to survive winter in any way they can. As with the hot spots I've already mentioned, when it comes to indoor living, rats tend to hide in warm spots.

Behind your giant refrigerator, a dishwasher, or dryer is a safe place for a rat to seek warmth. They love furnaces and hot water pipes, too. Anything that oozes warmth in an otherwise cold room. And don’t forget your loft — any fiberglass up there provides a lovely warm bed for them.

However, rats might also head straight to your garage, especially if you store extra food or pet food there, so it's worth rethinking what you store and where. If you can't change the storage spot, keep food in airtight, rat-proof metal containers. Inside your home, store food in plastic packets, away from your garage, and ideally move it to an airtight plastic or glass container.

For any external doors, like the one from your home into your garage, it's smart to invest in a few rodent-proof door sweeps. Just in case they make their way inside through a tiny door crack. They will also be handy when you turn on the heating, since they’ll keep valuable heat from escaping.

Heavy rain also drives rats indoors, so keep ahead of the weather forecast and secure your home before rats become a problem.

Amazon's Choice for a reason, you can buy a 4-pack to save more money and use these in more places than one. Easy to screw into your door, there's a rubber strip along the bottom of the stopper that ensures it is fully rat-proof. It can even seal gaps 1-inch wide.

If you religiously search your home for holes and fill them, ready for rat season, then bear in mind that what you fill them with matters. Rats can chew through plastic, rubber, or standard vinyl caulk. Instead, copper mesh wool is totally rat-proof. You can then seal it with silicone caulk, so it looks better.

You can only buy this in a large roll, but truly, you never know when you'll need it. Included is literally everything you need to secure your home from rodents, including safety gloves, scissors, and a packing tool to help push it into a hole or two.

#3406. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3405. iOS 27.2 adds new video feature that’s perfect for iPhone Duo

iOS 27.2 launched this week with many new features, including an upgrade for the Apple TV app that’s especially perfect for iPhone Duo: Multiview.

Apple TV’s growing lineup of sports content includes Formula 1, Major League Soccer (MLS), and Major League Baseball (MLB).

And a new video feature in iOS 27.2—Multiview—makes me hope the streamer adds even more sports soon.

Multiview lets iPhone users watch up to four live sports streams simultaneously. It’s available for all sports events included in an Apple TV subscription. Previously, Multiview was only available on Apple TV, iPad, and Vision Pro.

Activating Multiview is easy. Once you start watching a sports event you’ll see a new ‘Multiview’ button at the bottom of the Apple TV player.

Each sport’s implementation will differ a bit, but with F1 you can choose from a preset team Multiview or build your own custom setup that includes driver-view cameras, course maps, and more.

I gave it a try on my iPhone 18 Pro, where I assumed the smaller display would be a limiting factor on the number of streams. Fortunately that wasn’t the case, as I was able to set up four F1 streams from the Austin Grand Prix and could see all four on-screen at once.

Where I imagine this will prove especially nice is on iPhone Duo. Though it’s great that smaller iPhones support Multiview, the ability to stream four video feeds at once on the Duo’s large display sounds fantastic.

Do you plan to give Multiview a try on your iPhone? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.
